The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-nibandhana*. Treatise Volume One.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.

The preface is explained in two major divisions: first, up to the words "truly lies herein," which clarifies the benefit of the Bodhisattva’s appearance in the world and the flourishing of this treatise;
second, from "Chancellor of the Court of Judicial Review" (*zhengyi dafu*) onwards, which clarifies the reasons for the clergy and laity requesting the composition of this commentary.
The former section has two parts: first, a general praise of the thousand [treatises], and second, a specific elucidation of this particular treatise.

The initial term "yuè" (粤) is a particle used to introduce speech; it marks the beginning of an utterance. The term "hè" (赫) denotes a state of great magnificence, the ultimate degree of manifest clarity.

As for "kǎifēng" (颽風), it refers to the south wind; thus, the *Shijing* says, "The kǎifēng blows from the south, blowing upon the heart of the jī (hedge-hog tree)," and the *Erya* states that the south wind is called kǎifēng, the east wind guǒfēng, the west wind tàifēng, and the north wind liángfēng.
This is the same as in the case of the "Poem" (the *Sūrya-gāthā*). To say that he "rectifies the Great Teaching and saves the age" means to rectify and sustain.
It refers to the Bodhisattva rectifying and sustaining the Buddha-dharma to save the world according to the needs of the times.

As for the meaning above, because the sun has the power to dispel darkness and the wind has the function of maturing things, the Bodhisattva possesses the virtue of saving the world; therefore, these are taken as analogies.
The character *yuán* (pronounced with the *zhāng-yuán* initial) means "at" or "in"; *jué* means "his. Regarding *Shiqīn* (世親): in Sanskrit it is called *Vasubandhu*;

*vasu* means "world" (*shì*) and *bandhu* means "kinsman" (*qīn*). This refers to an Indian who was popularly known as Shiqīn because he was approached, honored, and supported by the people of the world;
thus he was named accordingly. It was from his parents that the Bodhisattva requested [the vow].
A Bodhisattva receives his name based on the place from which he was born; if one says "Devaputra" (Heavenly Relative), it should instead be called "Deva-bandhu.
Since he is not named Deva, it is clearly evident that calling him "Tianqin" (Heavenly Relative) is erroneous. Furthermore, the *Xiyu ji* (Record of the Western Regions) states:

"Vasubandhu" (translated in the Tang language as Shiqin; formerly called Baosupan dou; those who explain it as 'Heavenly Relative' are mistaken). To say that he "propagated the Way throughout the Five Indies" means that he widely disseminated [the teachings].
This is because it guides [beings] throughout the five regions of India; thus, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

"Formerly called Shendu (身毒) or Tianzhu (天竺), etc., but now following the correct pronunciation, it should be called 'Indu' (印度). 'Indu' here means 'moon. The moon has a thousand names, and this name is one such appellation.
It signifies that all sentient beings wander in saṃsāra without ceasing, through the long night of ignorance where there is no dawn; it is like the white..."
When the sun has already vanished from the heavens, the candle [of fire] succeeds it; yet though there is the illumination of the stars, how can it compare to the brilliance of the bright moon?
It is precisely because the sages and worthies have followed one another’s tracks in this land to guide the common people and govern all things—like the moon shining down—that it is called India.
The territory of the Five Indias spans over ninety thousand *li*; three sides are bordered by the great ocean, while to the north it backs against the Snow Mountains, which are broad in the north.

The southern part is narrow, shaped like a half-moon, with its boundaries demarcated into more than seventy kingdoms. At that time, the climate was particularly hot, and the land was abundant in springs and marshes.
Regarding those who composed a thousand treatises, the *Xiyu ji* (Record of the Western Regions) states: "When the Bodhisattva first studied the Hīnayāna, he composed Hīnayāna treatises.
Later, because he went to pay his respects to Asaṅga, Asaṅga then ordered his disciples to go out to welcome him as far as the monastery."

After closing the doors and windows, after the second watch of the night, he heard the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* being recited from within. Beholding a radiance, he was moved to realization and felt deep remorse.

He then sought instruction in the Mahāyāna from Asaṅga. Thereupon, he applied himself with refined energy and profound reflection, composing approximately one hundred Mahāyāna treatises, all of which were widely propagated and practiced.
(Some say he composed five hundred treatises each on both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; this should be verified against the original text. He said, "The Light is my teacher."
Regarding his orthodox footsteps, the *Shu* (Book) states that "high strides" are called *zhù* (footprints); this refers precisely to the illustrious traces of the Great Master’s teachings.

As for the statement regarding the resolution of the heterodox confusion of external paths, it means that by composing this treatise, he was able to resolve the disputes arising from the diverse attachments of non-Buddhist schools.
(The above is a general praise of his thousand works; hereafter follows a specific elucidation of this particular treatise.)
Regarding the phrase "including the six *pādas*," this means that by means of this treatise, the textual meanings of the six *pāda* treatises are encompassed.
The names of these six *pādas* will be described below in the commentary (*ṭīkā*). Regarding the "eight aggregates" (*aṣṭaskandha*), the *Vibhāṣā* states:

they are the Miscellaneous (*saṃyukta*), Knots (*saṃgīti-parivarta*), Knowledge (*jñāna*), Karma (*karman*), Lineages (*gotra*), Roots (*mūla*), Meditative Absorptions (*samādhi*), and Views (*dṛṣṭi*). This refers to the establishment of topical sections and the presentation of summaries within the various treatises on the Path spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding the composition of the individual chapters (*paryāya*) and the general aggregates (*skandha*): the discourse on the collection of various distinct characteristics is established as the *Saṃyukta-skandha*;
the discourse on the collection of conclusions is established as the *Saṃgīti-skandha*; the discourse on the collection of knowledge is established as the *Jñāna-skandha*;
the discourse on the collection of karma is established as the *Karma-skandha*; and the discourse on the collection of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is established as the *Mahābhūta-skandha*.

The principles regarding the faculties (*indriya*), meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and so forth, may be understood by applying [the same logic] accordingly. Although the tenets of various schools differ, the Master’s intention is free from partiality;
thus, he reveres all that is correct when discussing the doctrines of different schools. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "If there is no fault, it should be accepted as a tenet.
Regarding the statement "the sevenfold non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)... up to 'like painting,'" this refers to [the discussion on] karma.

This chapter extensively elucidates the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), fully revealing the core principle of the precepts; for those who transmit the Vinaya, it is like using colors and brushes to paint a picture.
Furthermore, regarding the "Three Categories" (*triskandha*) and the "Aggregates and Elements" (*skandhadhātu*), this serves as an embellishment for those who propagate the Sūtras;

within the "Elements Chapter" (*dhātuvarga*), the meanings of the three categories are presented in full detail, exhaustively investigating the fundamental sources of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Thus, it further acts as an embellishment for those who spread the Sūtras.

From this point downward, the section on requesting the composition of the text is divided into two parts: first, explaining how the clergy and laity made their request; second, the author’s own account of his intention for composing the work. The preceding section is further divided into two:
first, the request by the laity; second, the request by the monastic community. Regarding the phrase "endowed with a special and extraordinary breath":

this refers to an individual of eminent birth who receives a distinct and refined vital energy, setting them apart from the common flow of humanity. Regarding the phrase "the writing covers the clouds and the sound [resounds] between the heavens": [this indicates the vastness and resonance of the work].
Regarding "The Hero Beneath the Sun," the *Book of Jin* states that Lu Yun, styled Shilong, was a native of Wu Commandery. Xun Minghe was a native of Yingchuan.
At that time, Shilong was at the residence of Zhang Hua, the Minister of Works. Minghe arrived later than the others.
The guests already present had long heard of Minghe’s reputation and all rose for him. Minghe said, "When the pure wind arrives, the flying dust scatters; [so it is with] Shilong."
It is said that when the various birds have gathered and the phoenix soars, they settle; once seated, the two men, Xun and Lu, exchanged greetings regarding the weather.
Lu said, "Lu Shilong from among the clouds," and Xun replied, "Xun Minghe beneath the sun. Contemporaries called this an excellent pair of responses.

Now it is said that Jia Zeng’s prose excels that of Shilong, while his voice is more resonant than that of Minghe. As for those who say his character and bearing are profound and remote, "profound" (chong) refers to...

"Harmony" (*he*) means "profound" (*shen*); "distant" (*miao yuan*) means "far-reaching. Regarding the phrase "scholars who serve as mirrors for the girdled elite" (*jinshen gui jing zhi shi*), according to Wang Su’s commentary on the *Jia yu*, it says:

"The 'girdle' (*jin*) refers to the tablet [held in the hand], and the 'sash' (*shen*) refers to the great belt. (The character *jin* originally contains the radical for "hand," but here it follows the radical for "silk").

This is indeed the attire of court officials. As for "mirrors" (*gui jing*): the "tortoise" (*gui*) refers to its spiritual nature, which knows the omens of good and ill before they manifest; the "mirror" (*jing*) refers to its clarity, which reflects objects.
Regarding the beauty or ugliness of the image, it is said that its wearing of the robes of the gentry is like the clarity of a tortoise-shell or a mirror;

this is why [the text] follows with the monk’s request for words of diligent exhortation. "Diligent" (*zīzī*) describes an urgent appearance; thus, the *Book of Documents* says, "diligent and never indolent.
This means he constantly exhorted students to advance in their studies, not that he exhorted the Master of the Commentary (*shūshǔ*) to compose the commentary. It is said his resolve was set upon...

"Universal salvation" (*jiàn jì*) refers to the desire to benefit others; thus, it serves to express exhortation and entreaty. As the *I Ching* says: "In times of adversity, one perfects oneself alone;
in times of success, one universally saves the world.

From here, the Master of the Commentary (*shǔ zhǔ*) sets forth his intention for composing the work, stating: "To savor the True Word" (*zhūn quán*). "Savor" (*zhǔ*)—pronounced *cí jù*—means to chew. That is to say:

To discuss and savor the True Teaching means that those who speak of being intimate in a chamber of orchids refer to being close with virtuous friends such as Jia Zeng and Huai Yuan, just as one is intimate in a room filled with *zhī* and *lán* (orchid plants).
Thus, the *Zhuangzi* says: "Associating with an evil person is like wandering in a fish-pickle shop;

the longer one stays, the more one smells it. Associating with a good person is like wandering in a chamber of orchids; the longer one stays, the more fragrant one becomes. This speaks of the joy of hearing the truth in the morning.
Regarding those who perish at evening, the scripture says: "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die at evening.

This sentiment implies that having already savored the true teaching and further dwelt in the chamber of orchids, one values hearing the Right Path; even if death comes at evening, what regret could there be?

As for the statement that one should prune away the branches and leaves to reach the very roots: this means that if the branches and leaves consist of verbose words, they are omitted and not recounted, just as one discards the dross to retain the essence.

Regarding the statement that "the essential scriptures must exhaustively investigate the source," when it says "repeatedly citing before explaining," this means that first, at the beginning of the initial chapter, there is a general presentation, and subsequently, in the long prose section, there is a specific citation and explanation; thus, it is called "repeated.

Regarding the statement that "using wood and stone to dissolve the substance rather than relying on ornamentation," this means directly pointing to wood and stone to dissolve the meaning, without resorting to flowery rhetoric.

Therefore, the Book of Documents says: "Excessive refinement results in history; excessive simplicity results in rusticity. Only when refinement and simplicity are harmonized does one become a gentleman.
This commentary clarifies that the principle is the same as when one holds a *luán* mirror to reflect images: just as a mirror can reflect all manner of forms, so too is the meaning revealed here.
Regarding the "crane mirror" (*luán-jìng*): formerly, there was a man who saw a pair of cranes dancing and brought them to present to the King. On the way, one died.
The King did not dance, so he questioned his wise minister. The wise minister said, "The *luán* birds were able to dance as a pair because they saw their reflections in a mirror;

seeing themselves thus doubled, the *luán* birds immediately danced, and for this reason it was named [the Mirror Dance]. As for the phrase 'holding the Dragon Spring to cut things,' 'Dragon Spring' (*Lóngquán*) is the name of a precious sword.
Therefore, the *Wúyuè Chūnqiū* states that the King of Chu summoned Fēnghú Zǐ and..."
He said to him, "I have heard that Wu has Gan Jiang and Yue has Ouye. Would it be possible for me to request these two men through you to forge a sword?
Fenghu Zi then went to see the two men and had them forge one; the first was called Longquan and the second Tai'e.
Now, this [sword] distinguishes and severs principles and truths just as a sword cuts through objects. Some say it is wisdom.
The severing of afflictions is like a sword cutting through an object. Some say that wisdom severs afflictions as a sword cuts an object; however, this is not the intended meaning here.
When those of dull perception and unrefined insight speak thus, it is as the Book says: "I am not clever enough; how could I be sufficient to know this?
To be "not clever" (bu min) means to lack penetration. Now, this humble statement—that my own ignorant sentiments and views cannot be clearly understood—is likewise [an admission of such lack].
How could one possibly grasp the underlying principle?
Next, I shall explain the meaning of the six gates. Now, these six gates do not arise without cause;

the reason for clarifying the "Origination of the Treatise" first is that, when one intends to interpret its meaning, one cannot know the origin of this scriptural teaching—therefore, it is necessary to clarify the origination of the treatise as the first gate.
Although the dependent origination has been understood, the specific school and division have not yet been examined; therefore, secondly, the tenets of the treatise are clarified.

Although the tenets have been mastered, the Tripitaka and the teachings have not yet been comprehended; therefore, thirdly, the inclusion within the Tripitaka is clarified. Although the inclusion has been explained, one must know that this single treatise was translated on two occasions;
therefore, fourthly, the reasons for the translations are clarified. Only after the source of the tenets is known can the text be interpreted.
In explaining this work, one must first identify the title; therefore, there is the fifth section, the "Brief Explanation of the Title.

Having clarified that, one must next expound upon the meaning of the text; therefore, there is the sixth section, the "Extensive Explanation of the Textual Meaning. Furthermore, the preceding section consists of two parts:
although the first part reveals the reasons for the work's origin, it is also necessary to clarify the intent behind its composition; thus, it is divided into two subsections.

The explanation of the preceding section is divided into three parts: first, from "since the founding of this country" onwards, a general clarification of the original place where the Sarvāstivāda school arose;
second, from "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" down to "not allowing it to be dispersed," a specific clarification of the origins of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*;
third, from "Venerable Vasubandhu" onwards, a formal exposition of the causes for the arising of this present treatise. The first part [concludes here].

The first section has two parts: first, from "the subtle words still remain" up to "there have been no disagreements," it clarifies that while the sublime sages proclaimed and upheld [the teachings], the true doctrine remained unified;

second, from "it was only after the Venerable One and those below him" onwards, it reveals how the subsequent sages propagated the transformation [of beings] through diverse perspectives, causing the teachings to divide into different schools.
Regarding the initial statement that Kāśyapa concealed his form at Kukkuṭapāda: in Sanskrit he is called Kāśyapadatta (translated into Chinese as *Yǐnyǎng*, "Drinker of Light").
In ancient times there was a seer whose bodily radiance was so intense that it eclipsed all other light; the Venerable Elder Kāśyapa belonged to that lineage and thus derived his name from the clan.

"Concealed" (*dùn*) refers to his reclusion. According to the first fascicle of the *Fǔfǎzhuan* (Biographies of the Dharma Transmission), Kāśyapa entered into the *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from aspiration).
Having completed the collection of the Dharma-piṭaka without omission through his meditative contemplation, he then thought: "My years are advanced and I can no longer be relied upon;
I am constantly afflicted and harmed by various sufferings. What wise person would take pleasure in this body?
I should now enter parinirvāṇa. He then took leave of King Ajātaśatru and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda, whereupon he sat cross-legged upon a spread of grass.

And sitting there, he made this vow: "May I now wear these rag-robes given by the Buddha and carry my own bowl for a long time without them being damaged, even until fifty-seven koṭis and sixty hundred thousand years have passed.
When Maitreya Tathāgata appears in the world, may I perform the work of a Buddha and cause all his disciples to see my body and thereby give rise to [faith]."
Feeling weary [of his own body], he further thought: "If King Ajātaśatru does not see me, his blood will surely gush from his face and his life will not be saved.
If that king comes with Ānanda to the mountain, I shall open it for them to enter;
if they turn back, I shall close it again and then give up my life. As soon as he had performed this act, the great earth shook in six ways.
Śakra Devānām-Indra, together with the hosts of devas, moved to offer *mandārava* flowers and various celestial powdered incenses as offerings to King Ajātaśatru while he was asleep.
In his dream, the rafter of his house broke (symbolizing that the pillar of the Dharma had split). He immediately woke up in a state of terror and fear.
His attendants informed the Sovereign [of the situation]. Upon hearing this, the King lamented for a long time and then proceeded to the Bamboo Grove Monastery (*Veṇuvana*).
In accordance with the ritual inquiry, Ānanda, having learned where they were to go, proceeded together toward Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
Once they had arrived, the mountain opened of its own accord, and Kāśyapa was found within it, his entire body covered by *mandārava* flowers.
Upon seeing this, the King broke into loud lamentation and weeping, intending to perform the cremation using fragrant wood. Ānanda replied, "Venerable One, [this is due to] meditative concentration."
Maintaining their bodies, they shall wait for Maitreya; it is impossible that they could be burned.
When Maitreya appears, he will lead his retinue of nine hundred and sixty billion to this mountain to see Kāśyapa. At that time, the assembly of Maitreya will all think:
"The physical form of the disciples of Śākyamuni Tathāgata was so lowly and coarse; surely that Buddha must have been no different from them."
Kāśyapa leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations, manifesting a colossal form that filled the world.
At that time, Maitreya Buddha presented his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Kāśyapa. Then, the great assembly, witnessing this supernatural power, abandoned their pride and became *arhats*.
After the King had made offerings, they returned to their own country; at that moment, Mount Kukkuṭapāda closed back together.
As stated at the beginning, according to that tradition, it was asked whether Kāśyapa had entered *nirvāṇa* or had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
The answer, based on various sūtras and śāstras, is that for the most part it is said he entered *nirvāṇa*, and not that he entered the absorption of cessation. Question:

If he entered *nirvāṇa*, how could he leave behind his body so as to remain until the arrival of Maitreya and possess the power of transformation? Answer: This is the leaving behind of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). According to this treatise, it is through the power of his vow (*praṇidhāna-bala*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "that which is held" (and so forth): although the text merely recounts the succession from Kāśyapa to Madhyāntika, it specifically cites the *Kukkutapāda* mountain and the *Nāga-palace* as its textual basis;

this is why it is so. If one were to follow the sequence of transmission according to the *Five Masters’ Tradition*, Kāśyapa entrusted the Dharma to Ānanda, and Ānanda entrusted it to the two sages Śāṇakavāsin and Madhyāntika.
Since the details of these two holy ones' circumstances are not clearly explained in the extensive commentaries (*viśālā-vyākhyā*), I shall not recount them here either.
Regarding the statement that Matāṅga’s Pond is located in the Dragon Palace, in Sanskrit it is called Matāṅgika (translated here as "Golden Ground"). The *Xiyu ji* states:

"In the past, after the World-Honored Buddha had subdued the malevolent spirits in the country of Uddiyāna and returned to the Middle Kingdom, he traveled through the air above this country and said to Ānanda:
'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an Arhat named Matāṅgika.'"
At this site, one should establish a kingdom, bring peace to the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.
Fifty years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the disciple of Ānanda named Madhyantika, hearing the Buddha’s prophetic prediction, rejoiced in his heart.

He came to this place and sat in meditative seclusion within a forest on a great mountain ridge, manifesting great supernatural transformations. Upon seeing him, the youth developed deep faith and requested provisions.
The Arhat he desired said, "I wish for this pool to grant me enough space to rest my knees. Thereupon, King Tōṅ (Aśoka) withdrew the water to offer it as a gift;
the Arhat expanded his body through supernatural power, and the Dragon King exerted his strength to shrink the pool until it was empty and the water exhausted.
The King then begged for the remains of the pool, whereupon Maitreya left a single pool in the northwest, measuring over one hundred *li* in circumference, while all other branches were eliminated.
The Nāga King of the Adjacent Small Pond said, "I have already offered this pond in its entirety; I pray that you will accept my offerings forever.
Maitreya replied, "I shall soon enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Even though you wish to offer your invitation, how could it be possible for me to accept?

The Nāga King entreated him again, saying, 'May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the end of the Dharma. After the Dharma has ended, may they return to take possession of this kingdom.'"
When Māṭhara requested the lake from him, he granted it; then, employing great supernatural power, he established five hundred monasteries in various foreign lands.
He sold low-born people to serve as laborers to provide for the monastic community.
After Māṭhara entered parinirvāṇa, those low-born people established their own rulers, and neighboring kingdoms [attacked them].
Despising his lowly lineage, no one would associate with him; thus he was called Kṛtita (in the language of Tang, "Bought"). At present, the springs there already overflow in abundance;

this is the country of Kaśmīra (translated here as "Country of the Bought Name"; formerly called Jibin, which is a corruption). It lies within the borders of North India and is over seven thousand *li* in circuit.
Its four frontiers are backed by mountains that are extremely precipitous; although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted.
Since antiquity, no neighboring rival has been able to attack it. The kingdom’s great capital city borders the Great River to the west;

it is twelve or thirteen *li* from north to south and four or five *li* from east to west. It is suitable for sowing and reaping, abounding in flowers and fruits. It produces dragon-breed horses, saffron, incense, golden fire-pearls (*agnimāṇi*), and medicinal herbs.
The climate is cold and biting, with much snow and little wind. The inhabitants wear garments of wool, coarse hair-cloth, and white cotton cloth (*dukūla*).
The local customs are frivolous and the people are by nature gentle and weak; they are fond of learning and possess much knowledge, believing both in the heterodox and the orthodox.
There are over a hundred monasteries with five thousand monks. Although their discourse on the Great Meaning (Mahā-artha) is often slightly deviant, the subtle words (sūkṣma-vākya) still remain.
This is because, while their current understandings differ in depth, they have not yet split into separate sects; thus it is said that "the subtle words still remain."

In the *Gujia yu* (Discourse on the Old Family), it is said: "After the Master had passed away, his subtle words were lost; after the seventy-two disciples died, the great principles fell into discord.
This refers to this very meaning. Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha prophesied that in the future, the [Dharma] would initially divide into two schools:

ten thousand people outside the boundary (*sīmā*) would convene a council to form the Mahāsāṃghika school, while Kāśyapa and five hundred others within the boundary would convene a council to form the Sthavira school.
Regarding the division of the school into two sections, the names "Great Meaning" (*Mahārtha*) and "Slight Deviation from Sentimental Views" (*Alpavipratipatti*) differ;
the interpretation here does not accord with the intent of the original chapters.

Next, concerning the second point, the division of the school due to disputes: first, it clarifies that the path of the Kṣudraka was inferior, and subsequently, it clarifies the emergence of the dispute involving Deva.
Regarding the statement "from Upagupta to the Three Sages": the Sanskrit name is *Upagupta*, also known as *Uvaguḍa* (in the Tang language, meaning "Near Protector" or simply "Protector").
The fourth fascicle of the *Sūtra of King Aśoka* states: "When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Mathurā, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
'One hundred years hence, there shall be in this country a son of the elder Gupta named Upagupta, who will provide instruction.'"
Among the disciples of the Dharma of meditation, he was the foremost; although he lacked the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha, his transformative power for saving beings was equal to my own.

I shall provide a detailed commentary on the Tripiṭaka according to the various sectarian tenets. The Venerable One said: "O Great King, you have planted roots of goodness in past lives and are abundantly endowed with blessings and protection.

When he reached nearly eighty years of age, he left the household life to enter the Way in the city.
A young man among them said to him: "Foolish old man, how shallow is your wisdom! For those who have left the household life, there are two tasks:

From that time forth, whether walking, sitting in meditation, standing, or reflecting, he devoted himself to the study of principles and teachings by day and to tranquil contemplation and mental concentration by night. After three years had passed, his learning was thoroughly mastered.

Regarding the details of the five dreams, the *Māyā-sūtra* states: first, he dreamed that Mount Sumeru collapsed and the waters of the four oceans dried up;

A violent wind blew, and he was submerged in a deep abyss. In five dreams, five lions descended from the sky and bit Māyā’s breasts, entering her left side;
her body and mind were in pain as if pierced by swords and blades. These five evil dreams signify the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*.

As for the statement that he manifested extinction between the twin trees (*śāla-vana*), it means that the Buddha manifested entry into *nirvāṇa* between the twin trees, but it was not the ultimate reality.
"True cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to that which has arisen; "yu" (餘) means to cultivate, to narrate, or to begin. Here, it follows the sense of "beginning.
As for "ford and bridge" (*tīrtha*), this refers to the Buddha’s Dharma, which delivers one from the ocean of suffering by serving as a bridge—similar to a river-crossing bridge.
"Kui" (揆) means to measure or to gauge. Although the various schools differ in their interpretations, their purpose in delivering [sentient beings] remains the same.
The principle of "deliverance" (du) is one and the same. Regarding the metaphor of breaking a golden staff, the Sūtra states:
"In the King’s dream, the golden staff was divided into five segments," symbolizing that the Buddha's Dharma was divided into five schools (*nikāya*) (as verified in the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*).

The Dharma-Buddha causes [the teaching] to be equally bestowed, saying that all are the Saṃgha, just as broken gold staffs are all used for gold. (This sūtra does not reach the level of the former.

as for the phrase "rushing from ten thousand *li* like shooting stars," the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the King issued a proclamation to summon [monks] from near and far.

Those who had realized the fruits [of the path] remained, while those still bound by all fetters returned; even so, they were numerous. Again, he commanded that those beyond training remain, while those still in training returned; yet they were still many.

This is because the six supernormal powers depend upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*); thus, by citing concentration, the supernormal powers are implied. The four analytical knowledges arise from wisdom (*prajñā*); therefore, by designating wisdom, the analytical knowledges are expressed.

That is to say, being equipped with the six supernormal powers is called "fulfilled" (*pūrṇa*), and possessing the four analytical knowledges is called "perfected" (*pariniṣpanna*). Thus, the *Xiyuji* (Record of the Western Regions) refers to one who possesses them as "one who is equipped with the six supernormal powers."

"Perfection" (*pāramitā*) means "fulfillment. By extension, among the three types of fulfillment, attaining the meditative absorption of cessation is called "perfection of concentration" (*samādhi-pāramitā*), and attaining the knowledge of non-arising is called "perfection of wisdom" (*jñāna-pāramitā*).

The meanings of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) will be clarified below in their respective places, so there is no need for further elaboration here.

As for the five sciences (*pañca vidyāsthānāni*): first, the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), which explains terms, defines characters, and elucidates the conventions of its own linguistic system; second, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*)... [the text continues].

1. Arts and Mechanisms (*śilpa-vidyā*): This includes the principles of yin and yang, calendrical calculation, and the three medical sciences—namely, the mastery of incantations for warding off malevolent spirits, medicinal herbs and minerals, and acupuncture and moxibustion.

2. Logic (*hetu-vidyā*): This involves the examination and determination of the correct and the erroneous, as well as the investigation of the true and the false. 3. Inner Science (*adhyātma-vidyā*): This thoroughly elucidates the subtle principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles.

The single chapter refuting the "Self" (Pudgala-viniścaya) is not yet included in this count. As for the inclusion of the phrase "it is said" (*kila*) within the verses, it appears to serve as a form of moderation, as seen in numerous instances such as when it says "it is said that light and darkness [arise]," and so forth.
This intention is to clarify the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the Sarvāstivāda school.
It is said that there is no authentic canonical text upon which to rely for verification;

however, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that at that time, the Venerable Vasubandhu composed the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* in the eastern room of the Venerable Pārśva’s residence in the kingdom of Gandhāra, and out of respect for him, [the work] was sealed and recorded.
Regarding the original text consisting of eight thousand verses, in India, whenever a number reaches thirty-two, it is simply referred to as "eight."
For a single verse, it is called an *anuṣṭubh*; in a work of eight thousand verses, there are two hundred and fifty-six million characters.
This is calculated according to the number of syllables in the Sanskrit original.

The second section clarifies the intent for composing this treatise, which is divided into three parts: first, up to the point where it says "extensively upholding the World-Honored One’s teaching," it specifically clarifies the intent for composing the treatise;
second, from "furthermore, once the teachings of the Tripiṭaka have arisen" onwards, it generally clarifies the arising of the Tripiṭaka teachings;

third, from "furthermore, based on the *Vibhāṣā*" onwards, it again clarifies the composition of the treatise. Regarding the initial statement, "the three realms of existence" (*tridhātu*), this refers to the three worlds. It says:

Regarding those whose afflictions have not yet been extinguished, the subsequent text states: "Apart from latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), karma lacks the capacity to produce existence; it is only through latent tendencies that karma can grow and develop.
Thus, the cycle of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu-saṃsāra*) is precisely due to affliction. As for the statement that one must sever the conditions for affliction:
while karma is the cause that brings about results, affliction is the condition that moistens karma. Since we are now only severing the afflictions, they are termed the "conditions for affliction."

This refers to the conditions (*pratyaya*). Regarding the statement "the primary cause for severing delusions," this clarifies that the cause for being able to uphold the precepts is the purity of the path of wisdom, as this pure wisdom is the primary cause for severing delusions.
Regarding the phrase "the profound keys to the four Āgamas," they are: first, the *Dīrgha-āgama* (which contains many long verses);

second, the *Madhyama-āgama* (which contains many medium-length verses); third, the *Ekottarika-āgama* (meaning it begins with one dharma and increases by one up to many); and fourth, the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.

*Khanda* (translated here as "containing" [Sanskrit: *saṃgraha*, or "collection"] and also rendered as "various explanations") refers to a key. A key serves to secure a bolt; according to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it is that which strikes down at the bolt.
According to the *Fangyan*, those in the East call it *jian*, while those in the West call it *yue*; it is termed the "bolt and key," being the essential pivot of a gate.
Now, this treatise can reveal the profound and mysterious meanings of the Four Āgamas and Six Pādas, just as a bolt and key secure a gate.
Regarding the phrase "the source of the Dharma-characteristics river": the "source" refers to the fundamental origin of all streams;

this treatise is the primary source of the Dharma-characteristics school. Regarding the phrase "the ocean and rivers of its doctrinal gates": it reveals that the meanings are inexhaustible, like the flowing currents of the ocean and rivers.

Regarding the phrase "the text is pure and clear, as lustrous as jade": it means the text is as smooth and moist as jade, while the principles are as bright as the moon’s radiance, beautiful and exquisite. Thus it is said.
"To enlighten the obscured minds of students" means to open the dull and inferior minds of those who study the Dharma.
The phrase "I, in a corner [of the world]" refers to the verse at the end of the *Pudgala-pratiṣedha-pariccheda* (Chapter on Refuting the Self).

The expression "the blue lotus ceases its smile" means that while the Tathāgata’s eyes are pure, long, and wide like the color of a blue lotus, and his countenance is usually serene and subtle as if smiling, now he has entered [nirvana].
Because he has entered *nirvāṇa*, it is said that his smile has ceased. Regarding the phrase "the white tuft conceals its color," the "tuft" (*máo*) refers to a long hair;
the Tathāgata possesses the mark of a white tuft between his eyebrows, yet now that he enters *nirvāṇa*, the radiance of this tuft no longer appears, hence it is said that its light is concealed.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra* states: "When the Prince was born, the tuft extended five feet; beneath the tree, it grew to one zhang, four chi, and five cun."
After attaining enlightenment, its height increased by one zhang and five chi; externally it had ten ridges, while internally it manifested the sign of emptiness.

Both inside and outside were empty, and when released, it curled up like the full moon in autumn—distinct, bright, and pure, its color reflecting off white jade and snow, and being perfectly round like a three-inch sphere.

What is called "the confusion of heterodox followers" refers to the chaotic and entangled disputes of the various heterodox schools. As for the "rain of the assembly," [it refers to... three... (text fragment).
Regarding the term for "virtue" (guṇa), in Sanskrit it is called *guṇarṣi* (translated here as "rain"). Because they were born during the rainy season (*varṣā*), they are so named;
furthermore, because the disciples of these non-Buddhists were as numerous as the rain during the rainy season, they are called the "Rain-Assembly" (*Vārṣagaṇya*).

Moreover, in Sanskrit it is called *Sāṃkhyaśāstra* (translated here as "Number-Treatise"). This name is designated based on its subject matter: it refers to a treatise arising from numbers, and since the treatise can produce numbers, it is named accordingly.
The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists establish twenty-five principles (*tattva*). Here, when speaking of the "three qualities" (*guṇa*), one quality is mentioned by way of illustration.
According to their reckoning, there is a truly eternal self (*ātman*) whose essential nature is consciousness; it is merely the experiencer and not the agent.
The remaining twenty-four principles are what is experienced by that self. Regarding the two natures, they are the three qualities consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and [tamas].

The answer is: *māyā* (illusion) is the essence (*tattva*). This is translated as suffering, pleasure, and delusion; it is also called greed, hatred, and delusion; or suffering, greed, and pleasure; or sorrow, joy, and equanimity (*upekṣā*). Since *upekṣā* has the same meaning as *śama*, it is also called yellow, red, and black;
or valor, delusion, and darkness. These three are like my ministers who assist me. When I wish to enjoy objects, they transform for me;
when they have not yet transformed, each abides in its own nature, and thus they are called the "three natures" (*svabhāva-traya*). From these natures, the "Great One" (*mahat*) arises.
When I reflect upon the time of desiring to experience various objects, three factors immediately become known to be in motion;
because their substance is vast, they are called the "Great" (mahat). From the Great, the "I-grasping" (ahaṃkāra) arises—so it is called "I-grasping" because it takes the self as its object.

From the I-grasping, the five subtle elements (tanmātra)—namely, form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—arise, which together with the preceding [three] constitute nine. From these five subtle elements...
The five great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—are produced from the *pramāṇa* (the primal principle); these constitute the first fourteen.

From the five great elements, eleven faculties (*indriya*) are produced: the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, hands, feet, the organs of excretion and generation, and the organ of speech (which refers here to the internal tongue);
these constitute the twenty-five principles (*tattva*). All the dharmas asserted by this school are eternal, like gold being transformed [into various ornaments].
Just as the color of rings and bracelets remains unchanged while their forms differ, so too when I desire to experience objects,
[the elements] arise from the primal nature (prakṛti) through the Great One (mahat) down to the eleven organs; when I do not desire to experience objects,

they recede from the eleven organs back into the five gross elements (mahābhūta), from the gross elements back into the five subtle elements (tanmātra), and from the five subtle elements back into me.
Holding that [the individual soul] emerges from this [Prakṛti], and that from the Great One (Mahat) it returns to its own nature (Svabhāva)—now, these three *guṇas* are indeed the *svabhāva*.

Regarding the statement that they are called *guṇas* based on their capacity for transformation (*pariṇāma-śakti*), while they are called the *svabhāva* when speaking of the fundamental nature, there is the doctrine of the six categories of equality (*ṣaḍ-guṇa-samatva*).

The Sanskrit term for this is *Kāṇāda* (in Chinese, *Shí Mǐqí*; formerly mistranscribed as *Kāṇāda*). This refers to an externalist (*tīrthika*) whose physical form was ugly and who, during the day...
He hid in the mountain forests and would come among humans at night to beg for food;

because he caused a pregnant woman to miscarry by startling her, he thereafter ceased begging and instead subsisted on broken grains picked up from places where rice was being pounded. He was thus named after this practice.
He is also called Uṇṇābha (this name refers to the owl-heretic; his former name, Ulūka, is an error). This is likely because he resembled an owl that emerges at night.

Also known as Vaiśeṣika (translated here as *Shèngxī*; formerly called *Wèishì* or *Bǐshì*, both of which are erroneous abbreviations). It is so named because its treatise is superior, or because it was composed by a superior person.
Its followers are called the Pañcaśikha (so named because they have five tufts on their heads, from which they derive their name). They expound six categories (*padārtha*):

first, substance (*dravya*), referring to nine factors—earth, water, fire, air, space, time, direction, self, and mind—which possess the nature of substantiality; second, quality (*guṇa*), referring to twenty-one factors such as color, fragrance, and so forth; third, action (*karman*).

(This refers to the functional activities of grasping and discarding, contracting and extending, and so forth. The four great elements possess the capacity to give rise to all phenomena. The fifth is "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*): "sameness" refers to general identity, while "difference" refers to specific distinction.

The sixth is "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), which refers to the nature of combination. To say "they ravage my garden of flowers" means that these heterodox followers destroy the Buddha’s garden of the flowers of the True Dharma.
To say "they sully my clear stream" (the character *gū* is pronounced as *yú* or *gǔmò*; it refers to flowing water) means that the True Dharma is fundamentally pure.
Just as the clear flow of water is now turbidified by non-Buddhists who preach false teachings, thereby muddying the clear stream of the True Dharma.
The phrase "all for the purpose of widely upholding the teachings" refers to the subsequent text concerning the propagation [of the sutra].

From here below, the general intent for the arising of the Three Piṭakas is clarified; within this, there is a general manifestation of the basis upon which they rely, followed by a specific exposition of the four intentions.

Regarding the phrase "those who have long habitually perused the Piṭakas speak from the power of that which is their natural outflow (*niṣyanda*)," "power" refers to the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), "etc.

refers to the [four] kinds of equality, and "outflow" refers to the category of natural emanation. That is to say, because one speaks on the scriptural Dharma based on a mind that is an outflow of the Ten Powers and so forth, it is said to be "based on power."

Furthermore, the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) is explained as having the sense of being invincible through power. The Buddha taught that the principles of the sūtras are profound and far-reaching, transcending contemporary sentiments;
no heterodox paths are able to subdue them. Because these [powers] are called the "outflow of power," just like the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), the *Nyāya* states:

"If there are contradictions within the sūtras, they should merely be interpreted through reconciliation rather than being disbelieved. This refers to attaining the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).

Those who discourse on the Path maintain that the mind itself is concentration (*samādhi*), because the Sūtras explain concentration in this way; "preeminent" (*adhipati*) carries the sense of being superior or most excellent.

This is unique to the Buddha's Dharma and does not exist among non-Buddhists, and is therefore called "preeminent. One might ask: since concentration is a mental factor (*caitta*), why is it called "mind" (*citta*)?

The answer is that there is no error in calling a mental factor "mind" when it is the basis for the mind—that is, when the mental factor depends upon the king [of the mind]. Alternatively, it is designated as "mind" simply by referring to the aggregate as a whole.
The subsequent passage states: "One-pointedness of mind is called concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the "path of discourse," this refers to the teaching that expresses [the truth] through speech;
it means that because the teaching is established by way of verbal reasoning, sentient beings are enabled to obtain this teaching and the expressions of the path of discourse.

As for "various miscellaneous explanations," this refers to how, within the sūtras, whether concerning phenomena (*dharma*) or principles (*naya*), one speaks in accordance with the capacities of the audience; hence they are called "miscellaneous."

It is said that [the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*] primarily elucidates the principle of Buddha-nature, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* elucidate the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and sūtras such as the *Gopālaka* primarily elucidate conventional matters. Regarding the phrase "causing those who have not planted roots of goodness to plant them":

this refers to generating the five faculties, such as faith, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, thereby planting the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). Regarding the phrase "causing those who have not entered the True Dharma to enter it":
this refers to non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who, before encountering the Buddha, had only received false teachings; [upon meeting him, they are led to enter the True Dharma].
When the Buddha preached the sūtras, he entered the words of the True Dharma; as for the statement that the Vinaya Piṭaka is a natural outflow of compassion:

"compassion" refers to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because within the Vinaya there are many explanations of subtle deportment and detailed discourses, and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the essence of great compassion.
The phrase "attaining superior morality" clarifies the referent of what is explained; "the path of the treatise" refers to that which is capable [of leading to realization].

Regarding the explanation of the teaching: "Training rules" (*śikṣāpada*) refers to abstaining from killing and so forth; because they are the basis upon which training depends, they are called "training rules.
This means they are the points of training for a bhikṣu. Regarding the phrase "causing the continuum to achieve [perfection]":

some say that "continuum" refers to the body, meaning it causes the body to achieve roots of goodness. However, my current interpretation is not thus; as previously stated, the Sūtra intends for those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to do so.

The "roots" are the seeds; here, it is further explained that because the disciplinary rules (*vinaya*) continue in succession and reach fulfillment, they are not spoken of merely in terms of the physical body.

One who "upholds the True Dharma" (*saddharma-dhāraka*), having already entered the True Dharma by relying on the Sūtras, should rely upon the Vinaya to guard the body and speech so as not to fall back;
this is called upholding the True Dharma. Furthermore, the discourse on the treatises flows forth from fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
The Tathāgata possesses four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). In his treatises, he extensively elucidates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), thoroughly investigating their origins;

thus, the heterodox and erroneous doctrines of other paths are unable to shake him, and he thereby attains fearlessness. One should know that these [teachings] are either spoken with a fearless mind, and are therefore called "words based on fearlessness" (*vaiśāradya-vākya*).

Regarding "specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and so forth: "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the mode of appearance, such as [the characteristic] of form (*rūpa*).

Dharma has the characteristic of transformation and resistance; sensation has the characteristic of experiencing. These various characteristics are mutually exclusive and are termed "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Now, because one discriminates these meanings, it is called the "discrimination of specific and general characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vikalpa*).

Third, regarding "having already accomplished [the practice] so as to attain right liberation": this refers to the previously mentioned restraints (*saṃvara*), which merely cause one to accomplish roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*); however—
Because one cannot attain right liberation [merely through this], it is taught that one attains liberation only after subsequently expounding the Dharma;
or as a sutra says, "When precepts are pure and wisdom exists, one then attains the foremost path. Thus we know that without wisdom, one does not attain liberation.

Furthermore, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) attains true *nirvāṇa*, which is unlike the various false liberations imagined by non-Buddhists, such as the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*). Therefore, it is said:

Correct. To say that one "thoroughly penetrates the true nature of all phenomena" means that the true essence and characteristics of all phenomena, such as the five aggregates, are all made understood by the student through their differentiation via scriptural teachings.

From here below, the two preceding meanings within the section on the exposition of the teaching are further clarified. As for their distinction: the first meaning reveals that the Buddha’s teaching is to be upheld without error;
the second meaning is specifically intended to destroy the darkness of ignorance. Although both employ the metaphor of a lamp, these two meanings are entirely distinct.

Regarding the phrase "revealing the image of non-self": in the True Dharma, there is fundamentally no self; it is only through the false calculations of external paths that the deluded attachment to a self arises.

The image of selflessness was hidden and not manifest; now, by teaching the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and analyzing form (*rūpa*) and so forth, one finds that the substance of a self is entirely unobtainable, and thus the image of selflessness becomes clearly manifest once again.
"Image" (*bimba*) refers here to "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*); therefore, the Sūtra says, "the characteristics of selflessness," and so on.
The Buddha and sentient beings rely upon this to be fearless; the Treatise explains that this is the wisdom of the Buddha’s pure insight.

Sentient beings who have attained the realization of the fruits are likewise included; since the Buddha is one who has already realized them and others are those who shall realize them, they are mentioned collectively.
"Discriminating various phenomena such as the wholesome" refers to discriminating between wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

The above concludes the explanation of the first section. From here on, the clarification of the fundamental tenets (*siddhānta*) refers to the intent of the school’s doctrine, not the intent of the subject matter being explained.
This passage is divided into two main parts: first, a general enumeration of the sectarian tenets;

second, a detailed judgment of the doctrinal intent. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, a general account of how divergent views arose and established their doctrines; second, an examination of the specific tenets within those schools.
Regarding the statement that the traces of the initial teachings were divided into eighteen schools: "qu" (區) means to distinguish; "fen" (分) means to differentiate.
This refers to the eighteen schools when speaking of the branches alone; if the roots are included, there are twenty schools. The causes for these divisions have already been explained above.
Now, in response to this text, I shall briefly describe their names and numbers; first, the initial schism was solely for the sake of the superior [monks].
After the two divisions of the Mahāsāṃghika had emerged from the Great Assembly, they further split into eight schools through internal disputes.

Within the second century [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], three schools emerged: 1. **The Dharmaguptaka** (this school maintains that both mundane and supramundane phenomena lack any substantial reality and are merely conventional designations). 2.

**The Sautrāntika** (meaning they maintain that mundane phenomena arise from inversion, whereas supramundane phenomena possess a distinct and separate essence). 3. **The Kukkutika** (in ancient times, there was a seer who mated with a hen and fathered offspring).

The founder of this school was its patriarch. Two hundred years later, another school emerged named the Mahīśāsaka (the School of the Greatly Learned); because they extensively studied the Tripiṭaka and deeply realized the Buddha’s words, they were named for their virtue as the Mahīśāsaka.
Subsequently, another school arose called the Prajñaptivāda (the School of Designation);

Master Ci'en stated that this school asserts that both mundane and supramundane phenomena are all conventionally designated (*prajñapti*) and lack true reality, and thus differs from the Ekavyāvahārika and the Lokottaravāda schools. When the two hundred years had elapsed, they again examined five matters in detail, which led to further disputes.

It is divided into three schools: first, the Caitika school (Caitika is translated as "Spiritual Temple"; because the Buddha attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, and entered parinirvāṇa at four locations, there were spiritual temples established for offerings at each;

this school is named after a mountain where many Caitikas resided). Second, the Aparaseliya school (Western Mountain Dwelling School). Third, the Uttaraseliya school (Northern Mountain Dwelling School).

[These two schools both resided to the west and north of the Caitika mountains. These eight schools, together with the original one, constitute nine schools. Among them, the Sthavira school has existed for such a long time.
After the harmonious period of the *Vibhajyavāda*, at the beginning of the third century, a slight disagreement arose, leading to a division into two schools:

first, the Sarvāstivāda (also called Hetuvāda). [The term "all exists" (*sarvam asti*) has two aspects: first, conditioned phenomena exist as real entities throughout the three periods of time; second, unconditioned phenomena exist as real entities apart from the three periods of time.

The name of the school is derived from its established doctrine. Second, the Sthavira-vāda (the Snow Mountain School). This branch of the Sthaviras was weak and could not endure, like snow blown away by the wind, drifting without a place to settle; it was named after this metaphor, or alternatively, it was designated by its location as the Himavat-vāda.

It is also called the Sthavira (Elder) school, named after its founder to distinguish the sect. In the second three-hundred-year period, from the Sarvāstivāda school, one branch emerged called the Vatsīputrīya school.

(In ancient times, there was a seer who lived in a secluded mountain retreat; he became enamored with a mother cow and consequently had a son. Thereafter, the lineage of that seer was all called the Vatsīputrīya school, named after the descendant to distinguish the sect.

Subsequently, four schools branched out from the Vatsīputrīya: first, the Dharmottarīya school (the title of the leader of this school means "one for whom the Dharma is supreme," or alternatively, "one whose Dharma rises above the multitude").

The name Dharmottarīya is established based on both the person and the doctrine. Second is the Bhadrayānīya school: "Bhadra" refers to the leader of the school, while "yāna" has the meaning of "descendant," as they are the descendants of these noble Arhats.

Third is the Saṃmitīya school: that which weighs and determines is called "māna" (measure); that which is without error is termed "saṃmita" (correct). The profound doctrines established by this school are determined to be without error, and thus it is named Saṃmitīya.
Fourth is the Kṛṣṇagiri school: because the mountain forests nearby are lush and dense, it is named after its location. Next, the Sarvāstivāda school further divided into one more sect.

The Mahīśāsaka school (so named because its founder once served as a king who "transformed" [the earth] by spreading it out; he abdicated his kingdom to leave the household life and propagate the Buddha-dharma, and thus the school was named after him).
Next, from the Mahīśāsaka school emerged the Dharmaguptaka (or Dharmagupta) school (the meanings of "Gupta" and "Guha" in the names of their founders are essentially the same;

this master contained the esoteric True Dharma like a treasury, and thus the name was established based on the person). At the end of the third century, from the Sarvāstivāda school emerged the Kāśyapīya school (in Sanskrit, *Kāśyapīya*).

Kāśyapa (translated into Chinese as *Yǐnguāng*, "Drinker of Light") was a Brahmin clan name. In antiquity, there was a rishi whose body possessed a golden light that eclipsed all other lights; thus he was named Kāśyapa ("The One Who Eclipses"). The founder of this school was a descendant of his.

Furthermore, because the founder of this school possessed a golden light on his body capable of "drinking" [eclipsing] other lights, the school was named after this physical attribute as the Kāśyapīya.

At the beginning of the fourth century, a school named Sautrāntika emerged from the Sarvāstivāda. This school takes only the sūtras as its authority, not the vinaya or śāstras; thus, it is the Sautrāntika masters who, based on their established tenets, manifest the name of the school. The Sthavira school is distinguished by its primary and secondary branches.
It is taught that there are eleven schools; now, excluding the root and taking only the branches, there are ten schools.
When combined with the eight schools derived from the Mahāsāṃghika, they constitute eighteen schools.
Below this, the specific doctrines held by each are clarified; therein are three sections: first, it clarifies that the doctrines of the four schools are merely provisional, citing two sūtras.
Regarding the schools' tenets concerning the conventional and the real: the Sarvāstivādins maintain that all is real and not conventional.
As for the statement that "these four schools' cherished tenets are merely verbal designations," this means that the tenets venerated by these four schools are merely conventional and not real.
Now, upon careful examination, while it may be the case that the Ekavyāvahārikas hold everything to be entirely conventional, the Lokottaravādins admit that supramundane phenomena are indeed real.
Because they are of the same essence, it is known that the statement regarding the four [schools] as being merely provisional does not yet exhaust the full principle.

Furthermore, the statement that the Mahāsāṃghika school encompasses both the root and its branches refers to the school as a whole and is not restricted to the eighteen specific sects. Paramārtha states: "The Mahāsāṃghika school resides in the country of Aṅguttara; their territory lies within Rājagṛha.
This school widely propagates such sutras as the Avataṃsaka, the Nirvāṇa, the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda, the Vimalakīrti, and the Suvarṇaprabhāsa."
The Kukkutika school does not propagate the Sūtras and Vinaya, asserting that the Sūtras and Vinaya are merely provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*).

Because the Buddha himself, on certain occasions, refuted the Sūtras and Vinaya, they propagate only the Abhidharma (*abhidharma*) and the practice of seated meditation (*dhyāna*) for severing delusions. Regarding what the Sautrāntika school posits as partially real:

they claim that the past and future are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*), while only the present is real; furthermore, they hold that the three categories of dharmas—the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—are all conventional, whereas only the [eighteen] elements (*dhātu*) are real.
That these are real yet dissociated (*viprayukta*) and so forth is a mere conventional designation (*prajñapti*).

Regarding the Sarvāstivāda school (translated as "All-Exists"), in this chapter we shall first briefly examine their tenet that all things exist substantially across the three time periods; they maintain that even unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and dissociated factors possess substantial reality.
Within this system, the author first summarizes four positions in general, followed by the Master’s critique. As for Dharmatrāta, his name in Sanskrit is...
Dharmatrāta (translated into Chinese as Fajiù, "Dharma-Savior"), so called because he saves people by means of the Dharma, states that they differ due to their distinct categories (*jāti*).

"Category" refers to a genus; although the essence of the dharmas of the three periods of time is one, their modes of transition through the three periods constitute distinct categories, thereby establishing the divisions of past, future, and so forth.
This is illustrated by a golden vessel: when a bowl is fashioned into a cup, the name is established according to the category based on the change in form.

In reality, the essence of gold has never been different; the essence of dharmas is likewise. Although the past and future differ, their essence is not distinct (meaning that time has no separate substance established apart from the dharmas;
therefore, the essence of all dharmas is without difference). As for "Ghoṣa," in Sanskrit it is called Ghoṣa (in the language of Tang, "Capable of Resounding").

In the Western Regions, those who propagate and proclaim the name of the Dharma are called Ghoṣa; this refers to the Venerable One who, having long drifted through birth and death, has now attained sainthood.
Because wisdom contrasts with the past and is thus likened to it, it is called "capable of sounding"; or, because it is capable of proclaiming [the Dharma], it is called "capable of sounding.

Regarding the statement that their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) differ: "characteristic" refers to their mode of being, not to the four characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth. The old masters say: This teacher asserts that among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), there is a distinct category called "worldly characteristic" (*adhvalakṣaṇa*).
There are differences between the three time periods; each and every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possesses these three.

If a phenomenon has ceased in the past, its conjunction with the characteristics of the past is called "conjoined with the past," while its conjunction with the characteristics of the present and future is called "conjoined with the present and future," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is said that the past is not separate from the characteristics of the present and future, because all conditioned phenomena possess three characteristics.
Whichever world they reside in, one is manifest while two are latent; that which is currently manifest is said to be "properly conjoined," while the other two remain latent.
Although it is latent, its essence is not non-existent; thus it is also called "not separated from that characteristic. Furthermore, when a characteristic has function, it is termed "conjoined";
although it lacks function [at other times], because its essence is not non-existent as it conforms to the dharma, it is said to be "not separated.
Therefore, the treatise establishes an analogy, saying: "It is like a man who, while currently impassioned with one wife, is not said to be free from passion for his other concubines."
The past is as it is, and the future and present are likewise; these are all explained as distinct names based on their temporal designations.
Regarding the term "Vasumitra" (世友), in Sanskrit he is called *Vasumitra* (which in the Tang language means "Friend of the World"). This is the name of an Indian temple;

because the parents of that Bodhisattva feared that [the child] might be disturbed or harmed by ghosts and spirits upon his birth, they took that name in the hope of avoiding such affliction. This is what is meant by "based on [the context]."

Regarding the phrase "the states are different," "state" (avasthā) refers here to a temporal stage (*avasthāna*). The intended meaning is that while the substance (*dharmatā*) of a phenomenon is eternally existent, it is divided into three distinct stages based on the difference between the times when it possesses activity and when it does not.

As for the statement that "in each respective state, different functions are performed," this means that when the future reaches the present state, and the present enters the past state, they are designated by different names because the states are not one and the same.
When each stage reaches the present stage, it is called "present"; when it enters the past stage, it is called "past.

Because its essence does not undergo change, it is known through the metaphor of counting distinct units (*gaṇanā*). As for "Bodhadeva," in Sanskrit he is called *Bodhadeva* (in the language of Tang, "Jue Tian" or "Awakened Deva");
this title was established because the Buddha is regarded as a deva. As for "relative dependence" (*apekṣā*), it means looking toward one another; that is, with respect to the past...
The expectation regarding the present and so forth can be known through inference from what precedes it.

Below this, the Master of the Treatise offers his own evaluation, stating that Dharmatrāta, who maintains the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), attempts to establish the category of the present by analogy with the future—
just as the forms of vessels such as bowls and cups undergo transformation— and thus he should be classified among the ranks of the non-Buddhist Sāṃkhyas.
As for the "middle" [position], it refers to the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists who maintain that the three *guṇas* undergo transformation to become the twenty-five *tattvas*;
since the tenets of this school are identical to theirs, the term "this faction" (*spen*) is employed. Regarding the claim that all three times possess the characteristics of the three times:

first, Bandhuprabha states that when past characteristics are combined, it is called the "past"; furthermore, he says that it is not separate from the characteristics of the present and future, and that the present and future likewise [are not separate].
To be "separate from the past and so forth" means that the past is also called the present and future, and the present and future are also called the past and so forth.
Why? Because it is fixedly established as the past, the present, and the future, and so on; thus, confusion arises.
Regarding the statement by Buddhadāsa that the past consists of many moments (*kṣaṇa*), consider for a moment today at this very present time. Transversely...
Since everything prior to the present moment is collectively termed "past," the past consists of many moments;

thus, when these moments are viewed in relation to one another, they naturally constitute the three time periods. If it is argued that the future and the present should be understood in the same way, this would entail the same fault of confusion as in the case of the past.
Now, upon closer examination, while this may appear plausible at first glance, the reasoning is actually quite different. This is because the various phenomena of the future are already intermingled.
If they were disordered and indistinguishable as to priority and posteriority, how could there be distinctions such as mutual observation between prior and posterior moments?

Furthermore, since the present consists of only a single moment, how could it be the same as the past in having the fault of confusion? To this, the explanation is given: although the future has not yet been divided into priority and posteriority, because it contains many mental instants (*kṣaṇa*), it can possess priority and posteriority;
thus, it is similar to the past. As for the present, although it is indeed a single moment, [it is compared to the others].
Regarding the past, if one looks toward the future, it is the "prior"; if one looks toward the past, it is the "subsequent";
and if one looks toward both the prior and subsequent, it is called the "present.

Thus, although a single momentary dharma may receive the designation of the three time periods depending on its relation to what precedes and follows it—just as one person may be called a father, a son, or a husband—it is the same principle applied here.
Because she was the mother of a famous woman, there is no logical fault in the fact that her past status is similar to her present and future ones.
Regarding the statement that Vasumitra’s *Prakaraṇapāda* is superior, the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa* states: "The third [system] establishes the time periods based on activity (*kāritra*).
This is considered superior among the four positions currently under discussion, following the Sautrāntika critique of that [Vaibhāṣika] system. As for the Sautrāntika view on the past:
That the future has no substance means that they assert that phenomena (dharma) do not exist originally but come into being now, and having existed, return to non-existence;
as it is said below, "the moment a phenomenon attains its own essence is called one kṣaṇa. Thus, one knows that only the present is real.
In the following section on the classification of teachings (*p'an-chiao*), it says "the Exoteric School" (*hsien-tsung*): "exoteric" (*hsien*) means manifest;

this refers to the fact that because [Vasubandhu] composed this treatise based on the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it is manifest that he relies upon the Sarvāstivāda school. Regarding the "Esoteric School" (*mi-tsung*): "esoteric" (*mi*) means hidden;

although he composed the treatise based on the Sarvāstivāda school, he followed the Sautrāntika school according to his own secret intention (*rahasya*). Therefore, it is called the Esoteric School. Thus, the text below states: "The *Vibhāṣā*..."

Śāntipa says that because what I venerate is the Sautrāntika school, and because what they teach does not contradict reason, this single treatise constitutes two schools based on the distinction between the Exoteric and Esoteric.
Regarding the third collection (piṭaka), the text has two parts:
first, the formal explanation of their mutual inclusion; second, questions and answers for clarification. Within the first part, each begins as follows:
Next, I shall clarify the meaning of the translated terms. Regarding the term *sūtrapiṭaka*, what was formerly called *xiūduluó* (修多羅) or *xiūdùlù* (修妬路) and so forth is all erroneous.
As for the term "thread" (*sūtra*) and so on, it is a direct translation of the name of the teaching; that it "signifies meditative concentration" (*samādhi*) clarifies its intended meaning.
The *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*) states: "It is like flowers scattered upon a table; when the wind blows, [they are moved]."

Why is it called "scattered"? Because it was not originally strung together with thread; now, because the thread possesses the capacity to string flowers, the teaching possesses the functional utility of being able to string [the meaning].
Thus, by analogy with the thread, the name is established through metaphor.

Alternatively, it is called a "sūtra" (scripture) because, like woven cloth or silk, it possesses the function of expressing [meaning], which is identical in principle to the function of the thread. As the *Nirabhilāpyadharmatā-siddhi-śāstra* states: "It strings together."
Because it sews together [the teachings], it is called a *sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states that a *sūtra* has five meanings:

first, a spring; second, a carpenter’s line; third, a string of garlands; fourth, a thread; and fifth, a well-rope. Alternatively, according to secular etymology, *dharma* (the teaching) is glossed as *nitya* (constant).

Since it is something that even a hundred kings cannot alter, and because the teaching serves as a standard and a model, it is called a *sūtra*. As for the statement that it "correctly explains meditative concentration," this refers to the *sūtra*.

Although it clarifies ethical discipline (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), because it does not exclusively [emphasize] these, it is said that "correct" (*samyak*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the same may be understood by analogy for the other two *piṭakas*. Regarding *vinaya*, what was formerly called *pinaiye* or *binaiye* is both erroneous.

This is termed "subduing" (*dānta*) because it means to discipline the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and to suppress the three types of action (*tri-karma*). As the treatise states: "The term 'subduing' is intended to reveal the *vinaya*."
The Vinaya is so called because it can discipline the faculties; it is also termed *vinaya*, which means "extinction," though its many other names are not described here for fear of prolixity.
As for *Abhidharma*, what was formerly called *Abhidharma* and so forth is all a corruption; this is translated as "Dharma in Opposition" (*pratisaṃkhyā*), as will be explained below.
These three are all called "collections" (*piṭaka*) because they contain the essential meaning; thus, they are named "Pitakas."

Regarding the question-and-answer sections from this point onward: since the Sūtras and Vinaya both expound wisdom (*prajñā*), one might ask whether the Abhidharma-piṭaka also encompasses the other two [the Sūtra and Vinaya].

If one follows the answer in the *Nyāyānusāra*, which states that because the other two Piṭakas contain question-and-answer formats, they are subsumed here, it would imply they are not included in the other two.
This can be seen by examining the relevant chapters.

Explanation of the Fourth Gate: Regarding the translation of this treatise by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Chen Dynasty at Zhizhi Temple in Lingnan, the *Yijing Tujì* (Record of the Illustrations of Translated Scriptures) states:
"The śramaṇa Paramārtha (translated here as 'True Meaning') was a native of Ujjayinī in Western India.
His conduct was exemplary, his realization was profound, and his character was pure and serene. In the second year of the Taiching era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty..."
In the Baoyun Hall, eleven scriptures in total, including the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* and others, were translated by imperial decree.

Later, when Paramārtha arrived in Hengzhou and finished translating the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, he encountered the rebellion of Hou Jing and consequently sailed westward across the sea. Driven by the winds, he eventually reached Guangzhou.

It was during the first year of the Yongding era of the Chen dynasty that he finally began the translation of this treatise. This indicates that the previous translators had not yet fully mastered the [Indian] methods.
The phrase "the speaker" refers to myself, who have come from the Western Regions and recently traveled to the Eastern Lands, yet have not yet mastered the local dialects and terminology.
The phrase "wherein the meaning of the words differs or errs" means that there are discrepancies and errors;

this refers specifically to the section beginning with "unconditioned" (*asamskrta*), where I point out the nature of those discrepancies. Regarding the statement "unconditioned," the previous translation said "not," which does not mean non-existence.
Because it does not obstruct phenomena, it is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); because it is realized through the Path, it is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
Since it does not arise from the six causes, it is called "causeless" (*ahetuka*); since it cannot take up a fruit, it is called "fruitless" (*aphala*).

For this reason, people of old failed to distinguish between existence and non-existence, or right and wrong, and thus claimed that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is neither cause nor fruit, and that it is neither identical to nor different from its own nature.
