The statement that "Kātyāyanīputra compiled and arranged [the teachings] which were scattered throughout the Buddha’s sūtras" means that the name belongs to those two;

this is the same as the second explanation. Regarding the phrase "composed by Kātyāyanīputra and others, such as the *Jñānaprasthāna* and so forth," it refers to the selection and arrangement [of the material], while the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* and other treatises were composed by Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others. The word "etc. (ādi) [indicates these].
As the Venerable Dharmatrāta cites an example to establish [this point], this Venerable One appeared three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

"The formations proceed without ceasing and can traverse ten thousand li of paths; because impermanence is the world and conditioned phenomena are the path, and it serves as the path for the world, it is called the 'worldly path.
That is, it is the path of the world, which is an *upapada* (dependent) compound. He further says that although the term "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) does not [apply] in its literal sense...

To say that [the unconditioned] "falls within the three periods of time" means that because its essence (tattva) has the same meaning as the conditioned, although the word is so, the name "unconditioned" itself falls within the three periods of time.
Yet, because its essence does not undergo transition or flux, it differs from the former; thus, it is not coextensive with the name.
Herein, based on the expressive name and the expressed meaning both proceeding through the three periods of time, this explains the basis of speech (vāk-āśraya) in relation to the name.
Regarding the statement that "nirvana is the departure [from existence] because speech serves as its basis," the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

Because one is submerged in the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) within the various realms of existence (*gati*), nirvana is called "departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*) because it is the eternal relinquishing [of those realms]. This signifies the cessation of the constant flow and revolution of the realms of existence.

Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are like rafts, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) should likewise be abandoned; thus, one arrives at [the state where] all conditioned phenomena are relinquished.
Regarding the statement that "at the time of *nirvāṇa*, all things can be abandoned; therefore, 'thing' (*vastu*) has the meaning of 'cause' (*hetu*)," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:

"A 'thing' refers to that which is the basis (*āśraya*) or that in which something dwells; this is precisely the meaning of 'cause. This is because an effect depends upon a cause and arises from a cause, just as a child depends on its mother.

Alternatively, an effect may dwell within a cause and thereby obscure it, just as a person dwelling on a bed obscures the bed. Thus, the cause is said to be 'dependent' because it is eclipsed by its effect."

The Sautrāntika masters maintain that this entity exists in the sense that conditioned phenomena possess an essence while unconditioned phenomena lack an essence; thus, they know that "existent things" (bhāva) exclusively encompass the conditioned.
Since the intention of the author of the treatise is to clarify the Sautrāntika position, the treatise states: "The Vaibhāṣika masters transmit the tradition as follows."

Regarding the statement that "the aggregates belong to grasping," the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* says: "The aggregates are driven by afflictions; for example, due to greed or hatred, there arise acts such as killing.
Regarding the statement that "afflictions are called 'contention' (*raṇa*)," if one discusses contention in general, there are three types: first, the contention of afflictions;

second, the contention of speech, so called because contention arises from verbal discourse; and third, the contention of the aggregates, which refers to the two contentions of death and birth—that is, the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, what is currently referred to as "contentious" (*saraṇa*) refers to the contention of afflictions (*kleśa*), which harms both oneself and others.

As the Sūtra says: "A single moment of evil can open five gates of unwholesomeness: first, the destruction of wholesome qualities; second, the production of evil from evil; third, being censured by the Noble Ones;
fourth, the retrogression from the fruits of the Path; and fifth, falling into hell after death. Because it contradicts the mind of the Noble Ones, it is collectively termed [contention].
That which is suffering refers to the fact that the flow of contaminated results and the principle of impermanence are all suffering;
ordinary beings do not perceive this, whereas noble ones do. Therefore, it is said only that it contradicts the mind of the noble ones, as the following verse states:

"Just as when a single eyelash is placed on the palm of the hand, a person does not perceive it, yet if it is placed upon the pupil of the eye, it causes injury and discomfort—the fool is like the hand."

The hand does not perceive the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), yet for one with the wisdom of the eye of insight, it gives rise to extreme revulsion and fear when encountering the ultimate [truth].

Furthermore, the *Nyāya* states: "The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*) are the locus of all oppressions; because their intrinsic nature is coarse and unstable, they are termed 'suffering' (*duḥkha*).

This refers to the suffering of the aggregates themselves, rather than the suffering of painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*). Now, there are three types of suffering: first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), which is exclusively...

The suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) pertains to the desire realm; the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) pervades the form realm; and the suffering of conditioned formations pervades all three realms.

Thus, when the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three realms are collectively termed "suffering," it is said with reference to the suffering of conditioned formations, and not in the sense of the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).

Regarding the four types of destruction: first, "destruction by the characteristics" means that conditioned phenomena are subject to transformation by arising, abiding, and ceasing. Second, "destruction by antidotes" refers to contaminated phenomena.

Because it is that which is to be countered by the path of remedy (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), the *Nyāya* states: "As the Blessed One said, because its nature is subject to destruction, it is called 'the world' (*loka*).

If this were so, the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) would also be the world; but it is not. It is only that which is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and possesses both [characteristics] that is called the world.
Since the Truth of the Path lacks one of these [characteristics], it is not the world, for being untainted (*anāsrava*), it has no faults to be countered. Furthermore, regarding the four...

Regarding "distinguishing by way of disintegration" (*bhaṅga-viveka*), it excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Regarding "distinguishing by way of the antidote" (*pratipakṣa-viveka*), it excludes the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

As for the statement that they are also called "bases of views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), the treatise says: "Because views abide within them and increase as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Regarding the term "the three existences" (*trabhava*), this is a synonym for the three realms (*traidhātuka*).

Regarding the term "causes of the three existences," this refers to the contaminated aggregates (*sāsravaskandha*) acting as the cause for the three existences. Regarding the term "bases of the three existences," this refers to...

The contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*) serve as the basis for the three conditioned states (*saṃskṛta*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), which includes those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*):

according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, this "and so forth" refers outwardly to include the defiled; however, if one follows this treatise’s own internal logic, it would simply include the aforementioned categories.
The phrase "such categories as these" is a summary.
These eleven types are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Whereas the Sautrāntikas do not establish unmanifest form (*avijñapti*),

the Vijñānavādins do not establish derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), and the Mahāyāna establishes further forms within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), this school establishes the name "aggregate of form" based solely upon the measure of these eleven types of form.

Regarding the verse’s statement that "that consciousness relies on pure matter" (*rūpa-prasāda*), the ancient commentary explains: If one were to say merely that "that consciousness relies on matter" (*rūpa*) without specifying "pure," then the four objects that support the sense organs would also be able to serve as its basis;
furthermore, since these objects are also included within the category of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), they should then be designated as "eye" and so forth.

Conversely, if one were to say merely that "that consciousness is pure matter" without specifying "reliance," then clear ponds and bright mirrors would also be pure matter and should thus be designated as the "eye."

If one were to speak only of those consciousnesses without mentioning the pure matter that serves as their basis, then the five consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and so forth—would have to be named after the eye and so on themselves.

If they are stated fully, including the pure matter upon which they depend, then there is no fault in the terminology. The term "the former" refers to the five sense faculties mentioned in the preceding opening section;
that is to say, the pure matter which is the support for that eye-consciousness is called the eye-faculty, and the same applies to the ear and the others.
The same applies here; the treatise contains two explanations, and this chapter cites only the second, the definitive one. However, the first explanation states:
"That [view] holds that the consciousnesses of the five objects—form and so forth—are the consciousnesses of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch;

the five kinds of pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) which serve as the supports for those consciousnesses should be understood, respectively, as the five faculties, beginning with the eye. The Master [Vasubandhu] critiques and adopts [the second view].

Since the sense-faculties and consciousnesses constitute the primary [subject], the treatise states: "In this way, it accords with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. As that treatise explains: 'What is the eye-faculty?
It has as its nature the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) which is the support of visual consciousness. Thus it is explained at length. The correct principle is likewise.

Regarding the five kinds of translucent matter, the treatise states: "As the Blessed One said: 'O Bhikṣus, you should know that the eye is an internal base (*ādhyātmikam āyatanaṃ*), consisting of the four great elements (*mahābhūtāni*...'"
The nature of the derived translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) is as explained at length in the *Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa*:

"If that were so, since there would be no distinction in the characteristics of the translucent matter, the five [sense-faculties] would not be established. This is not the case, because their functional capacities (*śakti*) are distinct. How is this known?

Because they are the fixed supports for the consciousnesses of their respective non-common objects (*asādhāraṇaviṣaya*), and so forth, as explained at length. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the five faculties consist of translucent matter.
Regarding their essential natures, the Mahāsāṃghika school holds that the body is composed of a mass of flesh, while the Vijñānakāya school holds that it is composed of the four great elements.

In the verse explaining the five sense objects, it is stated that taste precedes fragrance. An ancient commentary notes that all treatises composed in India follow the rules of *śabda-vidyā* (grammar):

if fragrance were placed before taste, it would constitute a grammatical fault (*śabda-doṣa*), whereas placing taste before fragrance does not violate the rules of grammar. Now, following this [principle]...

The original translation places "taste" first and "odor" last; according to correct reasoning, one who speaks out of sequence does so to demonstrate that the arising of those faculties, objects, and consciousnesses is not fixed.
Regarding the statement that "matter is of two kinds," there are generally two types:
"color" (*varṇa*), which refers to appearance, and "shape" (*saṃsthāna*), which refers to dimension. As for the twelve types of color, they are blue, yellow, red, and white.
The fourth [category] consists of the four fundamental colors; the eight [remaining categories], such as shadow and light, are their fourfold distinctions. Thus, the treatise states:
"There are four primary colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—and all other manifest colors are distinctions of these four. The ancient masters held that light is subsumed under yellow;
however, when the sun first rises, it appears red because it is reflected by other objects, or else light is subsumed under red, or else light is a color that is both yellow and red.
Dark blue is subsumed under darkness; light blue, yellow, red, and white are all subsumed under illumination because they all possess luminosity.

Clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are all subsumed under the colors blue, yellow, red, and white. The moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, and various flames are termed "illumination"; by analogy, one should know that gems, lightning, and so forth are also subsumed under illumination.

Regarding what is called "shadow" among these, where other colors can be seen, it refers to... [the area] wherein... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist Abhidharma treatise concerning the classification of colors and light. The final sentence is incomplete, but the translation reflects the extant portion.)

Within the shadow that obstructs light, other objects can still be seen; this is what is called "remaining color" (*avaśeṣa-rūpa*), and it does not mean that the shadow itself is called "remaining color.

To say that the opposite of this is "darkness" (*andhakāra*) likewise means that within the shadow, other objects cannot be seen; this is called "darkness," and it does not mean that the non-perception of the shadow itself is darkness.

This refers to the fact that among the colors within the obstruction of light, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness: that which is light is called "shadow," and that which is heavy is called [darkness].

The preceding section on darkness has been explained according to the chapters; those points not yet explained shall now be briefly distinguished. First, regarding visible color (*varṇa*): that which is the vapor of dragons is called "cloud" (*megha*);
that which arises from fire is called "smoke" (*dhūma*); that which has not yet dispersed is called "dust" (*rajas*); and the rising vapors of earth and water are termed "mist" (*nīhāra*).

The four fundamental colors—blue, yellow, and so forth—are easily understood. There are also variations such as azure, crimson, purple, and green, all of which differ only in degree of lightness or depth. Furthermore...
They are not established as distinct [categories]: light blue is called "azure" (*bì*), thin red is called "scarlet" (*hóng*), and the combination of blue and yellow is called "green" (*lù*).

Red and black combined are "purple. Regarding secondary forms (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*): that which is level and even on its surface is called "regular color" (*samyak-varṇa*); that which is uneven on its surface is called "irregular color" (*asamyak-varṇa*). That which grows predominantly on one side is called "long color" (*dīrgha-varṇa*);
that which grows sparsely on one side is called "short color" (*hrasva-varṇa*); and that which is equal on all four sides is [called "square"].
That which is called "square color" arises pervasively in all directions; that which is called "round color" is convex in the center;
what is pressed down and concave is called "low"; and what is said to arise on "one side" refers to one of the six faces.
In reality, it arises on two of the six faces, but because this might be difficult to understand, it is said to be on "one side," as in the case of bamboo shoots and the like.
On one hand, the "small" is the opposite of the aforementioned [large], which can be understood; "long" corresponds to "fine" (sūkṣma), while "short" corresponds to "coarse" (audārika).

Therefore, among the eight kinds of matter, coarse and fine are not established as distinct categories. These forms such as length, however, consist of two types: first, those produced by external conditions, such as gold or stone, which attain length, shortness, and so forth through the agency of craftsmen and the like;
second, those whose intrinsic nature (dharmatā) differs, such as salt, which, through its inherent property, transforms into water when dissolved.
Later, when returning to their original state (the commentary explains that north of [Ding]yánfāng there are corners), the *guā* is naturally long and the *gǔlóu* is naturally short;
the walnut is high and low, the cherry is naturally round, and the bean pod is naturally flat—such distinctions among species are like a needle:
though it is short in comparison to the *gǔlóu*, it is long in color; though the *gǔlóu* is long in comparison to dates and the like, it is [short].

Regarding the "short color" (and so forth), the treatise further states that some other masters claim that the "single manifest color of space" is merely a portion of the matter of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*),
subsumed under light and darkness, and possesses no separate intrinsic nature.
This view of the dissenting masters asserts that the single manifest color of space is not light or darkness, but is established as a distinct color.

21. Furthermore, among the twenty types of matter (*rūpa*), each has its own "reflected image-matter" (*pratibimba-rūpa*), which may be included within the primary [matter] or not included within the primary.
Regarding the "eight kinds of sound," the *Abhidharmāmṛta* and the *Vibhāṣā* (in its non-canonical interpretation) state that there are eight kinds of sound;
the *Nyāyānusāra* newly asserts that this treatise [the *Abhidharmakośa*] differs from both [the aforementioned works]. However, according to this treatise, there are eight [kinds of sound].

Regarding the "various sounds," the treatise states: there are four types based on the distinction between those caused by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*), and those designated as sentient (*sattva-nāman*) or non-sentient (*asattva-nāman*).

Each of these four is further divided into the pleasant (*manojña*) and the unpleasant (*amanojña*), resulting in eight types. (The commentary explains: examining this passage from the treatise, [the first] appropriated, [the second] non-appropriated, [the third] sentient designation, and [the fourth] non-sentient designation are each further paired with the pleasant and the unpleasant; thus, eight kinds are formed. It does not [pair them with] existence...)

Sentient and insentient are paired with the appropriated (*upātta*) and the non-appropriated (*anupātta*), and when combined, these constitute eight categories. Thus, the *Xin* (New) commentary states: "Among sounds caused by appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*), there are those called 'sentient' and those called 'non-sentient'; among sounds caused by non-appropriated primary elements, they are exclusively called 'insentient'.

However, within this present treatise, even among non-appropriated sounds, those called "sentient" are also included, such as the speech of a magically created person (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*). The *Xin* commentary further states: "This sound has neither karma nor possession (*prāpti*); like a sound detached from vocal action (*vākkarman*), it is not designated as 'karma'.

Since one understands these distinctions, one should also interpret [the text] according to this treatise. Regarding the phrase "caused by primary elements," it means that all sounds have the four great elements as their cause.
Because they are produced by striking, they are called "sentient beings. Those called "agreeable sounds" refer to the production of pleasant sounds, such as songs and praises.
Those called "disagreeable" refer to speech that produces harsh sounds, such as insults and abuse. The third refers to hands and so forth producing pleasant sounds.
The fourth refers to hands and so forth producing harsh sounds. The fifth refers to emanated persons (*nirmāṇapuruṣa*) producing virtuous sounds. The sixth refers to [emanated] beings...
Seventh, humans produce unpleasant sounds; eighth, non-sentient things produce pleasant sounds, such as wind through flutes and the like;

ninth, non-sentient things produce unpleasant sounds, such as wind through forests and the like. These are described merely in terms of being agreeable or disagreeable, without mentioning neutral sounds;
for apart from what is agreeable, all else is disagreeable, and thus they encompass all sounds, since even those that are neutral are [included] because they do not conform to one's wishes.
Because this is disagreeable, by analogy one should also say that there are agreeable and disagreeable forms (*rūpa*) and so forth;
however, because the nature of sound is difficult to discern, its distinctions are explained in terms of causes and so on, whereas form is easy to discern and thus is not mentioned here.
As for the phrase "clapping hands and so forth," it explains the cause of appropriation (*upātta*), since it refers to the sounds produced by the hands and other such parts. However, this...

The hand is possessed by the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which take it as their support; thus, it is called "appropriated" (*sopādāna*) when experiencing sensations such as pain or itching.

Similarly, sounds produced by speech and so forth are all appropriated. The *Śāstra* states that some say (referring to the masters of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*) that sound can have both appropriated and non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its cause, such as the sound produced by the contact of a hand and a drum. This is what was previously referred to as "sound caused by both."

The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "If it is not admitted that a single atom of visible form (*varṇa-paramāṇu*) is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), then the same should apply to sound.
Regarding the six types of taste, the *Nyāyabindu* states: "Taste refers to that which is consumed; it has the sense of being palatable. The *Saṃgrahaṇī* explains [it as] being mixed.
Taste and the others are not separate from these six; however, because the various distinctions among these phenomena differ manifoldly, they cannot be treated by a single rule.
Thus, the five sense objects are unequal in their differentiation: visible form has twenty types, sound eight, taste six, odor four, and the tangible eleven.
Regarding "odor," that which is fragrant is called *gandha*; as the *Pañcavastuka-śāstra* states: "That which is pleasing is designated as [fragrant]."

That which is a pleasant fragrance but disagreeable to the mind is called an "unpleasant fragrance. Regarding the terms "equal" (*sama*) and "unequal" (*viṣama*), there are two explanations in the *Nyāya* (Principles):

first, it is said that an increase [in intensity] is called "equal," while a decrease is called "unequal"; second, it is said that what is weak is called "unequal," while what is intense is called "equal.
Furthermore, the treatise states: "In the *Mūla-śāstra*, it is taught that there are three kinds of fragrance: pleasant fragrance, unpleasant fragrance, and equal fragrance."
Regarding "fragrance.

As for what is called "contact" (*sparśa*): although it was previously said that even when a sense faculty encounters its object, they do not actually touch but arise in immediate succession, the faculty is the basis of consciousness and is thus metaphorically said to be able to contact.

Contact itself is not the basis of consciousness; therefore, we do not say that contact is the agent of contact. It only contacts the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), and is thus designated as the "object of contact."

Furthermore, because "contact" (spraṣṭavya) is in extremely close proximity to the body-faculty (kāyendriya), it is designated as "contact. Although the two types of odor and taste also reach their respective faculties, they are not like that [proximity] regarding their objects, and thus are not called "contact.
As for the term "weighable" (guru), it means that which can be pulled by a scale.
That which is the opposite of this is "unweighable," including things that rise upward such as smoke and flames; all these are termed [unweighable].
The commentary on "cold, hunger, and thirst" consists of three parts: first, explaining the names of the results; second, concluding by attributing them to their causes;

and third, citing examples to establish the proof. Regarding the statement that "cold, hunger, and thirst are what the mind desires": because the term "desire for food" is used to designate hunger and so forth, the names "cold, hunger, and thirst" refer to what the mind desires.
This means that it is frequently due to the power of contact within the body that these desires arise.
Heat possesses the power of contact that causes the desire to eat; cold possesses the power of contact that causes the desire to drink.
The "desire" produced is termed "cold," "hunger," and "thirst"; these are the results, while the contact that produces them is the cause.

Because the characteristics of the producing contact are obscured and difficult to perceive, one names the causal substance after its resulting fruit, thus calling it "cold," "hunger," and "thirst. Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "By this, within the body..."

There are distinctions among tactile objects (*spraṣṭavya*) that oppress the body, causing one to desire food and drink; these are the causes of hunger and thirst, and are thus termed "hunger and thirst," etc.
Now, regarding the term "tactile object" (*spraṣṭavya*): according to the underlying meaning, it should be understood as "tactile objects other than cold, hunger, and thirst.

When we speak of "cold, hunger, and thirst" here, this is a designation based on their effects. If one were to say that cold, hunger, and thirst are not tactile objects, then the term "tactile object" used here would be confused with its cause.
Regarding the statement that [the objects] are "perceived," there is a minor point of inversion in the meaning, though the principle remains consistent. Some explain it thus:
this essence of cold, hunger, and thirst is actually the *spraṣṭavya* (tangible object). Because there are tangibles such as hunger within the body, they cause one to desire food and drink;

thus, food and drink themselves are mental factors (*caitta*). Now, to explain hunger and so forth: when one says "hunger" refers to the desire for food, this is because the name of the effect is applied to the cause.
There is an interpretation that agrees with the *Vibhāṣā*: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world can produce the fruit of happiness. Here, "happiness" (*sukha*) refers to *nirvāṇa*;

because the cycle of rebirth within the three realms has completely ceased, it is called happiness. Because the appearance of the Buddhas in the world enables them to preach the Dharma and realize the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, this fruit serves as the cause of happiness;
thus, it is designated as "happiness" by way of its result. The following three phrases should be understood accordingly.
Knowing this is the fruit of the Path, it is called "pleasure," yet it is not identical to the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*). Question:

Since roughness and smoothness, heaviness and lightness each stand in mutual opposition, why is "warmth" (*uṣṇa*) not mentioned as the counterpart to "cold" (*śīta*)? Answer: Because warmth is of the nature of fire, it is not mentioned separately.

Question: If that is so, then cold should be subsumed under water; why then is it mentioned separately? Answer: Water has moisture as its intrinsic nature and thus cannot subsume cold. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There exists..."
Other masters say: because water and fire increase, there is smoothness; because earth and wind increase, there is roughness; because fire and wind increase, there is lightness;

because earth and water increase, there is heaviness; because water and wind increase, there is cold; and because wind increases, there is hunger—meaning that the striking and movement [of the body] cause food to be digested, which induces the sensation of hunger and gives rise to the desire for food.
Because fire increases, there is thirst—meaning that fire parches and oppresses [the body], causing drink to be digested, which induces thirst.

Contact gives rise to the desire for drink; furthermore, the *Nyāya* states that "dullness" (*mūḍha*) is not separate from the power of "smoothness" (*snigdha*), as it is subsumed within the natures of "roughness" (*khara*), "heaviness" (*guru*), and "weakness" (*manda*), which are included within "softness" (*mṛdu*) and "lightness" (*laghu*). Therefore, these eleven [qualities] exhaustively encompass all types of contact.

Regarding the statement that "wholesome and unwholesome [actions] both apply to the distracted and the non-distracted": this means that each of these two categories possesses its own *avijñapti* (non-informative action).
When viewed from its own perspective, it is "non-distracted"; when viewed in relation to others, it is termed "distracted.

Furthermore, this designation "distracted" is applied in terms of the mind, because it clarifies that *avijñapti* is present within all these various states of mind. As for the statement "there is no *avijñapti* of the neutral (*avyākṛta*)," this clarifies that a neutral mind is merely so named.
Distraction is not termed "non-distraction" because it lacks a non-informative (avijñapti) counterpart of the same class; therefore, a neutral mind is merely termed "distracted.

That neutral [minds] do not produce non-informative matter will be explained below. When it says "this other mind," it refers to the wholesome non-informative as "this," while the unwholesome and neutral are "other minds";
or, in contrast to the unwholesome non-informative, this [neutral] is "this."

Regarding the statement that wholesome and neutral [states] are "the remainder" of the mind, the term "mindless" (*acitta*) refers to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Question:
Why is the fruit of non-conception (*asaṃjñika-phala*) not mentioned? Answer: Because it lacks unmanifest form (*avijñapti*), it is not mentioned.

Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Although there are other states that are fruits of the mindless, because unmanifest matter does not flow forth [as a result] in those cases, the term 'mindless' is used."
The statement that "it does not include those" indicates that the phrase "with an undistracted mind" applies to both [cases] within the verse; the word "etc. (ādi) serves two functions:
first, it includes the undistracted mind, and second, it includes the state of being with a mind. The *Nyāyānusāra* criticizes this, saying: "Furthermore, to claim that the word 'etc.
extends to the state of being without a mind is useless, because it has already been included previously; the phrase 'distracted mind' and so forth has already subsumed it."
Regarding the phrase "the second and so forth" in the context of all other states possessing mind, what does it encompass? The Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) should reflect on this.

If he were to say that "the latter [states] and so forth" encompass the non-confused mind, while the preceding [state] is useless, this would not be correct; for there is no possibility for such inclusion. How could the latter and so forth encompass the non-confused mind?
The principle of exclusion (*pratiṣedha*) applies to cases where similarity arises; it does not apply to cases where there is no such arising. Thus, the principle is not established.

Furthermore, because there are other [cases], it is not a complete inclusion. Master An-hui (Sthiramati) provides this defense: "The master Saṃghabhadra did not grasp the intent of the Ācārya Vasubandhu and arbitrarily criticized him with the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*).
There are two pairs: first, the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) versus the non-distracted state; second, the distracted mind versus the non-mindful states of concentration (*samāhita*).

By 'distracted mind' and so forth, one includes the non-distracted scattered minds that are similar to themselves; by 'non-mindful' and so forth, one includes the non-mindful states of concentration."

Because the possession (*prāpti*) of the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is similar to itself, these statements apply to both locations; this reveals the skillful phrasing of the verse. Furthermore, it is objected:
"Moreover, since that which is produced by concentration does not flow on during the distracted or mindless states, it should not be considered non-informative (*avijñapti*). The defense states:

"The mention of 'four states' is said according to what is applicable; it does not mean that non-informative matter pervades all four states, just as [non-informative matter] is not present in all cases where concentration is absent."

In the state of manifest [action] (*vijñapti*) where there is a mind, one performs unwholesome non-manifest action (*avijñapti*); in states of mind that are either distracted or undistracted, one performs wholesome non-manifest action when it is scattered.

You assert that even in the state of no-mind (*acittaka*), it constitutes a distinct state; how then could non-manifest action associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) possibly be performed?
As for what is called "similarity of nature," the older tradition says this means it is similar to the manifest action and the mind, or that they are mutually similar in succession.

The *avijñapti* that resembles a new cloud is similar in its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and continues in a series; it is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome, but does not resemble informative action (*vijñapti*) or the mind (*citta*).
Regarding this "continuity," the *Nyāyānusāra* objects: "The first moment cannot be called a 'similar continuity';

otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the *avijñapti* of the first thought-moment is not included within the characteristics [of continuity] described by the *Abhidharmakośa* masters."
Jiūyún (救云) says that "continuity" (*saṃtati*) refers either to the former continuing to the latter, as in the case of the non-informative (*avijñapti*) of the first moment;

or to the latter continuing to the former, as in the case of the non-informative of subsequent moments; or to both the former and the latter being continuous, as in the case of the non-informative of intermediate moments. Therefore, both the first and the last are termed "continuous.

Furthermore, even if a particular non-informative exists for only a single moment, it is still called "continuous" because it belongs to the same category of continuity. This is what is meant by the term.
Since that which is pure or impure must necessarily rely on a strong manifestation (*vijñapti*) to be able to arise, it does not extend to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The ancient masters said this was "to exclude the other [view] that considers indeterminate non-manifestation. To clarify its nature as being exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*), the term "wholesome" excludes the indeterminate within the pure, while the term "unwholesome" excludes the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) within the impure.
The statement that "creating" (*kṛti*) has the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) is for the purpose of exclusion.

Buddhadeva and others say that "produced" (*kṛta*) has the meaning of "established" (*siddha*), and "derived" (*upādāya*) has the meaning of "conceptualized" (*prajñapti*); that is, because it is established by being derived, one conceptually designates it as "derived matter.

The phrase "it is said" (*ucyate*) indicates that this is the tenet of the master [Vasumitra]; "the Vaibhāṣika school says" indicates that this is the statement of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* according to correct reasoning.

The word "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates that these are the words of other masters which the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) does not accept. Although [the opponent] uses the term "matter-action" (*rūpa-karman*) up to the point where they are identical...

Regarding "informative action" (*vijñapti-karman*): although its substantial nature (*dravya-svabhāva*) is the same as that of [uninformative] matter, its functional activity (*kriyā-vṛtti*) is entirely different from that of the informative.

To explain the non-informative (*avijñapti*), one must first distinguish its informative aspect. "Informative" means manifesting to others so that they may know whether the internal mind is wholesome or unwholesome;

it is like the physical forms of joining palms, killing, binding, and so forth. Thus, the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* states: "It is like a fish submerged in a deep pool that manifests itself by stirring up waves."
Now, regarding the term "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*): it is called "unmanifest" because it lacks these characteristics.

As for the statement that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) pervade all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), this is because the nature of solidity and so forth exists within every aggregate of matter.

Regarding the two aspects of "greatness," these are explained in terms of the conventional (provisional) four great elements. As for their ability to give rise to various great functions, these refer to the internal four...

The elements (*dhātu*) are the basis for sentient beings because they can externally bring about their formation and destruction. Regarding their serving as the support for derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:

"Some say that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) exist below [the derived matter], acting as its causal support; this must be so for the supporting dharma. Others say they coexist in a state of intermingling;
the primary elements are on the outside and the derived matter is in the middle. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* asks: "For what reason..."

Regarding the term "great elements" (*mahābhūta*): why are they called "great"? Because when various derivative forms (*upādāyarūpa*) arise, these [elements] are able to produce their specific categories;
therefore, they are called "great. The Venerable One said: "Although space is great, its essence is not a seed (*bīja*), as it cannot produce [anything];

other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), though they can act as seeds, are not 'great' in essence, because their characteristics are not all-pervasive (*avyāpin*). Only these [four] possess both qualities."
Regarding the question of why the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are designated as only four, the Vaibhāṣika masters all state:
"If there were fewer, they would lack functional capacity; if there were more, they would be redundant. Therefore, there are only four. This is like the four legs of a bed or seat.

As for the statement that the earth element performs the function of supporting, it means that the earth can sustain objects by virtue of its hardness. Water can cohere objects by virtue of its moist nature.
Fire is able to bring things to maturity so that they do not decay. Regarding wind being able to cause growth, the *Śāstra* states:

"Growth means increasing in intensity (*upacaya*) or flowing and drawing forth (*preraṇa*). Increasing in intensity is like a seed producing a sprout; this refers to vertical [growth]. Flowing and drawing forth is like oil spreading upon water; this refers to horizontal [movement]. Because the activity of wind is somewhat subtle, it is explained separately. As for the statement that wind moves, the *Śāstra* says:
"By means of this, it can draw the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), causing them to arise in succession and reach other locations."
It is called "movement" because it is like the flickering of a lamp's light.
As for the question of how the various levels (*bhūmi*) and elements (*dhātu*) are distinguished:

this refers to contrasting the conventional (*prajñapti*) with the ultimate (*paramārtha*) to clarify the distinction between the conventional earth and so forth and the ultimate earth and so forth as elements. Regarding the phrase "indicating by means of color and shape": this refers to the world...

In the interim, one does not know that the four objective fields, such as earth and so forth, are collectively constituted, nor does one know that there are the four elements, such as solidity and so forth;

rather, one speaks of "earth" and so on based solely upon their manifest form (*saṃsthāna*). Question: Within the conventional designation of earth and so forth, since there are causes such as fragrance (*gandha*) and other qualities, why is it said that manifest form and color (*varṇa*) alone constitute its essence?

Answer: Although earth and so forth are composed of four objective fields, the world establishes the conventional characteristic of "earth" and so forth based upon the sense-field of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). Thus, [the essence] is established in relation to the visible form.
Just as when observing the four great elements, one observes only form (*rūpa*) and not odor and so forth, because form can be pointed out as being here or there even when separated from its objects;
whereas sound is not always present, as it is known only when three objects come together.

When the treatise does not state that "wind is itself an element," it is because in the world people also perceive motion as wind, and they also designate a black mass or similar forms as "wind" for this reason.
Regarding the wind [element], there are two masters who explain it as beginning with the eye faculty and ending with the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).

The previous explanation—that the eye faculty is the first and the unmanifest is the last—was an exposition of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) because, having finished explaining "form," it was necessary to identify the names of the forms of consciousness.
Therefore, the question now arises: "The commonality of the group (*nikāyasabhāga*) is impermanent" refers to the end of a single lifetime. Furthermore, regarding "transformation":

To demonstrate the destruction of subtle impermanence, it is said that "gross impermanence is new. Herein, transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is identical to destruction (*bhaṅga*), just as it is said that "transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*) are one.
Regarding the statement "touched by hands and so forth," a question is raised: since the five sense organs and four objects are not themselves tangible, how can they be called "destroyed"?
The answer is: although they are not touched by the hand, because they arise in a collection together with that which is touched, if [the object] were touched...
Because it perishes at the moment of contact; furthermore, the *Nyāya* states that it is called "changeable" (*vipariṇāma*) because it can be altered.

Regarding the phrase "in the section on the meaning of collection" (*saṃgraha-artha-varga*), this refers to what was previously explained: the Buddha collected the meanings of impermanence (*anitya*) into verses on impermanence, and so forth, up to the meanings of non-self (*anātman*).
Because they are likewise [collected], it is called the "section on the meaning of collection. This refers to the character "zhong" (or pronounced with the departing tone) at the end of the verse.

[The term is] pronounced with the level tone (*ping sheng*). If it were read with the departing tone (*qu sheng*), it would mean "as if an arrow struck the body"; if read with the level tone, it means "as if an arrow is within the body.
Most schools follow the departing tone, but the intent of this chapter follows the level tone (one should consult *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* 34 for a detailed explanation).

Regarding the statement that not even a single atom (*paramāṇu*) exists dwelling in isolation, there are two theories in the *Nyāyānusāra*: one theory agrees with this [position], while another says: "Furthermore..."

There are solitary atoms (*paramāṇu*) that are capable of transformation and resistance (*pratighāta*) yet do not give rise to consciousness, because the bases and objects of the five consciousnesses must necessarily be accumulated.

Just as it is established that although atoms lack spatial parts (*digbhāga*) and lack tactile contact (*sparśa*), they are nonetheless admitted to have the functions of being resistant (*sapratigha*), having an object (*sālambana*), and being obstructive (*savibandha*);
one should know that the meaning of "transformation and resistance" is likewise [applied here]. The phrase "and those of their kind" serves to preempt [objections].
It is difficult [to maintain that] the subtle state of non-arising is eternally unimpeded; nevertheless, because it belongs to that same category, it also receives the designation "form" (*rūpa*).

Just as when a tree perishes, its shadow necessarily perishes along with it, the *Śāstra* states: "This is the Master’s refutation of the *Abhidharma-nava* (New School). [The opponent replies: "This is the Master’s restatement of the *Vibhāṣā*’s refutation.
The *Nyāyānusāra* does not accept this refutation, claiming there is the fallacy of "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntika*), just as in the case of the cessation of a father, a craftsman, or a seed.
Because the teeth and other features of the palace of King Aśoka do not perish along with him, they demonstrate that those [unmanifest forms] themselves follow the mind.

This refutes the Master of the *Miśraka* (Saṃghabhadra) as cited in the commentary, which states that the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) relies directly upon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), meaning that it is acquired through the formation of the unmanifest by means of the primary elements;
therefore, it is a direct support. As for the five sense organs in relation to the five consciousnesses, they are merely auxiliary conditions and not [direct supports].

Because it is produced by [the primary elements] themselves, it is called a "distant condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). According to that school, since shadows and light each possess their own primary elements (*mahābhūta*), trees and jewels are likewise auxiliary conditions for their arising, acting as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This principle should be understood as analogous to the case of the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). Furthermore, it is said that the designation "form" (*rūpa*)—defined as being subject to transformation and resistance—is established as a general name based on a partial classification; one should not raise an objection on the grounds that there is no distinction [within the category]. Thus it is said: [as in the verse: "Just as the eye sees forms... and so forth. This is because the eye and its objects are both included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). Therefore, it is not the case that the eye does not see itself. Consequently, the objection that the eye cannot see itself is invalid. It is like the case where the eye sees the reflection of a face; although the face is not the object of sight, the reflection is seen. Similarly, although the eye is not the object of sight, it is nonetheless seen. Furthermore, the eye is not seen by another eye, yet it is seen by the mind (*manas*). Likewise, the eye is not seen by itself, yet it is seen by the wisdom of the Dharma (*dharmajñāna*). Moreover, the eye is not seen by the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), yet it is seen by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
