"Cow-sleeping" (*gośayanīya*) and "peacock-crying" (*mayūrakrośaka*): [the former] refers to a cow named "Earth-Sleeper" (*bhūmi-śayana*) and [the latter] to a peacock named "Earth-Crier" (*bhūmi-krośaka*);

it does not mean that they sleep at all times or cry constantly. Furthermore, as is commonly said in the world, one who eats quickly and walks quickly is called a "horse"; yet not everyone who eats and walks quickly possesses the qualities of a horse—it is only because they resemble it that they are so designated.
Regarding the statement that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis [for derived matter] do not necessarily perish along with it: this refers to the third *karmavācanā*.

When the polishing is finished, one acquires the unmanifest (avijñapti) that coexists with the form; because it arises once and continues to manifest, it is said not to perish along with [the physical action].
Although the unmanifest of the first moment also perishes simultaneously with the primary elements (mahābhūta), this statement is made in reference to the majority of subsequent moments.

Regarding the "basis of transformation and resistance": first, the five sense organs that serve as its support are themselves matter characterized by transformation and resistance; second, they perish immediately [after arising].

"Mind" (manas) refers to the fact that the arising of all consciousnesses depends upon the past mind. Furthermore, although the five consciousnesses rely upon the five sense organs, the mental consciousness does not rely upon them;
because the mental consciousness does not rely upon the five sense organs, it is not the case that the self-nature of the six consciousnesses is of a single kind of dharma.
Moreover, they are neither form nor non-form, and there is no unmanifest (avijñapti), because they do not rely upon form. Therefore, [they are not the same].
The same applies here.

Regarding the statement that "the ten bases and elements are admitted," this refers to the *Vibhāṣā*’s admission that the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) constitute the ten bases and elements.

However, the Sautrāntikas maintain that while the bases (*āyatana*) are conventional (*prajñapti*), the elements (*dhātu*) are real; they do not take the bases themselves as the substance of the elements, because there is a distinction between them. Therefore, it is said [that the two are not identical].
The term "permitted" (*kṣānti*) indicates that this is not a point of common consensus.

Regarding the explanation of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), there are two interpretations: the first concerns the experiencing of contact (*sparśa*), while the second concerns the experiencing of objects in accordance with the causes of contact. The four characters [of the phrase] all refer to the cause of contact;
they do not designate feeling itself as the object. This can be seen by examining the relevant chapters. Although contact and feeling arise simultaneously, [the former is the cause of the latter].
However, it must be admitted by those who maintain that cause and effect are simultaneous that feeling arises dependent upon contact, just as a shadow and its body exist at the same time.
As for the statement that they are "similar," this means that just as a painful contact gives rise to a painful feeling, the same applies to pleasant feelings and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "One experiences what is agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral, in accordance with the contact."

That which is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) has the meaning of "experiencing" (*upalabdhi*), which is to say, the capacity for enjoyment. Based on this, feeling is defined as the experiencing of contact (*sparśa*), rather than the experiencing of an object.
[The commentary] Chapter Two provides an explanation of this; it represents the traditional interpretation (*pūrvavyākhyāna*), which itself contains two expositions.

The first exposition is as stated in Chapter Two. Furthermore, it says: although all mental states (*citta*) share the same object of focus (*ālambana*), they differ in that they grasp the object through various factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth.

While it is established as a distinct category [of the aggregates], "feeling" (*vedanā*) has no separate name; although it is designated by a general term, it is immediately understood as a specific name, just like the "sense-field of form" (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.

Regarding its definition, the former interpretation is superior, for neither [the old nor the new] schools accept that it is merely the experience of an object. Rather, feeling is defined as the experience of contact (*sparśa*);

it is not called the experience of an object. As for the nature of feeling, there are two types: first, "appropriating feeling" (*upādāna-vedanā*), which refers to all mental factors (*caitta*) that grasp.

Apprehending objects of the preceding [moment] is all termed "clinging. Regarding the two types of self-nature feeling (*vedanā*), feeling is that which can experience what it encounters in accordance with its own nature.

To say that it "apprehends contact" (*sparśa*) as a portion of clinging is to say that it experiences contact; this is what is meant by "self-nature feeling. As for the phrase "conforming to the object of contact," it means that the object conforms to the contact;
that is, the object of the conforming contact. According to the former interpretation, the substance of the conforming contact is precisely that which conforms to this.
"Understanding" (*vijñapti*) refers to the object (*viṣaya*) that follows from contact (*sparśa*) and verbal expression (*abhilāpa*). To say "there are three kinds" is an enumeration;

briefly there are three, but in detail there are six, namely, because they are the sensations (*vedanā*) associated with the six consciousnesses. Regarding the phrase "images such as male and female," it means that this perception (*saṃjñā*) is able to grasp the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of various phenomena;
thus it is called "grasping images. For example, when perceiving blue, the perception is able to delineate its boundaries.
Since the entire realm is blue, the same applies to yellow and so forth; because other mental factors (*caitta*) cannot grasp these perceived images, they are not termed "perception" (*saṃjñā*).

While perception arises with a distinct function, it is designated by the name of another [aggregate], such as feeling (*vedanā*), based on its specific activity. This [aggregate] is also established as sixfold, just as was explained previously regarding feeling.

As for why the other four aggregates are specifically given the name "formations" (*saṃskāra*), it is because they are designated by the names of their respective specific functions, such as the "feeling aggregate" and so on.

Although this category is designated by its general name, "formations" (*saṃskāra*), it receives specific names just as the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and others do; therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"Although the five aggregates are formations, one [of them] receives the specific name 'formation'."

Next, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is explained. Question: Why are the three aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) explained collectively, while the aggregate of consciousness is explained separately?

Answer: There are three distinctions among phenomena: first, matter (*rūpa*); second, mind (*citta*); and third, mental factors (*caitta*). Because matter and mind are distinct categories, matter is explained separately.

Within the category of mind and mental factors, the three—feeling, perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—are all mental factors and are therefore explained together. Consciousness, however, is the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) and is therefore explained separately once again.

Regarding the statement that they "individually cognize": this means that because the six [consciousnesses] cognize their respective objects differently, they are called "individual. Question: Since the five consciousnesses cognize non-common objects, they can be said to be "individual";
however, since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of universally perceiving all objects, how can it also be called "individual"?

Answer: Because the five consciousnesses operate in relation to their own specific objects, they are termed "individual"; furthermore, because the mental consciousness operates in relation to distinct phenomena (*dharma*), it is also termed "individual. Moreover—

The *Śāstra* says: "Because each [consciousness] individually discriminates its respective objects and grasps the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of those objects, it is called 'vijñāna' (cognition).

The commentary explains that there are two meanings of "object" (*viṣaya*): first, the general characteristic, such as form, sound, and so forth; second, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), such as the agreeable or disagreeable.

Because it grasps the image-like aspect of its own object in a general way, without specifically grasping the image for the purpose of confirming it and so on, it is called "general" (*sāmānya*); this does not mean it is a universal (*samudāya*).
Within the particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one grasps the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). The *Nyāyabindu* states:

"One grasps only 'blue' and so forth, but not 'it is blue' and so forth" (the phrase "not 'it is blue' and so forth" serves to exclude *adhimukti*, as it means "it is not non-blue" and the like); nor does it grasp what is agreeable or disagreeable (this excludes the objects grasped by touch and feeling);

nor does it grasp [them] as male or female, or as a person or a tree-stump (these serve to exclude the mind and mental factors as appropriate). Just as that visual consciousness, with respect to its own object, grasps only the general [characteristic].

The characteristics of the other consciousnesses should be understood accordingly. To say that the six consciousnesses "transform and pass away" (pariṇāma) to become the manas means that the present consciousness and its support for the subsequent consciousness are designated as the manas;
"manas" has the meaning of "that upon which something depends. "Transformation" (pariṇāma) means "passing away," or it may be interpreted as "changing."
Regarding the statement that it is "the mind-element" (*manodhātu*), the treatise says: "Just as this son is called the father of another, and just as this fruit is called the seed of another;

therefore, one knows that while the substance is one, the names differ according to the perspective. The old [commentaries] say: "This is stated based on its manifest function when it exists in the past.

However, the substance actually pervades all three time periods. From the side of being produced by others, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); from the side of producing others, it is called "mind" (*manas*). The analogy is as stated above.

Furthermore, it is said that because the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is manifested through its functional activity, the mental element (*manodhātu*) does not exist in the future;

yet because it exists according to its substantial essence (*dravya*), the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) all pertain to the three periods of time. Furthermore, it is asked: "In a single present moment, the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously.
Since the faculties and consciousnesses are analytically distinguished, there can be at most thirteen [elements]; how then can there be eighteen? The answer is: this is based on the manifest [state].
If one considers a continuum of multiple thoughts or multiple persons in a single moment of the present, one speaks of eighteen [mental factors];
however, if based on a single person in a single moment, the maximum is thirteen, while the minimum is indeterminate.

Regarding the statement that the six consciousnesses and the mind (*manas*) mutually include one another: if the six consciousnesses are subsumed within the mind, there would then be only twelve [bases];
if the mind-element (*manodhātu*) were divided into the six consciousnesses, then the mind would simply be subsumed within the six consciousnesses and there would be no separate entity for the mind.
In that case, how could there be eighteen elements instead of seventeen? To establish this basis, the *Śāstra* states: "If that were so..."

It might be argued that the final mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) should not be the mind-element (*manodhātu*), because no subsequent consciousness arises immediately after its cessation, and thus it would not qualify as a mind-element.
This is not so; for it has already established itself in the nature of the mind, and the subsequent consciousness simply does not arise due to the absence of other necessary conditions.
Regarding the question of why each of the three categories (skandhas, āyatanas, dhātus) cites only one representative when these three collectively exhaust all phenomena:

here, in every case, citing a small portion serves to encompass the many. For instance, the name "form aggregate" (*rūpaskandha*) is a general term; thus, if one cites the form aggregate, it encompasses all forms without exception.

However, if one were to cite the "form base" (*rūpāyatana*) or the "form element" (*rūpadhātu*), they would each encompass only one part, and thus would not fully encompass all that is form. Therefore, with respect to the phenomena of form...

Although the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is cited because it subsumes the seven [bases] within the mind-base (*manāyatana*), and although the mind-base is cited because it exhaustively subsumes all states of mind, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) likewise universally subsumes all minds.
Nevertheless, since the aggregate of form has already been treated under the category of form, and one is now treating the category of mind, only the mind-base is cited here.

Furthermore, although the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) are identical in their breadth and narrowness, the dharma-element is cited here because one intends to comprehensively encompass all three categories (*skandha*, *āyatana*, *dhātu*).

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*) are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), this refers specifically to the truths of suffering and origin as they pertain to the sense bases such as the eye;
it does not mean that all instances of suffering and origin are subsumed under the aggregate of form, because suffering and origin pervade all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena.

Moreover, regarding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*)—the word "etc. here including the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)—although the path does indeed include form-factors (*rūpa-dharma*), since the present treatise concerns the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), it is likewise not included therein. Furthermore...
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "When all phenomena include their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is not like grasping the index finger with the hand or pinching a garment;
rather, each phenomenon maintains its own essence so that it does not disintegrate, and for this reason it is called 'inclusion' (*saṃgraha*).

Furthermore, here 'inclusion' is spoken of in the sense of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as including only one's own intrinsic nature. However, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), it also includes other phenomena, such as the four means of attraction (*catuḥ-saṃgraha-vastu*)."
Regarding the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*): these are generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
By means of these four, one attracts and gathers the assembly so that they do not disperse.
As for the statement that "the body is not majestic," the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: for what reason do the eyes, ears, and nostrils each have two locations?
Question: Are the tongue and body faculties each singular? Answer: The various material sense-faculties exist as ornaments for the body.
If there were two tongues, it would be a matter of vulgarity, and the world would mock it, saying: "How can this person have two tongues? It is like a poisonous snake.

If there were two bodies, it would be like two fingers placed side by side. The second [position] is the correct interpretation: that [a second faculty] serves to produce consciousness with clarity. If that were so, [regarding] the tongue...

Why does the body not require two? The answer is twofold: first, because the tongue and the body are large in form and sufficient for the function of generating consciousness, they do not require two;
second, the *Nyāyānusāra* also states that when one observes in the world that a certain function is superior and complete, it is described as "excellent" (*praśasta*).
If any of the faculties, such as the eye, were missing even one part, the functions of seeing, hearing, or smelling would all be unclear; if both parts are present, these functions are clear.

Regarding the statement that "if one wishes for consciousness to arise with clarity, it is sufficient merely to have the great [elements]; what need is there for two locations?"—according to the correct interpretation, this is said:
"The distinctions in these full causes and conditions are such that, depending on whether these causes and conditions are obstructed or unobstructed, [consciousness] arises.
This is just like the various arrangements and types of the body-faculty, such as the locations of the head, crown, belly, back, hands, and feet."
One should not harbor doubts or difficulties regarding this.

To say that the meaning of "collection" (*skandha*) is "aggregate" (*piṇḍārtha*): in Sanskrit it is *skandha* (translated into Chinese as *yùn*, "aggregate"), while the old translations called it *yīn* ("cover").
If one were to claim that *yīn* is the original Sanskrit term, the Sanskrit text should have read *prāvaraṇa*. Recently, various masters have vied with one another to provide divergent explanations.

Some claim that the term *skandha* refers to a collection (*caya*) of discourse; this interpretation is incorrect, for medical treatises speak of "drinking" (*pāna*) and do not use the term *skandha*.
Within the treatise, there are two further explanations: first, that *skandha* has the meaning of being able to bear the heavy burden of the fruit (*phala*), which is the sense of *skandha*;
for this reason, the world speaks of the shoulder as a *skandha*, because it is a place where things are gathered. Others say that the meaning of being divisible (*prakaraṇa*) is *skandha*.
For this reason, there is a worldly saying: "If you return my three aggregates, I shall give them back to you" (this is not the correct principle).
Regarding the phrases "whether past or future," etc., this is intended to refute the assertions of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Specifically, it refers to those who lived during the Buddha’s lifetime, such as the renunciant non-Buddhist named Daṇḍapāṇi, who denied the existence of the past and the future. To counter their views, the Blessed One said: "Whatever form... [and so forth].

Whether past or future, and so forth as explained at length—to say that "manifestation" (*vijñapti*) is briefly summarized into a collection means this is a brief designation (*nāman*), not that its substance (*svabhāva*) is condensed.
This is because the matter (*rūpa*) of the three time periods cannot be condensed into a single collection; rather, it is simply designated by the general term "one collection.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Although the substances of past and future matter cannot be condensed into a collection, they are [nevertheless] briefly [designated as such]."

It should be understood that the same applies to the collection [of factors] from name up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "They are also called 'aggregates' (*skandha*) because they are concise in name, not because they are concise in substance.
If this were so, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) would also have to be called aggregates, since all unconditioned phenomena can be concisely gathered together.

The explanation says: Because conditioned phenomena possess functional activity, they have the sense of being "concisely gathered"; although their substance may at times be such that it cannot be concisely gathered, [they are still so called].

Briefly summarizing their names, one establishes the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth. Since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) lack functional activity, they do not possess the sense of being "summarized";

although one may briefly summarize their names, they cannot be established as "aggregates" (*skandha*). That which has already ceased after being impermanent is called "past," because that which is currently ceasing is the present;
thus, by saying "already ceased," it is distinguished from cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-deliberative cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Because it has been extinguished, it is further called "impermanent. Having already been extinguished, that which is called one's own body is termed "internal.
That which is accomplished within one's own body is called internal; that which is not accomplished, as well as the bodies of others and insentient things, are all collectively termed "external.

Regarding the statement that "the wholesome and the indeterminate are called non-defiled, while the unwholesome is called defiled," this statement contains an error, because the indeterminate includes the defiled; therefore, it should be stated as follows:
Wholesome and non-obscured [phenomena] are called "non-defiled," while unwholesome and obscured phenomena are called "defiled.

According to the *Saṃgītiparyāya-pāda-śāstra*, with respect to unwholesome, obscured, and contaminated wholesome form, as well as uncontaminated wholesome form, they are designated as "coarse" in relation to what precedes them, being inferior, and "subtle" in relation to what follows them, being superior.
Thus, the four aggregates associated with the five consciousnesses are termed "coarse" because their bases—the five sense faculties—are coarse.
The four aggregates that depend [upon the form aggregate] are likewise coarse; the sixth [aggregate, consciousness], may be inferred accordingly.

Regarding the coarse and subtle nature of the nine stages, within each individual stage—whether viewed in comparison to those above or below—it is possible for both coarse and subtle aspects to exist. However, the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) is exclusively coarse, while the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is exclusively subtle;

the seven intermediate stages possess both coarse and subtle aspects. As for the term "place" (sthāna), it is called *āyatana* in Sanskrit (translated into Chinese as "place"); it was formerly translated as "entrance" (*rù*).
This is also not the case. If one says "entering" (*praveśa*), the Sanskrit original should have been *praveśa*;

furthermore, there are older translations where it is rendered as "station" (*sthāna*), such as in "the station of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and "the forest hermitage station" (*āraṇyaka-sthāna*), which are identical to the current usage.

Regarding the sense of being the "place where mind and mental factors arise and grow," this is the meaning of the term based on its etymological derivation (*nirukti*). If, however, one insists on using the term "entering," [it would be as follows].

It has only the meaning of cessation and disappearance, and no meaning of arising. Regarding the term *dhātu* (translated as "element" or *jie* in Chinese): the Sanskrit is *dhātu*, which in the Tang language means "element.

Some translations render it as "holder" (*dharana*), but this relies on only one specific sense and does not exhaust the full meaning. There are two interpretations of this: first, an interpretation based on the cause; second, an interpretation based on differentiation.
Regarding the phrase "the continuity of a single dharma": this is a general designation. A single body is called "one dharma," but it is not [a single] dharma-entity.
This refers to one portion among the eighteen [dhātus], as it corresponds to the preceding metaphor of "one mountain. Furthermore, the ancient commentary explains:
"One body" refers to the body of a single sentient being; "one continuity" refers to the continuity of a single lifetime. It further states: "One body" means the body of a single lifetime;
"one continuity" means the continuity of a single sentient being (since "continuity" is a synonym for "body," we know this is a collective reference).
Regarding the statement that [the *dhātu*] is the basis for the arising of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), the *Nyāyānusāra* raises an objection:

"If that were so, the meanings of 'base' (*āyatana*) and 'element' (*dhātu*) would become confused, as both are the basis for the arising of mind and mental factors. Consequently, it provides a distinct explanation of the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*):

just as ore, gold, rice, and yellow [pigment] are called "lineages" because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) differ when compared with one another, so too are the eyes and other [faculties] [distinguished].

They are called "lineages" (*gotra*) because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) differ when compared to one another. If that were so, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) would have no distinct nature when compared to the six consciousnesses, and thus it should not be a separate element.
This objection is not valid, because the essential natures of the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*) are different.

Furthermore, some say it is because there is a difference in the timing of their establishment; others say it is because the six [consciousnesses] are preceded by the mind, whereas the mind is not preceded by the six.

Knowing that there are differences, one should follow the correct principle (*nyāya*) and adopt the latter interpretation of this treatise. Regarding the statement that "all three categories (*skandha*, *āyatana*, and *dhātu*) are substantially real," and specifically that the aggregates (*skandha*) are real:

although an aggregate is a collection, even a single atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses the characteristic of an aggregate because it is capable of being accumulated; therefore, the aggregates are also real. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"Furthermore, a single atom is subsumed within the three time periods and so forth; when analyzed by wisdom, it is briefly reduced to a single mass."
Although the aggregates (*skandha*) are indeed collections, their meaning as real entities is established; other phenomena are likewise so. Therefore, the aggregates are not merely nominal.

Furthermore, since the term "aggregate" is applied to each individual phenomenon—for instance, it is said that "simultaneously arising feeling is called the aggregate of feeling" and "perception is called the aggregate of perception"—the Sautrāntikas and the Master [Vasubandhu] claim that the aggregates are nominal because "aggregate" has the sense of a collection. Consequently, the treatise refutes this, saying: "If..."

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'collection' (*caya*) is the meaning of 'aggregate' (*skandha*"): the aggregates must be provisional (*prajñapti*), because they are established by the accumulation of many real entities, just like a collection or like a self.

(The commentary explains: This master of the treatise establishes an inference (*sādhana*) to refute the Sarvāstivāda position on reality: "The five aggregates, such as form, are necessarily provisional" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because they are established by many real entities" is the reason (*hetu*);

"like a collection or a self" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). A "collection" refers to a gathering of grain and the like; although it is accomplished by many real entities, the collection itself is provisional. A "self" refers to the provisional self consisting of the five aggregates. Furthermore, the treatise states: "As the Sūtra says, all this is summarized as..."
Because a collection (*rāśi*) is designated as a "skandha" (*skandha*), the skandhas are certainly nominal (*prajñapti*). According to the Sautrāntikas, the bases (*āyatana*) are also nominal;

this is because "basis" has the sense of being that which produces, and since the sense-faculties and their objects must be accumulated (*saṃcita*) before they can produce [consciousness], they too exist nominally.

The Master [Vasubandhu] accepts that the bases are real, because within each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) within a mass of many [atoms], there exists a cause [for consciousness]. Otherwise, [if atoms were not real,] the sense-faculties and objects...

If [the sense bases] were to co-arise with consciousness and so forth through mutual assistance, they would not be distinct locations; thus, there would be no distinction between the twelve *āyatanas*.

Furthermore, the nature of their essence (*dharmatā*) and their status as the basis for arising are identical, and it is accepted that these are real because each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses a real nature.

Based on what has been stated above, the Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) maintains that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are provisional (*prajñapti*), which contradicts the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s position that the bases (*āyatanas*) are real. This differs from the Sautrāntika school’s view.
Taking reason as the authority, one does not cling to a single school; rather, whichever [explanation] is superior is adopted as established for oneself.

Regarding the statement that "there are three types of delusion," "delusion" refers to being bewildered and lacking comprehension of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Its essence consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the view of a self and what belongs to a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
The treatise states: "It is traditionally said that there are three kinds of delusion in sentient beings. It is called "traditionally said" because the Buddha’s intention is difficult to fathom.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Although the intention of the Sugata is extremely difficult to discern, when one investigates it through reasoning, it should be understood as follows:

regarding the statement that 'ten bases (*āyatana*) are matter,' one should say that ten bases in their entirety and a small portion of one base are matter, because the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding the statement that 'ten elements (*dhātu*) are matter,' one should likewise say that ten [elements] in their entirety and a small portion of one [element] are matter."
Regarding the statement that the remaining eight are mind: in reality, seven elements (*dhātu*) are entirely mental, while one portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is also mind.
This is because the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) and so forth are not mental. Thus, the present mention of "eight" is stated in terms of their general characteristics.

Furthermore, although the mental factors (*caitta*) within the element of phenomena are not mind, there is no error in collectively designating them as "mind" when contrasted with other categories. All that precedes has been...
Because one grasps at a self and phenomena in a general way amidst all dharmas, the detailed discrimination of the attachment to a self is thereby already established;
thus, it is said that the three categories (triskandha) each serve to destroy such attachment, for the objects of delusion for the ignorant do not exceed these three.

As for the statement that there are three faculties (indriya), this refers to the slowness or speed of comprehension, or alternatively, the difficulty or ease of receiving instruction; the faculties are divided into three parts, with the dull faculty (mṛdv-indriya) being the briefest.

Regarding the faculties (*indriya*) within the aggregates (*skandha*), they are explained as the superior faculties (*uttamendriya*). Having already discussed the faculties within the elements (*dhātu*), it is said that "faculties" refers to the spiritual capacity (*indriya*), which has the five faculties—faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth—as its essence.
As for "delight" (*ruci*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Delight means resolute conviction (*adhimukti*. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* states: "Delight means aspiration (*prārthanā*);
it has resolute conviction, faith, and desire as its essence."

Regarding the statement that householders are attached to various desires due to the power of the sensation of pleasure (*vedanā*), this means that because of their attachment to pleasant sensations, they give rise to the strife of craving.

Regarding the statement that renunciants are attached to various views due to the power of distorted perception (*saṃjñā*), this means that by virtue of distorted perceptions, they are able to produce the strife of views.

Regarding the statement that the sequential causes will be explained in the immediate following section, this refers to the subsequent chapter which analyzes the sequence of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This is clarified in the middle [section].

Regarding the first explanation—that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*)—the initial portion concerns its lack of correspondence with the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) and so forth;

the subsequent section, beginning with the question, concerns its lack of correspondence with the meaning of the aggregates themselves. As for the statement that "the unconditioned does not have the sense of an accumulation," the treatise says:

To clarify the basis of defilement: "grasping" (*upādāna*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). When we speak here of the "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*), it indicates that these aggregates are the basis for the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) afflictions.

Regarding the statement that the term "aggregates" reveals both the bases of defilement and purification: if one were to omit "grasping" and simply say "aggregates," it would generally indicate both types of bases—defiled and purified.
To say that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lacks both of these meanings means that it lacks the capacity [to serve as such a basis].
This reveals that the defiled basis (*saṃkleśāśraya*) and the pure basis (*vyavadānāśraya*) constitute the two meanings; it does not mean that defilement and purity themselves are the two.

Regarding the statement that "the cessation of the aggregates (*skandhanirodha*) is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)," the new masters say that the old masters’ intended meaning was that "cessation" refers to the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), which is called "cessation" because it is manifested through the cutting off and extinguishing [of defilements].

All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) have two kinds of cessation: cessation through abandonment (*prahāṇanirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). The term "cessation" (*nirodha*) and "extinction" (*kṣaya*) together reveal emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Regarding the statement that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) consists only of the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), the Master [Vasubandhu] uses the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu) as examples:
if one says that the unconditioned is manifested through the cessation of the aggregates (skandha), then it would not be included within the aggregates;

likewise, since the three types of unconditioned phenomena are manifested through the cessation of eleven bases in their entirety, one base in part, seventeen elements in their entirety, and one element in part, it follows that the unconditioned would also not exist.
Regarding the principle that the cessation of the aggregates occurs within the sphere of the bases (*āyatana*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Up to the point where one maintains the view of a self regarding the aggregates, when entering the state of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), the cessation of the aggregates does not occur within the sphere of the bases, because [in that state] the aggregates do not arise at all. Wherever the characteristics of the aggregates are entirely absent, it is called the 'cessation of the aggregates.

Since the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack the meaning of a 'collection' (*rāśi*) altogether, they cannot be said to be the cessation of the aggregates, nor can they be said to arise."

Since the meaning of "gate" (*mukha*) does not apply there either, it should not be used as an analogy. (The intended meaning of that [previous] explanation is that "cessation" (*nirodha*) means "absence," which refers to the sense of "non-existence";

because within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) there is no sense of "aggregates" (*skandha*), it is said that the cessation of aggregates reveals that the Master has erroneously taken the ancient meaning to be that "cessation" implies "annihilation").
Regarding the statement that "coarseness within the formless" refers to the exclusion of form—thus termed "formless"—it does not refer to the name of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) itself.
Regarding the phrase "according to the sequence of defilement," here all [factors] follow the order of effect first and cause later;
therefore, form comes first and consciousness follows. Regarding the statement that "such afflictions arise dependent upon consciousness," this passage speaks only of...

Because the afflictions arise dependent upon consciousness, consciousness is explained last. [In older translations] it is said that these formations (*saṃskāra*) and the preceding three—form, feeling, and perception—are all capable of defiling consciousness;

therefore, consciousness is explained last. Question: Since the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) contains delusions that can defile consciousness, how do form, feeling, and perception—the other three—defile consciousness?
Answer: Although form, feeling, and perception are not by nature delusions, they are able to serve as conditions [for them].
A defiled consciousness arises with either birth or form as its condition; the feeling and perception associated with afflictions that can defile consciousness are termed "defiled consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "first seeking a vessel for food," the *Zhengli chao* (Notes on Correct Principles) states:

"It is like first seeking a precious vessel when wishing to welcome a guest, because such a vessel is difficult to obtain. Regarding the phrase "having superior joy, etc.," the "etc. includes superior pleasure (*sukha*).

Regarding the statement "the three formless [aggregates]," this excludes the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Regarding the statement that "feeling and perception are established as separate aggregates apart from formations":

feeling and perception are both mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) that originally belong within the aggregate of formations; however, because of four reasons—such as perception being coarse—they are established as separate aggregates outside of the aggregate of formations.
The reason for the sequence mentioned previously applies here as well; this refers to the prior establishment and exclusion of the aggregates.

The gateway [of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] has three causes and two causes, which have already been clearly explained; as for the third cause, it is said: "The immediate sequence shall now be analyzed.

This very passage should be understood as follows: the term "sequence" (*anukrama*) fully manifests the four meanings, such as "according to coarseness" (*audārikatva*), and so forth, because they are not singular. Therefore, the treatise states:
"Precisely by means of such causal factors of sequence (*anukramakāraṇa*)."

Regarding the statement that "the sequence of consciousnesses can be known from these objects," this merely distinguishes the sequence of the six faculties because the sequence of objects and consciousnesses is established in relation to the faculties.
However, within this verse, the sequence is clarified by summarizing five points: first, [the eye and ear] are mentioned first because they apprehend only present objects;

second, [the nose and tongue] are mentioned first because they apprehend only derived matter (*bhautika*); third, [the body] is mentioned first because it apprehends objects that are separated [from itself].

The four [objects] are mentioned first because they are more distant; the five [objects] are mentioned first because of their vertical sequence. First, the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) are collectively contrasted with the mind (*manas*);
next, the four [faculties] are contrasted with the body (*kāya*). Regarding the body, it is said that its objects are indeterminate; therefore, it is mentioned last. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"When an object is designated as determinate, its function is free from confusion and its characteristics are distinct; for this reason, it is mentioned earlier."

Regarding the statement that "the objects are not fixed" because their functions are intermingled and their characteristics are not distinct, it is explained later by saying "other than body and mind.
This means that since the [faculties of] body and mind have already been clarified above, while the four faculties have not yet been distinguished, they are now being explained;
thus, the others are mentioned in contrast to body and mind. Furthermore, among these four, the two types—eye and ear—are alike in perceiving objects at a distance, and thus both are explained first.

The two faculties of nose and tongue both perceive their objects through contact; they are discussed together later. Furthermore, among the four [faculties], the eye and ear are first distinguished, followed by the nose and tongue, which differ slightly from the preceding two sections.
This can be understood by reflecting on the convenience of the textual arrangement.

As for the statement that the nose can apprehend subtle fragrances within flavors: this means that while the tongue merely tastes flavor, the nose also perceives fragrance; however, [the text specifies] "within flavors" because the nose’s perception of fragrance occurs simultaneously with the tongue’s tasting of flavor.
When smelling an odor, the tongue does not perceive taste. As for the statement that the eye is situated at the highest level, this refers to the relative position of their physical bases;
however, with respect to the actual substance of the faculties themselves, there is no such hierarchy of high and low. Therefore, the subsequent treatise states:

"These first three faculties are arranged horizontally in rows, with no variation in height, like a crown or a floral topknot. As for the statement that the body mostly resides below, this means it also occupies a small portion of the upper regions.
The preceding statement that it is "not the sixth consciousness" means that the sixth consciousness does not arise based on the five sense organs; thus, it is said to be "not the sixth consciousness.

However, because the mental organ (*manas*) integrates the six consciousnesses to form [the seventh], there are cases where it relies solely on the mind and cases where it arises based on various sense organs;

it is not entirely uniform in this regard, which is why it is said that "it exists. Although in the Formless Realm it relies solely on the mental organ, this is discussed in the context of the general discourse on all three realms.
Therefore, this statement was made. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Moreover, it is because they accord with the sequence of the coarse and the subtle.
That is to say, among the six internal bases, the eye-base is the coarsest, and thus it is mentioned first; continuing in this way until the mind-base, which is the subtlest, is mentioned last."

Regarding the statement that although a general designation is used, it immediately receives a specific name: because the term "form" (rūpa) applies universally across all ten [bases], it serves as a general designation;
yet, when distinguished by the other nine, it becomes a specific name. This is like a herd of horses with many owners where each has a distinct seal, while one owner has no seal;
thus, the one without a seal is distinguished from those with seals. Here, too, it is the same: this very [base] is without [a seal].

Because there are distinct names for individual [categories], although a general designation is presented, it specifically receives its own particular name (that is, the *rūpāyatana* receives its specific name, not the other nine bases).
As for why the *rūpāyatana* is said to receive the general name, it was previously distinguished by clarifying the ten types individually rather than treating them as a single collective name;
this now explains the reason why the *rūpāyatana* alone receives the general name, despite the differences such as form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth.

The two meanings are distinguished as follows: first, "resistant" (*sapratigha*) refers to that which undergoes transformation and decay when touched by hands and the like; second, "visible" (*sanidarśana*) refers to that which can be pointed out as being "this" or "that.

Furthermore, the aforementioned explanation does not include the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), because it is so minor that the name "sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*) is established for it in the same manner as the "sphere of form" (*rūpāyatana*).
Moreover, the treatise states: "Other masters say that within the sphere of form there are two [types]."

The ten types of form are established as the category of "form" (*rūpa-āyatana*) because they are the coarsest and most manifest, and because they are the objects of the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, and the three eyes respectively.

The sphere of phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) is established as the category of "phenomena" (*dharma*) because it contains the names of all dharmas and because it is the object of the knowledge of all dharmas.
In the sūtras, all other categories such as the aggregates (skandha) and bases (āyatana) have been explained, yet the five bases of liberation (pañca vimukty-āyatanāni) were not distinguished;

therefore, they are now explained. As for the "five bases of liberation": first, attaining liberation by hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma; second, attaining liberation by reading and reciting it oneself;
third, attaining liberation by preaching the Dharma for others; fourth, attaining liberation through meditative concentration and reflection; and fifth, skillfully grasping [the teachings].

Through the characteristic of concentration, one attains liberation; liberation refers to *nirvāṇa*. Because one attains liberation by means of these five factors, they are called "bases of liberation.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Among these five dharmas, upon attaining even one, one immediately understands the meaning.

From understanding the meaning, joy arises; from joy, the body becomes tranquil; from tranquility of the body, pleasure is felt; from feeling pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated; and through concentration of the mind..."
Therefore, one sees things as they truly are; because one sees them as they truly are, one is able to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*); because one has exhausted all outflows, one attains *nirvāṇa*.
These five preceding factors are the provisions for liberation and are called the "bases of liberation" (*vimukty-āyatana*). Regarding the statement that the number of verses is eighty thousand:

it is traditionally said that the numerical system of the West generally takes ten and hundred as its factors of multiplication to form larger numbers; from the hundreds and thousands upward, [the units] are multiplied by a hundred.

Because it was less than one hundred thousand, multiplying it by ten results in eighty thousand being referred to as "eighty-thousand" (now, upon detailed examination, these "eighty-thousand" are a rounded figure;

if stated fully, they are actually eighty-four thousand). Regarding those who say that the Buddha’s teachings have speech as their essence: "speech" refers to vocal action (*vāg-karman*), which constitutes the essence of the teaching.
This refers to the sequential arrangement, placement, and combination of the sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*).

This refers to the Buddhist teaching (*śāsana*) as distinct from the essence of Buddhism itself. When it is said that the "teaching" (*śāsana*) is the essence, this means that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) constitute the essence of the teaching.
As for the expression "articulated speech" (*vāgvijñapti*) and so forth, these are the successive causes;

just as sons and grandsons are born in succession, it is said that speech arises and each is capable of manifesting meaning. The commentary states: "As for 'speech' (*vacana*), it is the karmic action of speech (*vākkarman*)."

Because it is taught by one who has realized the Buddha’s intent based on what was heard from others, another question is asked: "For what reason is the Buddha’s teaching exclusively vocal action (*vāg-karman*) and not unmanifest action (*avijñapti*)?

The answer is: "It is called the Buddha’s teaching because it produces correct understanding in others; and this production of correct understanding in others occurs solely through manifest action (*vijñapti*), not through unmanifest action.
According to these two preceding explanations, each has its own basis. Both interpretations are fully transmitted in the Western regions (India). If one relies upon them...

The teaching must accord with the capacity of the recipient; without sound, it could not be heard. If one relies on the words to seek the ultimate meaning, there would be no means to manifest it without names.
Thus we know that the objects addressed differ, each having its own basis of reliance; if even one is lacking, there is a deficiency, but when all are complete, there is no flaw.
Regarding the statement that "each individual measure is equal to the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*," the intended meaning of this explanation is as follows:

although the Buddha taught eighty thousand sections of the *Dharmaskandha*, each section consists of eight thousand stanzas, equal in quantity to the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra* among the six *pādas*.

This refers to the fixed measure of the expressive words and phrases. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "according to the [categories such as] the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth," it refers to the five [aggregates] that were taught.
The terms "aggregates" (skandha), "twelve bases" (āyatana), and so forth, constitute the measure of the *dharmaskandhas*. Regarding the question:

"Since it has already been stated that they are defined by their meaning (*artha*), why are they further referred to as 'teaching-gates' (*śāsana-mukha*)? Answer: By mentioning these teaching-gates, one reveals the meanings they express.

That is to say, according to the number of distinct categories of the expressed meanings—such as the aggregates and so forth—there are eighty thousand [teachings]; these are the expressive *dharmaskandhas* that correspond to those expressed meanings.

The meaning is likewise. Regarding the statement that the third [category] is determined by its practical application (*yòngliàng*), the old name was "determined by its functional application" (*jìngyòng dìngliàng*).
"According to reality" (*rúshí*) means judging according to the correct principle (*dàolǐ*). As for the "eighty thousand," the old tradition says this is the calculation of the Dharma Master Zhéntí;
the new tradition says it is verified in Zhéntí’s *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, though there is no such text. If one follows the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, it begins from the *Prabhāsa* [kalpa].
(This refers to the time of entering the womb: from the final arrival at Dhānyakaṭaka (at the time of dividing the relics), there are three hundred and fifty *pāramitās* in total;
each has six *pāramitā*-vehicles, forming two thousand one hundred pairs. For each of the four great elements and the six *āyatanas*, there are two thousand one hundred, forming twenty-one thousand.
Greed, anger, and delusion, etc., each have twenty-one thousand parts, and when multiplied, they form eighty-four thousand.
However, the aforementioned eighty thousand *dharma-skandhas* are spoken of only in reference to the *śrāvakas*; if one discusses the *pratyekabuddhas* and others, their number is even greater.

In such texts as the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* and the *Anantārtha-sūtra*, it is stated that there are eighty thousand for the *śrāvakas*, ninety thousand for the *pratyekabuddhas*, and ten billion for the *bodhisattvas*.

Regarding the "five aggregates" mentioned within these scriptures, they refer to the untainted (*anāsrava*) five aggregates; thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The untainted discipline of body and speech."

The aggregate of morality of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-śīlaskandha*) is designated as such; the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samādhiskandha*) is the meditative absorption of one beyond training.

What is the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-prajñāskandha*)? Answer: It is the knowledge of right view of one beyond training. What is the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*)? Answer:

It is the mind associated with the mental attention of one beyond training that has already attained resolve, is currently attaining resolve, or will attain resolve—namely, that which is associated with the right view of the exhaustion [of outflows] and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-aśaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Adhimukti (resolute conviction) is established as such because it possesses mastery over its object; it does not mean "separation from fetters" (visaṃyoga). How is the aggregate of knowledge and vision (jñānadarśana-skandha) to be understood? Answer:

The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are called the aggregate of liberation-knowledge-and-vision. Question: For what reason is this knowledge called the aggregate of liberation-knowledge-and-vision? Answer:
Because it exists within the body of liberation (vimukti-kāya), and because it is most capable of definitively discerning the matter of liberation; thus it is so termed. Prior to this [statement],...

Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*) having non-attachment (*alobha*) as their nature: this means that by contemplating the primary elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as well as the derivative forms—blue, yellow, red, and white—one ensures that attachment does not arise toward these eight objects.
Because non-attachment is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), it is subsumed under the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

When it is said that they "take the form associated with meditative concentration" (*samādhisaṃprayukta-rūpa*), it is because they are tainted (*sāsrava*); thus, they do not pertain to the form associated with the [supramundane] path, but only to that which is co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja*).
Regarding the inclusion of the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):

the first eight spheres of mastery consist of four in which one perceives internal forms while observing external forms—both few and many—and four in which one has no perception of internal forms while observing external forms—both few and many; these are followed by four observations of the four colors, such as blue and so forth.
Since these also have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their essential nature, they are identical to the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). As for the first sphere...

Regarding the inclusion within the ten bases (*daśāyatana*): the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) belongs to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). It consists of the six faculties and four objects, making ten; among the twelve bases, it excludes only odor and taste.

Since non-conceptual sentient beings always possess sound, they are endowed with the base of sound. Question: Since they lack ideation (*saṃjñā*), how can there be the base of mind (*manāyatana*)? Answer:

At the time of experiencing the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), although the mental faculty (*citta*) is absent, [the base of mind exists].

Because there must be a mind at the moment of initial birth and subsequent death, there is also "mental discourse" (*manojalpa*). As for the "subsequent station," it refers to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);

its inclusion [within the stations] can be understood accordingly. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: For what reason did the Blessed One frequently designate the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as "stations"?
The answer is: There are certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to these two places as being liberation; the Buddha [designated them as stations] in order to refute them.

That [text] explains them as the bases of rebirth (*upapatti-sthāna*). In the aforementioned Sūtra, the chapter on the five bases of liberation (*pañca-vimukti-sthāna*) does not clarify their inclusion;

however, the present *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states that the five bases of liberation have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, and thus they are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

If their associated factors (*sahabhū-saṃprayukta-dharma*) are also taken into account, it should be understood that they are included within the spheres of sound (*śabdāyatana*), mind (*manāyatana*), and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Regarding the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, it also enumerates six [bases of liberation] within the Āgama.
The twelve *dhātus* are named in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*. This is derived from the "Bahudhātuka" chapter of the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*.
Sixty-two *dhātus* are subsumed within the eighteen *dhātus*. Regarding the first eighteen *dhātus*, they are subsumed according to their own names.

The first six—the four elements of earth, water, fire, and air—are subsumed within the *spraṣṭavya-dhātu* (tangible object element). The *ākāśa-dhātu* (space element) has shadow, light, and darkness as its essence. The *rūpa-dhātu* (form element)...

The consciousness element (*vijñāna-dhātu*) is subsumed under the category of "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*), taking contaminated consciousness as its essence. Regarding the second group of six [elements], the five beginning with suffering and pleasure have sensation (*vedanā*) as their nature;
ignorance (*avidyā*) has delusion (*moha*) as its nature; these are all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and are thus subsumed under the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*).

Regarding the third group of six, desire (*chanda*) has greed (*lobha*) as its nature, hostility (*vyāpāda*) has hatred (*dveṣa*) as its nature, and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*) has cruelty as its nature; non-desire (*vairāgya*)... [is the opposite].
Non-attachment has non-greed as its nature; non-hatred has non-aversion as its nature; and non-harming has non-injury as its nature.

These six are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and are all subsumed within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). (According to the New and Old Commentaries, the second group of six is in the third [section], and the third group of six is in the second.

Regarding the four types: feeling, perception, and formations are subsumed in the dharma-element; consciousness is subsumed in the seven mind-elements. Among the three groups of six, the first group of three is...

The eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are subsumed; the fourteen elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are subsumed, excluding odor, taste, and the two consciousnesses [of nose and tongue];

the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is subsumed by the mental element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*). Regarding the second three realms: the form realm is common to both the desire and form realms because both possess form;

thus, they are collectively termed the "form realm" within the subsumption of the eighteen elements. The last three elements of the formless realm and the cessation element (*nirodhadhātu*) are subsumed.

The first [category], having analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its nature, is comprised solely within the *dharmadhātu*. The third [category], consisting of phenomena of the three times, is comprised within the five aggregates (*skandha*) because they have the nature of the five aggregates;
it is comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The fourth [category], the wholesome elements, has all wholesome phenomena as its nature;

the unwholesome [elements] have all unwholesome phenomena as their nature. These two are comprised within the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*), the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*), and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). The neutral element (*avyākṛtadhātu*) is comprised by one... [text ends].

All indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena are by nature comprised within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The fifth [category], the three inferior realms, have the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) as their nature;

they are comprised within seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*), the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*), and the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). The intermediate realm has impure wholesome (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena as its nature;
it is comprised within the eighteen elements. The sublime realm has untainted wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*) phenomena as its nature; it is comprised within the final three [elements].

Regarding the inclusion within the *dhātus* (following the Great Commentary, which lists the fifth as the fourth): the sixth, the *dhātu* of those in training (*śaikṣa*), has the five untainted (*anāsrava*) aggregates of one in training as its nature;
the *dhātu* of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has the five untainted aggregates of one beyond training as its nature. These two are included within the latter three *dhātus*.

The *dhātu* of those who are neither in training nor beyond training has the tainted (*sāsrava*) five aggregates and the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena as its nature; it is included within the first eighteen *dhātus*.
Second, the contaminated realm (*sāsrava-dhātu*) has the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its nature and is subsumed within the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*);

the uncontaminated realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) has the five uncontaminated aggregates and the three unconditioned phenomena (*trividha-asamskṛta*) as its nature and is subsumed within the final three realms.

Second, the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*) has the five aggregates as its nature and is subsumed within the eighteen realms; the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) has the three unconditioned phenomena as its nature and is subsumed within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the inclusion within the *dhātus*:
the question "Is it that space itself is called the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*), up to the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*)?

intends to ask whether it is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) space itself that is called the space-element, or whether all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses constitute the consciousness-element. As for the term "aperture" (*chidra*):...

Regarding the term *kṣaṇa* (隙): the *Guǎngyá* states it means "aperture" (*qiào kǒng*) or "crack" (*kṣī-liè*). The *Shuōwén* states it means "hollow" (*qiào kōng*) or "the aperture at the junction of a wall" (*kṣī bì-jì kǒng*).
To say that transmission and teaching clarify light and darkness is because, in principle, they actually possess both. Light and shadow form a pair; light is clear while shadow is dark.
When one speaks only of "light," it is by citing the lighter element to manifest the heavier one. Shadow and darkness form another pair.
Shadow is light while darkness is heavy; by specifically mentioning "darkness," the heavier is cited to reveal the lighter.
This is a case of mutual abbreviation between the two, as the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The tradition says that those who speak of light and darkness specifically refer to the two heavy [elements].

Regarding the Sautrāntika position that the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*) is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The Sthaviras and all other Dārṣṭāntika masters unanimously maintain this."

The space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) is not separate from empty space (*ākāśa*); however, since the essence of that empty space is not substantially real, one should know that the essence of the space-element is likewise not substantial.
The Master [Vasubandhu] accepts this through the establishment of correct reasoning at length, even to the point of asserting that it has a substantial nature because it can contain all light.
He uses the effect to reveal the cause, showing that there is a characteristic of substantial reality; for if empty space did not exist, there would be no light.

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* further states: "This very [space] is called 'space-adjacent matter' (*ākāśānantaryarūpa*). It is traditionally explained that 'ākāśa' refers to accumulated matter that is extremely capable of being an obstruction; therefore, it is called 'ākāśa.
This matter of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is adjacent to that [obstructive matter], and for this reason it is called 'space-adjacent matter.

(This passage describes an alternate name for the matter of the space-element in the root treatise. *Āga* is translated as "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). The prefix *ā-* has two meanings: either "extreme" (*ati*) or "non-" (*an-*). Here it carries the sense of "extreme," referring to the space-element.)
"Form that is adjacent to this extremely obstructive form. Furthermore, it is said: "Some say that *ākāśa* (space) is the form of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*).

Because there is no obstruction within it, it is called *ākāśa*. This very form of *ākāśa* is adjacent to other obstructive forms; therefore, it is called 'form adjacent to *ākāśa*' (*ākāśa-sāmantaka-rūpa*).

This second [explanation] refers to its adjacency to other obstructive forms and to this space-element. Because it contains both meanings, the original name is retained. As for the statement that the six elements are admitted to be the basis for the arising of sentient beings, it means:
The six elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—constantly sustain birth from the moment of the mind that links rebirth until the mind at the end of life;
thus, all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena are not like this. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"These six elements function as the causes for the arising, nourishing, and growth of sentient beings; therefore, they are the basis of birth (where 'birth' refers to the element of consciousness, as it is the cause for linking rebirth, and 'nourishing' refers to the primary elements, as they are the basis for the growth of birth)."

Because it is quiescent, it is called "long" (the space element), as it provides room for the arising [of phenomena]. According to one interpretation, among material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are specifically taught as what is subsumed;
among immaterial phenomena (*arūpa*), the mind (*citta*) is predominant as what is subsumed, while other phenomena are subordinate.

Regarding the term "with vision" (*sadarśana*): in Sanskrit it is *sa* (meaning "with") and *darśana* (meaning "vision"). Vision contains three meanings: first, the sense of illumination;

second, the sense of manifestation; and third, the sense of metaphor. In the treatises, only the single meaning of manifestation is cited, whereas the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra* fully manifest all three meanings.
In this present chapter, however, there are only the two meanings of manifestation and illumination; the former is the sense of manifestation.
The term "seeing" (*darśana*) means "viewing," which is synonymous with "contemplation. Regarding the statement that the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) sees, the *Chao* (a commentary) states:
it means that the eye-faculty emits light to illuminate objects; because it illuminates objects so that they appear, it is called "seeing forms" (*rūpa-darśana*).

Because it causes both [the faculty and the object] to arise together, it is called "possessing seeing" (*sadarśana*), just as companions traveling together are said to be "possessing companions. Some further explain that this refers to forms [reflected] within mirrors and the like.
That which possesses a form capable of being manifested is called "visible" (*sanidarśana*), because it can be pointed out as being such and so forth;

therefore, it cannot be said that sound has an echo and the like, for [an echo] would otherwise result in being visible, since it is not co-arisen [with its source]. As for the remaining seventeen elements, they are termed "invisible" (*anidarśana*) because no such meaning has been stated for them.
Regarding the statement that what is composed of atoms obstructs one another: this is like an atom in the east obstructing one in the west.
If one atom were not to reach [another], there would be no obstruction in the east; the same applies to the west. Therefore, the treatise says:

"When [an atom] is obstructed by another at its own location, it does not arise, just as a hand obstructs a hand" (this refers to the mutual obstruction of the essential characteristics of the atoms). Furthermore, another interpretation states: "These faculties and objects are composed of atoms;

this demonstrates that the faculties and objects mutually obstruct one another" (this refers to the obstruction between the faculties and objects as they are constituted). Regarding the statement that "there are three types of resistance (*sapratigha*) in total," this is according to the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).

Since obstructive resistance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*) clarifies the other two types of resistance, the verse’s mention of "resistant form" (*sapratigha-rūpa*) refers exclusively to obstructive resistance and not to the other two.
Therefore, the treatise concludes: "It should be understood that here it is spoken of solely with respect to obstructive resistance;
for this reason, it is said that the ten material bases are resistant. By this same principle, the remaining [bases] are explained as non-resistant (*apratigha*).

The explanation of the three types of resistance (*sapratigha*) is summarized into three sections: first, the presentation of the headings; second, the enumeration; and third, the citation and explanation.

The first two may be understood according to the chapter headings. "Resistance" (*pratigha*) has the meaning of obstruction. Regarding the subsequent citation and explanation of "obstructive confinement," it is divided into three parts:

first, the presentation of the number; second, the explanation of the names and essential nature; and third, the distinctions. As for the phrase "a portion of the *dharmadhātu*": there are four categories of phenomena within the *dharmadhātu*. First...

Regarding the statement that "only a portion" [of phenomena] consists of mental factors (*caitta*), this refers to the two categories of mental factors, the three types of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), the four types of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*), and the unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Because it takes only the mental factors as its primary referent, it says "a portion. As for the phrase "toward objects such as form," this means that each of the aforementioned phenomena relates to its own respective object;

the "etcetera" includes the five sense objects, such as sound and so forth. Regarding the etymological explanation, one should say that these visual consciousnesses and others possess efficacy (*sāmarthya*) with respect to objects such as form.
Therefore, it is called "constrained by objects" (*viṣayapratighāta*) and "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).

Regarding the term "resistance with respect to objects," this refers to citing the apprehended object (*grāhyaviṣaya*) to indicate the resistance of the apprehending subject (*grāhakapratighāta*); thus, it is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound.

Next, the resistance with respect to the focal object (*ālambanapratighāta*) is also explained by citing the focal object to clarify the resistance of the cognizing subject (*ālambakapratighāta*). This is the resistance with respect to the focal object.
Regarding those that do not pervade the five sense faculties, they shall be analyzed in sequence. Next, concerning the analysis of their distinctions: first, the distinction of objects is clarified;

second, the differences are distinguished in relation to the focal objects (*ālambana*); third, in relation to obstructions; and finally, the objects and focal objects are analyzed again. These chapters may be understood by following the text.
As for the phrase "the eyes of people such as fishermen," this means that when fishermen and others see objects in the water, it is mostly described from the perspective of being on land.
"Obstruction. Regarding the Piśāca: formerly called the *Vijñā* or the *Piśāca*, this is a ghost among the most powerful of the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The Śiśumāra belongs to the class of animals (*tiryagyoni*); its form is like that of a wall-castle, though some say its shape is like a large bedstead.
In the older sūtras and vinayas, it is sometimes written as *Śicuma-ra* or *Śicou-ma-ra*; these are variations of the Sanskrit pronunciation.

A mistranslation calls it the "son-killer fish" (*putramāra*). The *Sudarsana-vinaya* calls it the crocodile (*śiśumāra*). It has four legs and resembles a fish or a tortoise; its teeth are extremely sharp.
When birds or deer enter the water, it bites their waists, and they are severed instantly. It exists in Guangzhou;

the small ones are twenty feet long, while the large ones may reach a hundred feet in length. According to the treatise, there are four further permutations regarding day and night; thus, the treatise says:
There are eyes that have obstruction at night but not during the day, such as those of bats, owls, and the like. There are eyes that have obstruction during the day but not at night;

this is stated according to the majority of cases, such as the eyes of humans and others. There are eyes that have obstruction at both times, such as the eyes of dogs, jackals, horses, *śṛgāla*, wolves, cats, and wildcats.
There are eyes that have no obstruction at either time, meaning they exclude the aforementioned characteristics. Next, to distinguish these differences, it says: "This is their function."
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "When a person possesses superior functional capacity (*vṛtti*) with respect to an object, that object is said to be one's 'sphere' (*viṣaya*). [Commentary:

This means that when a cognitive factor possesses the functional capacity to engage its own object through seeing, hearing, and so forth, it is termed a 'sphere. Mental states and mental factors arise by grasping an object; this is termed the 'object-condition' (*ālambana*). [This explains the object-condition.

Now, while the characteristic of these five sense-faculties as being 'resistant spheres' (*viṣayapratighata*) is well known, the characteristic of mental states and mental factors as being 'resistant objects' (*ālambanapratighata*) is easily understood: it refers to the sphere within the mental states and mental factors themselves."

Regarding the distinction between the two [types of objects]: those that arise from grasping an object and are termed "cognitions and mental factors" (citta-caitta) are called "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*) because they possess the distinct functions of apprehending images and maintaining them; those that differ from these cognitions and mental factors are called "spheres of experience" (*viṣaya*). Because these [latter] do not function with respect to anything other than their own specific domain, they are collectively termed "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).

This is what constitutes the distinction. As for the statement regarding the obstruction of substance and function: it is said that, for example, although the substance of the "homogeneous eye" (*sabhāga-cakṣus*) exists constantly, it is not called an "object of cognition" (*viṣaya*) when it lacks the capacity to see visible forms.
By this analogy, one should understand that "sphere of experience" (*viṣaya*) refers to function, whereas "object of cognition" (*ālambana*) is explained according to substance.

It is said that for mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*), a functional object (*ālambana*) must exist for them to arise; if there were no present object, they would lack substance.

Thus, we know that with respect to substance, the "homogeneous" eye (*tatsabhāga-cakṣus*), although it possesses substance, lacks utility and is therefore not termed "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).

We know that this is determined by utility. Furthermore, regarding other explanations, there are three traditional interpretations: the first says it is "resistance regarding the object" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*).

This refers to having the capacity [to perceive], not necessarily the actual arising of its function. For example, the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) has an object that is resistant (*sapratigha*), yet it only arises when it reaches the present;

that is, it arises when it exerts its function of grasping the result (*phala-grahaṇa-kriyā*). Thus, it is called "resistant" (*sapratigha*) because it arises when there is an object and does not arise when there is no object.

The second [definition] states: the function of obstructing the grasping of the object is called "obstruction of the objective field" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*), while the function of grasping the result is called "obstruction of the focal object" (*ālambana-pratighāta*).
