The atoms of the eye faculty are distributed across the pupil, lying flat and side-by-side. They are like the petals of a *kunda* flower, transparently covering one another so as not to scatter. There is [an arrangement].

The atoms of the ear-faculty are situated within the ear-cavity, arranged in a circular fashion like rolled birch bark. The atoms of the nose-faculty are situated within the nasal bridge, with their backs facing upward and their fronts facing downward, like a pair of fingernails.

These first three faculties are horizontally distributed across their respective locations. As for the body, it is said to be like a ball of accumulated matter; because its substance is transparent, it is like crystal (*sphaṭika*), and thus there is no mutual obstruction. The atoms of the ear-faculty reside within the ear-passage, dwelling in a spiral formation like a scroll of birch bark.
The atoms of the nose-faculty reside within the nasal bridge, with the back above and the face below, resembling a pair of claw-nails. These first three faculties are arranged in horizontal rows.
There is no variation in height, like a crown or a flower garland; the atoms of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya-paramāṇu*) are distributed over the tongue in the shape of a half-moon.
It is traditionally taught that the area in the center of the tongue, the size of a hair-tip, is not pervaded by the atoms of the tongue-faculty.

The atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya-paramāṇu*) reside pervasively throughout the parts of the body, corresponding in measure to the shape of the body itself. The atoms of the female faculty (*strīndriya-paramāṇu*) are shaped like the head of a drum (*mṛdaṅga-śīrṣa*), and the atoms of the male faculty (*puruṣendriya-paramāṇu*) are shaped like...

As with the fingers [the *veḍhaka*—referring here to the male and female sexual organs, which clarify the cause], next we shall distinguish the statement regarding the "equality" of the apprehension of objects.
"Equality" means that the measure of the object is neither less nor greater than the measure of the sense organ;

it does not necessarily mean being equal in size to a fingernail. This is because whether one apprehends a small or large object, it is all termed "equal," provided that a small object is apprehended by a small organ (and likewise for larger ones).

The essential point is that the object grasped does not exceed the size of a fingernail. For example, when one sees a grape, it is because the capacity of the eye is like that of a grape; thus, one sees the grape as new.
A modern explanation states that this also describes how the supporting sense organ and its object are of unequal size, and it is not necessary for them to be exactly like a grape fruit.
Even if the eye is the size of half a grape fruit, when it perceives an object the size of a grape, it is still called "grasping a large [object]," such as a mosquito.

The sound of a child is small, while the sound of clouds is great; the sound of a lute is likewise [variable]. According to the correct principle, the faculty of hearing also perceives the relative magnitude of sounds such as mosquitoes, clouds, and lutes.
To call thunder "clouds" is a designation based on their substantial nature.
The statement "the supports for these various worlds are likewise" refers to questioning the supports (*āśraya*) by means of the six consciousnesses as they take objects.

There are distinctions among the six consciousnesses taking objects—such as taking only the present or penetrating all three periods of time—and there are distinctions regarding whether the supports of the six consciousnesses are identical to their objects.
The phrase "not non-worldly" (*na-asaṃskṛta*) excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The reason the sixth [consciousness] relies solely on the past is that...

Because the mental faculty (*manas*) does not exist as a simultaneous support, the five consciousnesses depend exclusively on past [faculties]; because each of the five consciousnesses possesses its own simultaneous material faculty (*rūpīndriya*), they also pertain to the present.

Regarding the four alternatives concerning whether the nature of the support of visual consciousness is the same as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for that visual consciousness:

this is because the nature of the support of visual consciousness extends to both the eye and the mental faculty, and it further encompasses the meaning of the mental faculty as the equal-and-immediate condition.
Regarding the related questions arising from these points, because they possess mutual breadth and narrowness, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established, as clarified below: 1.
That which is the nature of the support for visual consciousness refers to the co-nascent eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which serves as the support for that consciousness. 2.

Regarding the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it applies exclusively to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); this means that mental factors and the like possess the power to induce the arising of the subsequent moment by way of immediate succession.

They are called "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) because they arise by opening up a space for the subsequent moment; however, since material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) arise either in small or large quantities and thus lack equality, they are not equal and immediate.

Furthermore, because they are not the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), they do not function as the dominant power (*adhipati-pratyaya*) upon which visual consciousness relies—just as the principle governing a king and his ministers does not apply here—and thus they do not pertain to the mental factors (*caitta*).
As for the fourth category, it includes the five objects such as visible form and so forth.
The dharmadhātu, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the dissociated (*viprayukta*) factors, etc., are both cases where neither [of the two conditions] applies.

If the nature of being the support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) were restricted to the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*), it would not constitute the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). However, since the preceding moment of mental consciousness serves as the support for the subsequent moment, it is termed the "nature of support.

Furthermore, because it provides an opening and induces the arising of the subsequent consciousness, it is also the "immediately antecedent condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*); therefore, it falls under the category of both [conditions]. Question: If one says...

If it is argued that that which serves as the support (*āśraya*) for mental consciousness must necessarily be an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), one might ask: "Is not the final mind of an Arhat not a support for mental consciousness, yet not an immediately preceding condition? The answer is:
In this context, the question and answer are framed specifically regarding the nature of being a functional support (*kriyā-āśrayatva*);

they do not refer to the definition of obtaining the support (*prāpti-āśrayalakṣaṇa*). The final mind of an Arhat merely possesses the characteristic of being a support and is thus designated as the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*); beyond that, there is nothing further.

Consciousness is not the basis for action; this is a statement of mutual negation. Furthermore, in explaining this, the question regarding the basis is posed by citing the fruit [of the path], yet the final moment of mind of an Arhat is not mentioned.

As for the statement that the name "basis" (āśraya) applies to the faculties (indriya) and not to the objects (viṣaya), one asks: why do only the faculties receive the name "basis," while the objects do not?
It is because they do not possess a basis [for being so named].
Regarding the statement that there is no "consciousness of form" up to and including "consciousness of phenomena," the question is:

why is it that one speaks only of "eye-consciousness" and not "consciousness of form," only "ear-consciousness" and not "consciousness of sound," and so on, until the sixth, where one speaks only of "mind-consciousness" and not "consciousness of phenomena"?

Is it consciousness? This differs from the previous section in that the previous section clarifies that while the eye and so forth are uniquely termed "bases" (*āśraya*), form and so forth are not bases;
whereas this section distinguishes that they are merely termed "eye-consciousness" and so forth, but not "form-consciousness" and so forth. Thus, the two sections are distinct.
Regarding what was previously stated, the intent of this response is to adopt the meaning of the previously mentioned eye as the "basis," as well as to adopt this internal [consciousness].
Regarding the meaning of "unshared cause" (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*), because two factors are combined, it is called "eye-consciousness," and so forth.

When it says "the eye is only for its own eye-consciousness," up to "its nature as a support," the phrase "its own eye-consciousness" excludes the eye-consciousness of another's body, because the eye is not the support for another person's eye-consciousness.

Furthermore, it is only the support for its own eye-consciousness and does not extend to being the support for one's own mental consciousness; however, in the case of visible form (*rūpa*), it does extend [to both].

The four types of consciousness are: first, one’s own visual consciousness; second, another’s visual consciousness; third, one’s own mental consciousness; and fourth, another’s mental consciousness. Therefore, they are called "shared.
Regarding the statement "like observing the moon," etc., the term "one" refers to the preeminent [consciousness], which was explained in the preceding section:

the consciousness varies according to the transformation of the sense faculty (*indriya*), and thus the sense faculty is preeminent. Consequently, the name of the consciousness is derived from the sense faculty and not from the object (*viṣaya*). This concludes the previous point.
The reason why [the consciousnesses] are called "eye-consciousness" and so forth, rather than "form-consciousness" and so forth, yet are termed "unshared causes" (asādhāraṇa-hetu), is as follows:

among the first five faculties, they are "unshared" in terms of their basis (*āśraya*) but "shared" in terms of their object (*viṣaya*). Now, this sixth faculty is "shared" in terms of its object but "unshared" in terms of its basis;

thus, it is said to be "reversed" compared to the former. Furthermore, the statement that "although the mind is not an unshared cause" serves to preempt an objection. This is the objection: [if the mind were not an unshared cause, how could it be established as such?]

It is said that because the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are not shared causes, consciousness is designated according to the faculty; however, since the object-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is also a non-shared cause, it should be called "consciousness of phenomena" (*dharmavijñāna*).
Therefore, this is refuted by stating: although the mental faculty (*manas*) is a shared cause, the object-field of phenomena is non-shared;

yet, the name of the consciousness is established according to the nature of its support (*āśraya*), rather than being established based on whether the cause is shared or non-shared. This differs from the case of the five faculties, which possess two meanings regarding their support.
Therefore, it does not follow from the object that [the mental consciousness] is established as a non-common cause. Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu* states:

"Since the object of the mental consciousness is non-common, it should be called 'dharma-consciousness' (*dharmavijñāna*). This objection is irrational, because whether taken generally or specifically, the dharma-object is common and not universal. [Commentary: If it were taken generally as "dharma," then the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) would also be dharmas;

thus, the mental consciousness would be common to the visual consciousnesses and so forth, as well as common to one's own and others' consciousnesses. If it were taken specifically as "dharma," the category would again be incomplete, as it would not encompass all mental consciousnesses. Since the general term "dharma-consciousness" cannot include them all, the designation of the consciousnesses is established solely based on their respective sense faculties (*indriya*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the dharma-realm has only the single meaning of being non-common and the meaning of having no basis, and is thus like the sound of a drum," this applies only to the five sense organs and is not equal to the mental faculty (*manas*).
To say it merely produces the sound of a drum means it does not produce the sounds of bells and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the hand lacks two meanings": first, the sound does not change according to the hand; second, [the hand] is not the superior basis (*āśraya*).
Because the two [factors] together produce all sounds, they are not an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*). Regarding the statement that "barley has two meanings":

first, the sprout changes in accordance with the barley; second, it produces only its own fruit. For this reason, although water and soil also produce the sprout by virtue of their power, they do not change in accordance with the sprout, nor can they universally moisten it;
because they are common causes (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*), the sprout is not named after the water or the soil.
It is said that eye-consciousness exists only in the desire realm and the first dhyāna;

from the second dhyāna upward, the dharmas of those stages are subtle, lacking vitarka and vicāra, and thus lack the three types of consciousness. While these may be compared to one another as being either superior or inferior, regarding the eye-element:

first, the eye is compared to the body; next, form and consciousness are compared to the eye; next, form and consciousness are compared to each other; and finally, form and consciousness are used to [compare with]...

In general, there are four sections regarding the body. It is not the case that consciousness of an upper stage does not rely on the eyes of a lower stage; rather, consciousness of a lower stage itself may rely on the eyes of an upper stage, as when those from the second dhyāna and above borrow the consciousness of the first dhyāna. Ultimately, there is no instance where consciousness of an upper stage relies upon the sense-faculties of a lower stage. The principle cited above is but a brief illustration of one corner of the matter. Most people fail to grasp the intended meaning here, though some offer this interpretation of the verse: [The verse: "Consciousness of a lower stage relies on the eyes of an upper stage; Consciousness of an upper stage never relies on the faculties of a lower stage. This concludes the section on the eye. As for the ear, it is similar. Regarding the nose, tongue, and body, they are each associated with their own respective stages. For example, when one in the first dhyāna smells a fragrance from the desire realm, the olfactory consciousness belongs to the desire realm while the nose faculty belongs to the first dhyāna; thus, the consciousness of a lower stage relies on a faculty of an upper stage. However, there is no instance where consciousness of an upper stage relies on a faculty of a lower stage. This is because the faculties of the upper stages are subtle and tranquil, whereas the consciousnesses of the lower stages are coarse and agitated; therefore, the coarse consciousness cannot rely upon the tranquil faculty. Furthermore, the faculties of the upper stages are superior, while the consciousnesses of the lower stages are inferior; thus, the inferior cannot rely upon the superior. Moreover, the faculties of the upper stages are subtle and refined, while the consciousnesses of the lower stages are coarse and dull; thus, the coarse and dull cannot rely upon the subtle and refined. Consequently, there is no such thing as consciousness of an upper stage relying on a faculty of a lower stage. This is the same for the tongue and body. Regarding the mind, it is entirely unrestricted, as it can rely on any of the six consciousnesses or the six faculties across all nine stages. Thus, the mind is distinct from the other five. This concludes the section on the faculties. As for the objects, they are all associated with their own respective stages. Consequently, there is no such thing as a mental state of an upper stage relying on a mind of a lower stage. This is the same for the other mental states. This concludes the section on the dissociated factors. This concludes the section on the association of the eighteen elements. As for the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), it is entirely associated with its own respective stage. For example, when one in the first dhyāna perceives a form of the desire realm, the form belongs to the desire realm while the visual consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna; thus, the form of a lower stage relies on a consciousness of an upper stage. However, there is no instance where a form of an upper stage relies on a consciousness of a lower stage. The text merely distinguishes the relative superiority and inferiority among the four categories of eye-consciousness and form-body;

it does not provide a comprehensive analysis of the remaining faculties and objects. Therefore, the claim that this passage is an abbreviated summary is incorrect. Even if the remaining faculties and objects have not yet been clarified, how could they be addressed in advance in relation to the eye-faculty?
For the subsequent verses will clarify those remaining faculties and objects on their own. Thus, my current interpretation is correct.

Regarding the "abbreviated" [treatment]: it refers solely to the four categories of eye, body, form, and consciousness. As for the reason why this is known to be abbreviated, it is as discussed above:
the analysis of the higher and lower realms was conducted merely by taking birth in the desire realm and the second dhyāna as examples, borrowing the consciousness of the first dhyāna and so forth;

thus, it did not explain the matter in exhaustive detail. If one were to rely on the full text of the treatise, there would be an extensive analysis based on birth within all four dhyānas and so forth.

Regarding their characteristics: first, it is based on being born in the desire realm; next, it is based on using the eye of the first dhyāna to see forms of the desire realm and forms of the first dhyāna;

next, it is based on using the eye of the second dhyāna to see forms of the desire realm, forms of the first dhyāna, and forms of the second dhyāna, as well as using the eyes of the third and fourth dhyānas to see forms of the lower stages and forms of one’s own stage (all of the above refer to being born in the desire realm); next, it is based on...
When one is born in the body of the first dhyāna, one sees the forms of one’s own level; this should be considered accordingly for the third and fourth dhyānas as well.

When seeing the forms of one’s own level or of lower levels, it should be considered according to the principle. If one is born in the body of the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, one sees the forms of one’s own level or of other levels with the eyes of one’s own level or of other levels;
this should be considered according to the principle. Since the detailed characteristics are such that they cannot be fully set forth here, the text concludes by saying "not yet."

It is a grave error to claim that the analysis of the remaining faculties is called "concise" (*saṃkṣepa*). The one who translated the preceding verse simply modified the verse previously clarifying the eye;
he merely changed "eye" to "ear" and "form" to "sound," while the rest of the text remains identical.

Regarding the statement that "body-consciousness [perceives] its own level through contact," this refers to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) in relation to the tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*); it does not mean that consciousness should be correlated with the body-faculty and the tangible object as being of the same level.
Furthermore, since the body itself is the faculty (indriya) and possesses no distinct characteristic apart from it, only three [faculties] are mentioned as being different;

this does not include the nose and so forth, which are distinct from the body-faculty, thus resulting in four types. Regarding the statement that "three grasp objects through contact" (*prāptaviṣaya*), these are the nose, tongue, and body.
This means that for the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) in relation to the body-faculty, its object is "touched. This is said because the higher stages lack body-consciousness.

Regarding "wandering through meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and at the time of taking birth": wandering through meditative attainments refers to proceeding through the eight attainments in forward or reverse order, either ascending from the lower to the higher levels or descending from the higher to the lower, as explained in the *Samādhi* chapter.
At the time of taking birth, one may die here and be born in Akaniṣṭha, or die there and be born in the intermediate or lower realms; the mind is entirely indeterminate.

Regarding the statement that "the remaining thirteen elements (dhātus) are cognized only by the mental consciousness," this refers to the six sense organs (indriyas), the six consciousnesses (vijñānas), and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu);

none of these are cognized by the five sensory consciousnesses. Regarding the statement that "a portion of the dharma-element is permanent," this means that the dharma-element consists of four categories, and among these, only the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is permanent;
therefore, it is said to be "one portion. As for the remaining dharmas, they are the mental factors (caittas) and the non-associated formations (viprayuktasaṃskāras).

The three categories of phenomena, such as visible form (*rūpa*), are [the first eight]. Regarding the statement that "the first eight, beginning with life-force (*jīvita*," this refers to the five beginning with the eye, the two of male and female, and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—making eight.

Because they are not mental concomitants (*caitta*), they have no objects of perception (*ālambana*). The fourteen beginning with the mind (*manas*) are mental factors (*caitta*), and therefore they possess objects of perception.
The five elements beginning with visible form are the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), namely, conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
Those conditioned phenomena dissociated from volition, contact, and desire, as well as all unconditioned entities that are not faculties, are merely the substance of dharmas;
because they lack the sense of predominance (*adhipatya*), they are not called faculties. (The Chapter on the Elements [Dhātunirdeśa] concludes above.)
Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa (Abhidharmakośakārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā) Treatise Text,
Part Three Narrated by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.

In this treatise, this chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Faculties" (*Indriya-varga*); in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, it is called the "Chapter on Formations" (*Saṃskāra-varga*); and in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, it is called the "Chapter on Distinctions" (*Vaiśeṣika-varga*). (In this context, "formations" has the meaning of "predominant function," while "distinctions" has the meaning of "activity.

Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the two chapters on the "Faculties" and "Worlds" are combined and named the "Chapter on Formations," which differs from this [present work]. However, as for this...
Within this chapter, three categories of phenomena are fully elucidated: first, the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*); second, the co-arising phenomena;
and third, the six causes and four conditions. Because the faculties are presented first and because their functional efficacy is preeminent, they alone are designated by the term "faculties."

Regarding the statement that "the most excellent, sovereign, and manifest [factor] is called a faculty (*indriya*)," the masters of Western grammar (Sanskrit) hold that there is a verbal root (*dhātu*), a suffix (*pratyaya*), and a prefix (*upasarga*).
"Most excellent" is the verbal root; "sovereign" is the suffix; and "manifest" is the prefix.

Because these together constitute the meaning of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*), the *Nyāya* states: "This meaning of predominance clarifies the meaning of the verbal root, thereby manifesting the root—namely, the root *ī* (pronounced with a rising tone) meaning 'to go'."
Some say that "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) is the meaning of *i*, while "illuminating clarity" is the meaning of *kṣānti*.
"Blazing radiance" is the derivative sense of the letter;
with this derivative sense of the letter assisting it, the compound name *kṣānti-bhūmi*—meaning "sovereignty" and "illuminating clarity"—is further designated as "supreme sovereignty" (*adhipati*).
This is the meaning of "root" (*mūla*). Now, this treatise takes "supreme sovereignty" as the meaning of the *iḍā* element;

"illumination" is the phonetic auxiliary for the meaning of supreme sovereignty in the *iḍā* [element], while "lack of blazing" is the phonetic auxiliary for the meaning of the *kṣānti* (patience) element.
In Sanskrit it is called *indriya*, which is translated here as "root. This intention generally elucidates the twenty-two [faculties].
Regarding the question of whether each of the dharmas possesses a superior function (*adhipati-kāritra*) in relation to one another such that they should all be established as faculties (*indriya*):
the answer is that only those which possess an extreme degree of superiority are specifically designated as faculties.

This is just as the lion king and the village headman are designated as such because they possess an extreme degree of superiority over beasts and villagers, respectively; the faculties are likewise so named. The verse uses the term "it is traditionally said" (*kila*) to indicate that this is indeed the correct position.
The *Li* (Principle) says: "The initial statement of the tradition indicates that the author of the treatise does not favor the explanations of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Regarding the explanation of the five faculties, when asked why the eye and ear are explained first, followed by the nose, tongue, and so forth, the answer is:

"The three [faculties] beginning with the nose, which apprehend objects such as odors and tastes, are of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); therefore, they are explained separately. This refers to their function in giving rise to the three consciousnesses and their respective characteristics.

That which corresponds to the Dharma refers to the fact that the sense faculties, such as the nose and so forth, each give rise to their own consciousnesses and associated mental factors such as feeling and perception.

Regarding the distinctions among sentient beings: it means that at the beginning of the eon, sentient beings were produced from two organs, causing the various classes of sentient beings to be distinguished by gender—namely, the differences in gait, speech, the arrangement of breasts and hair, and so forth; some say these also include differences in courage and timidity.
Because there are distinctions [in faculties], they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*). Because there are distinctions in clothing and ornaments, they are called "differently distinguished.
Some say that these female and male faculties also possess sovereignty (*adhipati*) over defiled and purified phenomena;

for those such as the *paṇḍaka*, the *ṣaṇḍha*, and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), because their natures are impaired, they lack the non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) of defiled phenomena, and likewise lack the restraint (*saṃvara*), the attainment of fruits, and liberation.
Regarding the statement that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) can continue the past homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*) of pure phenomena:

this means that when the preceding homogeneous group has ceased, it is continued by the subsequent life-faculty. Regarding the statement that it can sustain the present homogeneous group: this means that it maintains the present homogeneous group;
thus, in relation to the preceding, it is called "continuation," while in relation to the present, it is called "sustenance. As for "future existence" (*punarbhava*), it means:
Regarding the statement "there must be [an intermediate state]," the term "seeking fragrance" (gandharva) refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), because it takes fragrance as its food;

this is what was formerly called a *gandharva*. Regarding the statement "the mind can lead the world," it means that the mind possesses sovereign power over the two kinds of worlds and is thus able to guide them;
both kinds of worlds are produced by karma, and the mind is able to universally encompass them.
The recipient’s mind takes the objects of the two worlds as its conditions and is able to universally embrace them, following along with those objects;

the latter two phrases conclude the two preceding meanings. Regarding the eight faculties of faith and so forth—namely, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, and the three untainted faculties—it is because all dharmas of complete purity grow and develop in accordance with these eight faculties.
Second, regarding the presentation of alternative views: what has been explained above is the tenet of the *Vibhāṣā* school; from here on is the Dharmaguptaka school (that is, the Sautrāntika).

This school maintains that it is the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that are capable of discernment, such as being able to avoid dangers and receiving edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), and not by means of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

Therefore, this master does not merely deny that the eye sees and so forth, but establishes that it is consciousness (*vijñāna*) that is capable of discernment, and that consciousness discerns its own object through [the power of] consciousness itself.
Because the eye arises [from its cause], the eye is established as a faculty (*indriya*); the other meanings are largely the same. Question:

If the eye and so forth are established as faculties because they exercise sovereignty (*adhipatya*) over consciousness, then visible form (*rūpa*) also exercises sovereignty over consciousness and should likewise be established as a faculty. Answer: There are two senses of "faculty":
first, it serves as the common support for the various consciousnesses that cognize many forms, such as blue; second, the consciousness follows the faculty and possesses clarity.

Because they are obscure, objects lack two characteristics: first, blue color serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) only for the consciousness that cognizes blue, and not for the consciousness that cognizes yellow and so forth;
second, matter is subject to transformation and decay (*vipariṇāma*), whereas consciousness does not follow this [transformation].

Therefore, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*). As for why two faculties are established based on the body, the treatise states: "The essence of the female and male faculties is not separate from the body faculty. By virtue of this...

These two faculties possess predominant influence; because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) at this location differs slightly from that of other places, they are established separately from the body-faculty.

The *Nyāyānusāra* (Correct Principle) objects, saying: "This also does not transcend the meaning already presented in the previous section, where it was stated that these two faculties have predominant influence regarding the differentiation of sentient beings and the differentiation of their individual forms. This statement takes up the latter two phrases to explain the former two.
This means that one should understand that the latter two phrases—“the five faculties of sensation” and so forth—explain the former two phrases, “abiding together” and so forth.

It is said that the five faculties of sensation have a predominant function regarding defilement (*saṃkleśa*), which does not differ from the previous master’s view; however, there is a distinction between these and the eight faculties, such as faith, mentioned by the previous master.

While the previous master held that those eight faculties collectively have a predominant function regarding pure phenomena (*vyavadāna*), the present master maintains that it is faith alone [that has this predominance].

Regarding the five faculties such as faith and so forth, in relation to the pure dharmas, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) increase in clarity as one progresses through the successive stages of the path.

As for the statement that "in the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*), one subdues the afflictions," this means that although one has not yet definitively severed them while practicing various contemplative exercises in these stages, one is able to prevent the afflictions from manifesting;
therefore, they are said to be "subdued. Regarding the statement "unknown" in relation to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)...

Regarding the predominance [of the faculties] in abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*): it is because in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one is able to abandon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other delusions regarding the principles of reality.

Regarding the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) in relation to the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*): this refers to the abandonment of greed and other delusions regarding phenomena (*vastu*) through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) in relation to happiness in the present life: this refers to the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*) dwelling in various meditative absorptions within the present body.
This is because one intends to experience happiness in the present life.

First, regarding the exposition of one's own school (*svasiddhānta*): the "new" [tradition] states that the Master [Vasubandhu] established the characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*) for the Mahīśāsaka school.

According to this, it is called "one's own school" because it is contrasted with later divergent views; it does not refer to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as the Buddha-dharma itself constitutes one's own school.
Regarding the phrase "about to clarify the inquiry": this means that before clarifying its meaning, one first raises the point of inquiry. As for the objection raised by the Sāṃkhya school:
that school establishes twenty-five principles (*tattva*), and now [the author] raises an objection based on the five active faculties (*karmendriya*).

All those established faculties must be extensively refuted. Now, concerning the discussion of the faculties: their number and nature are fixed and limited; yet you claim that the fleshly tongue has speech as its predominant function.
If an infant possesses a tongue, why does it not speak? Must one wait for training and study before being able to speak?
Just as the eye can see forms and sees them immediately upon birth, we know that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) must be defined by their specific capacities.

If the hand has predominance (*adhipatya*) over grasping, then the mouth should also be established as a faculty since it holds objects; and if the foot has predominance over walking, why does an infant, though possessing feet, not walk?
Furthermore, a snake has no feet; how is it able to move? This is merely because when different thoughts arise in different locations, distinct movements such as "walking" or "going" are designated.
As for the expulsion of excrement, it is called "filth" because one considers it impure and casts it away, like an object in mid-air that is discarded without further utility.
Moreover, it is drawn out by the power of the wind. As for urine, it exists in those who engage in sexual desire, but it does not exist in infants who have not yet engaged in such desire.

Furthermore, because pleasure arises when these [organs] are present, one might argue that the throat, teeth, eyes, lips, and limbs should also be established as faculties (*indriya*), since they possess the functional power to swallow, chew, open and close, and bend and extend.
Therefore, there is no fixed limit; it is not appropriate to establish them as faculties.
As for how the five feeling-faculties cause the six faculties to become defiled, this refers to suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.

It causes the arising of greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth; it is called "defiled" (saṃkleśa) because it is associated with afflictions (*kleśa*)—this refers specifically to the mental faculty (*manas*);
and it is called "defiled" because it is bound by afflictions—this applies to all six faculties. Regarding these six faculties becoming untainted and pure (*anāsrava-viśuddha*):

the old [commentary] states that "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*) and "abiding" (*sthiti*) both encompass the six faculties; "the defiled provisions" (*saṃkleśa-sambhāra*) and "purity" (*viśuddhi*) alone [apply].

Regarding the statement in the *Yixin lun* (Treatise on the New Mind) that there are two kinds: if it is established as being untainted (*anāsrava*) in its very essence, it refers exclusively to the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*);
if it is called "pure" because it is free from the bonds of its own afflictions, it then pertains to all six faculties.
To say that the female and male faculties arise from those [faculties] is stated in reference to birth from a womb or egg in the desire realm;

however, this involves the fallacy of non-universality, as there are cases where they do not arise from the female and male faculties and thus would not qualify as faculties by measure (*pramāṇa*). To say that they "depend on those" means that the six consciousnesses depend upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) for their subsistence.
To say "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) refers to the stopping of birth and death, wherein the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) reach their ultimate end.
Because it is severed and extinguished, that which was originally due to afflictions and the cycle of birth and death now severs delusion and returns to the truth;

thus it is called "returning to extinction" (*pratyāgama-nirodha*). The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Flowing and turning" refers to taking further rebirth, while "returning to extinction" refers to proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the statement that these share the same four meanings as the preceding [section], they are: (1) the basis, (2) arising, (3) abiding, and (4) enjoyment. It is said that the five faculties beginning with faith are the "basis."
"Support" (*āśraya*) refers to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), which serve as the basis for attaining *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"The cessation of birth and death is the meaning of 'returning to extinction' (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The basis for this attainment consists of the five [faculties] beginning with faith, because they are the most excellent causes for the growth of all roots of goodness.
Regarding the phrase "first arising within the group of those fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), it means the attainment of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
The "group of those fixed in the rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) refers to those who are yet to know what is unknown (*ājñātāvīndriya*), situated in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Because the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) is at the very beginning of the path of seeing, it is said that this [attainment] arises for the first time. Regarding the statement "causing the attainment of nirvāṇa to arise in succession," this means that the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*), while in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), constantly maintains this attainment, causing it to arise in succession.
Regarding the statement "experiencing happiness in the present life," this refers to one who possesses full knowledge (*ājñātāvī*).

Since the faculties (*indriya*) within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) receive bliss only when delusions are exhausted and liberation is perfected, it is said that "thereby they neither decrease nor increase.

This means that there are only twenty-two faculties, with no further increase or decrease; this does not refer to the organs of speech and so forth, nor to ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, as these have already been refuted previously.
As for the statement that "the sequence is established by this very condition" in the Sūtra, it refers to the respective processes of saṃsāra and *nivṛtti* (cessation).
Regarding the principle of the four meanings established in the Sūtra, the sequence of the faculties (*indriya*) is as follows:

first the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are taught, next male and female, then life (*jīvita*) along with the five feelings (*vedanā*), and finally faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, including the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*).

It is not mentioned in the formal exposition because the masters of the Abhidharma teach the mind faculty (*manas*) after the life faculty; thus, it does not accord with this sequence of the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*). As for its...
The sequence has already been explained as previously established.

Regarding the statement that "the eight faculties have already been discussed in the Chapter on Elements," this refers to the fact that the aforementioned chapter concludes its explanation of the six faculties beginning with the eye, as well as the male and female faculties, though it does not provide a detailed analysis there;
this is fully clarified in the main treatise. As for the statement that "the life faculty and faith, etc., will be analyzed below," this refers to the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

In the section on the "Non-associated [factors]" (*viprayukta*), within the explanation of mental factors such as clarity (*ābhoga*) and so forth, it is distinguished that those associated with the five consciousnesses are called "bodily sensation" (*kāyikī vedanā*).

Generally, there are three meanings for the term "body" (*kāya*): first, the meaning of continuity (*saṃtati*); second, the meaning of substance (*dravya*); and third, the meaning of accumulation (*rāśi*).

If one says "the body of the six consciousnesses," then "body" has the meaning of substance. If one says "bodily sensation," then "body" refers to the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-rāśi*), and this aggregate of matter is termed "body."
Because these five faculties are collectively termed "body" (*kāya*)—in contrast to the mind—the feeling that relies upon this body is called "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*).

This shall be analyzed in detail in the commentary on the *Lokadhātu-paṭala*. Regarding the statement that the third dhyāna is "free from the craving for joy," it means that although the third dhyāna is a mental delight, its character is tranquil;
thus, it is designated as "pleasure" (*sukha*) and not as "joy" (*prīti*), because the characteristic of joy...
It surges and ebbs like waves upon water; it is also like a poor man who, having once obtained treasure, loses it all at once and consequently gives rise to sorrow and affliction.

In the first and second dhyānas, joy (*prīti*) arises as a pervasive sensation throughout both body and mind; because one relishes and becomes attached to this joy, it is termed "craving for joy" (*prīti-rāga*).

In the third dhyāna, because one is free from this craving, it is simply called "bliss" (*sukha*). Furthermore, because the third dhyāna lacks the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), [this distinction holds].
Question: Is it only the mind that is called "joy"? Answer: In the three dhyānas, the mind is extremely joyful and associated with pleasure (*sukha*);

in the hells, the mind is extremely displeased and associated with suffering (*duḥkha*). Question: How can extreme joy be associated with pleasure? How can extreme impairment of discrimination not be associated with suffering?
Answer: Regarding equanimity (*upekṣā*), there are two kinds: first, the feeling of equanimity, which is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).

Regarding the two types of equanimity (*upekṣā*): the equanimity that abandons lethargy and agitation is subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). However, the "equanimity" mentioned here refers to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), not the equanimity of formation.

To say it "exists in the body" is not [the case]; rather, "arising by the power of the object" means that it does not arise through internal mental discrimination, but arises solely by the power of the preceding objective field (*viṣaya*) as pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "Arhats and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes those who have attained the three lower fruits of the path.

Regarding the statement that "the noble ones are the same as ordinary beings": this means that although the Noble Ones have no internal discrimination, they still experience pleasure and pain according to the power of external objects;

how much more so for ordinary beings? As for the statement that "three faculties are established based on nine," within the five feelings (*vedanā*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*) are excluded because the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), being a state of distraction, lacks the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) faculty, and because sorrow is abandoned through detachment from desire (*vairāgya*).

Since the untainted (anāsrava) path of suffering is restricted solely to the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and likewise does not extend to the untainted [mental consciousness], both are excluded.

Regarding the statement that "the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is simultaneous with the acquisition of doubt," this means that at this time the essence of the affliction does not arise;

rather, it is simultaneous with the acquisition of the affliction because patience is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that directly severs this acquisition, just as when driving out a thief, one is still accompanied by the thief until the stage of knowledge (*jñāna*).

At that time, one attains liberation. [Question: Does this patience (*kṣānti*) not coexist with the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of other afflictions? Why is it spoken of as coexisting specifically with the acquisition of doubt (*vicikitsā*) alone? [Answer:

In reality, it does indeed coexist with the acquisitions of other [afflictions] such as greed (*lobha*), but because the name "doubt" is particularly opposed to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), only the term "doubt" is designated.
Regarding the phrase "the activity of 'never-before-known' and 'to-be-known'": the word "activity" (*pravṛtti*) means "arising" (*vartana*), and the word "arising" means "birth" (*utpāda*).
This means that one should know there will be the arising of a subsequent cognition (*anvaya-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement that "seven cognitions arise in the interim," this is discussed by way of a general overview of both the upper and lower realms, wherein there are eight truths (*satya*) in total. Since each truth has one cognition, there are eight cognitions in all.

Excluding the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent cognition of the path), because it knows the truths exhaustively, the preceding seven cognitions do not yet know the truths completely; thus, they arise in the interim. For example, this is like the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* (dharma-cognition of suffering).

Although the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the desire realm has already been known, the remaining seven truths have not yet been known. This is stated in reference to the eight truths collectively, rather than discussing them individually according to their respective truths.

At the stage of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), there are seven truths yet to be known; at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*), there are six truths yet to be known.
In this manner, it continues until the stage of the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), where [the truths of] form and formlessness...

Because one has yet to know what is to be known regarding the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), fifteen moments of mind are collectively termed the faculty of "knowing what is yet to be known" (*ājñātāvy-avindriya*).

This continues until, through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), one knows that the categories [of the truths] have been fully understood, at which point it is called the faculty of "having already known" (*ājñendriya*). Regarding the statement "eliminating the afflictions that delude one concerning phenomena":

this means that while the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) delude one concerning principles (*tattva*), the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) delude one concerning phenomena. Since we are here eliminating only those of the path of cultivation, they are said to "delude one concerning phenomena. "Phenomena" (*vastu*) refers here to objective entities (*viṣaya-vastu*). Question:

Within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are also the refinement of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) and the attainment of happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

Why, then, is it said that [the path] is solely for the purpose of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*)? The answer is: The refinement of the faculties is undertaken out of fear of falling back into the afflictions; furthermore, the attainment of happiness in the present life is itself a path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) for abandoning the afflictions.

Thus, the meaning of "abandoning the afflictions" subsumes all other purposes. For this reason, the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) spoke only of "abandoning the afflictions," implying that the others are already understood.
The "knower" (*ājñātṛ*) is that which was already known previously and is now known again; thus it is called the "faculty of having known" (*ājñātendriya*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:

"Since the sixteenth moment of mind should be similar to the preceding seven knowledges (*jñāna*), why is it alone designated as the faculty of having known, rather than being called 'correct knowledge' (*ājñā*)?
The answer is: This is stated from the perspective of the majority. That is to say, although the first moment resembles the seven knowledges, the subsequent moments...

Because each moment is distinct from the preceding one, it is designated as the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*) by way of its predominant state. Regarding the statement that it forms the cognition "I have known what was to be known":

this means that within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because afflictions still exist, one is unable to form the cognition "I have known what was to be known" regarding the principles of the Four Truths;
whereas in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), because there are no more delusions, one is able to form the cognition "I have known" regarding the objects of the Truths.
This refers to the understanding of what is already known. "Complete" (*samanvāgata*) means that one achieves this knowledge by relying on a person;

therefore, it is called "complete. Question: If that is so, should the first two faculties also be called "complete"? Answer: If we speak in terms of the meaning of "achieving," they are indeed the same.

However, because the meanings of "knowing" differ, there is a distinction. In the previous commentary within this chapter, both were explained in relation to the Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the Knowledge of Non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Regarding the second [type of] wisdom, the *Xinyi* (New Translation) states: "This refers to those of dull faculties who attain only the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)," which differs from the present chapter.

The second [explanation] interprets "endowment" (*samanvāgata*) in terms of practicing for the exhaustion [of defilements]. "Endowment" means that one who has practiced the aforementioned knowledge and thereby perfected its nature is said to be "endowed.

The *Xinyi* further states: "This refers to those of sharp faculties who attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). It also says: "One who is capable of practicing is called 'endowed'; such a person is endowed [with it]."

Regarding the statement that the root of the household is called the faculty of full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*), if one explains this as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound, it is because the names of these faculties—such as "not-yet-known" (*anājñātam*) and so forth—are applied to the person.
This is the correct principle for a *tatpuruṣa*. Alternatively, if the name refers directly to the phenomenon (*dharma*), it is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative) compound.

These two interpretations are not mutually contradictory, as each relies on a different sense. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Although the names of these faculties are twenty-two, among all the faculties..."

In substance, there are only seventeen [faculties], because the two faculties of female and male are subsumed under the faculty of body, and the three untainted faculties are subsumed under nine faculties.

Regarding the statement that those with form and the life-faculty are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*): there are two kinds of "contaminations" (*āsrava*). First, that which coexists with its own afflictions is called a "contamination.
Second, that which serves as an object for others is called "contaminated" (*sāsrava*). All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones in training (*śaikṣa*) possess both types.
For those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and for Buddhas, there is only one type [of faculty], which merely gives rise to the outflows (āsrava) in others while being itself without outflows (anāsrava).

Regarding the statement that the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) are both with and without outflows: according to the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* in the Mahīśāsaka school, the five faculties beginning with faith are exclusively without outflows, because the Sūtra states:
"If someone is entirely devoid of the five faculties beginning with faith, I declare that they abide in the category of external worldlings (bāhyapṛthagjana)."

Therefore, it is further said that the noble ones possess [this] while ordinary beings do not. To this, the Master replies: "That is taught in reliance upon the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), not in reliance upon the tainted faculties (*sāsrava-indriya*); thus, it applies to both types.

Regarding the question: "If life-force is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*), then who is it that prolongs the present body—already summoned by past karma—by means of extending its lifespan?"
Regarding the maturation (*vipāka*) that prolongs life, the treatise states: "It refers to an Arhat who has attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and mastery over the mind;
if, toward the Saṃgha or an individual, he makes a gift according to his means and immediately enters the meditative absorption of the limit (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*), he makes this vow:
'May whatever karma capable of producing the maturation of wealth be transformed so as to produce the fruit of the maturation of longevity.'"
At that time, those karmas capable of producing the maturation of wealth all turn toward producing the maturation of longevity as their result.
Regarding what constitutes the maturation of this [result], the Sarvāstivāda school offers several explanations. A new interpretation states that the correct explanation is as follows:

among the many karmas from previous lives capable of producing the result of wealth that have not yet been experienced, through the present act of giving, entering meditative concentration, and making a vow, one does not [further] deliberate...

By the power of deliberation, one may transform karma that was intended to produce the fruit of wealth so that it instead attracts the fruit of longevity; this [longevity] is also a *vipāka* (maturation), specifically the maturation fruit of the karma for wealth.

If one follows the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*), who asserts that it is the momentum (*vega*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) induced during meditative concentration (*samādhi*) persisting over time, and not a *vipāka*, then [one must consider that] joy (*saumanasya*) and the others are likewise [not *vipāka*], because sorrow (*daurmanasya*) pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and thus is not *vipāka*. If that were the case, then joy and the rest would also [not be *vipāka*].

If it were common to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, it would follow that it is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*); one should say that mental pain (*daurmanasya*) is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome, and therefore not a result of maturation.

The statement that it is "common" refers to its being common to the two categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome by way of their own names; it does not mean that it is common to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as is the case with joy (*saumanasya*).

Furthermore, for those who have abandoned desire, there is no result of maturation consisting of mental pain; since this is not the case [for other faculties], it is not a result of maturation. Moreover, the treatise states: "If the eight faculties, beginning with the eye..."

If it occurs in a happy realm, it is a wholesome fruition; if it occurs in an unhappy realm, it is an unwholesome fruition. The eight faculties refer to the seven material faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Regarding the "gate of having fruition" (*savipāka-mukha*): this refers to being designated as "having the former gate" based on the capacity to produce a future fruit of fruition.

Because their nature consists of maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth, these two categories rely on distinct bases; it is for the sake of excluding [other meanings] that the verse uses the term "certainly" (*niyata*).

That is to say, the basis for the meaning of "only" and the basis for the meaning of "excluding" are such that the verse states "certainly exists. Regarding the statement that the untainted (*anāsrava*) has no maturation:

because the untainted is neither moistened by afflictions nor does it destroy the three realms of existence (*bhava*), it lacks maturation. Regarding the four feelings with the exception of sorrow (*daurmanasya*): sorrow is necessarily...

The discussion regarding those with maturation (*savipāka*) has already been clarified previously. The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); thus, by simply stating "wholesome or unwholesome," it is understood that it possesses maturation.

The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are exclusively wholesome in nature; therefore, by simply stating "if they are contaminated," they are distinguished from the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

As for the eight faculties beginning with faith, which occupy the very end [of the list], the reason they are explained here first is that in the preceding section, faith and the others were explained later.
Now, because it follows from what precedes and is clarified by what comes before, the treatise states: "Although it occurs later, it is mentioned first because it relies on what precedes.

Regarding the statement that *daurmanasya* (sorrow) pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome: if one sorrows because the practice of virtue has not succeeded and this wholesome undertaking is not accomplished, this sorrow is called wholesome.

If one sorrows because the commission of evil has not succeeded, this is unwholesome sorrow; because it functions as a movement of mental distress (*daurmanasya*), it is not obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Because they arise from discrimination and are neither unobscured-neutral nor neutral, they are exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.
Regarding the subsequent meanings assigned to the first phrase: the first phrase introduces the three realms;

having now excluded the latter three, the first phrase is assigned to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the second phrase to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the third phrase to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding those whose bodies lack the female or male faculties, [the author] resolves this objection by stating that although the nose and tongue faculties may be of no use there, they are not unattractive;
rather, they serve to adorn the body. Furthermore, women and men do exist in that realm, for it is not otherwise.
Thus, the Sūtra says that the Form Realm is called "male," as the Sūtra states: "There is the possibility and the occasion for a male body to become a Brahmā. No such thing exists.

There is no place where a female body can become a Brahmā (the commentary explains: there are places where a male body can become a Brahmā, but there is no place where a female body becomes a Brahmā; "Brahmā" refers to the Pure Heaven).
Those who possess male characteristics (puruṣa-lakṣaṇa) have all the physical features, appearance, and bodily attributes belonging to a male body; however, they lack the male organ (*puruṣendriya*).
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that because their intense renunciation of desire resembles the function of a male, their bodies are pure and sublime.

Regarding "pure and sublime," the *Xinlun* (New Commentary) says there is no suffering resulting from outflow (*niṣyanda-duḥkha*). [The commentary explains: This means that if the bodily features were coarse, one would experience much suffering over time; since the body is now pure and sublime, suffering does not arise. This refers to what occurs in the present life, as it is not produced by prior karma; therefore, it is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*).

Those who possess no unwholesome deeds do not experience the suffering of karmic maturation (that is to say, those above [the desire realm] lack adverse conditions; unlike those in the hells and other realms, they do not possess unwholesome deeds accompanied by adverse conditions that result in the suffering of maturation).

According to the Sautrāntika school, pleasure and pain follow the body up to the fourth dhyāna, while sorrow and joy follow the mind up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—the intention of that school being that where there is a body, there is pleasure and pain, and where there is a mind, there is sorrow and joy.
The seven faculties that are material (*rūpa*) are the five beginning with the eye, as well as the male and female faculties; these are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Regarding the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), this means that although contaminated faith and the others are not abandoned by their own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), they are abandoned through the severance of their objects and fetters (*ālambana-bandhana-prahāṇa*), and are therefore included among those abandoned through cultivation.

As for the statement that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not what is abandoned, this refers to the case where [they are]... if there is... [if they were contaminated, they would be abandoned].

The outflows (*āsrava*) possess faults that can be severed and are therefore termed "to be abandoned" (*heya*); because the untainted (*anāsrava*) are without fault, they are not "to be abandoned. The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"Is it not the case that the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is also something to be abandoned? As the Sūtra says: "The Noble Path is like a raft," and so forth. The explanation is:

this [path] is not termed "not to be abandoned" in the sense of being abandoned by seeing or cultivation; rather, it is called "not to be abandoned" because it is relinquished at the stage of entering the realm of Nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Therefore, it is called "abandonment," and thus there is no contradiction.
Regarding the gate of obtaining rebirth through maturation (*vipāka*), the *Nyāyānusāra* asks: "The purpose of this gate is to refute the claim that a non-defiled mind can link rebirth.
The commentary explains: "The Mahāsāṃghika school maintains that one takes rebirth with a non-defiled mind, as in the case of a Bodhisattva."

Regarding the three periods of correct awareness, or the Sautrāntika position that the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) undergoes rebirth—this section is established to refute those views by asserting that one acquires only the two maturations of body and life.
This is because at the stage of taking rebirth, one only acquires these two;

it is only at the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), when the four [senses] beginning with the eye and the female or male faculty arise, that one intentionally abandons the two faculties, even though they are currently present.

Because at the moment of rebirth it is necessarily defiled, it is not a maturation (*vipāka*). Furthermore, there is no mental faculty (*manas*) that has already been acquired prior to that time, as it would not yet be called "possessed" (*samanvāgata*) at that moment.
Moreover, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*) is not produced by maturation, and the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth are likewise not maturation.
Furthermore, at the initial moment of taking birth, there are no faculties such as suffering, pleasure, or joy; thus, although they are possessed [at that time], they are not maturation.

This is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*). Nor is it said that the two faculties of mind and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are established [at birth]; since even their manifestation is not mentioned, how much less so the nine [faculties] such as suffering (*duḥkha*)?

It is logical that they are merely established but not manifested, for the principle lies beyond words. Regarding those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) who possess six, seven, or eight [faculties]:

at the initial stage of transformation, those born from moisture or from eggs may possess two [sexual organs], while those born by transformation possess both male and female organs. Transformation occurs only in the state of birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) and does not extend to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), because the intermediate...

Because there is a certainty of male and female bodies. For example, those without form in the desire realm—namely, those who are born by transformation (*upapāduka*) as gods with form—are necessarily endowed with the sense-faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life, yet they lack the female and male faculties.

When it is said that such beings in the desire realm are superior to those in the two lower realms, it means that while the formless realm has no physical location and does not exist above the two realms, here [in the discussion of superiority], it is merely by virtue of...

Regarding "superior in terms of cause and effect" and "superior to the two lower realms," it is called "superior concentration" because this concentration can induce a fruit of eighty thousand kalpas in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As for "superior to the lower realms," it means that one attains the long-lasting fruit of eighty thousand kalpas,
which is superior to those of the lower realms.

Regarding the section on the number of faculties that cease (*nirodha-indriya*), the reason the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) is explained first is that in the preceding section, the formless realm was mentioned last;

now, taking advantage of that immediate context, it is explained first. As for the eight faculties that cease in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), this is because during the states of death and birth there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and no joy (*saumanasya*) or pleasure (*sukha*);
furthermore, since beings there are born by transformation (*upapāduka*), they necessarily possess the eye-faculty and the others, thus totaling eight.
It should be understood that herein, all moments of mind that cease and enter the past at the point of death are termed "abandonment" (*tyāga*).
This is because for one who dies instantaneously—such as those who are killed—the eye and other faculties are all abandoned simultaneously;

furthermore, at the precise moment of death, there is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and thus there is no joy (*prīti*) or pleasure (*sukha*). As for the four gradual [deaths], they are as follows:
In one who is gradually dying, the eye and other faculties all cease first; at the actual moment of death, only four faculties cease.

Regarding the number of faculties required to attain the fruits [of the path], the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Although the fruits of śrāmaṇya are not themselves faculties, this discussion concerns the faculties;
therefore, it asks specifically about the faculties. Among the twenty-two faculties, why is it said that only nine faculties attain the fruits?

Answer: Herein, all [factors] are based on those associated with the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) that possess efficacy toward the fruit; only these are discussed, such as the five faculties and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Those that do not directly produce the fruit are not considered here. This is not because they are contaminated (*sāsrava*);

for if it were so, the path of the world (*laukikamārga*) which realizes the fruit would also be excluded, as it is contaminated. If one argues that although the mental faculty (*manas*) is common to both the uncontaminated and the contaminated, it is taken [here] because it is the master of sentient beings, [we reply: no. *Note: The original Chinese text contains a complex argument regarding the definition of the "faculties" (*indriya*) in the context of Abhidharma psychology.

It distinguishes between those factors that are associated with a concentrated mind and have causal power toward the fruition of the path, versus those that lack such direct productivity. It clarifies that the exclusion of certain factors is not due to their being contaminated, but rather due to their lack of specific functional efficacy in this context.*

Since one who delights in relinquishment is not the master [of the object], how could they take it? Therefore, we know that this is explained solely in terms of functional power (*vīrya*). Regarding the statement "the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) relies on the *anāgamya*":

this means that as long as one has not abandoned the defilements of desire (*kāmarāga*), one does not attain the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*), but relies only on the *anāgamya*. Within the *anāgamya* concentration, there is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*);

thus, the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) to induce the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyogaprāpti*). This refers to the path of immediate succession.

That which shares the same untainted nature (*anāsrava*) as the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). Arising prior to the acquisition, it is able to induce the arising of that acquisition and is therefore termed its "inducing cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).

Since this acquisition of dissociation is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), it is also called a "fruit.

Although the term "fruit of the śramaṇa" (*śrāmaṇya-phala*) also applies generally to other conditioned states of liberation, we now ask: how many [causes] are capable of realizing it, and what [is the result]?
Regarding the fruit of śrāmaṇya, for the time being, it is answered that it consists in the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).

As for the statement that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is called the "supporting cause" (*niśraya-hetu*), "support" (*niśraya*) means to sustain; that is, because this [acquisition] arises depending upon it, the path serves as the support for the acquisition.

It is not the case that the path which arises prior to the acquisition is called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Although the path of liberation is not a homogeneous cause with respect to the fruit of śrāmaṇya..."
However, because these are associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), there is no fault in saying that they obtain those fruits;

for the essence of the fruits of śramaṇaship arises through mutual dependence, and when viewed in relation to one another, they constitute results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Who could possibly prevent this?

(The commentary explains: Since it is stated here that these are associated and co-existent causes, it is clearly understood that conditioned liberation (*saṃskṛta-vimukti*) is taken as the essential nature of the fruit, because the acquisition of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*) is not an associated or co-existent cause. Because...

Regarding the Arhat’s penetration through the nine stages (*navabhūmi*), this means that within these nine stages there are all equally untainted paths (*anāsravamārga*). However, these untainted nine stages are not the same as the tainted nine stages. This is because [the untainted ones] exclude the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), taking instead the "Not-Yet-Arrived" (*anāgamya*) and the "Intermediate" (*dhyānāntara*) stages; whereas the tainted nine stages exclude the Not-Yet-Arrived and Intermediate stages, taking instead the Desire Realm and the Peak of Existence. This distinction can be known from the following: [The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The untainted path is cultivated in nine stages; the tainted path is cultivated in nine stages. This indicates that the untainted path is cultivated in nine stages by excluding the Desire Realm and the Peak of Existence, while the tainted path is cultivated in nine stages by excluding the Not-Yet-Arrived and Intermediate stages. Thus, the two sets of nine stages differ. Furthermore, the untainted path is cultivated in nine stages by excluding the Desire Realm and the Peak of Existence, while the tainted path is cultivated in nine stages by excluding the Not-Yet-Arrived and Intermediate stages. Therefore, it is clear that the two sets of nine stages are distinct. Finally, the untainted path is cultivated in nine stages by excluding the Desire Realm and the Peak of Existence, while the tainted path is cultivated in nine stages by excluding the Not-Yet-Arrived and Intermediate stages. Consequently, it is evident that the two sets of nine stages are different. Thus, it should be understood that the untainted nine stages and the tainted nine stages are not identical. This is why it is said that the Arhat’s penetration through the nine stages refers to the fact that within those nine stages there are all equally untainted paths.
