however, in its actual substance, it is one. Regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), there are four aspects in total. As for what is called the "reflected image" (*pratibimba*):

This refers to the category of mental phenomena that arise conditioned by the mind, appearing like various distinct images on the surface of a mirror reflecting objects according to their respective types.
These mental factors are neither permanent nor annihilated, neither identical to nor separate from the mind.

Just as the colors of the images reflected in a mirror are not different from the mirror itself—though there may be many blue appearances, they are all the same blue—so too are sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
Because each of these mental factors (caitta) individually bears the aspect of blue, it is said that although they are many, they are all identical in being a single aspect of blue;

thus, they may be called "possessing an aspect" (sākāra). [Question: Since it was already stated previously that they possess an aspect, why is it now said again that they "may be called possessing an aspect"?
[Answer: This should be understood as citing a treatise to establish the previous meaning, though it is slightly inconvenient to call them by four names.

Regarding "correspondence" (*yoga*): this fourth name is a collective designation for the five meanings—the three [factors] previously mentioned, such as the basis (*āśraya*), along with the two subsequent matters of time—taken together to form this term.

As for the word "category" (*jāti*) in the verse, the older translations state that "category" means "lineage" (*gotra*); that is, the fourteen different types of lineages. This is according to this [text].

In this treatise, there are only fourteen [factors]. According to the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle), because the nature of conjunction (*sāmagrī*) is added, it says: "and the nature of conjunction. This means that the nature of conjunction is added to the fourteen. Question:
Since this treatise does not mention the nature of conjunction, under what category is it subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed under the "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāyasabhāga*).

That is to say, when one receives the precepts, one acquires the homogeneity of the group; when one causes a schism in the Saṃgha, one abandons it. Question: Does causing a schism in the Saṃgha [not constitute a transgression]? [The text continues: ...no.

Question: If *saṃgha-sāmagrī* (concord) is itself non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), what is the harm? For concord has acquisition as its essence. Answer: When we discuss acquisition, there must necessarily be something acquired;
however, concord is characterized by the absence of anything to be acquired, and therefore its essence is non-acquisition. [Objection: This is merely a brief omission of mention;
it does not mean that apart from what is explained here, nothing else exists—just as among the mental factors (*caitta*), fear and so forth are not mentioned, yet they are included within them.

Because it is included within the category [of conditioned phenomena], according to correct reasoning, the addition of the nature of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga) is not the intention of either treatise; there is no contradiction here.
Regarding the "conditioned factors dissociated from mind" (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra), one should generally state that they are "neither matter nor mind.

Here, however, we speak briefly as "dissociated formations," which is sufficient to exclude all other dharmas. By stating "dissociated," one excludes all mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta).

Regarding the brevity of terminology for formations (*saṃskāra*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), because these do not belong to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), various treatises often preserve abbreviated names.

As for the attainment of accomplishment (*prāpti-siddhi*), there are general and specific explanations of its meaning; generally speaking, both "acquisition" (*lābha*) and "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) [refer to this].

Regarding the distinction between "acquisition" (*prāpti*) and "attainment" (*samanvāgama*): at the time of acquisition, it is not called attainment; at the time of attainment, it is not called acquisition.

Therefore, we know that "acquisition" is the general term, while "attainment" is the specific one. Furthermore, reaching the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) is called acquisition, and reaching the present is called attainment;
thus, even this usage of the term "acquisition" is a specific sense. Hence, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Although the meanings of acquisition, attainment, and accomplishment..."

This is a single entity, yet it is explained as having distinctions based on different perspectives (*paryāya*). Furthermore, the *Chao* (Excerpts) states that "attainment" (*prāpti*) applies to both the new and the old;

however, when referring specifically to attainment through accomplishment (*siddhi*), it refers only to new attainment and does not include established accomplishment (*niṣpanna-siddhi*). Based on what has been stated above, whether taken collectively or individually, non-attainment (*aprāpti*) should be understood by inferring it from the opposite of attainment.
If one considers it in relation to its own kind (*sabhāga*), then only the "characteristic of arising" (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) in the very first moment is called attainment.
The characteristic of cessation at the final moment is called "abandonment" (*tyāga*). At that time, non-possession (*aprāpti*) reaches the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).

Although, during the interval between these two, each momentary thought reaches its own characteristic of arising, such categories of phenomena are always termed "accomplished" (*samanvāgata*); because they are not newly acquired at this point, they are not termed "possession.
If one were to discuss the three characteristics of a single moment in terms of their sequence, the characteristic of arising would certainly involve acquisition.

At that time, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*); when it reaches the phase of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*), it is called "accomplishment" (*samanvāgama*); only when it reaches the phase of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is it called "abandonment" (*tyāga*).

That which has fallen away into the past is called "non-accomplishment" (*asamanvāgama*). Question: Why is it that at the very beginning, upon reaching the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is not called "accomplishment"?

Answer: Because within that [present] continuum, one still possesses non-possession (*aprāpti*). Non-possession is explained by analogy [to this case]. Next, according to the topical outline (*anukrama*), the explanation follows.
Regarding the [fault of] establishing another's body: if one were to establish another's body, there would be the fault of the confusion of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).

That is to say, if a human were to establish the nature of a ghost or an animal, that person should then be called a ghost or an animal. Furthermore, if one were to establish insentient things (*asattva*), there would be the fault of everything becoming a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) by common consensus, as well as the fault of the indeterminacy of insentient things, because it would destroy the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

(The commentary explains: Conditioned phenomena are not permitted to be established through common consensus; if they were so established now, then all people would simultaneously establish them, which is the fault of common consensus.)

Regarding the fault of "indefiniteness concerning insentient things": if one were to establish that what is non-sentient is precisely this sentient being, then would it be sentient or non-sentient? [End of previous section. If that is so, why does the Sūtra say:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that there is a Wheel-turning King who possesses the seven jewels," and so forth, at length? [The explanation says: The intention of the Sarvāstivāda school here is that "possessing" (*samanvāgata*) means having mastery over the jewels, not the actual acquisition (*prāpti*) of them.

According to the Sautrāntika school, they establish only seeds (*bīja*) and do not allow for real acquisition, because such acquisition cannot be perceived as a present reality in the same way that form (*rūpa*) and other phenomena can. A commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* provides a refutation, stating: "Among the seven jewels, the wheel, the jewel, and so forth, are non-sentient; the ministers..."

[The Sautrāntika objection: "If women and so forth become other bodies that are composed of the seven treasures (*saptaratna*), it is clear that they also become other bodies and non-sentient things (*asattva*). [The Abhidharma-kośa] response: "It is because the Wheel-Turning King possesses sovereign power over those seven treasures, and they revolve according to the King's will. (End of section above.
"Acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) exist only with respect to the two types of cessation (*nirodha*)," [this statement] excludes empty space (*ākāśa*).

"All sentient beings possess, from beginningless time, the 'non-arising dharma' (*anutpatti-dharma*) characterized by the deficiency of conditions (*pratyaya-vaidhurya*). Therefore, in relation to this...
Within the Dharma, who achieves the untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*)? It refers to all sentient beings, which is to say, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The phrase "the first moment" excludes noble ones (*ārya*) who are still bound by fetters (*sakalabandhana*) at the second moment; the phrase "bound by fetters" excludes those who have previously abandoned defilements.
Alternatively, this single clause directly designates the specific state [of the first moment] while universally excluding other categories and all others.

Ordinary beings bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana-pṛthagjana*) must be excluded because they have not yet abandoned the afflictions and have not yet attained analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
As for "all other sentient beings," this refers to those outside the aforementioned exclusions:

those from the stage of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna*) onwards, as well as noble ones (*ārya*) who have previously abandoned defilements through the patience regarding the suffering [of the desire realm] (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), and all other ordinary beings who have abandoned the afflictions; all such categories are included.
It is an error to state in the chapter on "That Which Is Called 'The Remainder'—the Attainment of Cessation through Analysis" that "the remaining sentient beings" refers to all noble ones (*ārya*).
Since the treatise explicitly excludes ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), it is clear that those not so bound are the ones intended.

Furthermore, there is no one who possesses space (*ākāśa*), because space is a non-obstructive phenomenon (*anāvṛti-dharma*) and does not arise; thus, it differs from cessation not through analysis (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Because it is not induced by the power of the Path, it is unlike *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation); therefore, there is no attainment (*prāpti*) of it. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Since space is not induced by the mind, there is no contradiction; it arises internally. Having already explained its essence and characteristics based on this treatise (*Abhidharmakośa*), we shall now clarify the distinctions of attainment according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
Within this, first attainment is explained, followed by non-attainment (*aprāpti*). It is said that these do not exist prior to or subsequent to [the dharma].

Regarding "simultaneous" (*saha*): because [the dharmas] are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and non-arising (*anutpāda*), it cannot be said that their acquisition (*prāpti*) occurs prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with them.
Above, we distinguished acquisitions based on the dharmas themselves, which yielded only four types. Below, we distinguish the dharmas based on their acquisitions;

here, the simultaneous acquisitions differ, resulting in six distinct varieties. Some say that among these there are also cases of simultaneous acquisition; this means that although wisdom (*jñāna*) is ultimately...
Because that which has not yet arisen shares its acquisition with what exists in the future, there is "simultaneous acquisition" (*sahabhū-prāpti*).

Furthermore, regarding those who do not habitually practice deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*)—meaning those who are not practiced, such as the deportment of Aśvajit or the craftsmanship of the *Sudhanu* devaputra—there would be three simultaneous acquisitions;
therefore, these must be excluded. Additionally, there is the "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) matter, which refers to the obscured mind.
The term "form" (*rūpa*) is used here to distinguish it from the mind and other factors, as it encompasses three types of acquisition (*prāpti*).

This form—such as the bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) of the first dhyāna—is that which is cultivated through acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), as will be explained below. There are four kinds of cultivation in total: first, cultivation by acquisition; second, cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*); third, cultivation by protection (*ārakṣaṇa-bhāvanā*);

and fourth, cultivation by removal (*vibhāvana-bhāvanā*). Among these, conditioned wholesome dharmas possess the first two types of cultivation; however, this present essence of wisdom (*jñāna*) does not arise [as such].

It is not that there is cultivation through habitual practice; rather, the mere arising of "attainment" (prāpti) constitutes cultivation. The rest is as explained below. Question: Why is it that the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*) does not arise? Answer:

Because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is tainted (*sāsrava*). Since these two types of mind—the tainted and the untainted—cannot coexist, [conventional wisdom] does not arise.
The phrase "only that which is based on the path of seeing" refers to the untainted basis of the body (*āśraya*), which is subtle and existent.

The support for the outflows (*āsrava*) is coarse; since one is now in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is only the support that is untainted (*anāsrava*), and no support that possesses outflows.
Because this support is absent, the superior conditions are lacking, and thus this conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) can never arise.

"Realization of the objective" (*vastu-abhisamaya*) means that this conventional knowledge shares the same name as the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), such as the knowledge of suffering and the abandonment of origination, because they both cognize these same objects.

Regarding "the second [stage] of the actualization of the truths concerning the objects to be realized": this refers to the three types of contemplation regarding the objects to be realized as complete.

It also includes the attainment of conventional wisdom through cultivation. Question: Since the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have not yet been severed, meaning that the origin has not been fully abandoned and cessation has not been fully realized, why is it called "complete"?
Answer: Although it is not yet complete at present, it will become complete in the future; therefore, it is not the same as [the previous stages].

The Path possesses the sense of being "entirely pervasive" (*sarvaga*); by this statement, it is meant that its activity is universal. This will be explained extensively below. Regarding the phrase "attainment prior to the arising of the dharma":
this refers to the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the edge of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), which is the attainment prior to the arising of that wisdom.

Within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), there has never been a "present realization of the object" (*vastv-abhisamaya*); this means that from time immemorial, one has never previously attained the untainted (*anāsrava*). (2)

Regarding "the realization of non-pervasive matters" (*aparyāptavastu-abhisamaya*): this refers to the fact that because there are differences such as the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and the distinctions between those of sharp and dull faculties, it is not possible to cultivate them all universally.
Regarding the term "pervasive" (*paryāpta*) applied to the three truths (*tisraḥ satyaḥ*): it means that within the context of the three truths, the verbal expression "pervasive" may be used.

As for the statement that even the Buddha does not exhaustively cultivate both the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*) regarding the Path: this means that the Buddha does not cultivate the [paths] of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Since the Path is neither cultivated nor attained through arising, both the cultivation of practice (*āsevana-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of attainment (*niṣpatti-bhāvanā*) are not fully exhausted. If even the Buddha’s attainment is not fully exhausted, how much less so that of others?

Regarding those whose power is weak because they do not follow the mind or form: the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the discipline of the Path (*mārga-śīla*) possess strong power because they function in accordance with the mind;
thus, they have three types of acquisition (*prāpti*). Now, as for the distinct liberation (*prātimokṣa*), its power does not follow the mind.
Because it is weak and inferior, there is no prior acquisition (*pūrvaprāpti*) for the present *mārgānvayakṣānti*. How could there be a dharma that has a prior acquisition?

This is because this type of patience (*kṣānti*) has never been practiced since beginningless time. Furthermore, if this type of patience had a prior acquisition, then at the moment of the *mārgadharmajñāna*, that patience would already have been established;
thus, there is no prior acquisition. Since there is no prior acquisition, why do you now say that it exists? It is for this reason that [this objection] is raised.

Question: Regarding the various patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) that arise before the realization of the principle (*tattva*), none possess prior acquisition (*pūrvaprāpti*). This is because the dharma-knowledge of the subsequent path (*anvaya-jñāna*) has no posterior acquisition;
since this [dharma-knowledge] itself serves as the cause for its own class, it is indicated that these patiences possess prior acquisition. Based on this, the question arises.

As for the other various patiences and knowledges, although they lack prior acquisition, they are not mentioned in the text, and therefore they are not questioned. If one speaks in terms of their general categories (*jāti*), it refers to those that have not yet...
Although the present and future [moments] differ, their patience (*kṣānti*) is the same;

therefore, with respect to present patience, although there is no prior acquisition (*pūrvaprāpti*) in the present, it is said that there *is* a prior acquisition when referring to the future. Question: Why is there a prior acquisition in the future? Answer:

Once the first moment of patience has arisen, the subsequent moments immediately possess its prior acquisition. However, this merely excludes the real existence of a prior acquisition for the very first moment.

It does not preclude subsequent moments. The second explanation states that even if [the patience] is absent from manifest presence (*samukha*), there is still the "prior acquisition" (*pūrvaprāpti*).
This means that while these various patiences arise with no fixed order of priority when they exist in the future, because the first moment arises prior [to others], there is no prior acquisition;
yet, if it remains in the future without arising, there is indeed a prior acquisition. This is stated in terms of the possibility of its non-arising, wherein a prior acquisition exists.

Because it has been acquired, it is said to be "liberated," which is not the same as the third interpretation. That interpretation states that there are dharmas whose prior acquisition (*pūrvapratilambha*) exists in the future;
this means that although the various dharmas of the future are intermingled, the nature (*gotra*) of their prior acquisition remains constant from beginning to end.

When they suddenly encounter conditions, they arise and reach the present, yet the prior acquisition of those dharmas still remains in the future. This is stated with respect to the horizontal perspective of the time periods (*adhvan*).
"Truly being posterior to the present" means that, viewed horizontally across the three periods of time, the future truly exists after the present;

thus they are collectively termed "dharmas posterior. This is because, by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*), this [dharma] is prior to other dharmas; therefore, although it is currently situated in the posterior period, it is still called "prior to dharmas.

(Note: "Vertical" refers to up and down, while "horizontal" refers to side-by-side, such as before and after. However, these three interpretations are all traditional ones; according to the new interpretation, however—
Regarding the guest’s [objection] that is similar to the second explanation, the refutation of the first three explanations is extensive and will not be described in full detail here.

Next, the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is explained as having two aspects: first, the non-acquisition is distinguished by way of the phenomenon (*dharma*); second, the phenomenon is distinguished by way of its non-acquisition.
That which is not acquired and lacks non-acquisition is, for example, space and insentient things (*asattva*), which are not [phenomena].

Regarding the dharmas attained, there is neither attainment nor non-attainment. Concerning the conventional knowledge at the limit of the three types of subsequent knowledge (*trividha-anvaya-jñāna-pṛṣṭhalabdha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*), a question is raised:
"The previous statement said that conventional knowledge has only prior attainment; now this says it has only non-attainment. Is this not a contradiction? The answer is:

The former [statement] refers to being at the limit of the direct realization (*abhisamaya*), and thus there is prior attainment; the latter refers to the period preceding the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and thus there is non-attainment. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Because the times differ, these do not contradict one another. Regarding the mind of maturation (*vipāka*), the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), and the mind that enters *nirvāṇa*:

it is because the nature of these two [latter] minds is weak and they are conducive to entering *nirvāṇa*. As for the two minds of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), because their natures are strong, they are not conducive to entering *nirvāṇa*.
"Having no support" means that after entering *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), the body and wisdom perish together.

When cessation occurs, there is no further basis for existence. Regarding the question of why "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is always present while "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) is not, it is asked:

"Why is 'knowledge of exhaustion' (*kṣaya-jñāna*) not mentioned? The answer is: Knowledge of exhaustion may involve regression, and there can subsequently be a non-acquisition of it; however, knowledge of non-arising does not involve regression, and thus there is no further non-acquisition of it. Therefore, knowledge of exhaustion is not mentioned.
Some individuals raise an objection against the Tripiṭaka master based on the view that the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are not seen-afflictions (*darśana-heya*).
This is the objection raised by Master Bao. The intent of his objection is as follows: previously, regarding non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), there were only three propositions and no fourth;

there was only the single proposition that "non-acquisition exists only after a dharma. Now he objects that there ought to be a fourth, and the words of the objection—as found in the chapter—are sixteen characters.
Regarding the phrase "it is not that from the beginningless past," this can be understood by continuing the reading directly from below the character "not" (*fei*).

It is also said that although those [defilements] have not yet been abandoned, it is not necessarily the case that their future species (jāti) will arise; this is not because they have not existed since beginningless time (*anādikāla*).

This is precisely because the opponent’s objection uses the phrase "since beginningless time" and so forth; therefore, we now fully cite that objection and categorically refute it by placing the character *fei* ("not") at the beginning.
To explain: when it is said that this is spoken in terms of "species," it means that although past views-afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) exist only as...

Regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) subsequent to the dharma, we now distinguish that which pertains to the future; this is explained collectively as including the non-acquisition prior to the dharma as well.

This is because both the future and the past are alike in being [objects of] those afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and are therefore termed "homogeneous" (*jāti*). If one follows the new interpretation, it differs from this:
that [interpretation] discusses only a single moment and does not speak in terms of homogeneous categories. Thus, it says: "One should say 'by means of non-..."

Because it is determined, there are two possibilities: it is not the case that one necessarily acquires [the state of being a noble one] upon reaching the past non-perception stage (*asaṃjñī-bhūmi*), for prior to the arising of afflictions, one may already have entered the state of a noble one. If these afflictions were to enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) beforehand, then those very afflictions would possess a "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) prior to the dharma.
If this explanation is adopted, it is identical to the other [cases] where both types of non-acquisition apply, because [it is] not...
Having grasped this intention, [the opponent] argued that the difficulty regarding the past afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) should result in four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*).

Since this argument could not be resolved, they subsequently revised the *Vibhāṣā* to present it as having four alternatives. Even now, the two editions circulating in Chang’an still maintain the four alternatives.

Several years later, the treatise was revised again to state that there are "only three alternatives," and a textual insertion was added to block the objection that [afflictions] are not without beginning (*anādikālika*).
Even these sixteen characters do not yet capture the original intent of the *Vibhāṣā*, for they have not exhausted the underlying principle.

As for why the question specifically uses the afflictions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as an objection, the answer is that the afflictions of the other stages have already been abandoned numerous times;

therefore, when they are abandoned in the interim, there exists a "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) prior to the dharma in the future. If this were so, then the cultivated afflictions of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception would have been established since beginningless time.

Why not raise the objection that it is difficult to understand? [The opponent might argue: "Since there can be regression from the abandonment of the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and since they arise again, it is clear that at that time their seeds were not entirely exhausted.
As for their future [arising], this is because there exists a non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) prior to the dharma itself;
therefore, none of these points are used as objections.

Regarding the statement that "the dharmas of the three periods of time are called the 'three' [categories]," there are two meanings: First, each of the three periods of time possesses its own three categories, regardless of whether a dharma exists before or after another.
Although it is a dharma that precedes others, it is still termed "future"; although it is a dharma that follows others, it is still termed "past.

Second, all dharmas—whether preceding or following—possess all three [periods] simultaneously, regardless of their distinction in temporal sequence. Thus, although it is a past dharma, it is still termed "following" [in relation to what comes after]; although it is... [the text here is incomplete].

That which is future is still called "prior to the dharma" (*dharmapūrva*). Now, when it is said here that each of the three time periods has three [subdivisions], this is based on how they are divided according to the three times, not based on whether the dharma is prior or subsequent.
Regarding the past, as for those acquisitions that are either prior to or subsequent to the dharma—for instance, suppose there is a single moment of mind in the past;
if one looks horizontally at all acquisitions that have already arisen prior to today, if [the acquisition] is in the dharma...
The preceding dharmas, the simultaneous dharmas, and those that follow are all termed "past. Regarding the phrase "such as past [dharmas] born of maturation (*vipākaja*), etc.," the term "etc.
includes those born of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), excluding those not habitually practiced.

As for "attainment in the present" (*pratyutpanna-pratilambha*), this refers to the moment of arising today; all dharmas subsequent to that moment are termed "future" attainment. This is based on the horizontal classification of time (*adhvan*).
I expect that what has been explained above represents the traditional interpretation (*pūrvapakṣa*), while from here on, the following will be consistent with it.

However, according to the new interpretation, for those who maintain that past dharmas do not exist in the future, the prior acquisition (*prāpti*) of a dharma cannot be established by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because priority and posteriority are spoken of only in relation to their actual arising.

Therefore, one cannot determine priority or posteriority based on intrinsic nature; nor can those who maintain that past dharmas exist in the future allow for the prior acquisition of a dharma based on such a determination. Regarding...
Regarding "attaining by way of category," this refers to the distinction between preceding and succeeding natures.

Regarding "speaking in terms of the capacity for the arising of function," although at the present moment they belong to the same world-period and thus have no [actual] precedence or succession, when considering the time of the arising of function, that which arises first is called "prior attainment" (*pūrvaprāpti*) and that which arises later is called "subsequent attainment" (*paścātprāpti*).
According to this sequence, there are three types of attainment: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
This means that wholesome dharmas have wholesome acquisitions (*prāpti*), unwholesome dharmas have unwholesome acquisitions, and indeterminate dharmas have indeterminate acquisitions.
Although these three types of natures—the acquisition and the acquired dharma—are of the same nature, they differ in terms of the conditions through which the acquisition arises.

Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states that there are three kinds of acquisition: first, the acquisition of conditioned dharmas; second, the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) follows the specific categories of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that are acquired, because conditioned phenomena possess functional efficacy and thus draw forth their own acquisitions.
The acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), however, follows the specific categories of the path (*mārga*) by which it is realized;
for analytical cessations themselves lack functional efficacy, being drawn forth only at the time they are sought through the power of the path.

Because it is acquired, if it were non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it would inherently lack activity and would not be sought after by the Path; its acquisition arises solely based on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Therefore, these factors of the three natures are called "acquisition by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prāpti*).

Although one acquires analytical cessation through this [intrinsic] acquisition, the acquisition of non-analytical cessation does not depend on what is acquired [by the Path], because the Path and analytical cessation share the same nature, whereas [non-analytical cessation] depends on the homogeneous class and so forth. Thus, they are of the same nature.
The distinction [of acquisition] is of the same nature as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

because these two types, although not acquired through the acquisition of what is obtained, must necessarily be of the same nature as that which is obtained, these three categories of dharmas must necessarily be of the same nature as their acquisition (*prāpti*). This has already been explained in general;

it will not be reiterated in the subsequent sections. Regarding the determination of non-analytical cessation according to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth, it is as previously stated in the section on the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). Since it is... [the text continues].

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) shares the same nature [as its associated factors], and now, in the section on the realms of bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*), it is likewise determined according to the life-faculty and so forth.

As for the attainment (*prāpti*) of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it is determined according to what is attained; this is because the Truth of the Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and possesses a remaining function, and thus its attainment is determined according to what is attained.
Therefore, summarizing the factors that are not bound (*abandhana-dharma*), they consist of the two kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the attainment of the Truth of the Path.

This general statement refers to the four types [of acquisitions] that pertain to the three realms as well as those that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*); it does not refer to the three categories of "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Here, only the acquisition of non-learner-dharmas (*aśaikṣadharma*) is indicated, yet it can encompass all three types of learners (*śaikṣa*).

Question: Why is only the acquisition of non-learner-dharmas cited to clarify the nature of these acquisitions? Answer: Because the verse is concise. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that because the acquisition of non-learner-dharmas can encompass all three types of learners, it is specifically singled out for mention. Moreover...
This single verse summarizes the three trainings. "Non-trainee" refers to dharmas that are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee;
"trainee" refers to trainee dharmas, and "non-trainee" refers to non-trainee dharmas. Regarding the distinction of "attainment by one who is not a trainee":

while for the former two categories of dharmas there is no further distinction between the attainment and that which is attained, within this present context, the dharma that is "not attained by a trainee" applies universally to all three.
The distinction between "learning" (*śikṣā*) and "dharma" is that their names differ. As for the statement that "outflow-tainted dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) cannot be cultivated":

this means that because outflow-tainted dharmas possess various defects and are merely to be abandoned, how could they be cultivated? Regarding the statement that "the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be made to increase":
because the essence of the unconditioned is eternal and lacks functional activity, it cannot be made to grow. Furthermore, outflow-tainted dharmas are determined according to what has been acquired.

In reality, although conditioned uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states are also determined according to what has been attained, for the time being we shall refer to this dharma as the subject of discussion.

This is because contaminated (*sāsrava*) states necessarily possess functional activity; therefore, they are determined according to the dharma itself. As for the acquisition (*prāpti*) of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) not induced by the Noble Path—that is the cessation through deliberation realized by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
If it is the case that even the acquisition of the path of training (*śaikṣa-mārga*) up to its final attainment is likewise [determined], then one asks: "What of the learner (*śaikṣa*)?"
Sentient beings generally employ two types of paths to sever the afflictions of the lower stages that remain within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Whichever path is employed, each is capable of inducing the acquisition of two types of disconnection (*visamyoga-prāpti*). Since this is so, how can one say that [the acquisition] is determined according to the path? Answer:

Although the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) severs afflictions, it is also capable of inducing the acquisition of the tainted; likewise, although the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*) severs afflictions, it is also capable of inducing the acquisition of the untainted.

The acquisition [of cessation] is not categorized according to both paths because it is acquired concurrently rather than being drawn forth by each individually; rather, it follows its own respective path.

Although that path capable of realizing it does not arise [at that moment], they cultivate one another, and since the acquisition of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) arises through the power of that [cultivation], it is each categorized according to its own respective path capable of realization.
If the acquisition of the analytical cessation realized by the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) is also [the state of] no-more-learning.

Question: Since the afflictions of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have already been exhausted, how can there be a realization of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and why is it said that [this cessation] "follows" the state of being beyond training?

Explanation: At the time when one beyond training attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), this path is able to maintain the acquisition of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*); therefore, because the acquisition follows this path, it is designated as "beyond training.

Alternatively, when one beyond training refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they exclusively induce superior acquisitions; these are also called the "acquisition of the path of one beyond training. It is simply designated as such [to distinguish it from others].

Furthermore, "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) is explained as being distinct because it applies to both types of attainment (*prāpti*); thus it is specifically designated. Alternatively, it is explained that within the verse, the three types of abandonment are fully indicated:
"non-abandonment" refers to the two kinds of abandonment—namely, those pertaining to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Accordingly, there are attainments of what is abandoned by seeing and what is abandoned by cultivation; since these two factors are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), their attainment follows the attainment of the factors themselves.

The determination of the dharmas is likewise [subject to] abandonment through both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*). To say that there are "two" in total refers to the general designation of two types of dharmas: the two unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
As for their specific differentiation, this refers to the distinction between non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation is abandoned solely through cultivation, because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) are abandoned through cultivation; therefore, their acquisition is likewise [abandoned through cultivation].
Indeed, the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) is attained through the Truth of the Path; it is untainted (anāsrava) and is also not subject to abandonment.
Regarding postures (īryāpatha) and crafts (śailpasthānika), these refer to the mind and not to matter (rūpa).

Since this is not the case for obscured-neutral (nivṛtāvyākṛta) matter—let alone unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) matter—how could there be the designation of "prior" or "subsequent"? As the old [commentary] says: "If [these] four—postures and crafts..."
Even for those who have cultivated the aggregates to the utmost degree, there is both prior and simultaneous acquisition;

furthermore, for all other resultant (*vipāka*) five aggregates, as well as a portion of the aggregates of deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*), along with a portion of the four aggregates of deportment and craftsmanship, and a portion of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) matter and formations (*saṃskāra*) by their very nature—these are acquired only simultaneously.
Regarding the training in deportment, it is like that of the Buddha or the Bhikṣu Aśvajit.
As for those who have practiced other arts, their skill is like that of the deity Viśvakarman and others well-versed in crafts;

the *Vibhāṣā* states that such mastery of craftsmanship is like the "Sublime Deeds" (*Sudarśana*) of the Buddha’s sons, and so forth. (The commentary explains: these cases refer to the acquisition of [results] across the three time periods based on the four aggregates that can produce them, rather than the matter and other elements produced by them.

Regarding the mind capable of transformation, this refers to the supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā*), which relies upon the four dhyānas to manifest in the desire realm and other locations.

There are fourteen types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*), as will be explained below. Because the supernormal powers of the eye and ear, as well as the transformative mind, possess two characteristics, they are common to all three [dhyānas].
First, they attain a powerful capacity; second, they are accomplished through preparatory effort (*prayoga*). It is by virtue of these that they possess the attainment of all three.

The bodily and vocal karma produced by the obscured (*nivṛta*) afflictions of the first dhyāna is, for example, like the King of Brahmās practicing deceit and guile, and so forth, within the desire realm.

Although within the realms there are the two views of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), because these are obscured afflictions that operate internally, they cannot initiate karma.

Furthermore, from the second dhyāna upward, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra, nor do [afflictions] initiate karma simultaneously; therefore, only in the first dhyāna and the desire realm are there non-concomitant material phenomena (*rūpa*).
This excludes those material phenomena that follow the mind as explained above regarding meditative concentration and the Path. Apart from what has been identified here, all else is included.
The four unwholesome aggregates (*skandha*) and all other wholesome five aggregates possess three types of acquisition (*prāpti*).

Regarding the gate of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), the old translations state: "If one follows the gate of acquisition, there should likewise be a distinction between the three trainings (*śikṣā*) and the three abandonments (*prahāṇa*).

Since the first phrase states that non-acquisition is pure and neutral (*avyākṛta*), it is clearly understood that it pertains exclusively to that which is neither-training-nor-non-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). Only this.
Because it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it is not mentioned separately among the wholesome or the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:

"In accordance with which category of nature (*dharmatā*) is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) differentiated? The answer is: It certainly does not follow the nature of the dharma that is not acquired, because they are mutually contradictory; nor does it follow the Path, because it is not sought by either the Path or the non-Path;

rather, it functions in dependence upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), and thus it is differentiated according to the nature of its basis.
The dissociation (*visamyoga*) follows only the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and not the maturation (*vipāka*), because it is not universal. Question:

Why does non-possession (*aprāpti*) not follow the dharma that is not yet possessed? Answer: If it were to follow the dharma that is not yet possessed, then one who has severed the roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*) would possess wholesome dharmas;

one who is already free from the defilement of desire (*vītarāga*) would possess unwholesome dharmas; and a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) would possess defiled dharmas, as would an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
It would follow that one could fall away from the untainted dharmas of the three vehicles, fall away from the fruits, and abandon the paths leading toward those fruits;
such errors would arise because non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) cannot be determined solely by the dharma not yet obtained. Regarding the non-acquisition of past dharmas:

it refers to the state of non-acquisition existing at the time when a dharma has not yet been obtained, even though that dharma is now in the past. As for the non-acquisition of future dharmas: this exists [in the present].

Regarding the two types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of a single dharma: after [the dharma] has not yet arisen, there is the non-acquisition of the second type; before [the dharma] has arisen, the non-acquisition exists in the future.
There is no present non-acquisition, because according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, a present dharma does not coexist with its non-possession (*asamanvāgama*).

Some say this is because their natures are contradictory. As for the non-acquisition of form and formless dharmas belonging to the three realms: first, regarding sentient beings of the desire realm...

The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is not possessed by sentient beings bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the non-acquisition of dharmas not belonging to the form realm is not possessed by sentient beings bound to the form realm;
and the non-acquisition of dharmas not belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is likewise not possessed by sentient beings bound to the formless realm.

Furthermore, regarding the non-acquisition of those that are unconditioned (*asaṃprayukta*) to the three realms, it follows the realm-bound nature of the sentient beings themselves. The treatise cites the *Mūla-śāstra* [Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna] as its source.

This refers to the *Mūlaprakaraṇa* (Fundamental Treatise) that induces knowledge in this very treatise. It is not reasonable to say that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is untainted (*anāsrava*).
That is to say, it is not logical to claim that the nature of an ordinary person is untainted.
If one asks, "What noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) are not obtained such that one is called an 'ordinary person'? the answer is: "It is all [noble dharmas]. If it were otherwise, then for all...

Since the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would also not have attained the lineage of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and would thus have to be called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is known that he did not obtain them all.
If this is so, one should say that he "exclusively" did not obtain them.

The answer is that it is not necessary to say "exclusively," just as when one says "this class [of beings] eats water" (referring to mosquitoes) or "eats wind" (referring to cicadas), it is understood that they exclusively eat water, wind, and so forth. Now, regarding the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).

It is called "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*). Regarding the statement that "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) with respect to the dharmas of an ordinary person should be called "the nature of a noble one" (*āryatva*):

the explanation is that since an ordinary person does not possess the dharmas of a noble one, it can be said that there is a non-acquisition [of them], which constitutes the nature of an ordinary person; whereas a noble one necessarily possesses the dharmas of an ordinary person, therefore their non-acquisition is not the nature of a noble one.

"Arising of views of a different class" refers to the various views such as the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth. "Various afflictions of a different class" refers to the creation of a different [state].

Regarding "similar karma" and so forth: this refers to the various afflictions such as greed and hatred creating various types of karma for the five destinies, thereby resulting in births of various classes within those five destinies.
It is not necessarily the case that there is acquisition (*prāpti*) where there is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).

The aforementioned [section] clarified the characteristics of acquisition and non-acquisition based on the primary tenet (*siddhānta*), establishing them in mutual opposition according to their respective stages (*bhūmi*). Now, however, we are considering different stages; thus, while there is acquisition, there is no non-acquisition.
It is said that this is not necessarily the case because it does not serve as a substitute for the state of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).

Although one does not universally abandon the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) in its entirety, this means that when changing levels (*bhūmi*), one merely abandons the nature of an ordinary being belonging to the level from which one departs; however, the nature of an ordinary being belonging to the level into which one is born and so forth still remains distinct.

One only completely abandons [the nature of an ordinary being] upon attaining the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). Question: Since non-acquisition is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature and lacks prior or subsequent acquisition, how is it that this...?
If at every single moment one abandons and does not acquire [the non-acquisition], how can it be said that "one acquires the dharma and later abandons the non-acquisition"?
The explanation says: Indeed, there is such a principle; however, what is here called "abandoning" refers to the exhaustion of an entire category, not merely a partial portion.

Furthermore, while the non-acquisition has not yet been abandoned, there is still the acquisition of that non-acquisition; once the non-acquisition itself is abandoned, that acquisition of it ceases to exist. Therefore, the treatise states: "Non-acquisition..."
When the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is severed and the acquisition (*prāpti*) arises, this is called "abandoning the non-acquisition. [The opponent] explains:

Since it is stated that the non-acquisition is severed, it is clear that when it has not yet been severed, there must already be an acquisition. [Question: Does the acquisition of a phenomenon (*dharmaprāpti*) also have a further acquisition? [Answer:
If the acquisition has a further acquisition, then that acquisition would also have another acquisition, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [Answer: No.
There is no fault of infinite regress, because it is admitted that they can successively establish one another: when a dharma arises, three dharmas arise together—first, the primary dharma;
second, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that dharma; and third, the acquisition of the acquisition (*prāpti-prāpti*).

This is because, through the arising of the acquisition of the acquisition within the continuum, the primary dharma and the acquisition of the dharma are established; and because the acquisition of the acquisition arises, the acquisition of the dharma is established.
Therefore, in this case, there is no fault of infinite regress. Thus, when each individual entity—whether wholesome or defiled—first arises, three dharmas arise together;
at the second moment, six dharmas arise together, namely the three dharmas and their three acquisitions (*prāpti*);
at the third moment, eighteen arise together, namely the six dharmas from the second moment and the [six] from the first moment.

The three middle categories of dharmas collectively constitute nine dharmas; for these nine dharmas there are nine acquisitions (*prāpti*), and these acquisitions together form eighteen. (This is based solely on the first moment of a dharma;

if one were to further discuss the mind and other factors arising in the second moment and so forth, they would become even more numerous. Thus, these various acquisitions increase progressively in each subsequent moment.

Furthermore, because the mental continuums of sentient beings are gathered together and lack mutual obstruction, they can accommodate one another; otherwise, a single sentient being... [would not be possible].
The Emptiness of Sentient Beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*) does not even admit of a second;
how much less so others.
*Abhidharmakośakārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Treatise Text, Volume Five.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.
Regarding the "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāya-sabhāga*): those who share the same dharmas are called a "group" (*nikāya*). That which serves as their cause is termed "homogeneity" (*sabhāga*).
The chapter states that the meaning of "many groups sharing homogeneity" is likewise the same. "Without distinction" refers generally to the equality of sentient beings.

All these [terms] are used solely to exclude non-sentient things and are thus called "undifferentiated. Regarding the absence of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) in non-sentient things, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"The Blessed One spoke of such homogeneity only with reference to sentient beings, as it does not apply to grass, trees, and the like;

for the Sūtra speaks of 'the homogeneity of this person' and 'the homogeneity of that deity,' and so forth, and thus does not mention non-sentient things. Sentient beings of a single class each possess [it]."
This means that because it distinguishes its own category from other categories, it is called "having distinctions.

The statement that "the bases of the homogeneous groups (sabhāgatā) such as realms and destinies are each distinct" clarifies that the *sabhāgatā* is that which depends [upon them]. "Similarity within its own class" refers to the similarity within its own class, such as that of form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth.
From "because there is a real entity" up to "mutual similarity," this clarifies that *sabhāgatā* is...

It is precisely because there is a real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) that dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) are each mutually similar. As for the statement that "sentient beings" (*sattva*) also includes "dharmas," this means that dharmas are not separate from sentient beings; the verse merely says "sentient beings" while also including dharmas. Regarding the question of whether the essence of the homogeneity of sentient beings and the homogeneity of dharmas are distinct or identical, the commentary explains: The homogeneity of sentient beings has as its nature the mutual similarity among those who possess mind (*cittavat*), while the homogeneity of dharmas has as its nature the mutual similarity among those things devoid of mind (*acittaka*). Therefore, their essences are distinct. Furthermore, the homogeneity of sentient beings is established based on the homogeneity of dharmas, and it is by virtue of this that the term "sentient being" is applied. Consequently, the homogeneity of sentient beings is not established apart from the homogeneity of dharmas. Thus, although they are distinct in terms of their specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are identical in terms of their essential substance (*dravya*). This is because the homogeneity of sentient beings is a derivative of the homogeneity of dharmas. The older [commentators] say: "The distinctness of their essential natures (svabhāva) causes sentient beings to be similar, which is termed 'homogeneity of sentient beings' (*sattva-sabhāgatā*);

that which causes all phenomena (*dharma*) to be similar is termed 'homogeneity of phenomena' (*dharma-sabhāgatā*). Although there are no sentient beings apart from phenomena, the homogeneities are distinct because they differ in their functional definitions.

Furthermore, another interpretation holds that since sentient beings have no separate essence apart from phenomena, one should know by inference that the essence of the homogeneities likewise has no distinction.
The names differ because their meanings differ; they do not depend on being distinct entities [as clarified in the current commentary, which follows the previous explanation].

If there were no real entity called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*), this section below would serve as a counter-argument to establish that the Sautrāntika school must admit the actual existence of the essence of homogeneity.

Within this, there are two parts: first, establishing it with respect to sentient beings; second, establishing it with respect to phenomena. Regarding the first, concerning "sentient beings": "sentient beings" refers to the fact that sentient beings are not one.

Regarding the statement that "the designation 'sentient being' and the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) would not allow for the occurrence of non-differentiated cognitions and designations regarding the name 'sentient being'":

the meaning of this is that if there were no real entity called "homogeneity," there could not exist the cognitive understanding that takes homogeneity as its object, nor the linguistic conventions that designate it as "homogeneity. Since such cognitive understanding and [linguistic] expressions do indeed exist...
Because it explains the conventional designations (*nāma-pada*) of the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*), one knows that *sabhāgatā* is a real entity.

Since there can be no arising of cognitive awareness (*buddhi*) without an object of cognition, and since there can be no initiation of verbal expression without a referent (*abhidheya*), it follows that when [the category of] "dharmas" is subsequently obtained, it is treated analogously to sentient beings.
Thus, it is said: "One should know according to reason that awareness follows conditions based on the homogeneous class. This explains the arising [of awareness] conditioned by the homogeneous class.

The conceptual understanding (*buddhi*) may be like the conceptual understanding of "sentient being" that arises equally toward humans and devas, or the conceptual understanding of "form" that arises equally toward phenomena;

this is termed "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) based on such conceptualization. Furthermore, this is merely cited as an example of the difficulty regarding the undifferentiated commonality, as it is not exhaustive.
Specifically, the Sautrāntika school asserts that homogeneity is a mere designation (*prajñapti*), for they claim it is not a distinct entity separate from the nature of the individual (*pudgala*).

There exists a generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), just as there is a generic similarity among those who are not of the human nature; furthermore, it is not directly perceived.

Moreover, an objection is raised: "Why do you not admit a generic similarity for non-sentient things (*asattva*), since grains, barley, gold, silver, and so forth also possess mutual similarity within their own respective classes?
The *Nyāyānusāra* responds: "One should not level such criticisms, for it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

Since you also admit that there are destinies such as humans and gods, and modes of birth such as the womb and the egg, why do you not likewise admit that there are destinies such as mangoes and modes of birth such as beans and wheat?

Furthermore, this is how I understand it: because those grasses and so forth lack the mutual similarity of karmic activity and volition, and because grasses and so forth arise only by depending upon sentient beings. Thus, [only] these [are destinies].
Regarding sentient beings, it is said that their *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) can be severed; this serves as proof that *sabhāgatā* exists as a real entity (*dravya*).

The Sautrāntikas say that the homogeneity of persons and so forth is merely a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), like [the categories of] wheat or beans; the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] intention is the same.
Regarding the cultivation of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are many explanations.

The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (the "Critical Evaluation" or *pūrvapakṣa-vādī*) states: "The ripening of non-conception is produced solely by the attainment of non-conception; the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*), as well as the material faculties such as the eye, are all produced by karma;

the remaining aggregates are produced by both [the attainment of non-conception and karma]. (This is because, with the exception of the life-faculty and so forth, the remaining aggregates such as sensation are produced by both the attainment of non-conception and karma. From this, it follows that there are causes of projection (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and fulfillment (*paripūraka-hetu*).

The passage in the *Madhyama-āgama* stating that "the two meditative attainments cannot induce [rebirth]" refers to their inability to induce the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*).

When it says "for a long time there is perception," this means it excludes the brief intervals [of unconsciousness] and thus designates them as "long"; it does not mean that there is no period of non-perception during the interval.

This is because there is no perception for a long duration of five hundred great eons (*mahākalpa*) during that interval; thus, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, the former [period] is long and the latter is short.

Alternatively, because there are distinctions according to one's inclinations—such as when there is little in the former life and much in the latter—one must necessarily have karma to be experienced in a subsequent life within the desire realm.

The *Vibhāṣā* states: "Some say that if one creates karma to be experienced in the next birth in the Realm of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), it is a natural law (*dharmatā*) that one also creates karma to be experienced in a subsequent life in the desire realm;
just as those who practice the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*) are born in the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), they must necessarily create [karma] for the desire heavens."

Because when cultivating this practice, one must necessarily possess ten karmic causes; thus, one might give rise to wrong views and slander the Śākyas and *nirvāṇa*—the latter meaning the repudiation of true *nirvāṇa*.
