The *Vibhāṣā* differs [in its analysis]: some give rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), reckoning the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) as liberation.

Now, "grasping of views" refers to clinging to that which is inferior as being superior; since this is not *nirvāṇa*, yet one clings to it as *nirvāṇa*, it is therefore the grasping of views. Alternatively, some give rise to the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);

that is, reckoning what is not the path to be the path is called the grasping of precepts and observances. Now, the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is truly not the true path.
Because one falsely conceives [these practices] to be the path, this constitutes the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Next, regarding "one who subsequently abandons desire":

this refers to first giving rise to unwholesome causes and only subsequently cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), detachment from defilements (*vairāgya*), and so forth; thus it is called "subsequent. Question: In the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), since the three types of nutriment (*āhāra*) have ceased, how can one remain there?

Answer: There are two kinds of nutriment: first, that which is capable of projecting [existence] at a prior time; second, that which maintains [existence] in the present. In that state, [it is the former that sustains one].
Although there is no present sustaining [force], it can still endure because it was previously induced by nutriment.
Regarding the statement that they are "the same" in terms of the cessation of mind, this refers to their being identical in the state of being mindless;

it does not mean that their nature, substance, category, or numerical count are the same as the fruit of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-phala*). Question: What is the mental state when entering and exiting the state of non-conceptualization? Answer: The *Vibhāṣā* states:
The "entering" and "emerging" [from the state of non-conception] both consist of the contaminated wholesome mind of the fourth dhyāna, as will be explained in detail later.
That non-conception relies exclusively on the fourth dhyāna and not on lower stages, as clarified in that [text];

yet it does not rely on the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu), because ordinary beings fear total annihilation, and they believe that if the mind were further extinguished within those formless realms, it would result in utter extinction.

Because it is feared by them, there is no attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Furthermore, since there is no fruition of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) to be reckoned in the formless realm, the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) itself does not exist there either.
It is traditionally taught that one who manifests this attainment in the present life must necessarily be able to arouse it again;

that is to say, at the time of falling from the attainment, one arouses the afflictions of a lower stage. If one does not arouse them again, then in the second birth one will not receive the fruit [of that attainment], because [the fruit] occurs within the next birth.
One will certainly regain that same state; thus, in the second birth, one immediately receives the fruit. Question:

Since this concentration is strictly *upapadyavedanīya* (to be experienced in the next life), and one has already previously attained the concentration capable of summoning the fruit, what further result is induced by entering concentration again? Answer:

It may be said that it induces the maturation (*vipāka*) of other aggregates (*skandha*), or that when the retribution for that [new] entry into concentration is felt, one enters late and emerges early, or enters early [and emerges late].
When the Sage emerges late from the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi*), it is as if he sees a deep pit;

that is to say, having experienced the great fruit of birth and death for five hundred great kalpas, it is empty and yields nothing, and thus the Noble One feels weary detachment toward it as if seeing a deep pit.
Regarding "having the mental attention of the perception of cessation as a precursor":

this refers to the Noble Ones who, because they find the coarse movement and exhaustion of feeling and perception to be wearying, enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in order to seek a temporary state of tranquil abiding. Question: Since the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arrived, and the present does not abide, what mind is it that ceases?
Answer: Abiding in the present, one obstructs the arising of future minds and mental factors.

Because there is no further continuity, it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*). It is like cutting off a city road, closing the gates, and erecting a banner so that people cannot enter or exit; thus, it is called "the removal of the enemy.

Regarding the fact that it relies solely on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the *Nyāya* (Principles) further states: "The previously mentioned attainment of non-ideation was at the limit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
now, this attainment of cessation is at the limit of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The body received in rebirth is drawn forth by the most superior karma."
Therefore, it is called the "Summit of Existence" (*bhavāgra*) or the "Limit of Existence. It is called the Summit of Existence just as the edge of a tree is called the top of the tree.
Regarding that which brings about the maturation (*vipāka*) of the four aggregates of the Summit of Existence, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:

"It receives the maturation fruit of the four aggregates of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*); because these are exclusively the fruits of karma, they cannot be produced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)."

This [attainment] has three causes in total: first, because of fear; second, because it is induced solely by the power of the Noble Path; and third, because of entry through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).

Regarding those who enter the Noble attainment of cessation through resolute conviction: this means that during the distant preparatory stage, they form the notion of entering nirvāṇa, yet it is not actual nirvāṇa;
it is like forming the notion of rest during the preparatory stage. When first attained, it is acquired as belonging to only one lifetime.
This means that because it is a state without mind (*acittaka*) and because no dharmas can be acquired prior to it, one acquires only [the dharmas] of a single lifetime. World-Honored One,
this objection implies that those who have not yet attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) until they become "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*)—

since Bodhisattvas prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are still ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and thus have not yet attained this absorption— and when they enter the Path of Seeing and become noble ones (*ārya*), [they possess] thirty [dharmas].

Because the four minds arise in succession, this concentration (samādhi) is not attained until the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna). Since this concentration has not yet been attained, how can one be called a person liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta)?
Answer: There are two [senses]. First, one is named "liberated both ways" based on mastery over the arising [of the concentration];

second, it is based on attaining the mind that enters and exits [the concentration]. Because the minds that enter and exit have a temporal sequence, when the knowledge of exhaustion attains the essence of the concentration, there is no mind and no dharma [present].
Because it was previously attained, it is not [attained] again. The West refers to the kingdom of Gandhāra, which is to the west of Kaśmīra.
Upagupta—translated here as "Near Protector" (Jìn hù) or "Near Treasury" (Jìn zàng)—appeared one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as explained above.
He was a teacher in the lineage of King Aśoka. Regarding the "sixteen moments of clear realization" (satya-abhisamaya) mentioned therein, they are as follows:
Because one contemplates each of the eight truths of the upper and lower realms with two moments of mind, sixteen [moments] are established, as explained in detail in the chapter.

Regarding the statement "one who has already attained freedom from craving for the sphere of nothingness," this means that it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) for Bodhisattvas to first become free from the defilements of the lower realm through the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*).

Just as Bodhisattvas, like Udraka Rāmaputra and others, cultivate the perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is clearly understood that at this time they have already become free from the lower [defilements].
Regarding the impossibility of a defiled mind arising [while in this posture], the Western masters say:

"It means that as long as I have not attained the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), I shall never untie this cross-legged sitting; I resolve with certainty not to rise. This refers to the determination of the mind, and does not mean that an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind cannot arise.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks: "How could it be that by this [resolution] one has already transgressed [the rules]? How then could a Bodhisattva..."
Having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), he cultivated the two paths—of seeing and cultivation—which had never before been attained;

desiring to uproot the seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and to eliminate the enemy of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation there, he made a solemn vow and sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

Before his task was complete, however, he abandoned that very vow and the untainted path of remedy (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa-mārga*), valuing instead the beginningless world that is capable of deception and delusion.

Because he was delayed in attaining the meditative absorption of cessation—which is common to those of his class—he thus successfully accomplished the attainment of enlightenment in thirty-four moments of thought;
according to the master’s intent, this is the same as the Western masters and differs from the Sarvāstivāda school.

Regarding the statement that there is no doubt as to why the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) does not rely on the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*): this is because the state of non-conception exists in the fourth dhyāna and is not a formless phenomenon;

therefore, it does not rely on those [formless] principles. As for the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), since it is a phenomenon belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), why does it likewise not rely on a formless body?
If there are those who do not admit that the state of non-conception can arise in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), what would they say?

It is asserted that one can arise in the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) solely through a mind belonging to the desire realm, because such a mind is sharp and possesses the power of [prior] resolve.
Some say it arises from all three dhyānas, because it can also be produced through the force of the application of effort (*prayoga*) cultivated with mindfulness and vigor.
Others say it can also be manifested in the fourth dhyāna, excluding the Heaven of No-Perception (*asaṃjñisattva*), lest the fruit and its cause be too closely proximate. These are the three views.
Among these, the latter two do not contradict the previous explanation; it is not unreasonable that these consist only of the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).

The aggregate of form is easily understood, while the aggregate of formations includes the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), acquisition (*prāpti*), the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*), and so forth, excluding the other three aggregates. This is because feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are not associated with the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta*).

As for the statement that the five aggregates are the five formations (*pañca saṃskārāḥ*), it is because the impermanent is termed "formations" (*anityatvāt saṃskāra iti*). Thus, [the text] says: "Bha..."
Śāriputra said: "The aggregates (*skandha*) are spoken of by the term 'formations' (*saṃskāra*).

The past Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas spoke of the aggregates by the name 'formations,' while the present Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha speaks of formations by the name 'aggregates.

This exposition in the Abhidharma explains the five formations in order to show that the five aggregates taught by the present Buddha are identical to the five formations taught by the Buddhas of the past."
Only among human beings can the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) be first produced. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:

Why is it that while one can first produce the dhyānas while born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one cannot first produce the attainment of cessation there? It answers: The dhyānas are first produced due to three conditions:

first, the power of the cause; second, the power of karma; and third, the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*). The attainment of cessation, however, is first produced by only one condition, namely, the power of instruction (*deśanā-bala*).

It exists only in the desire realm because it is taught by the Buddha; it can first arise not through the power of causes, because one has never previously produced the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in other lifetimes;
nor does it arise through the power of karma, because this attainment is not of the nature of karmic force;

nor does it arise through the power of natural law (*dharmatā*), because there is no destruction of the world-system in the formless realms. Regarding those who have never practiced this attainment of cessation: it means...

Only an *ārya* is capable of cultivating this [attainment]; since he was previously not an *ārya*, he had never cultivated it before. Regarding the phrase "preceded by falling away," the treatise asks:
"Does this cessation (*nirodha*) also involve falling away? One should say that it does, as in the *Udāyi-sūtra* (translated here as the *Chuxian jing*):
"There are certain bhikṣus who, having previously in this place possessed pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), were able to repeatedly enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling."
It is certain that they will be unable to diligently practice in this present life or at the point of death so as to bring their liberation to fulfillment;

consequently, upon the dissolution of this body, they will transcend the gods who subsist on edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). By "gods who subsist on edible food" is meant the gods of the six desire realms (*ṣaṭ-kāmāvacara-deva*), who possess bodies sustained by edible food.

"Gods of form" refers to the gods of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), who are born spontaneously according to their wishes without depending on semen, blood, or other such substances. "Gods who receive birth in a single place" refers to those who take birth in any one of these locations.

Once born there as a deity of the Mind-made Body (*manomaya-kāya*), one repeatedly enters and emerges from the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

Since there is no falling back once this attainment is obtained, how could one go to be reborn in the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*)? According to the Mahāsāṃghika school, there is also a cessation attainment in the fourth dhyāna;
however, their assertion that there is no falling back from that cessation attainment differs from this [position]. This is just as one also understands [the case of] feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.

This refers to the fact that although feeling (*vedanā*) is a mental factor (*caitta*), even though one knows it as a mental factor, it is not called "knowledge of other mental factors" (*paracaittajñāna*), but is instead called "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
The *Śāstra* says: "Now, since in the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) the mind has been interrupted for a long time, how can the subsequent mind arise again?

The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that the past exists, and that the preceding mind serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the subsequent one (as extensively explained in many treatises).

Question: If there is no mind at all, how can it be called "concentration" (*samādhi*)? Answer: It is called concentration because it causes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to function in equilibrium;
or, it is called concentration because the power of the mind reaches a state of equilibrium therein. Explanation:

Because this concentration resides in the body, it causes the various primary elements to abide in a state of profound equanimity, such that they cannot be harmed by water, fire, wind, or other such factors.

Therefore, it is called "equipoise" (*samāpatti*). Alternatively, because the mind prior to the meditative concentration leaves behind dullness and agitation and reaches equality within this concentration, it is called equipoise.
The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that equipoise has two meanings: first, it makes the mind equal; second, it makes the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) equal.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The term 'concentration' (*samādhi*) used here should actually be named 'equipoise,' but it is designated as 'concentration' for the sake of brevity."

(The commentary states: "The ultimate meaning of 'righteousness' (*yǐngzhèng*) and 'extreme meaning' (*jíyì*), according to the principle of equality, refers to the sense of 'accomplishment' (*chéngbiàn*). Regarding the statement that the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) have twenty-two entities as their substance, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are many explanations.
One says that this attainment has a single entity as its substance, because when a single cessation (*nirodha*) manifests, it is termed 'mindless.
Others say it has eleven entities as its substance, consisting of the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the mind-king (*citta-rāja*)."*)

Regarding cessation (*nirodha*), some say its substance consists of twenty-one factors: the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

Regarding this, the master of the critique (*viniścayakāra*) says: "According to those who speak thus, as many mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) as cease, so many factors manifest as its substance.
The present chapter, however, states that by adding "joy" (*abhinandana*) and "aversion" (*vidveṣaṇa*), it differs from the third master.

The *Xinyun* (New Cloud) states that the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is added with "joyful joy" because one rejoices in its fruit, whereas the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is added with "disgusted disgust" because one enters the meditative absorption of cessation through weariness toward sensation and perception.
Now, examining this closely, it appears that this is merely a single aspect and does not fully exhaust the principle;

for the attainment of non-conceptualization also involves weariness toward perception, while the attainment of cessation also involves joy in entering the absorption. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* explains that in the attainment of cessation, either joy or weariness may prevail.

If it were merely [a matter of] aversion, why would it be called "one of the two"? According to the Sautrāntika school, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is conventional (*prajñapti*); this differs from the present case.

"To meet" (*saṃnipāta*) refers to meeting with the designation of "life-force" (*jīvitendriya*). "To prove by function" means to provide proof based on the function of the sustaining consciousness and so forth.
It is known that there is a real entity called "life" (*jīvitendriya*) which is able to sustain warmth and consciousness; this is what is designated as "vitality" (*āyus*). Question:
By what factor is this vitality sustained? Answer: It is sustained by warmth and consciousness. If that is so, these three factors sustain one another like the three legs of a tripod.

Which of them perishes first? Answer: Because only one [of the three] perishes, the other two perish accordingly. According to the Sautrāntika school, the essence of vitality is not [a separate entity].
In truth, it is said that the *āyus* (vitality) is the continuum of the momentum (*vega*) of the homogeneous state (*nikāya-sabhāga*) projected by karma of the three realms;
because it remains for a determined duration according to what is appropriate, this momentum is called the essence of life.

It is like the momentum projected by seeds of grain and the like until the time of ripening, or like the momentum projected by a released arrow until the time it comes to rest. Thus says the treatise.

Since its fundamental tenet is the same as that of the Sarvāstivāda school, the treatise states: "There exists a distinct, substantial entity capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is termed the essence of life-force (*jīvitendriya*);
this explanation is considered correct.

Regarding the statement that "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to "defining marks," this means they manifest phenomena so that one may know them to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). If a phenomenon possesses these [characteristics], it should...
That which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is so called because it flows through the three time periods by means of the four characteristics;

thus it becomes conditioned. If it lacked the sense of flowing, it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The word "should be said" (*vaktavyam*) might seem to overlap with the phrasing of an objection, yet it is not an objection.

The *Vibhāṣā* asks: "For what reason was this treatise composed? There are those who hold that all characteristics are substantial entities (*dravya*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states: [text follows].
For what reason was this treatise composed? There are those who maintain that all conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such as the Vibhajyavādins;
there are those who maintain that the three characteristics are conditioned while the characteristic of cessation is unconditioned, such as the Dharmaguptakas;

and even those who maintain that the five aggregates, such as form (*rūpa*), at the moment of emerging from the womb are called the "characteristic of birth" (*jātilakṣaṇa*) at the time of their continuity.
The stage of abiding is called "decay" (*jarā*) at the time of transformation, and "cessation" (*nirodha*) at the time of death.

As the Sautrāntikas maintain this view in order to refute that [opposing] position, it is here stated that each and every conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possesses four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in every single moment. That which is able to give rise [to a phenomenon] is called "arising" (*jāti*);
that is to say, it is able to initiate its activity and cause it to enter the present, and is thus designated as "arising. If there were no characteristic of arising, then conditioned phenomena...
The nature of phenomena (*dharma*) is like space and so forth; they should be understood as originally unarisen.

That which is designated as "abiding" (*sthiti*) refers to reaching the present state and causing their functional capacity (*kāritra*) to abide temporarily, thereby enabling each to draw forth its own fruit; therefore, it is called "abiding. If the characteristic of abiding did not exist, phenomena would be unable to each draw forth their respective fruits.
Furthermore, by means of the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*), the capacity of those phenomena to draw forth their fruits is impaired, rendering them incapable of doing so.

Because it repeatedly draws forth its own fruit, it is called "differentiation" (*jarā*). Since its manifest activity has already declined and its function has ceased, it can further destroy that manifest activity of the present;

because this activity has ceased and entered the past, it is called "destruction" (*anityatā*). If the characteristic of destruction did not exist, activity would not cease, and all phenomena would be eternal.

Know that in this school, the characteristic of arising (*jāti*) resides in the future and exerts its function, while the three—abiding (*sthiti*), differentiation (*jarā*), and destruction (*anityatā*)—reside in the present.

It is said that although the stages of arising and ceasing do not occupy a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), because a single moment possesses three natures (*trikāya*), it is taught that the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are identical within one moment.

(The former [explanation] speaks in terms of function, while the latter speaks in terms of essence; each relies on a single meaning, and there is no commentary from the Master. The old [commentary] further provides another interpretation:
when the function of arising occurs, it is called one moment; when the functions of the three present characteristics occur, they are again called one moment. (Sarvāstivāda).

Many schools maintain that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), on the grounds that since these four characteristics possess functional efficacy, their substance must clearly be substantially existent.

However, according to the Sautrāntika school, the four characteristics are established in relation to the arising and ceasing of a single life-span; yet, as they are merely provisional and not real, the treatise asks:
"How can one analyze in this way? Space does not have the characteristics of arising and so forth, nor does it have the nature of a real entity, as previously stated."
Why is this so? It is because these various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) do not manifest in a fixed manner like form (*rūpa*) and other such entities;

nor can they be established as truly existing through authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*). Furthermore, it is not the case that a single moment possesses all three characteristics simultaneously. As the treatise states, the refutation of characteristics is extensive and will not be recounted here in full.
The main intent of the treatise is the same as that of the Sautrāntika school. Thus, the treatise says: "It is spoken of as existing in dependence upon a continuum (*saṃtati*)."

Regarding those who define the characteristics [of conditioned phenomena], they do not contradict correct reasoning and are well-aligned with the sūtras, causing sentient beings to give rise to weariness and fear.
A treatise provides an analogy, saying: "It is like a person situated in a dense forest who has three enemies wishing to cause him harm:

one drags him out from the dense forest (analogous to the characteristic of arising); one diminishes his strength (analogous to the characteristic of change/deterioration); and one destroys his life-faculty (analogous to the characteristic of cessation)."

[The mark of] arising (*utpāda*). One should know that the three marks [of arising, abiding, and ceasing] apply to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the same way. Abiding (*sthiti*) is not established [as a separate mark] because it functions to sustain and establish [the phenomenon].

The note states that this is the interpretation of the first master regarding the intent of the Sūtra; that is to say, it refers to the previous master’s explanation of why the mark of abiding was not mentioned in the Sūtra, which is why he is called the "first master" again.
However, within this chapter, there are three interpretations. If one follows the *Ratnagotravibhāga*...
The Master merely provides two explanations; since the first two interpretations are identical in stating that "abiding" is not mentioned, he combines them into one.
As for Śrī and Kālī, they are none other than the goddess Puṇyavatī and the woman Kālikā from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "the preceding clause answers the question, etc.": this means that the preceding clause answers the question of "further arising," while the following clause answers the objection of "infinite regress.

"Small arising" (sūkṣma-utpāda) is called "arising of arising" because it does not produce abiding and so forth, but produces only "great arising" (mahā-utpāda); therefore, it is termed "arising of arising.
"Great arising," however, produces abiding and so forth as well, not merely arising; therefore, it is not "arising of arising. The same applies to abiding and the other [characteristics].

According to the explanation by Sthiramati, this [interpretation] holds that the "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*) is the minor arising (*upapatti-jāti*), while the "arising itself" (*jāti*) is the major arising;

the *Nyāyānusāra* further states that by analogy, the "cessation of cessation" (*nirodha-nirodha*) is the minor cessation, and the "cessation itself" (*nirodha*) is the major cessation—meaning it is the arising of the major arising.
The same applies to duration (*sthiti*) and the other characteristics. The older tradition maintains two interpretations, asserting that these [characteristics] possess functional efficacy (*śakti*).
The treatise states: "That which is called the activity (*kāritra*) of a dharma, or what is termed 'human effort' (*puruṣakāra*), is designated as 'efficacy' (*sāmarthya*).

According to this principle, there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This means that because of the principle that a single [cause] possesses the capacity for [multiple effects], there is no error of infinite regress.

For instance, a small productive cause (*janman*) is able to produce a large productive cause; since this small productive cause itself arises from the large one, it does not require further [causes].
The other characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*), are established separately because this minor arising produces the major [characteristics].

While the major arising can produce only eight factors—namely, the four major characteristics (abiding, change, decay, and cessation) along with the primary dharma itself—and further produce the four minor characteristics, it is said that these eight factors possess the capacity [to arise]. For example, arising does not arise from itself;

rather, excluding its own self-nature, it can produce the four major characteristics (abiding, change, decay, and cessation) together with the primary dharma, making four, and furthermore, it produces the four minor characteristics.
They constitute eight dharmas because these eight all arise through the power of birth (*jāti*).

Regarding their subsistence (*sthiti*), with the exception of its own self-nature, the remaining eight dharmas are all caused to abide within a single moment by the power of subsistence. The other two [characteristics] are explained by analogy.
Thus, the treatise provides a metaphor: "It is like a hen that gives birth to many chicks, while another gives birth to only one; this is analogous to the birth of birth (*jāti-jāti*)."

The same applies to the power of eight producing one. The *Nyāyānusāra* asks: "Since there is no difference in their nature as 'arising' (*jāti*), how can there be a distinction in their functional capacity (*śakti*)?
For example, although the nature of sensation (*vedanā*) as apprehension (*anubhava*) is without difference, there are distinctions in its functional capacities for either harm or benefit.

Furthermore, regarding primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), there are differences in the scope of their objects; for instance, while the five consciousnesses have only a single object, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cognizes six objects."

"Causing one to know that this characteristic indicates that which is conditioned" (the old translation says: "Causing one to know that this defining characteristic [lakṣaṇa] indicates that the essence of the characterized phenomenon [lakṣya] is conditioned").

If one were to speak merely of "the characteristics of the conditioned," one would not know that these characteristics definitively indicate that the essence of the characterized phenomenon is conditioned.
The meaning of the preceding passage is the same as the new translation, which states: "The conditioned characteristic of the conditioned. The former...
After stating that the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute the essence (*svabhāva*), it is said that the preceding characteristics indicate that which is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

To say they do not indicate that the conditioned "exists" means they do not indicate that the conditioned has an existent essence; that is to say, the essence exists prior [to them] and does not come into being through the four characteristics.
Furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) lack the four characteristics yet their essence nonetheless exists, [the characteristics] are like a young girl’s... [virtue].
Regarding physical characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): this refers to having a pure and chaste nature; slender and rounded ankles; white teeth and thin lips; fine and long hair;
and arms that hang down past the knees—these are called auspicious marks. That which is contrary to these is called an inauspicious mark.

"Not apart from the conjunction of other causes and conditions" means that it is not the case that although there is the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it requires other causes before a phenomenon can arise;

rather, the power of the characteristic of arising alone cannot produce it. The Sautrāntika objects: "If that were so, a phenomenon arises when causes and conditions are in conjunction and does not arise when they are not;
therefore, we know that only causes and conditions exist—what is the use of postulating a 'characteristic of arising'?"
The Vaibhāṣikas replied: "How could all existing phenomena be objects of your knowledge? Because the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is profound and subtle, it is extremely difficult to know;
thus, although they exist as substantial entities, they cannot be known [and so forth]."

The sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) are explained by their respective synonyms—conception (*saṃjñā*), chapter (*vyañjana*), and letter (*akṣara*)—in that order.
Because conception arises from a name, it is said that "the name produces the conception"; this is because one uses the name of the effect [conception] to designate the cause [the name].

Furthermore, it should be understood that since the meaning of the name as it expresses the characteristics of phenomena is identical to that of conception, it is called "conception. This linguistic convention is termed "conception" (*saṃjñā*). Up to this point...

"Designation as perception" (*nāma-saṃjñā*) means that names are established through the conventional designations of the noble ones (*ārya*), which function as expressive designations; because this act of designation is itself perception, it is called "designation as perception.
Regarding the meaning of "converging" (*pratyāgama*): it refers to approaching its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), wherein there is an internal differentiation of characteristics;
to call out and express this with single-minded focus is the meaning of "converging. By means of such calling, one is able to lead [the mind] to its own essence. In Sanskrit, this is called *saṃgha*.
If one considers this [term] "saṃjñā" (here translated as "conceptualization"), it carries the meaning of grasping at signs with exclusive adherence, or the meaning of a convention.

Regarding the phrase "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and so forth: this refers to expressing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are known to be impermanent; because it articulates specific distinctions, it is called a "phrase" (*pada*).

As for "function, quality, and time": one interpretation follows the chapter [of the *Abhidharmakośa*]; a new explanation says it is like saying that "wholesomeness can bring about desirable fruits" or that "a sword [is capable of cutting]."
"Cutting things" and so forth refers to its *karma* (activity); "tranquility as bliss" refers to its *guṇa* (quality); and "three incalculable eons" refers to its *kāla* (time).

Alternatively, when explaining the characteristics of phenomena, they are called *saṃprayoga* (conjunction) because they accord with one another; when explaining their meanings, they are called *viśeṣa* (distinction) because the meanings differ.

An older source further states that "time" (*kāla*) is an auxiliary phrase and "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*) has the sense of "hooking and binding," meaning it distinguishes and clarifies activity, quality, and time.
Among these, that which refers to the uninterrupted attachment to names and meanings is called the "distinction of correspondence" (*saṃprayoga-viśeṣa*).
That is to say, whatever dharma possesses this functional activity, its variation according to time is called the "distinction of time" (*kāla-viśeṇa*).

For example, as an elephant has four tracks—meaning that by following the tracks one finds the elephant—so too, by following the phrases (*pada*) one obtains the meaning; therefore, it is translated as *pada*. As for the explanation of *pada* as a chapter (*varga*), this is the traditional [interpretation].
It is said that conventions differ between regions; in this land, verses (*gāthā*) are few while chapters (*varga*) are many.

In the legal tradition of India, both chapters and verses serve as the ultimate means of explaining meaning, and thus one may use chapters to explain verses. Furthermore, the *Zhengli chao* states: "In non-Buddhist texts, a verse consists of several words, which differs from a chapter;
here, a verse is defined by its expression of meaning, which is similar to a chapter. As for the term "word" (*akṣara*), it is [derived from] Sanskrit.
The term "akṣara" (in the Tang translation, *zi*) signifies the meaning of non-transmigration, in that it does not shift or change according to direction;
it also signifies the meaning of manifestation. What is here called "text" (*vyañjana*) refers to the function of the syllable (*akṣara*).

Regarding the syllables within the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), these refer to syllables that express through specific vocal modulations; they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind.
One who argues against the theory that characters are distinct from the *lipi* (scripts) asks: "Is it not the case that these characters are also named after the scripts? The answer is:
"It is not for the purpose of manifesting the scripts that the various characters were created; rather, it is for the purpose of manifesting the various characters that the scripts were created.
Why is this? It is so that even those who have not heard the teachings may still attain understanding. Therefore, the characters are not the scripts.

Furthermore, because one wishes to rely on the syllable "rūpa" (form) to retain non-associated [factors] and to transmit the syllable "rūpa" to other regions and future generations, one creates written characters.

Although this has already been clarified above, the specific characteristics of the distinctions between names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) have not yet been fully explained.
Regarding this, the Abhidharma states: "Those two depend upon the syllables, just as the patterns of brocade depend upon the silk; they are manifested by the arising of the threads."

Distinct from other locations, it is precisely based on this manifestation that they are arranged to form dragons and phoenixes; furthermore, by combining these dragons and phoenixes, one creates the fundamental pattern of a brocade.
All of this depends upon the manifesting phonemes (*vyañjana*) to produce the threads, just as sounds correspond to phonemes and phonemes correspond to syllables (*akṣara*).

Dragons and phoenixes are like phrases (*pada*), while the brocade pattern is like the syllables "a," "i," and so forth, which are manifest within the sounds. One then takes this manifestation as that which is capable of designating its own object.

The distinction between the meanings of the designations for gender and transformation arises from the differentiation of phrases; therefore, these names and phrases all depend upon syllables (*vyañjana*).
Question: What is the difference between a single-syllable name and a syllable? Answer: The *Chao* (Excerpts) states:

"In the West, the basis of syllables has existed since the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), based on various inflected sounds (*pariṇāma-śabda*). Having first established a standard, later people adopted them and applied them to this dharma, whereby names were produced."
When not yet designated, there is no name, but only a syllable (*vyañjana*); like a syllable without meaning, it is not called a designator (*abhidhāna*).

Therefore, one knows that the designator possesses a distinct name. When they arise in extreme proximity and their mutual resemblance is extremely difficult to discern—just as it is hard to distinguish between the two colors of a jade disk and its light—the general term for their collection is *saṃketa* in Sanskrit, which here means "general designation" (*sāmānyasaṃjñā*). *Saṃmoha* in Sanskrit [refers to] delusion.

Regarding the term *vaye*, translated here as "composite" (*hoji*), it refers to the condition of the phonemes (*akṣara*). For instance, in this land, characters such as those for "river" (*jia*) and "stream" (*he*) all derive from their constituent water;

thus, water itself is the "element" (*dhātu*), while the phonemes *ga* and *ka* serve as the "conditions" (*pratyaya*). It is because *ga* assists the water that "river" (*jia*) is formed, and because *ka* assists the water that "stream" (*he*) is formed.
As for the statement that the general designation arises from *uṣman*: since the conditions have already assisted, the *uṣman* [consonants] transform into a general designation.

The explanation of "knowing the collective" (samudāya-jñāna) begins with the statement that [words] such as *gaṅgā* arise from water; this makes it clear that the collective expression also arises from a combination.

Since the verbal root (*dhātu*) of the word *samudāya* is fundamentally "combination," and its meaning as a "collective" remains intact when it is transformed into the sense of a "general term" (*samudāya-śabda*), how could it not be a combination?
For instance, just as words like *gaṅgā* still possess the quality of water, a single name is likewise so.
Regarding "name" (*nāman*) and "name-body" (*nāmakāya*): it is called a "name" because it possesses expressive power; it is not a "body" because it has not yet been aggregated.

Furthermore, it is said that names are of many kinds—whether a name consists of one syllable, two syllables, or three syllables—regardless of their number, as long as they constitute a single name, they are all not "bodies.
Regarding "name-body," this refers to multiple names being designated as a single body.
"Name" (*nāman*) does not refer to a collection of many phonemes (*akṣara*). The same applies to phrases (*pada*) and sentences (*vyañjana*). Phrases also have various positions:

namely, the intermediate phrase (eight syllables), the initial phrase (six syllables or more), the final phrase (twenty-six syllables or fewer), the short phrase (fewer than twenty-six syllables), and the long phrase (more than twenty-six syllables).
The compositions of the Sūtras and Śāstras mostly rely on the intermediate phrase. Sentences are also of many kinds; for instance, a single sentence may be produced by multiple moments of sound.
Alternatively, a single phoneme may give rise to a single name, and so forth (as detailed in the full passage). For example, regarding the case of *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*:

one might ask why, previously, [the text] cited *a*, *ā*, and so on, whereas here it cites *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*. The traditional explanation states that the former refers to the sound (*śabda*) of the syllables, while this refers to the body (*mūrti*) of the syllables.

To demonstrate that both sound and body are equally "syllables" (*akṣara*), the first [example] is cited to subsume the subsequent ones; thus, a single category is established for these nine meanings.

Regarding the word "ghu," because the Sautrāntika school maintains that factors such as names (*nāman*) are not substantially real or fixed, whereas the Vaibhāṣika school asserts that there exists a distinct substantial entity called "name" and so forth,
the Master [Vasubandhu] employs a critique based on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) according to the Sautrāntika position that names and so forth are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
Regarding the statement that "because there is no form and no sound in the formless realm (ārūpya), there is no name," some other masters claim that names also extend into the formless realm;
however, they argue it cannot be so spoken because it would be useless. This is not the correct interpretation. As for "that which is not the meaning being manifested," the *Vibhāṣā* asks:
"Who accomplishes the name and so forth—is it the speaker or the subject spoken of? If it were the speaker, then [in the case of] an Arhat...
It would follow that defiled phenomena are established [as existing], because Arhats and others are also said to possess defiled phenomena.

If it is argued that what is spoken of [establishes their existence], then external unconditioned phenomena (*bāhyam asaṃskṛtam*) would also be established as having names and so forth, since they too are phenomena that are spoken of. Answer: Only the speaker establishes [the existence of] these things.

If that is so, the subsequent objection is well-answered; how then do you answer the previous objection? [We reply: Although an Arhat may possess defiled phenomena and the like, [they do not establish the existence of external objects].

They are designated as such but do not constitute defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas and so forth, because names such as "defiled" are all of the nature of non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because they are not produced by karma, and because they do not pertain to maturation (*vipāka*).
This means that they arise according to one's will rather than being a retribution for past karma; they are not maturation because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
they are not truly produced by a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); and they do not last for even a single moment. Only...
Regarding "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) and "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*): the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks, "What is the homogeneity that is maturation (*vipāka-sabhāgatā*)?

It refers to the homogeneity of destinies and births, such as those in the hells and those born from eggs. What is the homogeneity that is outflow? It refers to the [homogeneity] of the realms (*dhātu*).

Regarding the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of locations, castes, lineages, *śramaṇas*, *brahmins*, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), some say that what is projected by prior karma is the "maturation commonality" (*vipākaja-sabhāgatā*), while that which arises from present application (*prayoga*) is the "outflow commonality" (*naiṣyandika-sabhāgatā*);

the other two are to be understood as these same outflow and maturation types. Furthermore, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of dharmas are of the nature of "dissimilarity" (*visabhāga*).
The Matured and the Remaining are of the Nature of Outflow.

The word "qiě" (and/also) is used because this follows the analysis of the six types of causes within the four conditions; it is used here specifically to analyze the six causes.

Regarding why the *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) is placed first among the six causes, the *Xiǎnzōng lùn* (Treatise on Manifesting the Tenets) states: "The essence of the *kāraṇahetu* pervades all phenomena."
Therefore, it was stated previously that the essence of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) pervades all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and thus it is placed second;

the other [causes], such as the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth, each encompass a small portion of conditioned phenomena as appropriate, and are explained in their sequence for the sake of linguistic convenience.
Regarding the "contemplative" Kātyāyanīputra, the *Nyāya* states: "In the various sūtras, by the power of those to be converted, the world..."

The Venerable Master [Vasubandhu], employing a different method of exposition, states that the masters of Abhidharma, having observed certain partial signs, know for certain that there was a clear compilation [of this material];
thus some say that the meaning of these six causes was taught in the *Ekottarika-āgama* and the *Ṣaṭka-āgama*, but over a long period of time the text has been lost.
Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others...
Reflecting deeply, he sought a mystical response, and a celestial being (devaputra) appeared and bestowed upon him the *Devadatta-sūtra*.

This principle is necessarily so; although the meaning of the four conditions (*catur-pratyaya*) is fully set forth in this sūtra, there are those in other sections who do not recite it, as explained at length.
(The commentary says: When the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a bhikṣu named Devadatta who, while reciting the sūtra at midnight, omitted one chapter. Inside his room, a celestial being...)

Suddenly encountering this extraordinary report, I presented it to the World-Honored One at dawn, whereupon I received his confirmation and exposition. That the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*) should likewise conform to that principle is because they are present in the *Caturārpitā-sūtra*, just as the six causes are not recited in the *Mahīśāsaka* and *Dharmaguptaka* schools.
Regarding the statement "conditioned phenomena other than its own self," this excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because unconditioned phenomena lack arising;

therefore, they are not considered *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes) in relation to one another. As for why one's own self must be excluded: the meaning of *kāraṇa-hetu* is "non-obstruction," yet a phenomenon is always an obstruction to itself.
Furthermore, if all phenomena were to depend upon their own selves [as causes], it would lead to logical fallacies.

There would be faults such as the perpetual existence or the perpetual diminution [of the entity]. That is to say, if it were dependent upon its own self-essence, then because that self-essence exists eternally, there would be the fault of its perpetual existence.
If it were dependent upon a second self-essence, then because that second self-essence eternally does not exist, there would be the fault of its perpetual diminution.
Other masters say: "Because it does not perceive any utility in itself, it is not a causal condition, just as a thing cannot act upon itself."
A finger cannot cut itself, and an eye cannot see itself. Regarding the claim that all phenomena serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*):

if one asks how it is that when sunlight arises, stars and the like do not appear, and the consciousness that would perceive them does not arise due to the absence of its object—how can it be said that conditioned phenomena have all phenomena as their efficient cause, excluding only themselves?
The answer is: at the time of their arising, [all other phenomena] abide without acting as an obstacle.
Therefore, it is said that [a cause] is "capable" (kāraṇa), which does not mean that it is called "capable" only when it is not producing [an effect].
For example, people of a country say, "We obtain peace and happiness because of our sovereign," even though he does not actively harm them.

If this is so, since nirvāṇa and unarisen phenomena (*anutpattidharma*) fundamentally lack any obstructive function toward the arising of all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*), how can they be considered [causes]?
In response, it is said that although there is no obstructive function, it nonetheless serves as a cause, just as a powerless king may still be described as such.

As for the statement "abiding without obstruction," this means that the essence of this cause abides within the state of non-obstruction; thus, the cause that abides without obstruction is itself the "active agent" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
This is one interpretation according to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, which, in total, presents four views on this matter. This is the first.

The second interpretation states: Alternatively, this cause can be said to perform two functions; because it does not obstruct, it may be called a "cause," yet because it cannot produce [the result] itself, it may also be called "not a cause.
The third [interpretation] states: That which is capable of acting is the immediate cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*);

because this [condition] assists that [immediate cause], it is called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*). (The commentary explains: this means it assists the other five causes. The fourth [interpretation] states: Alternatively, this [condition] enables another to perform an action. That other...

This means that when a result has the capacity to act as a cause, it is termed a "productive cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*). (The commentary explains: this is like how a flower and fruit can serve as the seeds for subsequent growth.

Regarding the "sphere of form" (*rūpāyatana*): among the ten spheres such as the eye and so forth, all are material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*). While the other nine spheres each have their own distinct names, this "sphere of form" alone has no separate name of its own;
it is distinguished by being contrasted with those other nine. Thus, although this sphere of form bears a general designation, [it is specifically identified through that exclusion].

Regarding the distinct names: although "simultaneous cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*) is here used as a general designation, it also functions as a specific name (this explanation being based on the first of the four types of etymological interpretation).
As for the interpretation of mutual causality, the treatise states: "Just as three staffs stand by leaning against one another."

The principle of cause and effect regarding co-existent dharmas is established according to the *Vibhāṣā*’s master commentator (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the *Nyāyānusāra*, both of whom state that the meaning of "having the same fruit" constitutes the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Regarding what is meant by "having one fruit," it refers, for example, to how the mind and mental factors together produce a single fruit.
As for these four great elements being mutually dependent, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "That is to say, if the four great elements were to exist individually..."
If there is no partial increase, the elements serve as three causes for one another, and three serve as the cause for derived matter. Why is this?

Because an element does not depend upon another element to produce derived matter; for all phenomena do not depend upon their own nature (*svabhāva*) or their own kind (*sajātīya-bhāva*) to function as causes or effects for others.
The same principle applies to the remaining great elements. Regarding the mutual relationship between the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this sūtra distinguishes three [types].
Since categories are divided into five types, there are four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) that relate to one another.

However, according to the correct principle (*nyāya*), it is not said that the four characteristics and the mental concomitants (*cittānuvartin*) relate to one another. Therefore, the questioner asks: "The characteristics of causes described here are too few. Yet, he himself explains:
"Because they are taught in the *Mūla-śāstra* (the Root Treatise), these must be explained here. Thus, within this context, one should clarify the intention of the author of the treatise.

This is intended to demonstrate that it is only dissimilar types (*vijātīya*) that are taught as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), whereas similar types (*sajātīya*) are not taught as being causes for one another [as they are self-established].

(According to this treatise, only three categories are mentioned. Regarding what should be analyzed here: according to the new outline (*navavidha-krama*), the point to be clarified is which dharma is called "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*), forming a continuous sentence.
The present chapter states that this is the Master’s exhortation that the Sarvāstivāda school should understand the mutual causality.
Regarding the statement that "the effect exceeds the fault": this means that the minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) do not mutually serve as effects.

If the primary dharma (*mūladharma*) and the minor characteristics were mutual causes, then the cause would not be coextensive with the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), resulting in a case where the cause is narrower and the thesis (*pakṣa*) is broader.

Now, examining the *Vibhāṣā*, since the commentator (the *pūrvapakṣin*) explains the simultaneous cause (*sahabhūhetu*) by means of a single effect, and Master Vasubandhu himself explains it by means of mutual causality, why does the Master [Vasubandhu] instead propose [this alternative]?
Is there a fault in this school’s position? Because there is, the Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) critiques this treatise for the fault of mutual causality;

he subsequently explains the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) by means of a single effect. The old tradition states that "entering the Abhidharma" refers to works composed after this treatise, and that those who speak of mutual causality are students of our own teacher, Vasubandhu.
Based on such passages, it should not be [the case] that the Master [Vasubandhu] himself authored [this work].
There is a doctrinal error; we request that you examine this again. We ask the *Vibhāṣā* and other treatises: Is that which is called "a single fruit" simultaneous, or is it at different times?
If so, what is the fault? Both positions possess errors. If they were simultaneous, then how could that which is its own self be the fruit of that which is not its own self?
How could they both exist as having the same single fruit? Furthermore, the production of the great and the production of the small do not share the same fruit.
This is the cause of a single effect; how does it differ from the previous [position] regarding the non-pervasion of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*)?

If you claim that the effect occurs at a different time, then this is merely a minor characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that is of the same outflow (*niṣyanda*) as its primary dharma; why then would the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) not also serve as the cause for that primary dharma?

This is the cause of a single effect that extends even to heterogeneous instances (*vipakṣa*); its fault is even more severe than [the previous one], as it functions within those heterogeneous instances.

The new school [the Yogācāra] states that what is established in both treatises is free from fault. For example, the definition of "form" (*rūpa*) as "that which undergoes transformation and resistance" is not over-extended (*avyāpti*) to include non-manifest form (*avijñapti*).
Furthermore, although one speaks of a "horse" when referring to a horse eating quickly or walking swiftly, there are horses that eat slowly or walk at a leisurely pace;

yet this naming does not contradict worldly convention. This same principle applies to the mutual relationship of being causes and effects, as well as to the case of multiple factors sharing a single effect.
It should also be so; this entry into the Abhidharma does not contradict reason, as it cites both causes together.

Because this treatise is concise, it cites only one [of the two]. (The commentary explains that the "two causes" refers to being mutually effects of one another and having the same effect—these are the two causes.)

Regarding the phrase "those [characteristics] and the various characteristics of the mind," this single sentence refers exclusively to the four characteristics, such as arising (*jāti*), and so forth.

This is because the word "those" (*te*) subsumes two types of characteristics: first, the characteristics upon mental factors (*caitta*), and second, the characteristics upon the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*). When these are further combined with the characteristics upon the mind-king (*cittarāja*), there are, in total, three categories of the four characteristics.
As for the traditional interpretation: since it mentions "arising and so forth" but does not mention "the arising of arising" and so forth, it is thereby made manifest.
The secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) do not follow the mind in their activity.

Regarding future dharmas that have not yet reached the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*): when a future dharma reaches the state of the characteristic of arising, it becomes somewhat proximate [to the primary dharma], whereas otherwise it is not so;
this is because it has been raised as being adjacent to the characteristic of arising. For this reason, it is said to exist in the future.
Regarding "the preceding" and "past dharmas": this refers to dharmas that have already ceased and exist in the past world;

because they are not subsumed under the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is said that they are only "co-arising," which does not include the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) prior to them. Regarding the future, it is said that they are only "co-ceasing," which does not include the characteristic of arising prior to them.
Regarding the past, it is said that they are only "co-ceasing," which does not include the period after the characteristic of cessation; thus, there are three [distinctions].
Since the manner in which the characteristics (lakṣaṇas) mutually encompass one another is not exhaustive, the *Nyāya* states:
"Is it not the case that by merely saying 'one [characteristic] arises, abides, and ceases,' one already understands that it falls within a single time-period?

Yet, this has not yet clarified whether these characteristics and the dharma itself are inseparable across the past and future, or [whether this is] for the purpose of demonstrating those dharmas that do not arise. Thus, among the four characteristics, "change" (*anyathātva*) is not mentioned.

Answer: "Arising" (utpāda) indicates that [the dharma] exists together [with its causes] in the future and is about to enter the present; "cessation" (nirodha) indicates that it exists together in the present and enters the past;

and "abiding" (sthiti) indicates that this dharma is currently taking up its fruit. This thus reveals that the three times—past, future, and present—are simultaneous and possess a single characteristic without distinction, as they are capable of manifesting [their effects].
For this reason, the term "single fruit" is not mentioned here; rather, the intention is to include the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the fruit of disconnection (visamyoga-phala).

This refers to the fact that outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and ripening (*vipāka*) fruits are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), as they are understood to include the two fruits of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and disconnection (*visamyoga*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Regarding the term 'fruit,' it subsumes everything from the causal conditions.
Since the simultaneous cause is explained herein, the other two fruits should not be clarified; thus, the term "fruit" here subsumes only human effort and disconnection.

Fearing that there might be an objection regarding the fruit of the bond, one might say: "If that is so, then in explaining the meaning of 'concomitant' (*anuvartin*) here, one should only speak of one fruit;

one should not mention the other two types. To this, the present explanation says: in order to dispel such doubts and obstacles, it is necessary to explain the significance of those two. What is their meaning?
Generally, there are four kinds of *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort) [as in the examples in the treatise]. These four kinds all depend upon the agent who performs the action.
Because they are produced by the power of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) associated with the mind, they are all termed "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) according to this principle.

In this context of "concomitant transformation," the term "single fruit" does not refer to a successively transmitted fruit of human effort (*pāramparya-puruṣakāra-phala*), because its own essence is not the fruit of itself;

thus it does not constitute the sense of a "single fruit. Rather, it refers only to those other things produced within the state of co-arising that are acquired through effort, as well as others that follow immediately without interval.
To prevent those who have not yet understood from hearing the term "result" (*phala*) and assuming it refers to co-arising or reciprocal *puruṣakāra*-results,

or from clinging to the notion that there are only co-arising *puruṣakāra*-results, [the author] now separately demonstrates that outflow (*niṣyanda*) and ripening (*vipāka*) results are definitely results that do not arise simultaneously with their causes,
in order to refute the exclusive attachment to [only] simultaneous causes and results.

Within the collection of co-nascent and conjoined factors, there exists the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); therefore, it is necessary to exclude this fruit of human effort because it is not a single fruit.
Furthermore, why is it that one merely excludes the mutual fruits of co-nascent factors? It is also intended to simultaneously demonstrate the absence of a single fruit.
For this reason, *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit) and *vipāka-phala* (ripening fruit) are not mentioned, as they are not required and do not constitute a single fruit.
The *Shèjiùjiě* (Compendium of Old Explanations) is also the same as the new [commentary], which states: "This treatise negates the attainment of simultaneous fruits;

it does not intend to include the various *puruṣakāra-phalas* (fruits of human effort) that are either immediate or separated [in time], which differs from the explanation above" (the details are not fully recounted here). First, regarding the mutual *puruṣakāra-phala* of co-existent and associated causes:

this refers to the fact that the mind, mental factors, and the four characteristics (arising, duration, change, and cessation) act as mutual fruits for one another. Second, "and the rest" [refers to other such cases].
"Simultaneously produced and acquired" refers to those things other than the successive fruits (kṣaṇika-phala), which are termed "the rest. The *Zhengli chao* states:

"For example, the resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and so forth. According to this, since it mentions "resistant matter and so forth," it encompasses both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) matter.
Lin says: "This means that within a single assemblage (*samagra*), the [four] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the mind produce informative and non-informative matter simultaneously."
(Now, upon detailed examination, the reason why the name "kṛtaka" (produced) is applied according to its characteristics remains unclear).

That which is induced by the *samanantara-pratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition)—namely, the preceding moments of mind and mental factors—possesses the power to induce subsequent results such as those mentioned above, as will be explained below.
Second, regarding those produced by other immediate [conditions]: this refers to this very production.

Form (*rūpa*) is called "the remainder" because it is distinct from the fruit of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Since a subsequent moment is not separated by a long interval from the preceding one, it is termed "adjacent.
Here, the term "adjacent" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth of the preceding moment; the term "activity" (*abhisamskāra*) refers to the simultaneous primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, it is said that this applies exclusively to the two types of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*)—those of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*)—because form here follows the mind.
Regarding "fruits obtained after an interval" (*vyavahita-phala*) due to transformation: this refers to all fruits obtained from the third moment onward.

As for "fruits separated by an interval," the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Zhengli chao) states: "It is like when a person has finished plowing and sowing a field, and only at a later time do the sprouts and so forth arise;

these fruits are likewise. [The commentary explains: "This is just as the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the first moment remotely produce numerous future unmanifest forms (*avijñapti*); in relation to those prior primary elements, are these not indeed separated by an interval? Regarding this:

Among the co-emergent (*sahaja*) and human-effort (*puruṣakāra*) fruits, only those produced simultaneously are taken as the agent, because the nature of a successive fruit is neither its own essence nor a non-essence fruit, and thus it is not taken.
As for taking other heterogeneous [factors] that are immediate, the above explained that there are two types of immediate human-effort fruits:
first, the fruit of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and second, the fruit obtained through successive production. Regarding the latter:
In the middle section, both the same-natured and different-natured [causes] are discussed; here, setting aside the same-natured, we shall take only the different-natured.

For example, regarding the fruit of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), that which is of a different nature is as follows: when a preceding wholesome mind is followed by a subsequent unwholesome mind, these are of different natures.

The same-natured cases may be understood accordingly. As for the production of the attainment of the fruit, if one considers only the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) in relation to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*):
However, if one considers the "other-nature" (parabhāva) from both perspectives, it encompasses both the homogeneous (sabhāga) and the heterogeneous (visabhāga).
This is because the fruit of this other-nature, when considered generally with respect to the two categories [of cause and effect], encompasses both mind and matter.

Regarding the statement that "one fruit" refers exclusively to the virile fruit (puruṣakāra-phala) and the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyoga-phala), this concludes the previous point; yet, here we are taking all four fruits in their totality.
The results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) are: (1) simultaneous production; (2) attainment of a result of a different nature; (3) immediate succession; (4) distant human effort;
and (5) non-arising human effort. This accords with the traditional interpretation.

These ten causes for which a mental state is said to be "concomitant" (*anuvartin*) refer only to its general categories and do not require that all ten causes be present simultaneously, as it is impossible for the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) to coexist. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Because the outflows (āsrava) that follow [the mind] have no ripening fruit (vipākaphala), they are said to be "extremely few.

Regarding their being the co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu) for fifty-eight dharmas, this refers specifically to the ten mental factors such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth; since there is nothing subtracted from these, they are called "extremely few.

For instance, in the case of the two higher meditative attainments (dhyāna) and above, within the state of an unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind, there are only eleven dharmas, including the major and minor [mental factors].

Regarding the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are ninety-nine factors; among these ninety-nine, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) acts as a cause for only fifty-eight factors. (The commentary explains:

from the second *dhyāna* upward, because there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*), and because there is neither the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) nor faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, or delusion (*moha*) and so forth, there are only ten mental concomitants (*caitta*). Together with the mind-king, this makes eleven. Only in this state is it the absolute minimum.

In the desire realm and the first *dhyāna*, because there is applied and sustained thought, it is not the absolute minimum. Question: Why does this [mind-king] not act as a cause for the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) that follow upon the mental concomitants?
Answer: Because they are remote, the mind-king (citta-rāja) is not a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) with respect to them (meaning the power of the mind-king does not extend to the second [moment]).
If one discusses the maximum number, the mind-king acts as a cause for one hundred and fifty-eight dharmas;

that is, within the first dhyāna, there are ten universal (mahābhūmika) factors, ten wholesome (kuśala-mahābhūmika) factors, either the factor of joy (prīti) or aversion (vidveṣa), along with the seven branches of the meditative absorption including vitarka, vicāra, and samādhi, totaling thirty.
When the one primary dharma and its major and minor characteristics are totaled, there are two hundred and seventy-nine dharmas;

however, because the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), the *samprayukta-saṃvara* (concomitant restraint), and so forth—namely, the aforementioned minor characteristics—are excluded, only one hundred and fifty-eight dharmas serve as causes.

Regarding the statement that "the mind does not have the secondary characteristics as its causes," the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (*Kōsharon Jutsuki*) states: "Because the secondary characteristics have efficacy toward a single [primary characteristic], they function only in relation to that which they characterize (*lakṣya*)."
Regarding the reasoning for why the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) are not co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) of the primary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is also said:

because the mind follows its own characteristics, yet the mind does not arise by the power of those [secondary characteristics]; because the mind and those [characteristics] do not serve as mutual fruits;

and because, within the aggregate, they are for the most part not the fruits of those [secondary characteristics]. (The commentary explains: the minor characteristics merely characterize one dharma—the major characteristic—while other dharmas are not the fruits of the minor characteristics. It is precisely due to these many stated reasons.

The secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are not called "factors that follow the mind" (*cittānuvartaka-dharma*). (This is an incidental clarification that the secondary characteristics do not follow the mind.
If that is so, how can the mind serve as a cause for them? Answer: Because they proceed by following the various characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). Question:

Since the characteristics of mental factors (*caitta*) do not follow the mind-king, how can they mutually serve as causes for one another? Answer: Because they possess functional efficacy (*samarthya*) with respect to the mind-king.

Just as mental factors (*caitta*) relate to the mind-king (*cittarāja*), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that because primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) possess a power equal to that of the dharma itself, they act as co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for that dharma;
however, secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) do not act as causes for the mind-king because they lack such power.

This above explains how causes universally include the mental factors and their secondary characteristics. Other masters, however, maintain that only the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) together with the mind [act as co-existent causes].
The fourteen factors of the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute the mind-king (*citta-rāja*); therefore, this is not a correct argument, as it has been extensively refuted.

Regarding those which become causes by virtue of being co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), they must necessarily be co-existent. In the phrase "by virtue of the cause" (*hetu-yogāt*), the upper "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the reason or ground;

the lower "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). That is to say, if one attains the status of a cause through the principle of co-existence, it is called a co-existent cause.

Since these must necessarily be simultaneous, it is said that they "must be co-existent," etc. Alternatively, there may be cases where things are co-existent but do not constitute a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
That which constitutes such a cause refers to those phenomena which, although simultaneous, do not become co-existent causes by virtue of the principle of simultaneity;
this refers, for example, to the eight pairs of dharmas. Regarding the first pair among these eight pairs: [text follows].

Regarding the previous explanation in the commentary on the second pair, the phrase "mutually related, they do not share a single fruit" means that "mutually related" refers to the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) being related to one another.

"Not a single fruit of the mind" and so forth means that, for example, the minor *jāti* (birth-characteristic) produces only the major *jāti*, and the minor *sthiti* (duration-characteristic) sustains only the major *sthiti*;
thus, their fruits are not the same. This includes cases where they are not of the same *vipāka* (maturation) or the same *niṣyanda* (outflow).

The "New Translation" (Xīnyún) states: "This is not a single fruit; the meaning is extremely difficult to understand. Examining this in detail, it means that although they possess common power (*sāmarthya*), because they do not grasp [the object] together (*samudāharaṇa*), it is not a single fruit.

Although the fruit is the same, because the powers differ and they do not grasp it together, it is not a single fruit. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* says: "Within a collection, the majority are not its fruit.

[Commentary: This means: first, common power; second, grasping together—these constitute the meaning of being a single fruit.
