For example, as when two people together realize the unconditioned fruit of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); although the fruit is the same, it is not a single fruit.

Only when factors are associated and possess equal power can they be said to share a single fruit; now, although the four minor characteristics (lakṣaṇas) share the same ripening (vipāka), outflowing (niṣyanda), and so forth as the primary dharma, because their powers differ, they do not constitute a single fruit and so on. As it is with this pair, so it is with other similar cases.

Regarding the fifth pair, although form (rūpa), sound (śabda), and so forth are simultaneous, they do not mutually share a single fruit and so on; therefore, they are not co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu).
As for derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) and the primary elements (mahābhūta), however, the primary elements do possess the sense of sharing a common fruit, which is derived matter.

Because derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) has no sense of being a fruit in relation to the primary elements (mahābhūta), they are also not mutually fruits of one another. The treatise concludes by stating:

"Although such dharmas as these are called 'coexistent' (*sahabhū*), they do not constitute a cause by virtue of being coexistent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Causes are not of a single type, and their fruits differ;

[the fruits] are the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) and the uniform outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). Thus, this [category] does not apply to the previous seven pairs, as there is no instance of a single fruit. The eighth is acquisition (*prāpti*)."
Because that which is acquired is not fixed, it is explained separately. Furthermore, regarding the eight [categories] above in relation to the ten causes:
the first four pairs and the sixth pair all possess seven causes, but lack the three beginning with "result" (*phala*).

The fifth pair sometimes possesses the four beginning with "time" (*kāla*), lacks the three beginning with "wholesomeness" (*kuśala*) and the three beginning with "result," such as in the case of visible form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and those [factors] belonging to the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), as well as fragrance (*gandha*) and so forth.

Because it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the seventh pair is likewise so. Although the eighth [pair], consisting of the attainment (*prāpti*) and that which is attained (*prāpya*), share the same nature, their timing is not fixed;
because they may occur either before or after one another, coinciding by chance, there is the school’s teaching of simultaneous cause and effect, such as flame and light, or the body and its shadow.
According to the Sautrāntika school, however, the cause precedes and the effect follows, as in the case of mutual [dependence].
This involves mutual refutations with the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (and so forth).

Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), there are two interpretations: if it is called a "homogeneous cause" because it serves as the cause for similar dharmas, it is an *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the cause of the homogeneous";
if it is called a "homogeneous cause" by taking similar dharmas themselves as the cause, it is [an *appositional* compound].
This is an *ubhayapada-karmadhāraya* (appositional compound where both members function as the agent). A new explanation states that the latter does not reach the former;

"defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) and "the defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*)—this term "defilement" applies to both unwholesome (*akuśala*) dharmas and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas, because these two types of dharmas serve as causes for one another.

That is to say, the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are obscured-unspecified, and they can either serve as causes for the unwholesome or arise from the unwholesome.
Because they are "born" (*jāta*), the term "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*) is used to comprehensively include both types [of neutral states].

Regarding the statement that this clarifies the "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), the phrase "is also thus" follows the treatise’s explanation of the causes for wholesome and defiled states, where no other explanation is given.

As for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the neutral, there are four different explanations; however, since we are here merely recounting the correct view, it is said to be "also thus. Nevertheless, according to the treatise itself, there is further...
Regarding the three explanations: The first says: One [aggregate], the pure-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), is the fruit of the five; four are not the cause of matter (*rūpa*).

(The intention of this master is that because the nature of matter is inferior, it serves as a cause for what is superior; since the four aggregates are superior to matter, they are not the cause of matter. The second says: Five are the fruits of the four; matter is not the cause of the four.

(The intention of this master is that the power of the four aggregates is superior and can serve as a cause for the five aggregates; because the power of the aggregate of matter is inferior, it does not serve as a cause for the four. The third says: Matter and the four aggregates are mutually related.

None [of these] act as causes. (The intention of this master is that although the four aggregates and the form aggregate are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because they are inferior, they do not act as causes when viewed from the perspective of different categories.

Among these four explanations, the older tradition states that since there is no adjudicating authority, the latter interpretation should be taken as correct. The newer tradition states that the first explanation is superior;
for if, within the nature of the wholesome and the defiled, the five aggregates may mutually serve as causes for one another, why would it be otherwise for the indeterminate?

Because this contradicts the principle of the two natures (*dvividha-svabhāva*), those within one's own school—namely the five schools—correlate with the nine stages (*navabhūmi*). This results in forty-five categories (five times nine), each acting as a distinct cause.
Within this context, however, one excludes only different stages and different schools, but does not exclude different destinies (*gati*) or different locations (*sthāna*).
Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Afflictions arising in the same stage but different locations bind one another reciprocally; they bind one another according to their respective types."

It acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), yet with the exception of different categories (*nikāya*), because there are distinctions in the limits of the fetters of the five categories of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Regarding the phrase "arisen previously," as stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*: "What is the homogeneous cause?

It means that a previously arisen wholesome root is the homogeneous cause for subsequently arisen wholesome roots, as well as for their associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) factors, within its own realm (*sva-dhātu*). Thus it constitutes a cause.
However, to speak of the past in relation to the present and so forth is merely a coarse description.

If one seeks the meaning according to the principle, then only by considering the past that arose earlier in relation to the past that arose later, as well as dharmas of the present and future that have not yet arisen, and the past that arose later in relation to the present and future that have arisen or not yet arisen, can one fully exhaust the logic.
The same applies to the present when it is considered in relation to [the other times].

Subsequently arising dharmas and non-arising dharmas can all serve as causes for one another; however, future dharmas do not possess the cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*), because future dharmas abide in a state of confusion and their sequence has not yet been established.

Even when they approach the characteristic of arising, they have not yet transcended the future, and since they are fixed according to the time periods (*adhvan*), they are not considered "previously arisen.
Regarding the nine stages of the Path (*mārga*), the desire realm and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are excluded, as the desire realm lacks meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Therefore, because the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is obscure and inferior, and because the noble path (*āryamārga*) is entirely absent there, it is only these nine stages that—among all stages—abide as mere guests.

This explains why the aforementioned nine stages serve as causes for one another. There are three reasons they are like guests: first, they abide like sojourners; second, they do not fall under the bondage of the realms (*dhātubandhana*);
and third, they are not grasped by craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Because they possess these three characteristics, when compared across different stages, they can all function as causes for one another.

Regarding the statement that "only those that are equal or superior serve as fruits," although this refers generally to all nine stages being taken as causes, there are nonetheless distinctions among them;

this is what is pointed out by the phrase "this very [stage] and below" (*idam-adhas*). Within this section, there are two parts: first, pointing to specific instances to provide the formal explanation;

second, the commentary states, "The paths of the higher stages... and so forth, which serves to resolve potential objections. This latter part also has two sections: the first distinguishes [the stages] based on the three paths.

Next, regarding the section below, it specifically distinguishes between those of dull and sharp faculties to clarify that, according to this treatise, the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) serves as the cause for three [paths], while the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) serves as the cause for two;
the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) does not serve as a cause for the Path of Seeing.

If one follows the *Nyāyānusāra*, the three paths are mutually causes for one another. As previously stated, the Path of Cultivation of dull faculties also serves as a cause for future non-arising dharmas.

The previously arisen dull path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) that serves as a cause for the sharp path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) which is to arise also serves as a cause for the future non-arising sharp path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Alternatively, when one falls from the state of no-more-learning back to the stage of learning (*śaikṣa*) and transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), it also serves as a cause for the already arisen sharp path of cultivation.
As for the statement that it serves as a cause for three or two [paths], this is explained according to the sequence of their actual manifestation (as inferred from that).

This may differ from other treatises; perhaps this treatise provisionally bases its explanation on the present [state] as the cause. Next, regarding the division of the six types of noble ones (*ārya*) according to the three paths, the definitions and meanings of these terms are as explained previously in the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (*Āryavarga*), specifically within the section addressing objections.
First, superiority is established based on the paths; subsequently, superiority is established based on the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the former, there are two parts:

first, the distinction between superior and inferior is clarified by means of the two paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); second, within a single path, the distinction is clarified by means of the nine grades (*navāṅga*).

Regarding the phrase "inferior [faculties] such as the path of seeing," etc., the subsequent commentary on the "increase of causes" refers to the preceding treatise text that mentions the lowest-of-the-low grade of the path of seeing and so forth.
As for the fact that the treatise does not explain the "faculties" (indriya) themselves— meaning that although both "causes" and "faculties" were listed above,
only the increase of causes is explained in the commentary while the meaning of the faculties is not— it is because the meaning of "sharp" and "dull" is easy to understand.

Because it has already been explained, it is not further elaborated here. To say that the superiority or inferiority of the Path does not depend on whether the stages (bhūmi) are higher or lower means that even if one relies on the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) to give rise to a path of dull faculties, it is not superior to a path of sharp faculties arising from the Not-Yet-Arrived stage (*anāgamya*).
By this same principle, a path of dull faculties relying on the Sphere of Nothingness can serve as the basis for a path of sharp faculties arising from the Not-Yet-Arrived stage.

The differences between this and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* regarding their respective positions on the higher and lower stages are slight; as they are not of great significance, I shall not describe them in detail.

As for the resolution of objections, it concerns only the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because [the sūtras] speak of those who "follow by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who "follow by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*). The reason for this is that...

Regarding the claim that when cultivating the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), the characteristic of being "long" is manifest and thus not separately explained because the characteristic of being "swift" during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is obscure and therefore requires separate explanation—this can be understood as stated in the treatise.
As for the assertion that volition (*cetanā*) serves as the cause for cultivation (*bhāvanā*), I say this is not so.

This is because in the desire realm there is volition but no cultivation, while in the form realm there is cultivation but no volition; since these are distinct stages, they do not serve as causes for one another. How, then [can such a claim be made]?
Is it said that the wisdoms of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) are of the same class as causes (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
Furthermore, the statement that hearing (*śruta*) is the cause for reflection and cultivation is also a general statement; however, within this context, one ought to make a distinction.

This is because, for example, hearing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not serve as a cause for cultivation, and hearing in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) does not serve as a cause for reflection. Therefore, the treatise states: "As with that which is produced by hearing (*śrutamaya*) bound to the desire realm..."

Dharmas can serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those produced through hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*) within their own realm, but not for those produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*), because such [cultivated] dharmas do not exist in the desire realm.
Dharmas produced through reflection serve as homogeneous causes for those produced through reflection, but not for those produced through hearing, because the latter are inferior.

(By extension, it is not stated that they serve as causes for those produced through cultivation. As for dharmas produced through hearing belonging to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), they can serve as [homogeneous causes] for those produced through hearing and cultivation within their own realm.

That which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*) serves as a cause for [dharmas] produced through cultivation within its own realm, because such things do not exist in the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

Dharmas produced through cultivation are causes only for those produced through cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced through hearing (*śruta-maya*), because the latter are inferior. In the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), dharmas produced through cultivation serve as causes only for those produced through cultivation within their own realm, and not for those produced through hearing or reflection (*cintā-maya*), because those do not exist and because [cultivation] is inferior.
(The commentary explains: "Because they do not exist" means that hearing and reflection do not exist; even if they were present, they would still be inferior.)

According to this treatise, while the actual principle should be explained in terms of the specific realm itself, the present discussion speaks generally of different realms. As for wholesome factors acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) acting as causes for one another:
because they do not arise through the power of preparatory effort (*prayoga-bala*) but manifest spontaneously (*svarasena*), all nine grades may serve as mutual causes.
This differs from preparatory wholesome states, which do not act as causes for inferior states—just as the diligent effort required to plant rice or wheat does not yield results in other species.

Do not exert laborious effort if there is nothing to be gained. The traditional explanation states that innate wholesome states (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) serve as causes for applied wholesome states (*prāyogika-kuśala*), whereas applied wholesome states do not serve as causes for innate wholesome states because they are inferior.
However, in the present context, we are considering only innate states in relation to one another;
therefore, they encompass all nine grades. As for the four types of non-obscured neutral states (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), the maturation-born (*vipākaja*) arise spontaneously and are the most subtle.

The attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the inferior course of conduct (*airyāpathika*) has weak functional power; that arising from the superior course of conduct (*śailpasthānika*) has stronger functional power because it arises from a powerful conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
That arising from the transformation mind (*nairmāṇika*) is even more powerful than the course of conduct, as its power is supreme because it is the fruit of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*).
Thus, they are compared in their respective order, excluding the preceding ones.
Regarding the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), there are two meanings: first, the sense that mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) mutually accord with one another;

thus, taking associated phenomena as the cause is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). Second, if it refers to being the cause for associated phenomena, it is a *dependent compound* (*tatpuruṣa*).

The phrase "having a common basis" (*sāśraya*) indicates that they necessarily share the same object (*ālambana*) and the same mode of activity (*ākāra*), and so forth. This explains the verse which mentions only "common [basis]."
The reason for this [distinction] is that the meaning of a single basis (*āśraya*) is most essential;

therefore, it is specifically mentioned to exclude those cases where the object (*ālambana*) and the mode of apprehension (*ākāra*) differ, as well as those where the object and mode of apprehension are identical but occur at different times, or where they occur at the same time but belong to different bodies—such as when a multitude of people together observe the new moon and so forth. This is done to exclude all such instances by means of a single statement.
Because there are many such objections, it is said that they share a common basis (*sāśraya*), meaning they have a common object (*sālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), and so forth.

Question: Since the essence of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) among the mind and mental factors is identical to the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), what is the distinction between these two causes?

Answer: The simultaneous cause is established by the principle of mutual causality (*anyonya-phalatva*). It is like traveling companions who rely on one another to traverse a dangerous path together; they are equal to one another.

The meaning of mutual association (*sahāya*) establishes the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), just as fellow merchants perform tasks such as eating together; if even one among them is missing, they are no longer associated.
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "That which, through reciprocal power, arises, abides, and so forth together is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*);

that which, through reciprocal power, takes the same object as its condition is the associated cause. (Based on this, the co-existent cause encompasses the four characteristics [of conditioned phenomena] and is thus more extensive.)

Since "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) refers exclusively to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is understood that if something is associated, it must necessarily be a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). However, there are co-existent causes that are not associated.

As for the "pervasive cause" (*sarvatraga-hetu*), this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) and cannot be a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound), because while the cause has the sense of being "pervasive," the fruit does not have the sense of being pervasive;
therefore, one cannot say "the cause of the pervasive. The term "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) carries three meanings of pervasion.

Therefore, (1) they take all five categories as their object; (2) they pervade all five categories as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); and (3) they serve as causes for the defiled phenomena of all five categories.

Because of these three meanings, they are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*). Among the afflictions of the five categories, only these eleven possess the aforementioned three characteristics and are thus termed pervasive;
other afflictions do not, and therefore are not pervasive. The establishment and exclusion of these [categories] is as explained in the *Anuśaya-nirdeśa*.
However, while this universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) can take effects from other categories (*nikāya*), the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) takes effects only from its own category;
therefore, there is a difference in the breadth and narrowness of these two causes. For this reason, the treatise provides a fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi-vibhāga*) [and so forth].
Regarding the statement, "The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) consists only of unwholesome factors and those wholesome factors with outflows (*sāsrava*) that possess the quality of ripening":

this clarifies the essential nature of the cause by excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*). Unwholesome factors and wholesome factors with outflows are called "ripening factors" because they possess ripened results;

it does not mean that the essence of these wholesome factors and so forth is itself the ripened result. The older tradition explains that the term "factor" (*dharma*) means "to hold" (*dhāraṇa*), referring here specifically to the cause.

Because this cause can sustain the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*), it is called a "ripening phenomenon" (*vipāka-dharma*). This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound), meaning "the phenomenon that is ripening.

If one says "ripening itself is the phenomenon," this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative compound). Among the phenomena of the three natures, all unwholesome phenomena are entirely ripening causes;

the indeterminate are entirely not [ripening causes]. Regarding the wholesome, there are two categories: if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are ripening causes; if they are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are not.
Wholesome dharmas are not its cause. Regarding the explanation of the term *vipāka* (maturation): it may reside in the cause or in the fruit;

both the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) and *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) analyses apply, as has already been demonstrated above. Other dharmas possess both [the characteristics of being a cause and a fruit]; conversely, the two meanings of the untainted (*anāsrava*) can be understood by reversing the preceding [case].
According to the new [interpretation], the meaning is augmented by the intensification of functional efficacy, thus forming three meanings. Therefore, this alone [is the case].
Regarding the term "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*), the Vaibhāṣika masters establish it in contrast to other causes;

their intention is that although the name "maturation" (*pāka*) applies generally to all six causes, it is not [in this context] a maturation [in the technical sense], and thus only this one is called the "maturation cause. According to the Master’s (Vasubandhu’s) interpretation, the name "maturation" does not apply to other results;
therefore, the treatise states: "For this reason, one should instead explain it as follows: [it is so called because it is] a transformation (*vipariṇāma*)."
"Vipāka" (ripening) has the meaning of "maturation" (*vipāka*); it should not merely distinguish [this cause] from other causes (this is the Master’s correct explanation).
Regarding the determination by time, this means clarifying in which of the three periods of time the six causes are established. Therefore, there is this section [on time].

While the universal (*sarvatraga*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes do not extend into the future, both of these causes [the universal and homogeneous] exist prior to their effects and follow after them.
Since the future lacks priority and posteriority, this cause does not exist there, as has already been established above.

As for the associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) causes, because they require simultaneous arising, abiding, and so forth, they pertain to all three time periods. Although the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) also involves a cause preceding its fruit, it pertains to the future because it is determined by nature:
being of a wholesome or unwholesome nature as the cause, and of an indeterminate nature as the fruit. Thus, it extends to the future. Because it is distinct [from the other causes],...

The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established by way of its essential nature, whereas the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is established by way of its temporal position; thus, they are not the same.
The verse does not mention the efficient cause, for the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "It cannot be said that it has a fixed temporal period."
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has no taking or giving, it possesses no conditioned fruit (*saṃskṛta-phala*).

This means that although the unconditioned does not obstruct the arising of other phenomena and is thus established as a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because it lacks the function of taking or giving, it is not said to possess a fruit; therefore, unconditioned dharmas have no dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

To say that the two types of unconditioned are causes but not fruits refers to the two kinds of unconditioned—space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which are merely...
Regarding the statement that "not obstructing" constitutes the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), [the path] does not function within the world; therefore, it is not a result that is projected.

Furthermore, because it is neutral (*avyākṛta*), it is not the path that realizes the fruit. As for the claim that "all three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack both cause and fruit," this is a general discussion asserting that all three types of unconditioned phenomena may be termed "without cause and without fruit.
Regarding the point that "the path has efficacy with respect to acquisition" (*prāpti*), the intent of this objection is that since the path is indeed capable of projecting...
If [the path] possesses efficacy, it has efficacy only with respect to acquisition (*prāpti*), not with respect to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).

To say that analytical cessation is the fruit of the path means that, although the path is not a productive cause (*janakahetu*) with respect to analytical cessation, it is nevertheless a realizing cause (*sākṣātkārakahetu*); thus, it is the fruit of the path.

This is based on the explanation provided by the Sarvāstivāda school. According to the Sautrāntika school, however, they do not admit that an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta*) is a cause, as there is no sūtra stating so.
It is taught that only causes are conditioned, as the Sūtra states at length: "All causes and conditions capable of producing form are impermanent," and so forth.
The Sarvāstivādins respond: "Is it not also taught that only the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) is impermanent?
It is not based on unconditioned phenomena, which serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) solely by virtue of not obstructing [the arising of other dharmas]," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "first, the fruit of maturation (vipāka-phala) is obtained from this cause":

first, there are five fruits—(1) the fruit of maturation, (2) the fruit of outflow (niṣyanda-phala), (3) the fruit of disconnection (visaṃyoga-phala), (4) the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala), and (5) the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).

These are arranged such that those which are narrower in scope come first, and those which are broader come later. Regarding the sequence of the six causes, those which are broader in scope are placed first, and those which are narrower come later; thus, the preceding cause is contrasted with [the subsequent ones].
Regarding subsequent effects and subsequent causes in relation to a preceding effect, their disconnection fruit (*visamyoga-phala*) is not obtained through the six causes;

therefore, it is not discussed here. However, because it slightly overlaps with the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), and because it is narrower in scope than human effort, it is placed separately before the fruit of human effort.

This is for the reason of the sequence of the breadth and narrowness of the four fruits. It is not placed after the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), because it does not obstruct the attainment of dharmas.

Question: Regarding the term "predominance" (*adhipati*), if there is only the state of being unobstructed, what constitutes its predominance? Answer: It is precisely by virtue of being unobstructed that [a phenomenon] can arise;

thus, it receives the name "predominance. As for the statement that "the karma of sentient beings [exerts predominance] over the receptacle world," this means that because the receptacle world is perceived through the power of the karma of sentient beings, karma possesses a predominant force with respect to it. These two types of causes are equal.

Regarding the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): if it is the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it takes as its outflow fruit only that which belongs to the same realm (*dhātu*), the same stage (*bhūmi*), the same category (*nikāya*), and the same nature (*svabhāva*).
If it is the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), it takes as its outflow fruit only that which belongs to the same realm, the same stage, and is defiled (*kliṣṭa*) by nature.

Since the fruits obtained from these two causes both resemble their respective causes, although there are two types of causes, their fruit is only one. Question: As for "wrong" (*mithyā*)... *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "如邪" (as for "wrong"), suggesting the original source was incomplete.*
Seeing that the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and [other] views of arising are different in nature yet both are defiled, they are considered equal outflows (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Although wholesome states and the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are different in nature, since they are both pure, they should likewise be equal outflows. Answer: Because defiled natures are easily identical, they can function as results;
because pure phenomena are difficult to identify as identical, they do not function as results. This is stated in order to refute the Vaiśeṣika school regarding those that possess causal efficacy.
If functional activity were distinct from the essence of the dharma, then these two causes would possess a superior power;

however, since there is no "human effort" (puruṣakāra) that exists apart from the essence of human effort itself, it is by virtue of these two causes that a superior result of human effort arises simultaneously.

In this context, the "drunken elephant general" is specifically mentioned. One interpretation follows the chapter [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*]; another interpretation states that the drunken elephant resembles a general in its ability to charge forward.
Regarding the question: "If that is so, why is it said that only the *saṃprayukta* (associated) and *sahabhū* (coexistent) causes obtain the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort)?
The answer is: The two masters [Vasubandhu and Yaśomitra] speak according to the general designation (*sāmānya-nāman*), and thus other causes may also obtain it.
However, in this verse, the focus is on what is obtained directly by the coexistent cause; therefore, it distinguishes the other four causes and states that only these two causes obtain it.

Only the non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) has a ripening fruit (vipākaphala). This means that while there are four types of unspecified dharmas in total, among them, only one type is a ripening dharma;
therefore, it is said that [the ripening fruit] exists, and so forth. Question: Why is the ripening fruit not wholesome (kuśala) or defiled (kliṣṭa)? Answer:
If it were wholesome or unwholesome (akuśala), then the karma performed would have no point at which it could be exhausted; therefore, the ripening fruit is exclusively [unspecified].

Regarding the inclusion of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states, it is said that maturation (*vipāka*) does not extend to insentient things. This means that external objects such as the environment and so forth, which are produced by collective karma, are not maturation in this sense;
therefore, it does not extend to them. The *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) asks:

"Is it not the case that the insentient realm where Mahābrahmā dwells is the fruit of individual karma and should thus be called maturation? Why then do you say it does not exist? To this, it is replied: "Mahābrahmā dwells..."

Regarding the rebirth through the sovereign power of all the great Brahmā-karma, other masters state that as long as the continuity of the Great Brahmā’s abode has not been destroyed, it is logical for others to experience [the results] within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This is because it is not uncommon; furthermore, it is understood that these do not pertain to outflow-born (*naiṣyandika*) or nurtured (*aupacayika*) [matters].

In this school, the essential natures of the five categories are each distinct and different, and they do not mutually subsume one another; it is precisely because of this principle that [the following is stated].
Because it demonstrates the meaning of the school’s tenets, it is said that "clear knowledge" (vidyā) applies to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Its capacity to nourish (*puṣṭi*) may be understood as applying to all three natures; however, that which is nourished is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*), as has already been established above.

Furthermore, these two kinds of fruits are exclusively of the same class (*sabhāga-hetu*) and are not maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*). The *Abhidharmāvatāra* explains the names of the five fruits, stating: "A fruit is not like [its cause]."
It is called "ripening" (*vipāka*) because it is matured and fit for enjoyment; thus, the fruit itself is ripening, and it is termed the "fruit of ripening.

Because the fruit resembles its cause, it is called the "fruit of outflow" (*niṣyanda*); thus, the fruit itself is the outflow, and it is termed the "fruit of outflow. Unconditioned cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is called the "fruit of disjunction" (*visamyoga*);

because the fruit itself is disjunction, it is so named. The three fruits mentioned above are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds. [The fruit arising from] human effort is the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra*).
The term "dominant" (*adhipati*) is derived from its cause and is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Here, it is treated according to the traditional [commentaries], or alternatively:
the fruit that resembles its cause or fruit in type is called a "concordant fruit" (*niṣyanda-phala*);

the fruit of dissociation is called a "fruit of dissociation" (*visamyoga-phala*), because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and free from fetters; and finally, the dominant fruit refers to the collection of fruits.

Because it predominates over multiple entities, it is said that "the mind of transformation born of pure *dhyāna* is pure. This means that by saying "pure," one distinguishes it from the *āsvādita-samādhi* (tasting concentration) and others.
Regarding the term "non-arising" (*anutpāda*) as the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) such as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*):

[Question] Since this fruit does not arise, how can it be said that it arises through the power of that [effort], and thus be called the fruit of human effort? [Answer] The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "We clearly observe [that it occurs] in relation to acquisition (*prāpti*)."

It is also said that the term "arising" (*jāti*) is like saying "my wealth has arisen," which carries the meaning "I have acquired wealth. Question: What is the difference between this and dissociation (*visamyoga*)?

Answer: If the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized when the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) are abandoned by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is such a cessation, it is called the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

However, if one realizes it again at a time when the proclivities were not abandoned by the path of immediate succession—such as upon returning to the original state—it is [merely] the fruit of human effort.
"Analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is likewise; analytical cessation is not a fruit of disjunction, but only a fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala). (End of the treatise). Question:
Why is it stated that only five causes take up a fruit (*grahaṇa*), without mentioning the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?

Answer: The efficient cause takes up a fruit in the present, just like the other five causes. Among these, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has no fruit; therefore, it is not mentioned. This is based on the *Vibhāṣā*.
Regarding the two [theories] that accept the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*): the principle that only the present takes up the fruit (*phala*) is the same as this treatise.
Their statement that "taking up the fruit" means "drawing forth" (*ākṣepa*) refers to drawing forth the future so that it arises and so on.
Within its own homogeneous class (*sabhāga*), it acts as a seed; within a heterogeneous class, it does so by virtue of having the same fruit. Such distinctions are called [the efficient cause].
Regarding the first of the four propositions concerning the acquisition of the fruit of attainment (*prāpti*), it refers to the "acquisition of the final moment of relinquishment.

This means that although one has continuously possessed immeasurable innate wholesome acquisitions since beginningless time—so long as the roots of goodness have not been severed—at the moment the roots of goodness are severed, one relinquishes all prior acquisitions;
yet, it is specifically the acquisition of the very last moment that is taken up here. This is because the preceding acquisitions are also [included] in the act of giving.
Because it is a fruit, the various acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the future have not yet taken their fruit; therefore, this mindfulness is associated with acquisition, not with the second phrase.

Regarding the statement "the acquisition first obtained," the commentary explains that at the time of reconnecting the roots of virtue, the acquisition that first arises takes as its object the past acquisitions that were previously abandoned;
thus, it is called "the acquisition first obtained. According to the new interpretation, "first" refers to the acquisition that arises at the very first moment.

Regarding the statement that "at the time of first obtaining [the acquisition], this acquisition is the fruit to be grasped": by mentioning the acquisition that is obtained, it reveals the prior capacity to give;
it does not mean that what was previously acquired is taken up again. Both explanations are valid. One should say: "At that time, the continuity [is maintained] by the prior acquisition.
This intention is likely to prevent others from misunderstanding that one is taking up acquisitions of the past; thus, the word "prior" is used as a qualification to distinguish it. That is to say:
This refers to the acquisition (*prāpti*) that was relinquished at the very end of the first moment mentioned previously. The *Nyāyānusāra* objects:

"How can it be that while many moments of acquisition in the prior stage all serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) by taking up the present acquisition, at the present time you speak only of the acquisition of the final single moment as yielding the fruit of the present acquisition?
Therefore, it would be better to follow the original text (*mūla-grantha*) in composing the *Abhidharmakośa*."
The Master [Vasubandhu], in order to clarify the main point of the treatise, states: "If a dharma bestows its fruit from the future," and so forth.

This means that although all acquisitions (*prāpti*) of past dharmas bestow their fruits at the time of the continuity [of the stream], they are not mentioned here because they have already bestowed their fruits in previous moments and are thus subsumed under the category of "already given.

Therefore, only the last one is not mentioned, as it is this one alone that bestows its fruit at the present moment; hence, it is specifically singled out. Furthermore, there is another interpretation of the preceding passage.
Does "attainment" (*prāpti*) apply generally to all past wholesome [dharmas], or does it refer specifically to the attainment that is abandoned at the very last moment?
Since the attainments that are abandoned pertain to all three time periods, yet not all of them are capable of yielding their fruit, the preceding statement is used to select those that precede.
In this present chapter, however, we simply follow the previous interpretation. Why, then, is "attainment" alone mentioned as a single category?

Regarding the statement that other wholesome roots are not mentioned: the answer is that while the severance of wholesome roots occurs, because they do not manifest [at that time], only the possession (*prāpti*) of wholesome states manifests;
therefore, only possession is specifically mentioned.
As for the phrase "the remainder of the three," it refers to those two categories of phenomena that lie outside the first three categories, which is why they are called "the remainder of the three."
The remainder refers to the three dharmas; "having a remainder" means there are others, whereas for a single category such as the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), there is no remainder.

In the first phrase, "defiled dharmas excluding the ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*) is because the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and thus not of a defiled nature.

Those "arising from five causes" are mental factors (*citta-dharma*), and therefore they must necessarily possess association (*samprayoga*); within the associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), there must necessarily...
Because these are co-existent and share the nature of being defiled, they possess the cause of similar type (*sabhāga-hetu*);

because defiled phenomena also include universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) must necessarily exist, they possess five causes. The remaining four [causes] are to be understood by analogy with this and will not be explained further.

Regarding the ripening phenomena (*vipāka-dharma*), the universal causes are excluded; since universal causes function solely as causes for what is defiled, they are excluded. Therefore, the two aforementioned causes do not mutually [apply].
It can be understood through reflection that [dharmas] arise from other causes. Question:

Since maturation (vipāka) has wholesome or unwholesome states as its cause and neutral states as its fruit, how can it be said that it arises from a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu)? Answer: Subsequent maturation arises from prior maturation;
because there have been fruits of maturation since beginningless time, they exist by virtue of serving as homogeneous causes for one another. This applies to all remaining dharmas.

Excluding the two causes—maturation (*vipāka*) and universal (*sarvatraga*)—because it is not a maturation; excluding the maturation cause because it is not defiled; and excluding the universal cause [because it is undefiled].
Thus, the first untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma arises from four causes: the associated (*samprayukta*), co-existent (*sahabhū*), homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and productive (*kāraṇa*) causes.

Furthermore, excluding one type of homogeneous cause—namely, the essence of the patience toward the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)—it is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Because they are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), the receptivities to suffering (*duḥkha-dharmakṣānti*) do not arise from causes of the same kind; rather, they arise from three causes—namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)—as should be understood.
This refers to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as explained above, because these are dharmas that are mind and mental factors;

thus, they possess the associated cause. Below this, the material phenomena (*rūpa*) and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are explained, which are excluded from the four aforementioned categories.
Based on the external [classification], further excluding the four types among the non-associated causes—namely, the defiled and so forth:

first, non-associated defilement, which refers to the four characteristics (lakṣaṇas) and so forth upon defiled dharmas; second, non-associated maturation, which refers to the four characteristics and so forth of the five faculties, as well as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the homogeneous character of beings (nikāyasabhāga);
third, non-associated with all remaining dharmas, which refers to those excluding the two aforementioned categories and...

The initial untainted [dharmas], the remaining unwholesome tainted [dharmas], and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the aforementioned wholesome tainted dharmas—excluding the four characteristics of the aforementioned [dharmas] and the two types of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), such as those of the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—as well as the four characteristics of the initial untainted non-associated [dharmas], such as the four characteristics of the "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*):
among these, there is no dharma whatsoever that arises from a single cause. Based on what has been explained above, even the very minimum [of causes] still exists.
The two causes from which [phenomena] arise differ from the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) reckoning that all phenomena are produced by a single cause.
*Abhidharmakośakārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Seven.
Explication of the Meaning of the Four Conditions by the Fuchun Śramaṇa Dunlin.

This is divided into three sections: first, explaining the names and defining the characteristics; second, clarifying the mutual inclusion of the conditions; third, clarifying the similarities and differences among the conditions.
The first section follows the commentary for its explanation; here, we shall clarify only the remaining two sections, beginning with the mutual inclusion of the conditions.
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Do causes subsume conditions, or do conditions subsume causes? The answer is that they mutually subsume one another;

that is to say, the first five causes possess the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the capacity to act as a cause constitutes the nature of the other three conditions. Some say that conditions subsume causes, but causes do not subsume conditions;

this means that the five causes constitute the causal condition, while their capacity to act as a cause constitutes the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
