They are called "proclivities" (*anuśaya*) because they follow along with sentient beings; they are called "dormant" (*middha*) because their mode of activity is subtle, like that of a person who is asleep, for their mode of operation is difficult to discern.
Ānanda asked his fellow practitioners, "Do I not have pride at this moment? Even though Ānanda was sharp-witted, he did not even know [it was there];
therefore, they are subtle. Although this chapter also clarifies the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and impurities (*mala*), the proclivities are the fundamental [cause].

The title of the chapter is indicated, and since it is explained first at the beginning of the section, the designation is established from the outset. As for why the "Chapter on Karma" (*Karmavarga*) is explained last:

karma is caused by afflictions (*kleśa*), as it is capable of summoning future existence (*punarbhava*). While karma is specific, afflictions are universal; therefore, karma is explained first and the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are explained afterward.

If one follows the previous explanation, the causes of karma are afflictions and their conditions have already been analyzed above. Apart from latent dispositions, karma lacks the capacity to produce existence.

This means that karma must be moistened by afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to be able to produce existence (*bhava*); karma separated from afflictions cannot produce existence. It is like a solid seed that, lacking the moisture of water, fails to sprout;
therefore, it is said [to be "moistened" by] greed and hatred. Regarding the mention of "greed and hatred," this indicates that the term "greed" (*rāga*) extends to all ten afflictions.
Just as dust adheres to a garment when it is moist, so too does hatred increase in accordance with the moisture of greed toward its objects; thus, it is called "greed."

Since hatred is not only [present] in relation to hatred but likewise in relation to pride and so forth, the word "also" (*api*) is used; and regarding the phrase "and doubt" (*ca vicikitsā*), the word "and" (*ca*) is explained as indicating contradiction.

It is stated that the word "and" is placed there to clarify that the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the six types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are each distinct and different from one another.
The term "attachment to existence" (*bhavarāga*) refers to the craving for the two upper realms. Existence (*bhava*) is manifold; as it is said, the three existences are the three realms.

Here, "existence" refers to one's own personal identity (*ātma-bhāva*). Craving for the two upper realms consists primarily of attachment to this personal identity rather than attachment to external objects, because they are free from desire for sense-objects.
Therefore, the designation "attachment to existence" is established specifically for the two upper realms, though it may occasionally take external things as its object to a minor degree.

Regarding "objects" (*viṣaya*): either only the first dhyāna has three consciousnesses that take external objects—form, sound, and touch—as their conditions; or, from the perspective of the higher stages, they rely on consciousness belonging to a lower stage to take external objects as conditions.
As for the term "dharmas" mentioned in the commentary, it is stated figuratively; the meaning follows that which is designated as "desire-greed" (*kāmarāga*) in the desire realm.
Since the Master [Vasubandhu] has already stated that there is greed in the two upper realms, the greed of the desire realm is specifically termed "desire-greed."

Therefore, it is not separately indicated in the verse. According to the Sautrāntika school, that which is active is called an *paryavasthāna* (envelopment), while its seeds are called *anuśaya* (latent dispositions).
For the Mahāsāṃghikas and other schools, the essence of the *anuśaya* is a non-associated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), which is precisely the latent disposition of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*).

In the Sarvāstivāda school, sensual desire itself is the *anuśaya*. Regarding the two preceding [explanations], the former is a *tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound, while the latter is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound; this is explained in the treatises.
The mutual refutations are so numerous that they cannot be fully detailed here.

Although there are three [types of] views regarding origination and cessation, for the sake of this discussion, one should generally distinguish their characteristics of being universal (*sarvatraga*) or specific (*asarvatraga*). The two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise in relation to coarse fruits and belong exclusively to the category of the first part (*ekadeśa*).

As for those that arise in relation to the fruits of the precept-and-vow attachment (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), they are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) and do not [belong to the other categories].

That which arises with respect to the fruit takes only the general characteristics as its object and does not investigate cause and effect; because it is abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it pertains to both divisions [of the afflictions].

This includes false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), as they take the Four Noble Truths as their objects. If the view of holding to views as supreme (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arises in relation to cause and effect, it is abandoned by the Path of Seeing Suffering and Origination;

if it takes general characteristics as its object without investigating cause and effect, it is abandoned by the Paths of Seeing Cessation and the Path. These three are not delusions regarding the nature of things (*vastu*); therefore, they are not abandoned by the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Regarding the three—greed, hatred, and pride—that are to be abandoned: if they arise by taking the Four Noble Truths as their object, they are abandoned through the abandonment of those Four Truths;

if they arise from delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*), they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). This is because greed and the others are coarse and do not involve the investigation of principles; thus, they do not directly delude one regarding the principles [of the truths], unlike ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, this applies to those arising in association with the five views and doubt, as well as to greed that takes those Four Truths as its object and is to be abandoned through the abandonment of those Truths.

Regarding those associated with the [other afflictions] as well as those that are independent (*muktaka*), if they are abandoned by the vision of the Four Truths (*satya*), they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) when associated with greed (*rāga*) and so forth that are deluded regarding objects.
Therefore, since greed and the other [afflictions] each pertain to all five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), once these distinctions have arisen, they may be understood from the commentaries (*ṭīkā*).

Regarding the view that takes what is abandoned by the vision [of the truths] as its object, the *Nyāyānusāra* critiques this, saying: "If one follows the position established by the Master [Vasubandhu], it would not be logical."

Why is this? Because pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) take all five categories as their objects, the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin would also necessarily be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path.

Furthermore, regarding the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, which take non-abandonable phenomena as their objects, one must state through the vision of what they are abandoned.
Therefore, that [definition] is not a well-established characteristic of what is to be abandoned. He himself explains it as follows:

It should be said: that which takes the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) as its object is called "vision of suffering"; this refers to what is abandoned by the receptivities to the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna-kṣānti*).
In brief, these are called "abandoned through the vision of suffering," and so on up to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), which is likewise.

For one who has seen the tracks (*dṛṣṭa-mārga*), the repeated cultivation of the knowledges regarding suffering and the other truths for the sake of attaining the higher goal is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*); what is abandoned by this path is called "abandoned through cultivation."
That which is abandoned through cultivation is what is called "well-established as having the characteristic of being abandoned. The old [commentators] offer this defense:
"The Master of Right Reasoning (Nyāyācārya) has misinterpreted my text, thinking that [the afflictions] are abandoned solely because they take as their object those truths [abandoned by seeing];

it is for this reason that he raises this objection. Therefore, one should know that there are two meanings here: first, taking these [truths] as the object; second, taking that which is abandoned as the object. This is because other schools [assert that]..."

It should be understood that the "outflows as conditions" (*āsrava-pratyaya*) are subsumed under the category of "conditions consisting in views" (*dṛṣṭi-pratyaya*), because they take the [four] truths as their objects. Regarding the new critique which states:

"The *Nyāyānusāra* raises an objection based on the literal text; how can one resolve it by adding words? (meaning that the phrase "taking views as its object" is split into two functions within the sentence, thus constituting an addition), this new interpretation concerns only the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Thus, the refutation in the *Nyāyānusāra* is erroneous. This is clearly explained in the commentary.

If one investigates this, it can be understood that within this chapter, the author directly states his own interpretation while largely omitting the formal principles (*nyāya*) and difficult arguments.

Nevertheless, regarding the characteristics of direct objects (*pratyakṣālambana*) and indirect objects (*parokṣālambana*) under the Four Noble Truths: for instance, when wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) denies the existence of contaminated causes and effects, this is a direct delusion regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

Furthermore, when this view arises and gives rise to self-indulgent attachment, this is the mind of greed (*lobha*); and when anger (*dveṣa*) arises toward that view, it constitutes an indirect object.
As for "the one who sees," the subsequent text states that one will necessarily feel aversion and resentment toward views that contradict one's own;

furthermore, because one feels aversion and resentment during the stage of accepting or rejecting within one's own view and understanding, other afflictions can be understood as having similar modes of intense conditioning.

The statement "the patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti* and *anvayajñānakṣānti*) on the path of seeing" refers to the patiences of the knowledge of phenomena and the subsequent knowledge within the context of the four truths.

Because patience on the path of seeing constitutes the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) that abandons the afflictions, while the knowledge constitutes the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) that realizes cessation, only the patience is taken here.

When the term "knowledge-patience" (*jñānakṣānti*) is used, it expresses the cause by means of its fruit. As for the statement that "the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned only through seeing," this refers to those below...

Since all stages (*bhūmi*) possess both superior and inferior aspects that can be either delighted in or loathed, even the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) is capable of effecting permanent abandonment.

Although the afflictions destroyed by the forbearances (*kṣānti*) are generally abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) occupies the highest position; therefore, there is no further superior stage to be delighted in, and the path with outflows cannot abandon [its own level] again.

It must be that when a noble one (*ārya*) enters the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and gives rise to the forbearance of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), [only then can it be abandoned].

Because they can be abandoned forever, the term "cultivation" (bhāvanā) does not apply [to them]. Regarding the statement that "the noble ones abandon through vision alone and not through cultivation":

this means that as soon as a noble one perceives the principle of the truths (satyadharma), they are able to abandon [the afflictions], and thus there is no room for them to reach the subsequent stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). Regarding the statement that "ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) abandon through cultivation alone and not through vision":
this means that an ordinary person, who has not yet perceived the principle of the truths, must necessarily rely on repeated cultivation before they can abandon them.

Regarding the statement that "only those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) and not by vision (darśana-heya) are the ten subsequent latent dispositions (anuśaya)": this means that there are four in the desire realm and three each in the two upper realms, totaling ten.

Because they belong to the category of cultivation and are situated at the end [of the list], it is said that they are generally abandoned by both the untainted (anāsrava) and conventional (sāṃvṛta) wisdoms. "Untainted" refers to abandonment by the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna);
"conventional wisdom" refers to abandonment by the tainted path characterized by delighting in the higher realms and revulsion toward the lower ones.

Because it is subject to destruction, it is called *sat* (perishable). The Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*), citing the Sautrāntika interpretation, establishes this name in order to refute the notion of a permanent unity.
One must not assume that there is no object of cognition for those who conceive of a self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).

This is because the Sarvāstivādins maintain that since they do not admit the arising of a mind that takes non-existence as its object, the "self" and so forth must necessarily have an object of cognition. The Sautrāntika school, however, asserts that a mind can indeed arise even by taking a non-existent thing (*abhāva*) as its object.

The two schools differ in their explanations of the meaning of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity). Regarding this *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that if explained in terms of the aggregates (*skandha*), it may be twentyfold or sixty-fivefold;

if explained in terms of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), there are even more varieties. As for the twentyfold [classification] based on the aggregates: when one analyzes the objects of the formations (*saṃskāra*) as conditions for the aggregates, but does not analyze the specific locations where they arise, there are twenty. To explain "analyzing the objects of the formations": [Note: The text provided ends abruptly. The following is a continuation of the logical structure based on the standard Abhidharma analysis. In this context, "analyzing the objects of the formations" refers to examining the various modes of activity through which the five aggregates are apprehended as a self or what belongs to a self.

Since these modes are twentyfold, the resulting views are likewise twenty. Specifically, one perceives each of the five aggregates as a self, and further perceives each aggregate as belonging to a self; thus, for each aggregate, there are four permutations (self, mine, self, and mine), totaling twenty views. This classification is made by focusing on the objective formations themselves without specifying the particular sense-bases or elements from which they arise.

"Conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the mode of practice; "object" (*ālambana*) refers to the focal object. Taking the five aggregates as the focal objects, one divides their conduct and objects into four categories each.
The first is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). The second is that which is seen (*dṛśya*). The third is that form acts as a servant to the self, meaning it is bound to and dependent upon the self.
The fourth is that form acts as an ornament, meaning it adorns the self. The fifth is that form acts as... [text fragment]... the self.
The "receptacle" (also called the "dwelling") contains a self; thus, each aggregate (*skandha*) has four modes of activity, which, when combined, form twenty propositions.

If one distinguishes the bases from which these arise, they become sixty-five propositions. This means that for form (*rūpa*), there are three types [of objects] given to the self, such as servants, necklaces, and so forth;
this applies even up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), where there are likewise three types [of objects]. Thus, there are thirty or forty [propositions].
The two [views] together with the view of self constitute fifteen; the five aggregates each have thirteen, totaling sixty-five propositions.

If one says there are sixty-two views—meaning that the sixty views of the five types of grasping, excluding the view of self, plus the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, make sixty-two—that is entirely different from what is taught in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
This [text] does not describe the view of emptiness as being an adherence to annihilationism.

Regarding "permanence": if one reckons that the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are identical with the aggregates (*skandha*), such that the extinction of the aggregates is the extinction of the self, this is called the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Alternatively, if one reckons that the self and what belongs to the self are different from the aggregates, such that the self remains even when the aggregates are extinguished, this is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).

Or, if one reckons that the self is permanent because it can undergo rebirth in other worlds despite the disintegration of the aggregates, this is also eternalism. To deny [the existence of cause, effect, and so forth] is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This means that among the truly existent entities—the Truths of Suffering and so forth—to give rise to a view that denies their existence is called "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

While all erroneous views that function through inversion should be termed "wrong," only those that deny existence are specifically designated as "wrong view" because their fault is particularly grave.

This is like saying "stinking butter" or "extremely evil"; these terms apply only to what is subtracted (denied), whereas the others involve superimposition (affirmation). [As for the term *caṇḍāla*, it means "extremely evil. Within this context...

Even more extreme than this is what is called "extremely evil"; this view is likewise so. To "grasp" other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena as superior means that one takes those phenomena—which are termed "inferior" because they are abandoned by the Noble Ones—to be superior;

thus, it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). In reality, one should establish them as "clinging to views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭy-ādy-upādāna*), meaning the clinging to views and the like which are grasped by views. The *Nyāya* (Principles) further states: "Or..."

Because it views [inferior things] as superior, it is designated simply by the term "view"; taking view as the primary factor and grasping other dharmas, this is called "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Regarding "the five precepts, etc.," the "etc. includes the ten precepts and the full set of monastic vows. The *Śāstra* says:

"Or, one may cling to the notion that purity is attained merely through the observance of ascetic rules and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). As for the "prohibitions of the ox-herders and others" among the non-Buddhists: by means of... [text fragment].

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) lack the power of penetration to know what occurred eighty thousand kalpas ago; they do not know that the ox (*goṇaka*) possessed karma for rebirth in heaven in a future life.
Seeing only that the ox died and was reborn in heaven, they claim that eating grass and consuming dung are the causes for rebirth in heaven.
Therefore, they imitate this by establishing the "ox-vow" (*goṇaka-vrata*) and other such prohibitions. For this reason, the *Mūlaśāstra* states that various non-Buddhists arise [with such views].
Regarding such views and the establishment of such theories of practice, it is said:

"If there is a person (*pudgala*) who observes the 'cow-vow,' the 'deer-vow,' or the 'dog-vow,' they will thereby attain purification, liberation, and deliverance, forever transcending all suffering and pleasure, reaching the state that transcends both suffering and pleasure.
All such categories of clinging to what is not a cause as being a cause should be understood as the *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to rules and observances).
Regarding those things to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, as explained in detail therein: there are those who throw themselves into water or fire;

the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) who reckon that the waters of the Ganges can wash away all sins and thus regard it as a river of merit; the fire-worshipping non-Buddhists who reckon that fire can burn away all impurities because it burns all afflictions (kleśa), and thus throw themselves into it;
or those who, for the sake of mortifying the body or seeking rebirth elsewhere, engage in ascetic practices such as throwing themselves from cliffs.

The word "etc. refers specifically to those who uphold mere rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This means that while both morality and wisdom act as remote causes for realizing cessation, one must rely on concentration and wisdom to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Because they now cling to the idea that morality alone can bring about *nirvāṇa*, it is called the "clinging to rules and observances. Thus, the *Śīla-sūtra* says:
"With purity of morality and the possession of wisdom, one attains the foremost path. Those who calculate and reckon that intellectual knowledge can attain *nirvāṇa* are referred to as outsiders.

When the calculation of the path reaches an immeasurable number, it becomes impossible to count; this supreme wisdom is considered by some to be *nirvāṇa*, or they calculate that this wisdom can attain *nirvāṇa*.
The phrase "and so forth" includes the grasping at non-precepts and other dharmas;

that is, other non-Buddhists who calculate that non-causal factors and the like are [the cause], or who calculate that the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. Thus says the *Nyāya-ānusāra* (The Correct Principle).

Alternatively, because the [first] two are superior in terms of their observance of precepts and prohibitions (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), they are designated by the name "precepts and prohibitions. Furthermore, the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Moreover, because the first three views involve the estimation of their objects and their mode of grasping is sharp and intense, they are called 'views' (*dṛṣṭi*); because the latter two views involve the grasping of the subject that perceives and their mode of grasping is sharp and intense, they are called 'attachments' (*parāmarśa*)."
To say that they are reckoned as one means that non-Buddhists reckon those five aggregates as a single unit, and thus there is no distinction between the five.
To say that the inversion of permanence is subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) means that the inversion of permanence is subsumed under the view of extremes.

To say that they are deluded regarding coarse fruits means that both of these views arise based on the body, and since the body is a coarse fruit, it is said that they are "deluded regarding coarse fruits. This is according to the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Regarding those who conceive of Īśvara and the like as causes when they are not, they are certainly unable to investigate profound principles;
rather, based on the coarse objects of the aggregates of speech such as "Īśvara," they falsely claim these to be permanent, unitary, self-existent agents.

Taking these as their primary basis, they then cling to them as causes. Therefore, this view is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The Master [Vasubandhu] raises an objection: "If that is so, there are those who cling to [the practice of] throwing oneself..."
Various wrong practices, such as [immolating oneself in] water or fire, are causes for rebirth in heaven; or one might hold that merely observing ascetic vows (*śīla-vrata*) leads to purification.

Since these do not arise from the inversion of permanence or self, they should not be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The answer is: although they do not arise from the inversion of permanence or self, they nevertheless delude one regarding the Truth of Suffering;
therefore, they are said to be abandoned through the vision of suffering. One should know that the verse refers here specifically to [the case of] ascetic vows (*śīla-vrata*).

Regarding the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) that is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), while it is generally held to arise from the inversion of permanence (*nitya-viparyāsa*), in reality there are also instances where it does not arise from this inversion.
These two [types of] delusion regarding the coarse fruit of suffering—the first arising from the inversion of permanence—operate with respect to the fruit itself;

therefore, they are abandoned through the vision of suffering by virtue of these two inversions. Furthermore, although the objects of delusion encompass both suffering and its origin (*samudaya*), the fruit of suffering is coarse, whereas the origin is subtle.
Because of this subtle delusion, one takes its coarse fruit to be the causal path; therefore, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). The ancient masters said:

"This [delusion] operates only with respect to the fruit, because the characteristics of the fruit are coarse and manifest, making them easy to perceive. One reckons the cause of suffering to be the cause [of liberation], yet it is not entirely erroneous.

Since one is deluded regarding the characteristics of the fruit, it is also abandoned through the vision of suffering. This includes even the outflow-tainted precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*) for those who are deluded regarding the fruit.
Because these deluded deer manifest the appearance of a fruit, they are permanently severed at the very moment the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is seen.
Thus, the two types of attachment and the false views that slander the Path— namely, the false view that denies the true and authentic Path and the doubt regarding the true Path—
and the subsequent clinging to that false view as the means of liberation, are directly contrary to the Path regarding cause and effect.

Because they do not distinguish between the characteristics [of the objects], they are deluded attachments; thus, it is only at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) that they can be permanently severed.

As for the statement that those which contradict the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) are "strong," this is because one clings to these mistaken views as being correct, holding them firmly and refusing to relinquish them; therefore, they are called "strong. Thus, the *Nyāyapravēśa* states:

"Those that take up precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as their object have extremely coarse modes of activity (*ākāra*); because they do not follow closely behind [the truth], and because the inclination (*āśaya*) is not firm, little effort is required [to abandon them]."

Because the exertion [of effort] is immediately cut off and extinguished, those who perceive suffering as something to be abandoned and who are deluded regarding the proximate [truths] are contrary to the above;

they can only permanently abandon [their errors] when the Truth of the Path is perceived. Regarding the misapprehension of what is not the path as being the path, there are two types: one is abandoned through the perception of suffering, and the other is abandoned through the perception of the path.

When one slanders the Truths of Origination and Cessation, one negates the characteristics of the phenomena that are to be abandoned and realized; if one then clings to these as being the path, it constitutes [the aforementioned error].

Because the path is established based on the dharmas to be abandoned and the dharmas to be realized through the concentration on the non-arising [of phenomena], it is not the case that it is abandoned by the truths of origin or cessation;
thus, there are four objections which are omitted here as they would be too prolix.

As for the statement that "extremes" refers exclusively to the view of eternalism: this means that while both the views of annihilationism and eternalism are indeed extremes, [the term] here refers exclusively to [eternalism].

The view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) is established to eliminate the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); because one reckons what is impermanent as permanent, it is called the inversion of permanence.
To reckon what is suffering and impure as pleasure and purity is called the inversion of pleasure and purity; this refers to the grasping of the inferior as superior, which is all *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*.
However, here we specifically take the reckoning of suffering as pleasure and the impure as pure as the two inversions, while excluding other instances of reckoning [the inferior] as superior.
The statement "only taking up the view of self" means excluding the view of "mine. Because it says "not the view of mine," this is the interpretation of one master.
Regarding the phrase "because it takes as its object limited purity," this refers to attaining a degree of purity at another time;

that is, because the ascetic practices (duḥkha-caryā) reckoned by non-Buddhists can also eliminate the defilement of desire and thus attain a small portion of purity at another time, as well as internally...
If one reckons within the path that only the observance of precepts constitutes the Way, this is also because one attains purification at a time of slight conceptualization.

If that is so, then taking pleasant feeling as pleasure and taking wholesome phenomena as pure also functions with respect to a small portion of reality; why, then, are these considered perverted understandings?
It is because they grasp what is tainted (*sāsrava*) as being identical to the bliss of *nirvāṇa* and identical to the purity of *nirvāṇa*, [while it is only] in relation to existence (*bhava*)...
Within the outflows (*āsrava*), there is not the slightest pleasure or purity; because they are entirely inverted like *nirvāṇa*, they are called "inversions.

As for the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), although it is not the path, one reckons it to be the path; thus, because it shares a portion with the uncontaminated noble path (*anāsravamārga*) and the verified purity of *nirvāṇa*, it does not constitute an inversion.

Regarding the statement that they do not arise through the gate of non-existence: this refers to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) which clings to annihilation, and the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) which denies these two. Both [are included].

To rely on "namelessness" (anāma) as being "without gates" does not mean that there is no gate for its cognitive object (*ālambana*). Regarding the claim that the mind and perception (*saṃjñā*) are called "inverted" (*viparyāsa*) because they follow after views:

an external objection states that while perception and mind are associated with views and thus called inverted in accordance with those views, why are feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth not also called inverted when they are associated with views?
The answer is: in worldly convention, it is established that the mind and perception are inverted, whereas one does not speak of feeling as being inverted. As it is said: [text fragment].

It is said that this matter "disturbs my perception" (*saṃjñā*), rather than "disturbing my feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth; therefore, following worldly convention, one speaks only of "perverted perceptions" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).

When it is said that the twelve perversions are forever severed upon reaching the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), this is because perception and mind are associated only with views (*dṛṣṭi*); thus, they are also abandoned by the abandonment of views.

This is the correct position of the *Vibhāṣā*. As for the eight [perversions] that are abandoned only by the abandonment of views, these refer to the [perversions of] permanence and self, respectively.
The third [category] refers to the three—perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*)—regarding pleasure and purity, each being one; that is, taking only the view as eight.

These are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) because they are of the nature of discursive investigation and are associated with views. Regarding the four that are abandoned by both insight and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*):

if one clings to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) as being the purity of *nirvāṇa*, then this perception and mind, being associated with the view, are abandoned by insight; however, if one has not yet become free from desire for existence (*bhava*).
The arising of the perception of pleasure from tainted joy and bliss, the failure to know that these are the nature of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*),

and the grasping of pure and exquisite perceptions toward agreeable forms— all such tainted states are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If one were to claim that these are not abandoned through cultivation,
then since noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire have already previously abandoned the two inversions of pleasure and purity, why would they still grasp at purity regarding impure objects?
The Vaibhāṣikas generally maintain that one seeks pleasure within what is perceived as pleasure and thereby gives rise to sensual desire.

However, they concede that there are occasions when an Ārya may momentarily experience confusion, such that sensual desire suddenly manifests toward an object; this is due to the confusion caused by a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) or a painted yakṣa.

The Sautrāntikas, however, assert that there are eight types of perverted perceptions (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and mental states (*citta-viparyāsa*), and that those who have not yet fully abandoned them are as described in the Sautrāntika masters' citation of scripture.
The eight points that refute the Sarvāstivāda position are as follows: regarding the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), each consists of both perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*).

According to these two masters, views (*dṛṣṭi*) are abandoned only through insight (*darśana-heya*) because they are exclusively delusions regarding the principle (*tattva*); however, perception and mind are abandoned through both insight and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) because they arise from delusions regarding both principle and phenomena (*dharma*).

Nevertheless, this view differs from that of the Vibhajyavādins; for while the Vibhajyavādins maintain that only four of the inversions are abandoned through cultivation, these masters assert that all eight inversions are abandoned through cultivation.
Because [the Abhidharma] has been severed, the Master’s intention is to clarify the sūtras of the *Vibhajyavādins*;

for this reason, no further defense is offered here. Regarding the phrase "the modes of activity differ": "activity" (*caryā*) refers to the mode of understanding (*pratipatti*). The term "arising" (*vṛtti*) is explained by the *Nyāya* as follows:

"There are those who, being deluded, first compare themselves with others regarding things that exist and things that do not exist; when their minds become uplifted [as a result], it is called pride (*māna*)."

Due to the transformation of their modes of activity, they are divided into seven types. (The commentary explains: "having an object" means the cognition accords with the object; "lacking an object" means it does not accord with the object. Regarding the inferior as superior and regarding the equal as equal, the *Nyāya* asks:
"Is it not the case that these two both function in accordance with reality regarding their objects, and thus should not constitute pride?
For instance, when the mind gives rise to attachment toward a desirable thing, it functions in accordance with reality; how then can this be considered greed? However...

Since it is admitted that this [state] which arises from such [conditions] and can defile and distress the mind constitutes the affliction of greed (*rāga*), so too, although it actually arises in relation to superior or inferior objects, that which causes the mind to become haughty and defiled is called the affliction of pride (*māna*). What logical fault is there in this?

To claim oneself equal to others who are superior is called "excessive pride" (*abhimāna*). As the *Nyāya* says: "It is when one regards others who are equal as being of superior lineage, learning, and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "considering oneself superior among those who are equal in virtue," this is called *abhimāna* (excessive pride). As for the terms *māna* (pride) and *atimāna* (over-pride), the older treatises refer to them as *mānātimāna* (pride-exceeding-pride).
Regarding the attachment to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātma-ātmīya-grāha*), the treatise states:

"To grasp at a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), causing the mind to become uplifted, is called *asmimāna* (the pride of 'I am'). Regarding "claiming to have attained what one has not attained," the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "That is to say, regarding..."

To claim for oneself that one has attained the distinguished qualities of the stages, the paths, the abandonments, and so forth, when one has not yet attained them, is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
Regarding those who are superior in many respects, to consider oneself inferior in only a few respects is the correct principle; as it says:

"There are those, whether householders or renunciants, who, amidst the many superior qualities of others such as craftsmanship or ethical discipline (*śīla*), conceive in their minds that they are inferior in only a few respects."

Exaltation is called "inferiority-pride" (*ūnamāna*). In this context, one who is exalted toward oneself is so because, while regarding others as greatly superior, they consider themselves slightly inferior;

since this increases [the estimation of] oneself, it is also called "exaltation. (According to this treatise, pride of superiority (*adhimāna*) has a high locus, whereas pride of equality (*māna*) is said to have no high locus.

Regarding those who lack virtue, claiming to possess virtue is called "lack of virtue" (*aguṇa*), because various unwholesome actions (*akuśala-caryā*) are contrary to virtue. Thus, the name "lack of virtue" is established.
It is like when one who is unwholesome, regarding the attainment of such unvirtuous qualities as his own, relies on those evils and becomes haughty;
therefore, it is called "false pride" (*mithyāmāna*). As for the term "category" (*jāti*), it refers to a specific type of pride.

Regarding the phrase "though knowing oneself to be extremely inferior, yet holding oneself in high esteem," the *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) provides an analogy: it is like one who displays auspicious omens, or perhaps a *caṇḍāla*.
Although the Caṇḍāla knew that he was universally despised by the world, when presenting auspicious signs and performing his duties, he held himself in high esteem and thus became arrogant.

(The commentary states that "presenting auspicious signs" refers to the *naṭas* [actors/musicians]. They knew that the king, ministers, and great personages were about to depart from their residences or arrive from outside;

they would then take various kinds of flowers, fruits, and the like to welcome them, raising them up for a *li* [a measure of distance] to signify good fortune. Because this brought joy to the people's hearts, they were granted many precious gifts. The Caṇḍālas—namely, hunters, butchers, and the like—presented these as commissioned by the king. Yet, although they knew themselves to be of the most lowly class, they nonetheless exalted themselves.)
[The term] "all" (*sarva*) refers to those who possess craving for existence (*bhavarāga*); it means that one does not wish to be born anywhere within the three realms.

This is different from having craving [for specific states], as one merely wishes to become a dragon-elephant (*nāga-hastin*) and does not seek birth throughout the three realms in general. Regarding the phrase "the great dragon kings, etc.," according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, the word "etc.
(*ādi*) is used to indicate the asura kings, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, the beings in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), and so forth—these being a portion of those with craving.

Regarding the statement that "the Most Holy One does not arise," this means that because such craving for the bodies of animals and so forth would necessarily lead the Noble One to be born in the evil destinies, he does not give rise to it;
furthermore, it should be understood that all such [cravings] as killing and other entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for the statement, "There is no craving that takes the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) as its object and gives rise to craving for impermanence" (and so forth), since the *nikāyasabhāga* is abandoned through cultivation, this [craving] is also [abandoned through cultivation].

Non-existence-craving (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is also abandoned through cultivation; since existence-craving (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*) takes it as its object and is abandoned through cultivation, it too is abandoned solely through cultivation.
All types of pride that are augmented by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) are directly increased by the view of self;

this means they are directly led, guided, and continuously brought into manifestation by it. As for the statement "by giving rise to false views, one commits killing and so forth," it means that due to false views, one does not...
Because one believes in the retribution for sins such as universal killing and so forth, these various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are increased by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);

thus it is said that noble ones (*ārya*), having severed wrong view, will certainly not commit killing and the like. Regarding the statement that "view and doubt are the 'back'": this means that the categories of pride (*māna*) and so forth arise based on view and doubt;
since view and doubt possess the power to support pride and the others, they are like a back.
Regarding "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*), the *Zhengli chao* states that it has two characteristics: first, that which arises through its own power;

second, that which is exclusively abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*). There are two types of the former: that which is unshared because it does not coexist with other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), termed "unshared," and that which is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Furthermore, there is also the view that it is a pervasive latent disposition (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) throughout the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*), meaning this affliction pervades all five categories rather than remaining dormant or suppressed. This refers exclusively to [the latter].

Eleven [types of defilements] are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) because they possess three of the four characteristics; the remaining ones lack these characteristics entirely and are therefore not pervasive.
As the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Why is it that among the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin, only these are pervasive?

It is because only these universally take all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) as their object, and because their underlying intention is uniform, their power is firm and stable, and thus they are able to act as causes."

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path, which pertain to all five categories, possess only the capacity to take a portion of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object;
because their objective support is distinct, their power is not pervasive or firm, and they cannot serve as causes to pervasively produce all five categories.

Therefore, only the first two categories possess universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*). By what means is it known that defiled phenomena to be abandoned through cultivation are [abandoned] by means of those to be abandoned through vision?
How can it be that those who have cultivated the universal bases (*sarvatraga*) as causes do not perceive the self as it is commonly seen in the world?

This is because, through the power of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), attachment toward external objects increases; if the view of a self were absent, attachment toward external objects would be slight. Furthermore, according to the authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*), it is said:

"What are the factors that have the factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) as their cause? Namely, all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) factors. Moreover, the treatise states: "As for what is called..."

Regarding the universal cognition (*pariṣpharaṇa*) of the five categories (*pañca-varga*): is this in terms of gradual succession or simultaneous apprehension? If it were gradual, then other [categories] would also have to be universally cognized.
If it were simultaneous, who could ever universally conceive of all phenomena within the desire realm as being superior, capable of attaining purification, or as the cause of the world?
Answer: It is not said that there is a simultaneous apprehension of everything within one's own realm and stage; rather, it is said that there is the power to do so simultaneously.

The factors that take as their object even a small portion of each of the five categories are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*). Since afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*) and pride (*māna*) are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*), they lack the power to take [all objects] simultaneously;
therefore, they are not pervasive. Only these eleven are pervasive; other afflictions such as attachment and hatred are not pervasive.

By this principle, it is established by implication that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride need not be mentioned separately. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Afflictions such as attachment rely solely upon what is seen or heard."

The object that is being contemplated only then manifests; for when one gives rise to desire and so forth toward a wife or others, one takes the manifest color (*varṇa*) as the object, not the shape (*saṃsthāna*), and takes the shape, not the color.

Thus, it is known that desire and the like do not take everything as their object. Regarding the statement that "nine [types of afflictions] can take what is above as their object," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:

The preceding statement primarily clarifies taking the higher realms and higher stages as objects, while incidentally showing that there are no latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) that take what is below as an object. If an affliction were to take what is below as its object, [it would contradict the principle].

Because the objects to be known are superior and the realms are destroyed, there is no such fault in taking them as objects; furthermore, regarding the false view abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the desire realm,

which denies the existence of the fruits of suffering in the form and formless realms, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) clings to them as supreme, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*) reckons what is not a cause to be a cause,

and doubt (*vicikitsā*) harbors hesitation, while ignorance (*avidyā*) fails to comprehend them— each of these being abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) as appropriate.

It should be understood that the case of form (*rūpa*) being the condition for the formless (*arūpya*) is to be known by analogy with this. Since it is thus regarding the conditions of the realms (*dhātu*), it is likewise regarding the conditions of the stages (*bhūmi*).

As for the statement that the two views do not take the higher [stages] as their object, the treatise raises an objection: "If one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) gives rise to the view of a sentient being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) or the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) toward Mahābrahmā, how is it that the view of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not take the higher [stages] as its object? The answer states: "One does not grasp the higher realms as..."

In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (and other treatises), it is further argued: "If that is so, then the conception of those [aggregates] as a sentient being and as permanent—what kind of view (*dṛṣṭi*) does this fall under?
The Abhidharma masters reply: "These two are not views; they are subsumed under false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). Furthermore:

"How is it that while other [cognitions] taking those [aggregates] as their object are views, this [conception] also takes them as its object yet is not a view? They reply: "This is established by taking our own tenet (*siddhānta*) as the authority."

This is explained as the correct principle: because those born in the desire realm do not form the attachment "I am Mahābrahmā," nor do they form the attachment "Brahmā belongs to me," the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is absent;
since the view of a self-body is absent, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is also absent.
Furthermore, the characteristics of wrong conduct induced by the view of a self-body refer to cognitions that are not associated with afflictions such as doubt or greed.
Therefore, up to those that take the eight stages as their object—[the questioner asks: why are those of one's own stage not combined with them to form nine objects of cognition? [The answer is:

because there is a distinction between those that increase in accordance [with the defilements] and those that do not. Thus, stages belonging to oneself and others cannot be combined as objects. As for the other accompanying factors (*anuvartaka*), they are also subsumed under the category of universal (*sarvatraga*):

if they are associated (*samprayukta*) dharmas, they possess both the sense of being a cause and the sense of being universal; if they are dissociated (*viprayukta*), they possess only the sense of being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because they share a single object, they are all subsumed under "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding the statement that "the remaining afflictions are to be understood by analogy," this means that apart from these six, the other afflictions of the five categories (*pañca-varga*) all take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their objects;
since this is established by analogy with the present case, the verse does not mention them. Within this passage, there are two main divisions; first:

Because they are not capable of being antidotes, it is explained that [the afflictions] have untainted objects; having clarified the two types of greed, hatred, and pride, what follows explains those with tainted objects.
The preceding section has three parts: first, up to "the analytical cessation of all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*), it clarifies those that take the Truth of Cessation as their object;

second, from "taking the Path as an object" onwards, up to "each has three objects," it clarifies those that take the Truth of the Path as their object; third, from "furthermore, the treatise says" onwards, it additionally reveals those that take the higher realms as their objects.
Regarding the statement that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is neither cause nor effect across different levels:

this means that cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and since the unconditioned is without arising and without characteristics, it lacks the sense of producing cause and effect. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"If there are dharmas that are moistened by craving for a particular level and grasped as 'self' or 'mine' by the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) of that level, then the cessation of those dharmas is likewise abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) of that same level."

Regarding the focal object (*ālambana*) of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): because one is attached to the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) of this particular stage, if one hears it said that the formations of this stage are subject to cessation, one then gives rise to a wrong view regarding this stage and denies them.
Since there is no attachment to a lower stage while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), how could one possibly give rise to a wrong view denying the cessation of a higher stage?

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*, depending on the source cited as *Xianzong lun*) states: "Thus, for those of virtuous wisdom who realize the principles of their objects, it is possible for them to apprehend [them] simultaneously."

Regarding the statement that "the cessation of various formations (saṃskāra) is the elimination of all false views," this refers to those who, due to delusion regarding objects and being obstructed by the grasping of causes, are unable to take all formations as their collective object.
When it says "the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of formations," it means that afflictions are termed "formations";

because the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is realized through the cessation of formations, the term "formations" is used to designate their analytical cessation. A formal inquiry asks: Is the false view that slanders cessation considered a "view of cessation"?
Is it that you do not see its cessation? If you do see its cessation, how can you slander it as non-existent? If you do not see it, how can it be called "dependent on cessation"?
You should say that you see its cessation; yet, by merely following the teaching, you see it and then slander it.

This is like a person with sight who, seeing a man standing at a distance in a place full of tree stumps, denies his existence, saying he is not a man; even though he is directly perceiving the man, [he slanders him].
It is not that they do not slander [the Dharma]; rather, having seen its cessation, they deny it and declare it non-existent.

Next, regarding the statement that the path has six stages, the "dharma-knowledge category" (dharmajñāna-pakṣa) refers to the arising of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) through contemplating the dharmas of the Four Truths of the desire realm while in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the six stages;

this is called dharma-knowledge. If one relies on the meditative absorptions of the nine stages to contemplate the objects of the Four Truths of the higher realms and gives rise to untainted knowledge, it is named... [path-knowledge].

Question: Regarding what will be explained below concerning subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), why is it that dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) pertains to only six stages (*bhūmi*), whereas subsequent knowledge pertains to nine stages?

Answer: Dharma-knowledge observes the objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Since the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are fourfold distant from the desire realm, they cannot observe the desire realm;

therefore, the three formless stages are excluded. Subsequent knowledge, however, observes the higher realms and thus extends through all three formless stages. Furthermore, the desire realm lacks the capacity [to observe them].

Regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said that the paths taking the desire realm as their object (*ālambana*) are not uniform; this is because they are manifested by the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) resulting from the abandonment of afflictions.

Thus, one speaks of the analytical cessation of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm. When it is said that all six stages (*bhūmi*) take those [phenomena] as objects, consider, for instance, the arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*):

it acts as both cause and effect with what arises in other stages. This is because the untainted truths of the path (*mārgasatya*) are not bound to any specific stage (*aniyata-bhūmika*). Therefore...

The mutual causality between different stages (*bhūmi*) arises from the fact that through wrong view one slanders the fruit and thereby slanders its cause, and by slandering the cause one also slanders its fruit.
This is not the case for their cessation (*nirodha*), as they are not reciprocal causes; it refers only to slandering within one's own stage and does not extend to the higher or lower stages.

The phrase "although the dharmas and their aspects (*ākāra*) are likewise mutually causal," etc., serves to resolve an anticipated objection. The objection is raised: "If they are mutually causes for one another..."

If seeing [the truths] is the cause for both subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) and dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), and these two are likewise mutual causes for one another, why is it that wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth of the desire realm do not take subsequent knowledge as their object?

To resolve this difficulty, it is known that although subsequent knowledge is a cause, it does not counteract the desire realm and so forth; as stated in the treatise: "For example, regarding dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge being mutual causes:

when the patience toward the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) gives rise to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), or when the subsequent knowledge of suffering gives rise to the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*), and so on. Question: Since one must first be free from the afflictions of the desire realm before relying upon the higher stages...

Question: When the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises and one has already attained untainted vision (*darśana*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), how can these [previously abandoned afflictions] still serve as conditions for the three delusions?

Answer: Regarding the statement that the views and doubts of the lower stages serve as conditions for the path of the six stages, this is said only with reference to the time before one has realized the state of an Arya when they take another’s body as their object;

it does not refer to taking one’s own untainted [body] as the object. If one personally gives rise to the untainted, then the untainted itself is devoid of views and doubt; that is to say, they do not exist.

The untainted (anāsrava) [state] first arises at the initial moment of the patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-kṣānti). Since one has already attained non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) regarding the afflictions of the higher realms during the stage of supreme patience (agradharmakṣānti), it cannot take its own untainted state as an object.
The treatise states: "Since dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) can counteract the three types of delusion pertaining to the form and formless realms, it takes those as its objects.
The intent of this objection is that conventional knowledge (anvayajñāna) does not know the desire realm, nor what is not desire.

Regarding the statement that since the *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) realized through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) can counteract [afflictions] of the higher realms, it should therefore serve as the object for others:

there are two explanations for why the afflictions of those respective stages each have three [aspects]. First, among the four truths capable of counteracting [the afflictions], the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) are missing.

Second, within the categories of what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the counteractive factor for what is abandoned by seeing is absent. From the passage "This is not so" onwards, this represents the first interpretation.

Moreover, the treatise states, "Because the two [types of knowledge] do not initially exist," which is a citation from the treatise serving as a concluding response; its meaning is the same as before.

Next, it simultaneously clarifies the statement regarding the higher objects of focus. The phrase "precisely by this cause" (*anenaiva hetunā*) carries the sense of "by means of" or "on account of"; that is to say, by virtue of...

Separated by intervals, the suffering and origination of the nine stages arise and mutually entangle one another; furthermore, as they establish their bases and serve as causes for one another, all false views can thus possess four conditions.

Question: Did you not previously state that only the six types of latent dispositions from the lower realms—excluding those to be abandoned by the path of cessation and the path—can take the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) as their object?

Question: Now, why is it said that these universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) universally take the five categories (*pañca-nikāya*) as their objects? Answer: In principle, these universal afflictions are actually unable to take the essence of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) as their objects;
they only take the various categories of subordinate afflictions within those [categories] as their objects.

Since the essence of those afflictions consists of views regarding Suffering and Origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), and since these can directly delude one regarding Suffering and Origin, it is said that they pervade the five categories. second, they are contrary to the afflictions (*kleśa*). This is because pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) that have a higher realm as their flow do not increase by way of object, and non-pervasive latent dispositions that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object do not increase by way of object.

rather, because the word "or" (*vā*) is used when asking about one or the other, it is intended to show that these are separate questions regarding whether it is superior or inferior. Therefore, [the text] says this.

Question: Regarding the "setting aside" (*sthāpanīya*) among the fourfold classification of questions, the objection asks: "How can it be established as a 'determination' (*vyākaraṇa*) while being set aside?

The response is that it is called a "determination" because one determines that question by stating, "This should not be answered. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "This too is said to be a matter that should be set aside.

Within the category of questions to be set aside, one should say: 'It should be determined by setting it aside. If one were to provide an answer using some other discourse, the determination would not be established. (Only this...)

Because answering a question does not constitute the full principle [of the teaching]. Regarding the term "barren woman" (*śilāputrī*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that she is called a barren woman because her female body is incapable of pregnancy and is empty of offspring.

Is this the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha? Are the teachings he has spoken well-spoken? Do his disciples practice the sublime conduct?

Regarding the first type of specific answer (*vibhajyavyākaraṇa*): if one with a straightforward mind requests, saying, "I pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for me," one should provide a detailed analysis.
All phenomena (*dharmas*) are manifold, namely those of the past, future, and present. Which of these do you wish me to explain?

and so forth; this should be set aside. Next, as for the reliance on scripture, this is the teaching of the Mahāsāṃghika school. Its general substance is largely consistent with this treatise.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun. *Yue shi ming xi men* (A Concise Clarification of the Gates of Bondage).

The intention here is to explain, based on the defilements (*kleśa*) of the three time periods that act as the "binder" (*bandhana*), how they are distinguished in relation to the "bound" (*bandhya*) meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) across the three time periods, thereby clarifying the extent and limitations of bondage.
What is here termed "bondage" refers to the object that is bound; within this object, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) reside.
That which increases [in accordance with its object] is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*); that which does not increase in accordance is not called a fetter.

As for that which increases in accordance, it does not necessarily require a present condition; even if they exist in the past or future, as long as they have not been abandoned, they all increase in accordance. There are two types of such increase:

first, increase through association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*), and second, increase through the object (*ālambana-anuśaya*). In the state where they have not been abandoned, all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) [increase in both ways].
Regarding their own associated [factors], they all increase concomitantly without distinction; regarding their own objects, they increase pervasively without distinction.
Because the object is fixed, one cannot say that there is pervasion or non-pervasion with respect to their own objects.

Although the afflictions have both specific and general characteristics, and the mental consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses differ in the breadth or narrowness of their objective spheres and their functional power, they are nevertheless pervasive.

Since there is no difference in the characteristics of their respective objects, when one examines the distinction between the bondage and non-bondage of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three time periods with respect to the objects they bind—whether it be greed, hatred, pride, or the afflictions of specific character—one finds therein the distinction between those that are pervasive and those that are not.

In this chapter, the main section is divided into two parts: first, up to the point where it is stated that [these] "necessarily bind pervasively," it clarifies the specific characteristics of greed, hatred, and pride.

"Affliction [consists of] two; the remaining [afflictions] are past and future, and are pervasive," and so forth. Below this, it clarifies that the common-characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), such as views and doubt, are explained.
Within this section, there are two parts: first, regarding the two periods of the past and present, it clarifies that there are no pervasive [dispositions] across the six consciousnesses;

second, regarding the future, it clarifies through the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the five sensory consciousnesses whether there are pervasive or non-pervasive [dispositions]. As for the statement "arising in dependence upon many factors," it refers, for instance, to how wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) denies [the existence of things].

The phrase "all causes and effects as a collective object" means that greed, hatred, and pride are specifically characterized delusions (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*). Regarding this, the *Nyāyānusāra* cites a sūtra, stating:
"The Buddha told Mātṛceṭā: 'If your eye does not see a form, would desire-greed arise with that form as its condition?
No, Venerable Sir,' and so on at length" (the above is the text of the treatise). This is because the arising of greed, hatred, and the like is not fixed [to a specific object].

In this context, that which has already arisen and is not yet abandoned is bound to that very object. Past greed and so forth cannot universally bind all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) across the three times.
Having arisen in the present, they are bound according to the breadth or narrowness of their respective objects;
as soon as they arise, they are bound. Although there may be instances where [greed] takes phenomena of the three times as its object, there is no present greed or the like that can [bind them].
Because they exhaustively take as their object all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the three times, those of the past and present are not "universal" (*sarvatraga*).

To say that there are objects which are taken as objects while others are not, is like how one may still give rise to desire for the visible form (*varṇa*) of a particular person, yet not give rise to desire for all other objects.
As previously cited from the Sūtra, the statement that "objects flow through the three times" explains what it means to be universal across time; this refers to the future mind.

Greed and other afflictions associated with consciousness are definitely bound to their objects; although the consciousness itself exists in the future, because its objects shift and it flows through the three periods of time, it is called "pervasive across the worlds" (*adhvavyāpin*).
This refers specifically to being bound to objects, not necessarily to being currently engaged with them.

Regarding the phrase "the types are limitless," this explains "pervasiveness of entities" (*vastuvyāpin*); that is, although the distinct-characteristic afflictions associated with the future mental consciousness are not yet exhausted...

Based on the general category, it is stated that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) of the three time periods are taken as objects; even if something is not bound by this [category], it is nonetheless bound by that [category].

Therefore, it is said that the types [of objects] are infinite and so forth. Next, regarding the five consciousnesses, they are distinguished by whether they arise or do not arise, and by their being pervasive or non-pervasive.

Thus, within the context of those that can arise, it is stated that the object must necessarily coexist with its support; that is to say, the support and the object of the five consciousnesses must be identical.
At that time, the arising [of consciousness] takes only the present as its object and does not take the three periods of time; therefore, the object must necessarily be simultaneous.

Regarding the non-arising of consciousness in the intermediate period, there are two types of universality (*sarvatraga*): first, regarding distinct objects, each flows through its own respective period; second, regarding a common object, they proceed in a staggered manner.
The reason for this is that objects such as form (*rūpa*) flow through the three periods by their own nature without depending on consciousness; thus, when consciousness arises...
Because they necessarily rely upon objects, although their temporal periods differ, their nature and bondage are fixed; therefore, they are called "pervasive" (*vyāpaka*).

When it says "all of one's own objects of cognition," this means that for the five consciousnesses, visible forms, sounds, and so forth constitute their respective objects; or for greed and hatred, agreeable and disagreeable things and so forth constitute their respective objects.

Regarding the statement "simultaneous or disparate [objects] of the three times," this means that when the binding consciousness simultaneously apprehends the six objects together, they are called "simultaneous."
At that time, those which are bound are each situated in a different world-system; this is called "disparity.

Regarding the "infinite categories of non-arisen fivefold consciousnesses," although a single momentary consciousness lacks the capacity for universal perception, when infinite consciousnesses are considered in relation to a multitude of objects, how could there not be universal engagement?
Since what is bound here is not necessarily bound there, the following explains the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as common characteristics.
"Views" refers to the five views; "ignorance" (avidyā) applies to both associated and independent [factors].

These, because they are associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), are necessarily able to universally bind the three time periods—past, present, and future—because they are universal characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa). Regarding their own objects of perception, they are necessarily able to universally bind them.

Although the statement mentions two types of universality, it is because those that are not fixed [in time] are necessarily associated with the mental consciousness and thus must possess universality across the time periods.
Because they are universal afflictions (*sāmānyakleśa*), although they have the capacity to pervade objects of experience, they do so in two ways.
However, because they exist only for a single present moment, there are times when they take only this particular object and not others; thus, they are not pervasive.
Since they do not necessarily pervade all objects, they differ from the past and future [afflictions], which possess multiple moments and therefore can be truly pervasive.

To speak of clarifying the existence or non-existence of the three times is also to clarify the bondage of the three times. According to the Sautrāntika school, since the past and future do not exist, how could there be bondage?
Therefore, from this point onward, the existence of the three times is established.

Regarding the statement "diligently cultivating aversion and relinquishment," it means that because one contemplates the impermanence of form (*rūpa*), one diligently cultivates aversion and relinquishment toward the past. Regarding the statement "diligently severing longing and seeking," it refers to contemplating...
Because it is impermanent, one can sever the longing for future form; this longing is precisely craving that takes future form as its object.
Furthermore, it is explained that by contemplating the impermanence of form, one diligently severs longing; because one does not hope for or desire it, one diligently severs seeking.

Regarding the statement that if the past and future did not exist, there would be no objects of cognition: this means that since mental consciousness takes the three periods of time as its objects, the existence of the past and future is established as a logical proof.

It is also said that those who claim to be followers of the Sarvāstivāda school [assert] that there is a difference in the substantial entities (*dravya*) of the past and future, whereas the existence of the present is not different from them;
however, this is no different from the non-existence of a rabbit’s horn. If they were the same as the present, they would not be past or future;
if they were like a rabbit’s horn, they could not serve as objects to give rise to cognition. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "That is to say..."
The establishment that the past and future are neither existent like the present nor non-existent like a horse's horn,

and the statement that "that which gives rise to cognition as its object is the characteristic of true existence," are fundamentally no different from the established tenets of the *Nyāyānusāra* as introduced in the preface.
If one says that the three time periods would consequently be destroyed: since the essence [of conditioned phenomena] is permanent, their function should likewise be so;
thus, they ought to be called "present," and how could there be a distinction between past and future? Therefore, the three time periods would be destroyed. The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense:

"Because conditioned phenomena are designated as 'future' when not yet arisen, 'present' when already arisen, and 'past' when already ceased, what is untenable about this? Thus, [the argument is] repeated.

[The opponent] refutes [the Sarvāstivāda position], saying: "Who has not yet been born? and so forth. This refutation targets the underlying intention [of the Sarvāstivādins]: since you maintain that the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena exists eternally, they ought all to be exactly like those in the present.

What, then, is lacking such that something is called "future" because it does not yet exist? Furthermore, what phenomenon is lacking such that something is called "past" because it has already ceased?
To say that one does not admit that phenomena "did not exist before but now exist" is merely a counter-refutation of the Sarvāstivāda school; it is actually used to establish one's own position.

"An independent creator" refers to Īśvara; whatever he intends to do, he does immediately. Now, the masters of the Sarvāstivāda school speak whenever they wish to speak, and thus they are similar to that [creator].
As for the Sautrāntika position regarding the three times: the past is called "existent" because it once existed;
the future is called "existent" because it will exist; and the past existence is the present effect, while the future is the cause that once existed.
Regarding the existence of present causes and the statement that future fruits will exist, there are differing views among various schools (*nikāya*) which contradict one another;

these are omitted here as they would be tedious to recount. To clarify disjunction (*visamyoga*) by way of abandonment (*prahāṇa*): "abandonment" refers to the severance of the afflictions (*kleśa*), while "disjunction" refers to the objects (*vastu*) to which one is bound.

This is because, although the afflictions have been severed, the object has not yet become disjoined from them; therefore, this category is established. In the dialogue concerning both the subject and the object, only [the following] is obtained:

It is said that when an object is dissociated from a defilement, that defilement must necessarily be abandoned; however, it cannot be said that when a defilement is abandoned, its object is necessarily dissociated. For this reason, the following section specifically asks about abandonment rather than dissociation.
In the explanation, first regarding the defilements of insight (*darśana-heya*), and then regarding the defilements of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*):

it says that although [a defilement] has already been abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), it remains bound to the [object] up to the stage of the origin (*samudaya*) because the pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are able to take all five categories as their objects.
