Thus, even though [the defilement] is associated with suffering...
The statement that one has already abandoned the lower grade yet remains bound by the subsequent grades is made with reference to the nine grades;
it means that as the nine grades of fetters and the acquisition of the first fruit arise along the middle path,
although the acquisition of the preceding grade has already been relinquished— its self-nature having been severed and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) realized— one remains bound by the lower [grades].
Because they are bound by the fetters of their respective categories (*pakṣa*) of afflictions (*kleśa*). The phrase "still bound" refers to subsequent categories that have not yet been abandoned;

it does not mean that the preceding categories are already disjoined from their fetters because they are no longer bound to other objects. As the *Śāstra* states: "That which can take this preceding category as its object is still bound to that preceding category.

The term "not yet abandoned" serves to distinguish it from what has already been abandoned, such as one who has previously become free from desire (*vītarāga*) and subsequently enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding these [afflictions]:
Because one cannot be bound within that very state, it is said that [the defilement] has not been abandoned.

The term "able to take as an object" (*ālambana*) serves to exclude those that are unable to take it as an object—namely, those taking other realms as objects, those taking other categories (*pakṣa*) as objects, and those taking wholesome states such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth as objects, since these do not take this [defilement] as their object.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states that the word "and" (*ca*) also clarifies that while the preceding [categories] have already been abandoned, the succeeding ones remain unabandoned; both constitute the sense of being bound.

Regarding the gate of the increase of delusion (*paryavasthāna*), first there is a question and answer, followed by an explanation. As for *Vibhāṣā*, the *Vibhāṣā* says it means "extensive exposition" (*vistara-vyākhyāna*).
Here, because the afflictions are extensive and difficult to survey, while the objects and consciousnesses are summarized for clarity, it is called the *Laghu-vibhāṣā* (the Concise Vibhāṣā).

Regarding the phrase "the great stream of questions that transcend," this means that since the characteristics of the questions are numerous, they are like a flowing stream. The word "and" (*ca*)... [text ends].
Regarding "untainted phenomena" (*anāsrava-dharma*), it was stated above that the five categories (*pañca-varga*) refer only to cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).
However, since this section concerns the actual substance (*svabhāva*) of cessation and the path, untainted phenomena are established separately from those five categories.

As for the question of which phenomena are the objects of which consciousnesses: among the aforementioned sixteen phenomena, which phenomena serve as the objects of which of the sixteen consciousnesses? This point should first be understood.

Regarding the phrase "the dharmas and so forth," since the pervasive increase (*anuśaya*) has not yet been distinguished, the objects of consciousness are clarified first; thus it says, "for now" (*tāvat*).

To explain this passage, it is divided into two parts: first, up to the point where it says "can serve as the objects of the ten consciousnesses," which clarifies the commonality and exclusivity [of the objects] by correlating them with the consciousnesses;

second, from the words "The Treatise says" onwards, which distinguishes the pervasive increase by correlating the entities with the afflictions. The phrase "three of its own realm" refers to the universal [afflictions] belonging to the lower levels of suffering and origin.

Because they take other categories (*nikāya*) as their objects, the contaminated wholesome minds and the non-obscured neutral minds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) can also take suffering and its origin as objects;

thus, there are three [types of] cessation and paths that sever infinite afflictions (*anuśaya*). Because these are severed by the paths and take only their own category as objects, they do not take others as objects.

As for the statement that "the attainments (*prāpti*) of the form realm’s abandonments through cultivation take the desire realm as their object," this refers to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*).
All such wholesome minds, as well as the resultant (*vipāka*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), and neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds, take the lower realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) as their object.

Regarding the statement that untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) also takes the suffering and origin [truths] of the desire realm as its objects: this is because various untainted minds, such as the patience and knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti-jñāna*), take the objects of suffering and origin as their domain.

Furthermore, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) cannot take the desire realm as its object because it possesses the four types of remoteness (*dūratā*) from the desire realm. Moreover, all higher [realms]...
The defilements of the [lower] stages do not take the lower as their object; for this reason, these three objects are perceived only by the five consciousnesses.

Furthermore, this is stated in terms of the general categories that are potentially perceivable, and does not mean that everything necessarily takes them as its object. For example, when [defilements] of the lower [stages] take other categories of afflictions as their object, or when those of the higher realms take the lower as their object, they do not take suffering as their object;
the rest may be understood by analogy. Next, the three [objects] of the Form Realm within its own realm are analogous to those of the Desire Realm.

Regarding the explanation of the three categories of the lower realm (*adhodhātu*): it refers to the afflictions of the lower nine [stages] that take the upper [realms] as their object, because they are able to take the upper [realms] as their cognitive object.

Furthermore, the wholesome consciousnesses—both acquired through application (*prayoga-ja*) and acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*)—of the desire realm can take the upper realms as their objects, such as when the mind aspires to the upper [realms]. For this reason, these also constitute the three categories.

As for the statement that the consciousness abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the formless realm can take the form realm as its object, this refers to the wholesome mind cultivated during the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Because it takes the fourth dhyāna as its object, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "What kind of phenomena can the wholesome consciousness of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the formless realm take as its object? Answer:
It can take all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of its own level and the levels above, as well as the contaminated phenomena of the level immediately below;

furthermore, regarding uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) pure consciousnesses, those that take [these] as objects—such as the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) of the subsequent classes (*anvaya*) concerning suffering and origin—are all able to take them as objects. Others do not take them as objects."

The four categories of the formless realm do not take lower realms as objects; because those abandoned by the [path of] cessation and the path take their own category as objects, there are thus only eight consciousnesses that take them as objects.

Next, regarding the three consciousnesses of the desire and form realms in the formless realm: these also take the nine higher objects through afflictions directed upward and through impure wholesome minds, all of which take the upper realms as objects.
This merely excludes the formless realm from taking the desire realm as an object below, but it does not exclude the desire realm from taking the upper realms as objects.
Regarding the statement that "all [defilements] can take the formless as their object," this means they may or may not take it as an object; it is not definitive.

As for the statement that "the five consciousnesses are as before," this refers to the fact that the defilements belonging to the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) are taken as objects by the universal (sarvatraga) consciousnesses belonging to the Truths of Suffering (duḥkha) and Origination (samudaya);

furthermore, they are taken as objects by the wholesome universal consciousnesses of both the Desire and Form Realms, as well as by uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds. Thus, they constitute five [objects], and when one's own consciousness is added, they become six.

Question: Why do cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) not mutually increase [their objects]? Answer: Because below the levels of cessation and the path, there are no universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*), and because they do not take other categories as their objects, they do not mutually increase.
As it is with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so it is with the higher realms. Regarding the statement that untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are the objects of ten consciousnesses:
this refers to the essence of cessation and the path; since what was previously mentioned is that which is abandoned by cessation and the path, it is not the same as the [universal] ten.
Regarding consciousness, there are ten types: the final three consciousnesses of each of the three realms, plus the untainted (anāsrava) consciousness.

If distinguished further, the untainted consciousness that takes only cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object—namely, that which is abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) within the first three realms—constitutes three types.

Furthermore, the untainted-object consciousnesses abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) within the three realms, which take only the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) as their object, constitute another three; added to the previous six, these form nine. Finally, there are those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the three realms.

The wholesome consciousnesses that penetrate and take the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) as their objects constitute another three bases; added to the previous [seven], they form nine untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses.

Furthermore, those belonging to the category of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) that take the cessation and path of the desire realm as their objects, and those belonging to the category of Subsequent Knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*) that take the cessation and path of the higher realms as their objects, constitute one [additional] base;

thus, there are ten. It should be understood that the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states abandoned through cultivation do not take the untainted as their objects. Now, regarding the universal [defilements] of suffering and origin: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.]
Since [the afflictions] take the five categories as their objects, why do they take only three consciousnesses as objects regarding cessation and the path?

The answer is that taking the five categories as objects refers to taking what is to be abandoned as an object, not taking the untainted essence of cessation and the path as an object, as previously explained; for it is only the six types of underlying tendencies belonging to the lower realms that take the untainted [cessation and path] as their objects.

From here below is the second section, which clarifies how the afflictions increase by association (*anuśaya*). This is divided into three parts: first, up to the point where it says "if someone were to ask," it clarifies the objects associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and how the afflictions increase in relation to them;
second, from "if someone were to ask" onwards, it distinguishes the increase by association in relation to consciousness that takes a single object;

third, from "if again there is one who asks about the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object" onwards, it clarifies the increase by association in relation to consciousness that takes an object of an object (*ālambanālambana*). Regarding these terms: [the text proceeds to explain].
To briefly indicate the general direction: this refers to taking a single dharma—the pleasure faculty (*sukhendriya*)—from among the twenty-two faculties as a provisional illustration.

It is explained that Kātyāyana, in the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, first establishes the analysis based on the twenty-two faculties by first questioning regarding the eye faculty and then questioning regarding the consciousness associated with simple objects (*ekālambana-vijñāna*).

Within this discussion of the pleasure faculty, there are further two parts: first, the enumeration of the names and categories of the pleasure faculty in the first dhyāna; second, the formal determination of its nature.

Regarding the statement that "pleasure" (*sukha*) increases accordingly and exists within the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), it is said to be abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);

this is because joy (*prīti*) is defined as mental satisfaction belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while pleasure is defined as physical satisfaction, and thus, existing within the five sensory consciousnesses, it is abandoned only by cultivation.

Regarding the "five categories" (*pañca-prakāra*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this refers to the third dhyāna, wherein mental pleasure (*manobhūmika-sukha*) is universally associated with all five categories. Regarding the "seventh," which is untainted (*anāsrava*), this refers to its basis.
When one arises from the third dhyāna and engages in untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*), it is associated with untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*).

Since there is only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no untainted faculty of pleasure; therefore, among the sixteen objects, it is associated only with seven.

Next, in correctly analyzing the increase [of defilements] (*anuśaya*), regarding the statement "the untainted faculty of pleasure is as previously explained," this refers to the previous explanation that the untainted is like a stone heated by fire.

Because the foot does not abide accordingly, there is no mention of "increasing accordingly. Regarding the statement that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase in accordance with [their objects]:
this refers to the latent dispositions to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm, as well as the universal (*sarvatraga*) ones.

Taking the pleasure of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as an object—whether it be the pleasure of the desire realm or the entirety of the form realm—the four types of latent dispositions, namely greed, anger, pride, and ignorance (*moha*), which are to be abandoned by cultivation in the desire realm, increase accordingly within the pleasure of their own respective categories; the universal ones [increase] across all.
Because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can take other categories as their objects, they increase accordingly.

Within the thirty-one latent dispositions of the third dhyāna stage of the form realm, when taken collectively among the ninety-eight latent dispositions, these total forty-six latent dispositions that increase with respect to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

Among these, fifteen belong to the desire realm, while the thirty-one of the form realm consist of the non-universal [dispositions] of the lower [realms] regarding suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) within the desire realm.

Because the delusions (*kleśa*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the cessation and path truths do not take other categories as their objects, they likewise do not increase in accordance with them.

Although there is an object that takes non-pleasure as its condition within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it does not increase in accordance with it; therefore, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) does not extend to the formless realm through such increase.

Furthermore, although it is said that "all" [faculties] exist within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one should know that this refers only to the stage of the third dhyāna; in the other three stages, [the faculty of pleasure] does not exist.

Because there is no underlying intention (*āśaya*) and because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of other stages do not increase in accordance with them, it is now stated in general terms that "all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm increase [in relation to their objects].

Although within the first dhyāna there is pleasure associated with the three consciousnesses, which belongs to the category of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and is thus similar to that of the desire realm, it will not be recounted again here.

Question: The three types of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which are abandoned through the cessation and the path, take only non-existence as their object. How can they be said to increase?
How can it be said that the outflows (*āsrava*) increase in accordance with all afflictions belonging to the five categories?

In reality, these afflictions take only the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; however, because they are associated with pleasure and are thus "increasing," even though they do not increase by way of being objects, they do so by way of association.
Therefore, one should understand that in this context, the term "increase" (*anuśaya*) applies to both association and the object.
Each [type] is obtained according to its respective application.

Next, the second section clarifies the consciousnesses that have single objects (*ekālambana-vijñāna*); this is divided into two parts: first, up to the point where it establishes the fixed number of twelve consciousnesses;

second, from "according to what is applicable" (*yathāyogam*) onwards, the actual analysis of how they increase accordingly. It should be understood that the "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*) mentioned here are...

Regarding those consciousnesses associated with the afflictions that increase in dependence upon the previously mentioned faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), those sixteen consciousnesses are also the consciousnesses associated with the afflictions within these twelve [consciousnesses].

There are no other consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure as their object—namely, the universal [defilements] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) such as those pertaining to the suffering and origin [truths]—referring to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) faculty of pleasure associated with the five sensory consciousnesses; this is the desire realm.

Because it is subsumed under the Truths of Suffering and Origin within the [desire] realm, it is generally associated with consciousnesses abandoned through seeing suffering and origin; because it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it is also associated with consciousnesses abandoned through cultivation.
Regarding the mental consciousness taking the untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) of the desire realm as its object:

as previously stated, because it can take the path-factors of the six stages belonging to the category of Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) as its objects, it is able to take the untainted pleasure of the third dhyāna as its object.

Furthermore, the essence of the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) is not the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), because the essence of the Truth of Cessation is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and thus not pleasure.
Regarding the "five categories (*pañca-varga*) of the form realm," since pleasure extends through all five categories, consciousness likewise extends through the five categories.

Regarding the statement that "the Path Truth (*mārga-satya*) up to the untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) of the third dhyāna takes [the third dhyāna] as its object," this means that false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth within the Path Truth directly take [those states] as their objects.

When the Truth of the Path takes one stage as its object, it simultaneously takes the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across nine stages; therefore, it can take the untainted pleasure (*anāsrava-sukha*) of the third dhyāna as its object.

Regarding the wholesome states—both those acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) and those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*)—of the formless realm that take the path of the category of subsequent knowledge across nine stages as their objects:

this means that while an impure wholesome mind can take the untainted as its object, it does so by taking only a single stage, yet it thereby encompasses all nine stages, just as in the case of [the previous] example.

Because I observe all phenomena through observation, in principle this also extends to the observation of impermanence (*anityatā*) and so forth. The twelfth [category], the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), is capable of taking the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object;

that is to say, untainted consciousness universally takes the faculty of pleasure belonging to the third dhyāna as its object. Next, to distinguish those [defilements] that increase accordingly (*anuśerate*):

regarding the four categories of the desire realm, excluding those abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) in their entirety, the remaining twenty-nine latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase accordingly.

Furthermore, for example, regarding the four categories of cultivation—suffering, origin, path, and cessation—the pervasive and non-pervasive afflictions that take the consciousness perceiving pleasure as their object all obtain "increase" (anuśaya).
Moreover, the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the lower realms of the origin category both take the consciousness perceiving pleasure as their object and constitute increase.

Other heavy-objective afflictions, such as greed and hatred, only obtain increase but do not take the consciousness perceiving pleasure as their object. The same principle applies to the direct and indirect [afflictions] of the path category in the lower realms.
Regarding the statement that the four afflictions of the [Nirvāṇa] Section are both objects and increase:

among the twenty-eight latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the five sections, excluding the three—namely wrong view and the others—associated with the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), all remaining ones increase in accordance with consciousness.

This is because the three afflictions associated with the Truth of Cessation take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object; therefore, they do not take the consciousness of pleasure as their object, nor do they increase therein.

However, false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). When greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth arise conditioned by such views, they are able to take that pleasure as their object;
this is a consciousness that takes pleasure as its object. At the moment this consciousness arises, greed and the other afflictions necessarily increase concomitantly (*anuśerate*).

Therefore, those very instances of greed and so forth are what "increase concomitantly. Previously, it was explained that the faculty of pleasure increases concomitantly throughout the realms from the Desire Realm down to the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); now, this is clarified [further].

Question: Is it not the case that while [the defilements] increase in accordance with consciousness (*vijñāna*), they do not [necessarily] pervade it? Answer: Although views (*dṛṣṭi*) and so forth take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object, they arise in association with the mental faculty (*manas*) and its desires;

therefore, they are said to "increase in accordance" (*anuśerate*) by way of association (*saṃprayoga*). Because they do not take the consciousness associated with pleasure as their object, one cannot say that they increase in accordance with that consciousness.

Regarding "the two categories of the formless realm" (*ārūpya-dhātu*), this refers to the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) which are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), including greed (*rāga*).

The three [types of] *anuśaya* associated with the wholesome mind abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) take the consciousness of pleasure as their object; therefore, greed and the others all increase therein.

Since those that are universal toward suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-sarvatraga*) take other categories as their objects, the twenty-one *anuśayas* of the entire formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) increase collectively.

Specifically, there are seven from the category of the path (*mārga*), three from the category of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and eleven from the categories of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*). Thus, in total, seventy-eight *anuśayas* increase collectively within the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

[The section on] "Increase" (vṛddhi). This is the third part from below, which clarifies the consciousnesses that serve as secondary conditions (*anuśaya-pratyaya*). Within this, there are two sections: first, up to the point where it says "all are able to take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object," which establishes the sequence of consciousnesses;
second, from "accordingly, as appropriate" onwards, which correctly analyzes the increase (*anuśaya*). Regarding the first [section], there is first a question and answer, followed by...

Regarding the statement "the consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)," the preceding twelve consciousnesses are those that take the faculty of pleasure as an object-condition;

since these current fourteen consciousnesses further take those preceding twelve consciousnesses as objects, they are called "consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure as an object-condition. As for the statement "further adding two types," this refers to taking the pervasive [mental factors] (*sarvatraga*) of suffering and origination as the two.

One might ask: why are the pervasive [mental factors] of suffering and origination excluded when considering direct objects? [The answer is: because they are already included within the aforementioned categories.

Question: What is meant by "repeatedly taking as an object" (*punarālambana*)? Answer: It is because the pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin do not take the untainted faculty of pleasure (*anāsrava-sukhendriya*) as an object, nor do they take the tainted faculty of pleasure belonging to lower realms (*adhobhūmika-sāsrava-sukhendriya*) as an object.
Therefore, that which is called "repeatedly taking as an object" refers to the pervasive latent dispositions taking all tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as their objects;

whereas those [dispositions] abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are capable of taking the untainted faculty of pleasure as an object. Furthermore, regarding the views (*dṛṣṭi*), [the same applies].
The false views, doubt, and so forth abandoned through the Path also take uncontaminated pleasure as their object;

these are consciousnesses that take pleasure as their object because they are all objects of the pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the lower realms of suffering and origin. Thus, they take it as an object repeatedly, and since they also include the pervasive [dispositions] abandoned through suffering and origin, they total fourteen.
Next, to distinguish how they increase in accordance with their respective objects, it is said that they extend to the desire and form realms as described above.

This means that the two realms of desire and form are no different from the aforementioned single-conditioned [defilements], except that they subsequently give rise to a second condition for the preceding consciousness.

In the formless realm alone, there are two additional categories; specifically, in addition to the number of pervasive latent dispositions (anuśaya) that increase upon the single-conditioned consciousness, there are further non-pervasive latent dispositions—namely, greed, pride, and so forth, belonging to the levels of suffering and origin. Therefore, they take suffering and origin as their objects.

The universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are the heavy conditions for consciousness, because greed, pride, and so forth arise conditioned by these universals; therefore, they are all included.

One should exclude only those that do not increase [in intensity] below their own level, as there is no sense of "increase" (*anuśayana*) therein. Question: Why are only three layers established as the limit? Answer:

Because these three layers encompass all phenomena exhaustively. For example, regarding "increasing in accordance with pleasure" (*sukha-anuśayana*), this refers exclusively to the afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as it is only there that pleasure is exhausted.

The "unrestricted" [category] does not include the consciousnesses that take only the formless realm as their object; although it does include the two divisions [of the formless realm] and those universal [factors] pertaining to suffering and origin, it does not include the non-universal [factors].
To exhaustively account for these non-universals, one must further distinguish the "repeatedly conditioned" [category], for only with these three categories is the analysis complete.
Were one to analyze further beyond this, it would be no different from what has already been stated.

The statement "if a mind is said to be 'with latent dispositions' (sānuśaya) by virtue of them" means that a mind is called "with latent dispositions" because those afflictions (kleśa) exist within it.

The question "is it certain that they increase in accordance with this mind? asks whether those afflictions necessarily increase in accordance with the mind when they are associated (samprayukta) with it;
the answer is that this is not determined. The phrase "namely, those associated with the mind and those [which take it] as an object" refers to these two types.
That which is associated with a mind that has not been abandoned increases through association; that which has not been abandoned as its object increases through the object.
The two terms "not abandoned" apply to both of the aforementioned positions. Regarding "associated [factors] already abandoned do not increase":
this means that although the latent dispositions (anuśaya) associated with that mind have been eternally severed and thus do not increase, they are still said to "possess [latent dispositions]."

Because they are dormant, it is said here that if the fetters [of the object] have been severed, one is no longer said to possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) toward it; therefore, this is not mentioned.

The first refers to a defiled mind associated with afflictions (*kleśa*); that is, when the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are associated with afflictions, the afflictions increase in accordance with them.

The second refers to those whose latent dispositions directed toward this defiled mind have not yet been severed; that is, when other latent dispositions take this defiled mind as their object, they likewise [increase].

Regarding the statement that "where there are latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they increase with respect to their objects," and that "once associated [factors] have been abandoned, they no longer increase":

this means that when afflictions such as greed have not yet been abandoned, they are associated with the mind and possess mutual power; thus, they bind the preceding object together, which is termed "increasing.

Once the noble path has abandoned them, they lack the capacity to bind the object; therefore, they do not increase. As for the term "not abandoned": [it refers to those factors that have not yet been severed].

Regarding those [defilements] that have association as their nature (*sahabhū-saṃprayukta*): this refers to those such as greed (*rāga*) and so forth, which necessarily arise simultaneously in association with the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Even when the Path of the Noble Ones (*āryamārga*) arises as an antidote, it cannot cause these defilements to become dissociated from the mind; therefore, they cannot be abandoned through [the severance of] association.

Although they may be abandoned, they are said to be "possessing latent tendencies" (*savāsanā*), because while the associated [factors] are severed, the objective conditions (*ālambana*) remain distant and are not yet severed.
It should be understood that both defiled minds—whether abandoned or unabandoned—are termed "possessing latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*).

As for non-defiled minds, this designation applies only when [the latent dispositions] increase therein; once they have been abandoned, they are no longer termed "possessing latent dispositions. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:
"Since the past lacks functional activity, how can it be said that [latent dispositions] increase therein? The Venerable Ghosa replied as follows:

It is said that although those [latent dispositions] lack the function of grasping an object, they possess a binding efficacy with respect to their objects and associated mental factors as if they were present;
therefore, those latent dispositions have the sense of "increasing along with" (anuśaya).

Regarding the statement that doubt arises next due to non-comprehension: this means that upon hearing two conflicting paths, one harbors hesitation as to whether [suffering] is suffering or not, and so forth, as explained at length.
From this hesitation, false views arise; that is, through improper hearing and reflection, one produces a false certainty that denies the truth of suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the statement that one reckons what was previously clung to as being "able to purify": this means...
If one reckons that what was previously grasped as a means of realization is now called a "purifying statement" that contradicts one's own view, one will certainly feel hatred and aversion;

this refers to the arising of anger toward the bodies of others. Furthermore, the treatise states: "Other masters say that because one gives rise to hatred and aversion during the stages of accepting or rejecting one's own views and understandings, when greed and other afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths arise, they take the views within one's own continuum as their object."

Regarding the object, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (New Translation) states: "If [hatred] that arises toward what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) were to arise, it should be as other masters say;

[hatred] that arises toward what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) also takes the mental continuum of another as its object. As for the statement that there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of before and after, this means that at times one may simultaneously give rise to greed and hatred toward objects that are respectively agreeable and disagreeable.
Why must it necessarily arise after what has been seen? Other cases should be understood according to this principle. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "All..."
There is no fixed sequence for the arising of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), because they can all arise after any other.
When it is said that "due to the non-abandonment of latent dispositions," this refers to the moment when one is about to give rise to the entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) of sensual desire;

since the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that desire has not been abandoned, it acts as a causal force, and by virtue of that acquired force, the desire arises. As for the phrase "like an Arhat of the 'regressive' type (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth," the "and so forth" [includes others].

This applies to non-returners and ordinary beings who have abandoned desire: in their case, afflictions arise solely through the power of the object and not by the other two causes, because their afflictions have already been severed;
because their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that remain unsevered do not exist; and because their mental disposition is pure, there is no improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
One should explain other cases by analogy with this.
Regarding the statement that there are thirty-one root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
this means that while there are thirty-six afflictions in the desire realm in total, because delusion (*moha*) is excluded from each of the five categories, there are only thirty-one.

The statement that although the two higher realms possess two envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), they are not established as outflows (*āsrava*), is an explanation intended to resolve an external objection. Therefore, the treatise asks: "Is it not the case that those [higher realms] also possess lethargy (*styāna*)?"
Regarding the two types of restlessness (*auddhatya*), the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* (Jñānaprasthāna) also states: "What are the outflows (*sāsrava*)?

They are the fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to the two realms of form and formlessness, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*).
Why, then, is it not mentioned here? The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr say that the envelopments in those realms are few.

Regarding the statement that they are identical in their neutral nature (*avyākṛta*) because they lack autonomy: this means that while the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm are mostly unwholesome (*akuśala*), those of the form and formless realms are both exclusively obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Regarding the claim that these two are identical in functioning through the internal door (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), the *Nyāyānusāra* refutes this, stating:

"The afflictions of those realms function by taking external objects—visible forms, sounds, and tangibles—as their conditions; how then can it be said that they function solely through the internal door?"
One should further separately explain the second reason for their conjunction: namely, that those two realms share the same path of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).

The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* offer this defense: although those upper realms also function as "external" (*bahirmukha*), they are described as "internal" (*antarmukha*) because this is said according to the majority of cases.

Just as when one speaks of the "Form Realm" (*rūpa-dhātu*), does it not [also] include feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates? Since these fifteen entities constitute the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), [the objection is thus addressed].

Because the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) have both been eliminated by means of [the elimination of] ignorance (*avidyā*), one knows that the fifteen instances of ignorance within the three realms are established as the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*) by analogy.
Although the verse does not explicitly mention the number fifteen, it simply says "ignorance is the root of all existences" (*avidyā sarvabhavānām mūlam*);

since the remainder outside of the outflows of desire has already been revealed by this [statement], it is said that "ignorance is the root of all existences" to explain the reason for its separate establishment as an outflow. Ignorance.

Because it gives rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, it is called the "root of existence" (*bhava-mūla*); it is not, however, the member of ignorance (*avidyā-aṅga*) among the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is because the member of ignorance within the twelve links has all afflictions as its essential nature. Thus, the *Nyāya-ānusāra* states:
"In order to manifest the preeminence of the faults of ignorance—that is, that it alone can act as the root of birth and death—it is said in the Sūtra: 'Ignorance is...'"
"Because it gives rise to craving and defilement," and so forth, as explained at length—is this not indeed the member of ignorance?

As for the statement that "view does not abide in accordance [with its object]" and so forth, they are collectively termed "outflows" (*āsrava*) because, within the categories of floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*), view is established separately as one;
thus, while there are four yokes including the yoke of views, there are only three outflows, as view is not established as a single outflow. It is for this reason that this explanation is given.

That which is called the "enemy of the noble path" refers to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), because by reckoning what is not the path to be the path, one abandons the true path;

this is the complaint of the noble ones. As for reckoning self-starvation and the like as the way to heaven, they merely reckon self-starvation and the like to be the way to heaven, yet do not practice the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*);
therefore it is said that they reckon abandoning desirable objects. This should be understood as follows:
Wearing coarse garments, eating rough food, abandoning pleasant objects, and observing the two hundred and fifty precepts are considered the path of true purity;
yet one fails to realize that these are merely auxiliary conditions for the path and consequently does not practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).

As for the statement that ignorance (*avidyā*) is not the grasper (*grāhaka*), this is but one interpretation; furthermore, another commentary explains that it is because the characteristic of ignorance is not sharp or intense.
They may be established separately, yet they can only be explained together.

Regarding the fact that the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the root afflictions are difficult to discern: this is as Ānanda asked whether there was pride (*māna*) and so forth among his fellow practitioners of the holy life;
[the Buddha] replied that it exists, because it increases (*anuśaya*) even within moments (*kṣaṇa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*), and is therefore called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*). This is the second point.

Regarding "increasing along with" (*anuśaya*), the *Nyāya* further states: Just as an enemy seeks out a vulnerability, and just as the poison of sight [is harmful], one should know that afflictions have the sense of "increasing along with" (*anuśaya*) in relation to their own objects (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, just as a red-hot iron ball can cause water to heat up, and just as the poison of touch [is harmful], one should know that afflictions have the sense of "increasing along with" in relation to their own associated factors (*saṃprayukta*). According to this, the characteristics of the object are established.
The meaning of this metaphorical illustration differs from the preceding one: the former refers to the *ālambana* (object-condition), while the latter refers to the *saṃprayoga* (association).

When it is said that these afflictions (*kleśa*) "follow along with" (*anubadhnanti*) sentient beings, it is because the substance of the afflictions does not always exist; rather, they are sometimes absent.

Since only their acquisition (*prāpti*) remains constantly present even when the mind is wholesome or neutral, it is simply stated that the acquisition follows along with sentient beings. As the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "That is to say..."
Regarding the statement that "since beginningless time, within the continuum [of beings], afflictions arise and follow along, persisting with sentient beings," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"Because they are extremely difficult to abandon, like quartan fever or rat poison.

Some say "following and binding" (*anuśaya*) means that acquisition (*prāpti*) constantly follows [the being], like the movement of the ocean or the shadow following one who travels through the sky. The *Xinlun* (New Treatise) states that these four meanings are combined as a whole.
In the "Chapter on Latent Dispositions" (*anuśaya*), the first explanation of *anuśaya* and the subsequent three explanations of *anuśaya* represent the traditional interpretation (*pūrvārtha*).

Furthermore, it is said that the designation "*anuśaya*" used in the two treatises is not a derivative etymological definition (*nirukti*), but rather that these ten types of afflictions (*kleśa*) are established as having the four aforementioned meanings and thus receive the name "*anuśaya*.
What is the correct principle (*yukti*) for why only the ten [afflictions] such as greed (*lobha*) are called *anuśaya*, while others such as anger (*krodha*) are not?

These ten types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are firm and solid because they are not like anger and the other [afflictions]; that is to say, these ten alone are firm and solid such that once they arise, they are difficult to cease.
Regarding the phrase "abiding in the flow" (*pravāha-sthiti*): "abiding" refers to the prolonged detention of sentient beings within saṃsāra;
"flow" refers to the process of transmigrating through saṃsāra from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) down to the Avīci Hell. Because their continuity [is maintained] in these six...

Because they leak out through the wound-like gates (āśraya) without end, they are called "outflows" (āsrava). Regarding the statement that they "sweep away wholesome qualities," it is like a torrential flood that sweeps away all manner of objects;
as the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states, the meanings of "staying fixed" (*sthiti*) and "sweeping away" (*prasravaṇa*) constitute the meaning of "flood" (*ogha*).

As for "yoking" (*yoga*), it refers to causing sentient beings to be joined together with the realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and modes of birth (*yoni*); thus it is called a "yoke" (*yoga*), just like the yoke of a chariot.
Regarding the statement "clinging to birth and death," this refers to being able to grasp the self-substance (*ātman*) of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) as a basis;
this is according to the explanation of the Sarvāstivāda school. However, according to the Master’s own explanation, it differs from the above. Thus, the treatise says:

"If one explains it correctly, one should say that because [the mind] flows, dwells, continues, and leaks through various objects without interruption, it is called an 'outflow' (*āsrava*)," as stated in the Sūtra.
The Sūtra says: "Venerable ones, you should know that it is like pulling a boat against the current; even with great effort, its movement remains difficult.
If one lets this boat go with the current, although one abandons effort, its movement is not difficult.

You should know that the arising of wholesome or defiled minds is likewise. (According to this treatise, when afflictions are uninterrupted within an object, it is called an *āsrava* [outflow]. If their momentum is predominant, they are called...)
They are called floods (*ogha*) because when sentient beings fall into them, they can only follow along and have no power to resist;

because they surge, overflow, drift, and rush with such force that they are difficult to oppose. When they are active, they are not said to be "yokes" (*yoga*) because they are not extremely predominant;
rather, they are called yokes because they cause sentient beings to be joined with various kinds of suffering, or because they manifest repeatedly. Thus, they are grasped as yokes.
Because they are characterized by desire and so forth, they are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).
(The above meaning has been fully set forth for the sake of conciseness). *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 21.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.
Regarding the statement that "the nine fetters" (*nava saṃyojanāni*) are so named: when asked for what reason all nine types are called "fetters," the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains:

"Because they have the power to bind one to objects and to rebirth, they are called 'fetters. Alternatively, because these exist, they cause all sentient beings to conjoin with a multitude [of sufferings]."
Because it is suffering, it is called a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*); it is the locus where these manifold sufferings and afflictions find their footing. Regarding the single "fetter of craving":

this refers to greed based on the three roots, which takes the bodies of the three realms as its support and the objects of the three realms as its conditions. Because it is the greed that has not yet abandoned the defilements of the three realms, it is called "greed for the three realms.
As for what is called "greed," it refers to a mental factor (*caitasika*) that is characterized by delighting in and being grasped by agreeable signs; it functions precisely with respect to...
The attachment arising from all forms of existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*) is called greed (*lobha*). For what reason is this greed called craving (*tṛṣṇā*)?

Because it is a defiled mental factor (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*) that pursues and delights in its object. Regarding the fourth, the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"Ill-will refers to causing the mind to feel aversion toward disagreeable perceptions and toward actions characterized by the desire for separation. Fourth is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The "fetter" (saṃyojana) refers to ignorance regarding the three realms; this is defined in terms of its basis (*āśraya*), not its object (*ālambana*).

This is because all untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena do not fall within the realms, yet ignorance also takes them as its object. This is analyzed in detail in the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

As for the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), they both consist of false deliberation; their specific characteristics are revealed separately, as when it is said that "one thing" is [the object] among the five views.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks: What is the purpose of stating that these [factors] are "equal"? It is because it is seen to be beneficial for establishing the meaning of the "fetters" (*saṃyojana*).

The intent of this statement is that just as greed, hatred, and so forth, each individually, can constitute a single fetter, so too do the three views and the two graspings—each consisting of eighteen factors combined—constitute a single fetter. If it were otherwise, one would have to say there are five [fetters].

Since views (*dṛṣṭi*) and grasping (*parāmarśa*) each consist of eighteen distinct entities—just as greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth do—they are established as single fetters (*saṃyojana*) only when combined;

otherwise, they would merely rival greed and the other afflictions. If that were the case, then the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the grasping after views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) would each consist of eighteen entities, and the grasping after precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) would likewise consist of eighteen entities.
Would this not mean that the number of entities is equal? It is not so; for in the *Mūla-śāstra*, the reasoning for their classification is definitively established.
Regarding the phrase "because they are equal in being grasped": the three views (*dṛṣṭi*) are equal as the objects grasped (*grāhya*), while the two views are equal as the graspers (*grāhaka*).

(The commentary explains that "equal" means "identical," and that the character "equal" is read in conjunction with what follows; thus the treatise says: "the three are equal as the objects grasped, and the two are equal as the graspers. As for the statement "due to the predominance of the two afflictions," this means that among the *paryavasthānas* (outbursts), only these [two] uniquely possess both characteristics, whereas the others do not.
Furthermore, shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) and do not arise through their own power.
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) arises through both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and it arises solely by one's own power; the other two [mental factors] do not arise in this way.
These three are sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*styāna*). Regarding their being causes for low birth and poverty, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Even if one is born within the two happy destinies (*sugati*), one is oppressed by the heavy suffering of low birth and poverty; we see that those who are base and destitute of wealth are not even treated with affection by their closest relatives."
"Veneration. Regarding the phrase "disturbing the two superior destinies of humans and devas," it is as the Blessed One told Kauśika:

"Because of the fetters of envy and stinginess, humans and devas are disturbed. Regarding the phrase "one should know that this includes the latter four types of the two groups," this means that from the fourth [category], "those who have gone forth," downwards, there are four types in total; they occupy the latter positions among the seven meanings.
Regarding the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni*), the older translations state that they collectively take thirty-one factors as their essence:

namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the three realms, which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, constitutes three; the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the three realms, each abandoned through the vision of suffering and the path, constitutes six;

doubt (*vicikitsā*) in the three realms across the four truths, constitutes twelve; and greed and hatred (*rāga* and *pratigha*) in the five categories of the desire realm, constitute ten. Thus, there are thirty-one in total.

Regarding the statement that "greed and hatred do not transcend the desire realm": even if a noble one (*ārya*) has severed the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), they still possess these two [afflictions] and thus do not ascend beyond it, because those in the first two fruits have not yet abandoned desire.
Regarding the statement that "by means of the three beginning with the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one returns to birth in the lower realms":
even if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has severed greed and hatred and attained birth in the higher realms, by the power of these three, they return to the lower realms.
Returning once more to birth below, these three delusions are not abandoned by ordinary beings. Question:

Since the three views—view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and so forth—pervade the higher realms, why are they not called "factors conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*)? Answer: It is not because of these three that one is born in the higher realms;

for even those who are *āryas* (noble ones) have already abandoned them and may still be reborn there. Rather, it is because craving and other [afflictions] moisten birth in the higher realms; therefore, only craving and the like [are so designated].

It is called "conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*), as will be clarified in the following text. Regarding the statement that one abandons six afflictions, these consist of the five views and doubt, all of which are abandoned by the noble ones (*ārya*).

As for the statement that they are "subsumed under three gates," a question is raised: since the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) pertains to all four truths, why does it speak of only three gates?
The answer is: the term "three gates" refers to a classification based on three types [of objects], not to a classification based on the truths (*satya*) themselves.

Therefore, the treatise states that among those [afflictions] to be abandoned, there are three types: one that pertains to only one category, one that pertains to two, and one that pertains to four categories.

Regarding the statement that "the view of extremes arises based on the view of a self-entity": it means that one first clings to a self, and subsequently clings to [that self] as being either annihilated or eternal. Regarding the statement that "the clinging to views arises based on the clinging to precepts and observances":
it means that one reckons what is not a cause to be a cause and clings to it as supreme. Regarding the statement that "false view arises based on doubt": it is due to...

Because doubt does not resolve itself and gives rise to false views, [the three poisons] follow the three [objects] and revolve around them; since the objects followed are stated, the followers themselves are thereby revealed.
Thus, those who fear liberation think, "I shall attain nirvāṇa through my own annihilation," and thus do not wish to set out upon the Path.
Those who are hesitant mean that they doubt whether right view is the Path or not. Therefore, while the Buddha specifically mentions these three, he also implicitly reveals the others.
Therefore, six are not mentioned.

Regarding the term "fettering to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*): because these fetters do not transcend the higher realms and instead conduce to the benefit of the higher realms, they are called "fetters conducive to the higher realms.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The substance of these five kinds consists of eight entities, because three—restlessness (*auddhatya*) and so forth—are distinct in the two realms."

Because the two upper realms are each divided into six, [the fetters] are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Once the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have been abandoned, those [fetters] then manifest;
even when views have not yet been abandoned, they can still serve as a basis for causing one to be reborn in the lower realm. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:

Why are only those abandoned through cultivation established as the "fetters conducive to the higher realms" (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)? Answer: That which causes one to proceed toward birth in the higher [realms] is called "conducive to the higher. The fetters abandoned through views do not [function in this way].

Furthermore, because they cause one to fall back to the lower realms, they are not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). Moreover, that which is practiced by those "above" is called conducive to the higher;
these "those above" are the noble ones (*ārya*), not ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Since the fetters abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) arise only in ordinary worldlings, they are not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms. However, among the noble ones, only those fetters arising in non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are established as such.
Following the inquiry into the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), this discussion arises:

Why are the various fetters produced by those who have attained the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms? The answer is that "conducive to the higher" means tending toward rebirth in the upper [realms].

Since the various fetters produced by Stream-enterers and Once-returners also cause one to be born in the lower [realms], they are not established as fetters conducive to the higher realms. As for the statement that "the fault of craving is heavy," it refers to the Vātsīputrīyas.
Furthermore, craving causes distinctions among realms (*dhātu*), levels (*bhūmi*), and classes (*nikāya*).

Craving can increase all afflictions (*kleśa*), and since craving and the objects of craving are said to have many faults, they are established as two fetters (*saṃyojana*) based on the distinction of realms.
Since such [faults] do not exist in the three states such as restlessness (*auddhatya*) and so forth in the two higher realms, these two realms are combined and established as one.
Regarding the statement that there are three types of bonds (*bandhana*): they are called "bonds" because they fetter sentient beings.

They are established as three types based on differences in their associated feelings (*vedanā*), and because they increase (*anuśerate*) in relation to one's own continuum (*sva-santati*) through the objects of perception (*ālambana*), mental association (*samprayoga*), and coexistence (*sahabhū*). As for the continua of others, they function solely as objects of perception. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Bonds have the sense of obstructing progress toward freedom from defilement (*vairāgya*); although there is no difference between the characteristics of 'fetters' (*saṃyojana*) and 'bonds,' [they are distinguished by their functions]."

Distinguishing them, it is taught according to the *Mātṛkā* that there are three bonds (*bandhana*). The remaining categories of fetters (*saṃyojana*) are subsumed within these three because their types are identical:

the five views, doubt, and delusion are of the same type as the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*); the two fetters of pride (*māna*) and greed (*lobha*) are of the same type as the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*);

and [the remaining fetters] are of the same type as the fetter of malice (*vyāpāda*). Furthermore, the Buddha specifically taught these coarse characteristics of the afflictions for those whose wisdom is inferior.
Therefore, only three bonds (*bandhana*) are taught. Regarding the statement that "craving increases in accordance with pleasant feeling" (*sukhāyām vedanāyām rāga-anuśete*), the *Nyāya* states:

"To a small extent, [craving] also increases in accordance with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, with one's own suffering, with the suffering of others, and with the pleasure of others; hatred and delusion should be understood accordingly.

Thus, the Blessed One, relying on the principle of the majority of cases, established the three bonds in accordance with the three feelings. Furthermore, it is only their active manifestation (*samudācāra*) that is designated as such.
If the bonds were different from this, they would all become threefold; consequently, one would be absolutely prevented from proceeding toward the state free from defilement (*vairāgya*).

Regarding the statement "conforming to the root afflictions" (*mūlakleśa*) and "conforming to the secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*): these refer exclusively to the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) and so forth, which are designated as "secondary.
According to the treatise, however, the root afflictions are also called "secondary afflictions" because they all conform to the mind and act as causes of disturbance. Furthermore...

Because these other various afflictions (*kleśa*) arise as secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) subsumed within the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), they are also called "secondary afflictions" since they are not fundamental.
Regarding the two explanations in the treatise, only the latter is accepted. As for the term "these others" (*ataḥ śeṣāḥ*):

it excludes the aforementioned [fundamental afflictions] and takes the remainder; according to the preceding explanation in the treatise, this term "these others" includes both the aforementioned and the rest. Furthermore, this is the interpretation of the former [section].

That is to say, the mind is the "concomitant" (anuśaya) and the secondary afflictions are the "concomitants"; likewise, the root afflictions are the "concomitants" and the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and stains are the "concomitants.

Regarding the term "entanglement," the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "These ten kinds of entanglements bind sentient beings and place them within the prison of birth and death; therefore, they are called 'entanglements' (*paryavasthāna*)."
Because they act as the cause for the arising of various unwholesome deeds that lead one toward the miserable realms (durgati), they are called "entanglements" (paryavasthāna).
This treatise further states that the root afflictions (mūlakleśa) are also called entanglements.

Regarding the statement in the Sūtra that the entanglement of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*) serves as a condition, the phrase "contrary to the skillful giving of wealth and Dharma" means that because of stinginess (*mātsarya*), one is unable to skillfully give away wealth and the Dharma; therefore, it is called "contrary. It says:

"Sleep" (*middha*) refers to that which causes the mind to become dull and withdrawn. Tan-shan says: "This means that while the six consciousnesses manifest during the waking state, sleep arises only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

because the other five do not function, it is termed 'withdrawn' (*saṃkṣepa*). Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that 'dullness' (*mūḍha*) distinguishes it from being in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and 'withdrawn' distinguishes it from the time of awakening.
Moreover, the *Nyāyapraveśa* states: 'It causes the mind to be dull and withdrawn; associated with torpor (*styāna*), it is unable to sustain the body.'"

Although the characteristic of *middha* (torpor) also includes dullness (*styāna*), it is not associated with *middha* itself; this statement is made because the present discussion concerns only the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments).
"Not accepting reasoned admonition" means not following wholesome counsel. "Resentment" (*upanāha*) refers to harboring a grudge; as the treatise states:
"It is the repeated reflection upon the object of anger that constitutes the binding of a grudge. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Resentment has the same characteristics as anger."
Regarding their distinction: anger (*krodha*) is like a fire on birch bark; its root is fierce and sharp, yet its residual force is weak. Resentment (*upanāha*) is like the heat in a winter room;
although its manifest characteristic is subtle, its residual force is strong. For this reason, some state the definition of resentment as follows:

"When anger has subsided, that which continues to arise and turbidifies the mind is called resentment. (Regarding "winter room," the *Chao shi* commentary states: "In the customs of the Western Regions, one values [heated] dwellings...")

Small defensive rooms are all constructed with brickwork, plastered on both the interior and exterior; they are cold even in winter. At the top of such a room, a hole is made through which a rope is passed to suspend a large iron pan, shaped like a *cau* (a griddle). This is tightly sealed at the bottom, and a fierce fire is lit beneath it until the intense flames fill the interior of the room.

Only after the heat has subsided and the floor has been swept clean can the offerings be brought into the room. It is as hot as a newly fired kiln; if one remains inside while the residual heat persists, one will break into a sweat and fall ill immediately.

Regarding "flattery" (*śāṭhya*), this refers to a crooked mind. The *Śāstra* states: "Because of this, one is unable to manifest oneself according to reality; one may either feign what is not so or deny what is."
To employ skillful means with the intent of causing another to develop a mistaken understanding—without explicitly stating one's deception—is what is termed "deceit" (*śāṭhya*).
According to the *Nyāya*, this is called "deceitful speech" because one first deliberates and devises such a means so that the other person subsequently develops a perverted cognition.

It is said to be a "concomitant outflow" (*niṣyanda*) of malice (*pratigha*) and the view of grasping at inferior things as superior (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because by clinging to what is inferior as being superior, one fails to accept reasoned admonition and instruction, thereby giving rise to it.
Regarding "deceit (*śāṭhya*) is the outflow of the five views": this means that wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are called "crooked" (*vaṅka*) because they resemble deceit and guile (*māyā*).

Thus, the *Abhidharma* states: "Those who harbor views are mostly deceitful and crooked. As for the statement regarding "deceit and crookedness," which refers to all wrong views, the section on the three types of abandonment and the three natures does not explain it.
Regarding the statement that "flattery and deceit exist only in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna," the treatise asks: how is it known that flattery and deceit exist in the Brahma-world?
It is because the Great Brahmā King concealed his true intentions and manifested deceptive signs to mislead the Bhikṣu Aśvajit.

Although these two have already been analyzed previously, they are discussed again here as their meaning is related. As for the phrase "the remaining secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) and so forth," this refers to the ten [secondary afflictions].
Among the six categories of afflictions, five have been distinguished as before; the remaining eleven are bound exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding those that arise solely on the mental level (*manobhūmi*), such as the abandonments by insight (*darśana-heya*) and so forth, there are three classes: first, those abandoned by insight; second, pride (*māna*) and sleepiness (*middha*);
and third, the autonomous secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Regarding the statement that greed is associated with joy and pleasure (*sukha*): this means it is associated with the feeling of pleasure when co-occurring with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), and associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) when co-occurring with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Hatred may be understood by analogy. Regarding the "first four feelings": if delusion (*moha*) occurs with the five sensory consciousnesses, it is associated with the feelings of pain (*duḥkha*) and pleasure;

if it occurs with the mental consciousness, it is associated with the feelings of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy. The neutral feeling (*upekṣā*) is distinguished according to the sequence [of the preceding]. Doubt is associated with the feeling of sorrow.

"Those who are 'responsive' (yogya) refers to those who harbor hesitation; at the time they seek definitive knowledge and are in a state of correct doubt, because they lack certainty regarding the object, they give rise to sorrowful speech.

Regarding the 'four [afflictions] such as the view of a self-body' (satkāyadṛṣṭi): since wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi) has already been clarified previously, only the four beginning with the view of a self-body are mentioned.

They are explained as operating through a mode of joy (prīti-carita), which does not apply to sorrow, because they exist only on the mental level (manobhūmi). This distinguishes them from the feeling of pleasure (sukha-vedanā) by way of their characteristics."

Regarding the statement that "at the time of the cessation of the continuity, one must abide in the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)," this means that the state in which afflictions (*kleśa*) subside is termed "cessation. As the treatise says:

"At the stage when the continuity is severed, because its momentum has exhausted, one necessarily abides in the feeling of equanimity; for within the feeling of equanimity, there is no contradiction with either joy or grief.
Regarding the statement that [afflictions] "pervade and correspond with their own consciousnesses throughout the higher realms," this refers to those existing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because sorrow and suffering involve the movement of afflicted mental states (*daurmanasya*), they do not occur in the higher realms;
because there is no movement of afflicted mental states there, consciousness in whichever stage it may be is associated with joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the statement that stinginess (*mātsarya*) is associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), the *Śāstra* says: "Because the characteristic of stinginess is extremely similar to greed (*lobha*), it exists only on the mental level (*manobhūmi*).
This indicates that it does not extend to the mode of activity of pleasure (*sukha*). Furthermore, it indicates that it does not extend to sorrow (*daurmanasya*). The *Xin lun* (New Treatise) states:

"There is a separate text which asserts that it must be associated with sorrow; one should investigate this. It means that when stinginess is attained, there is joy, but when it is not attained, there is sorrow. Thus, these four [types of attachment] are said to be associated with both sorrow and joy.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states that some masters claim that because deception (*māyā*) is an outflow (*niṣyanda*) of greed (*lobha*), it should only be associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and not said to be associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Furthermore, at the very moment of deceiving, one should not be dejected. Alternatively, they say deception is an outflow of delusion (*moha*).
As for those who claim it is associated with all [mental] equanimity (*upekṣā*), if it is predominant from the third dhyāna downward, it is as previously stated.
It is said that when the continuity [of consciousness] is severed, one relinquishes all associated factors of the four *dhyānas* and beyond;

whether they are flourishing or severed, all associated dharmas of the stages are relinquished because there is no longer any remaining sensation (*vedanā*). Furthermore, relinquishment (*tyāga*) and joy or sorrow (*prīti-duḥkha*) are universally associated with all six consciousnesses across the higher and lower stages without any obstruction, just as ignorance (*avidyā*) is universally associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is said to be "non-existent" [in its specific manifestation].

Regarding the statement that "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*) and "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*) extend to all five feelings: this is because these two are among the two great unwholesome universal mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Consequently, they are associated with all unwholesome states; since unwholesome states pervade the six consciousnesses and all five feelings, [these two factors] likewise do so.

As for "sloth" (*styāna*) and "restlessness" (*auddhatya*), because they are among the great afflictive universal mental factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*), they are associated with all defiled minds; all defiled minds are likewise [associated with them].

Because they pervade the six consciousnesses, the five feelings, and the upper and lower stages, it is said that the Buddha taught there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). "Hindrance" has the meaning of covering and obstructing;

the *Vibhāṣā* states that bearing a burden is the meaning of "hindrance," while the *Nyāyānusāra* further states that they are called "hindrances" because they obstruct the Noble Path and the preparatory practices for the Noble Path. This treatise will explain this further below.
This refers to the premonitory signs of sleep that obscure the five aggregates; "displeasure" (*anabhirati*) is explained as a lack of joy;
"sighing" (*vijṛmbhikā*) arises from exhaustion caused by strenuous activity and can give rise to yawning;

"uneven eating" (*viṣamabhojana*) means eating in excess, or when any of the [objects of sense—]smell, taste, or touch—are disproportionately increased, which causes the body and mind of the eater to become dull and obscured. Body and mind...

"Dullness" (*mūḍha*) means that by the power of those [states], the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is unable to apprehend its object clearly; this is called "dullness. "Weakness" (*hīna*) means that the power of the apprehending subject is feeble;

this is called "weakness. These two are "non-nutriments" (*anāhāra*) because the previously mentioned perception of light (*āloka-saṃjñā*), which is the antidote to lethargy (*styāna*), does not provide them with any benefit;
thus they are called non-nutriments. Regarding "thoughts of immortality" (*amara-vitarka*), it refers to, for example, reflecting: "Since I have not yet died, I shall do such-and-such."
Regarding such activities, what joy can there be in not recollecting one's own death? As for "recollecting things experienced," the treatise states:

"Recollecting various things experienced in the past, such as play, laughter, pleasure, and service—since these phenomena cause the mind that recollects them to become distracted, they give rise to restlessness (*auddhatya*);
and because the mind is not restrained, they lead to remorse (*kaukṛtya*). This is according to the correct [explanation].

The principle is even clearer regarding the objects (*āhāra*) of the three hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), such as greed, and their respective remedies (*pratipakṣa*). First, the object of the hindrance of greed (*rāga-nīvaraṇa*) consists of attractive things;

its remedy is the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*). The object of the hindrance of anger (*pratigha-nīvaraṇa*) consists of repulsive things; its remedy is the roots of goodness consisting of loving-kindness (*maitrī-kuśalamūla*).

The object of the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) consists of phenomena belonging to the three periods of time. As the Sūtra says: "Regarding the past, one gives rise to doubt; its remedy is the ability to perceive according to reality (*yathābhūta*)."

Regarding the statement that "observing the nature of conditions and dependent origination necessarily obstructs concentration (*samādhi*), it should logically follow that wisdom (*prajñā*) is obstructed first":

this is because the Sarvāstivāda school, following the sequence of the *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances), states that torpor and drowsiness (*styāna-middha*) obstruct wisdom and are therefore mentioned first. However, the intention of the author of the treatise is as follows:

since he previously stated that restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) obstruct concentration, and among those things obstructed, wisdom is primary; furthermore, the very essence of what constitutes an obstruction also causes concentration to be placed first. Thus says the treatise.

If one explains the intent of the sūtra in this way, then according to reason, restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) should logically be mentioned before lethargy and sleep (*styāna-middha*), because wisdom necessarily arises based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and thus the hindrance to concentration should likewise precede the hindrance to wisdom.
