(This passage, following the same logic, remains a counter-objection directed at the Sarvāstivāda.
Based on such reasoning, other masters state: "Among these five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), lethargy-sleep and restlessness-remorse respectively obstruct concentration."
Regarding the aggregate of wisdom, this sutra states: "One who cultivates meditative concentration (samādhi) fears lethargy and sleep;

one who cultivates the discernment of dharmas (dharmapravicaya) fears restlessness and remorse. This is a direct explanation of the sutra's intent. Since restlessness and remorse are not placed first [in the sequence], it is clear that lethargy and sleep together obstruct concentration.
Because of the dullness of lethargy, one cannot attain concentration; because of the agitation of restlessness and remorse, one cannot attain wisdom.
The first verse explains the cause for severing delusions; following the previous question and answer, this verse now provides the formal analysis. Within the question, there are two parts:

first, the question regarding the nine types of delusions that take the upper realms as their object; second, the question regarding the delusions that repeatedly take the lower realms’ cessation and path as their objects.

As for the statement, "If one has severed [delusions], one will not know the suffering and origin of the upper realms," this means that although the nine types of delusions taking the upper realms as their object take the objects of the upper realms as their referents, they are nonetheless [delusions] directed toward those realms themselves.

When the *dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma) regarding the truths of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-satya* and *samudaya-satya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) eliminates its objects, these objects—namely the suffering and origin of the higher realms—are only known by the subsequent *anvaya-kṣānti* (receptivity to the subsequent [truths]).
Therefore, at the time of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), those objects are as yet unknown, because the *anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti* has not yet arisen.

As for the statement regarding the abandonment of the cessation and the path when they have outflows (*sāsrava*) as their objects, this explains the abandonment of the views regarding cessation and the path.

The afflictions that take lower greed and so forth as their objects are abandoned, yet one does not know those objects [of the afflictions] (the two preceding categories both refer to abandoning afflictions while remaining unaware of their objects).

As for the statement "because they have already been abandoned, they are not abandoned," this means that when the preceding *dharmajñānakṣānti* arose, [the afflictions] were already abandoned; because *anvayajñāna* has now arisen, they are no longer abandoned.
Furthermore, it is said that the essence of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

Since all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena have the accumulation (*samudaya*) of suffering as their cause, they are the fruit of accumulation and are thus suffering itself. Since these wrong views and so forth are contaminated, their essence is suffering and accumulation.
When the knowledge of suffering and accumulation arises, one clearly knows suffering and accumulation; it is therefore evident that one has already known those wrong views and so forth.
If it is said that those wrong views and so forth are not abandoned, then one should likewise say that those cravings and so forth are not abandoned.

It is an error to say that [the afflictions] such as wrong view are not abandoned; for among these two categories, the former have already been abandoned and thus are not [further] abandoned, while the latter have not yet been abandoned and thus are not [yet] abandoned.

To say that they are not abandoned because it is not necessary to fully comprehend their objects is incorrect, for there are cases where afflictions are abandoned even when their objects are not clearly understood, due to other causes.
Since the meaning of the four causes will now be explained, this preliminary discussion is presented first.

Question and Answer, Part One: Because they are abandoned through the thorough knowledge of their objects, the delusions are severed across two categories: first, those delusions within one’s own realm that take suffering and its origin as their objects;
second, those delusions that take the untainted (anāsrava) truths of cessation and the path as their objects.

Although craving, hatred, pride, and so forth regarding suffering and its origin do not arise from a direct delusion regarding the principles of the Truths themselves, because their objective referents are suffering and its origin, the Patience toward Suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) arises taking suffering as its object.

Because the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) has already been abandoned, although there are two meanings, it is said that [abandonment] occurs through the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of its objects; thus, it is also abandoned because [the Truth of Origination] is an object of thorough knowledge.

Furthermore, the statement regarding this Truth of Suffering and Origination as having "conditions within one's own realm" (*sva-dhātu-ālambana*) refers exclusively to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Even if they have conditions in other realms or other stages (*bhūmi*)—namely, the Form and Formless Realms—they are also abandoned because they are objects of thorough knowledge.
This is because when the Patience of the Subsequent Knowledge of Suffering and Origination (*duḥkha-samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises, one thoroughly knows the two upper realms.

Therefore, when it is said that wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth take cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects, this refers generally to the untainted objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path within the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Regarding the statement that "afflictions taking their own realm as an object" and "afflictions taking another realm as an object":

since afflictions taking their own realm as an object take the suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) of their own realm as their objects, while afflictions taking another realm as an object—though they take the objects of a higher realm—have as their essential nature the suffering and origin of this very realm, [they are thus categorized].
Regarding the afflictions that have other realms as their objects (*ālambana*), since they take the higher realms as their object, they do not take the afflictions of their own realm as their object.

As for the statement that when the afflictions taking one’s own realm as their object are abandoned, [the others] are abandoned accordingly: this is because the afflictions taking other realms as their object depend upon the power of the afflictions taking one’s own realm as their object to be able to take the higher realms as their object.
It is like a weak person leaning against a pillar and looking upward; if the pillar breaks, he falls along with it.

Therefore, [the sequence hereafter is reversed]. As for the statement that "if the object (*ālambana*) is severed, that which arises in dependence upon it is also severed accordingly," the *Nyāyānusāra* says:
"It is like a weak person walking with the aid of a staff; when the staff breaks, he falls down along with it. [The sequence here is forward. Question:
When various knowledges (*jñāna*) arise and all afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed, for what reason do you specifically state that either the object is severed or the subject (*ālambaka*) is severed?

The reasoned answer is as follows: Although it is indeed the case that both [the afflictions of the desire realm and those of the higher realms] are abandoned at that time, because there are superior and inferior among those to be abandoned, when the superior are abandoned, the inferior are also abandoned accordingly.

This is because the arising of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is directed specifically toward the enemy [of the afflictions], exerting effort for that purpose; thus, they are called "superior," while the remainder are called "inferior.
The clear realization (*abhisamaya*) that arises with respect to the suffering and origin [truths] of the desire realm, regarding what is to be abandoned by itself—

Among the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth, those with objects within their own realm (*svadhātu-ālambana*) are the primary adversaries; the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) arising from the paths of cessation and cultivation acts as the antidote to them.

Among the afflictions to be abandoned by one’s own [realization], those with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) are the primary adversaries; because these are abandoned through superior means, the inferior ones are abandoned accordingly.
Regarding the statement that "afflictions of the realm of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are abandoned by their antidotes," the *Nyāyānusāra* raises an objection: "Is it not the case that all..."

When the afflictions to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are abandoned, they are also abandoned through the arising of the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), because when the counteractive path for a particular category arises, all the afflictions within that category are abandoned;

this is indeed the logical reality. However, in this context, the statement is made in order to demonstrate that there are no afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across the three realms that are not abandoned by the nine grades of the path, and thus to establish the certainty of the counteractive path.
It is with reference to the afflictions abandoned by insight that this [previous] statement was spoken.
Among those [afflictions] to be abandoned, only the antidotes for the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) are determinate, as has already been explained [above]. Furthermore, it is said:

"Alternatively, [the term 'determinate'] refers to abandonment through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in its specific sense, while [abandonment] through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is considered in its general sense."

Regarding the statement that the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*), in reality it only abandons the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions and does not abandon the essence of the afflictions themselves;

the present mention of "afflictions" is spoken of in terms of their general characteristics. Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The first is the counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path that directly and immediately abandons the acquisitions of all afflictions—namely, the path of uninterrupted transition.
The 'counteragent of distant separation' (*dūribhāva-pratipakṣa*) refers to the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*). According to this treatise, there are further [categories].

Other masters say that it also pertains to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because just as that [path] can cause the abandoned afflictions to become further removed, so too does this [path] arise from a profound sense of revulsion toward the truths of suffering and origin.
Regarding the statement, "If there is a path that perceives the faults of this realm and gives rise to a profound sense of revulsion," this sequence is the explanation of the *Vibhāṣā* masters;
the Master of the Treatise [Vasubandhu], however, maintains that revulsion occurs [only] at this [stage].

Since the latter point is not correct, the former must be revised; thus, the Master [Vasubandhu] holds this view. If one wishes to explain these remedies (*pratipakṣa*) correctly according to the actual principle, they should follow this sequence:
first, the remedy of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) arising by taking suffering and its origin as objects;

the remaining three follow in order. Furthermore, these four types constitute the fundamental doctrine of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*; according to the seventeenth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there is further...
The antidote of abandonment is like the abandonment of the precepts and so forth.
As for the statement that one cannot cause [the defilements] to be separated from their associated dharmas, it is because their nature as companions is not severed; thus the *Mahāvibhāṣā* says this.

Herein, it is taught that while the various latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can be abandoned with respect to their objects (*ālambana*), they cannot be abandoned with respect to their associations (*saṃprayoga*); this is based on the fact that they are said to "exist" in relation to one's own mind.

The meaning of "sleeping" (*middha*) is explained in terms of non-arising, rather than in terms of "increasing" (*anuśayana*), because that which increases can be abandoned simultaneously. As for the statement, "it causes [the defilement] not to arise again with respect to its object," the Master [Vasubandhu] raises an objection: "While it may be logically possible to say that future defilements are abandoned—since one can prevent them from arising again toward their objects—how can past defilements be said to be abandoned? Regarding the Sarvāstivāda position on the abandonment [of defilements], it is established that by the power of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), the defilements within one's own continuum are brought to abandonment.

Because they have been abandoned, past and future [defilements] lack the power to increase [their influence] (*anuśayana*) with respect to their objects; thus, they cannot bind those objective spheres.
Consequently, the defilements within the continua of others, as well as all matter (*rūpa*) and non-defiled phenomena, are not bound.
It is also called "severed" because it is not bound by the afflictions within one's own continuum.

To say that the four great elements are "distant in name and characteristic" means that although earth, water, and so forth arise together in a single aggregate and are extremely close to one another,
they are called "distant" because their characteristics differ— just as in the case of those who uphold and those who violate the precepts, even though they both reside within the same body.
Although they are situated extremely close together and share the same characteristic of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), they are not distant;

yet, because the counteractive factors (*pratipakṣa*) and the factors to be countered (*vipakṣa*) differ, they are also said to be distant, like the eastern and western oceans. Although these are within the same world-system and share the same characteristic of being water, they are not distant;
nor are they distant because they are both present; yet, because their locations—the east and west—are separated, they are called distant.

Regarding "distance in place," such as the past and future, that which is called "distance in time" refers to cases where, although both are established upon all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as their characteristics, they are not distant in terms of spatial location nor are they separated by physical barriers;
nevertheless, because they are separated by time, they are also termed "distant. This is the position of the Vaibhāṣikas.

Furthermore, because the natures of the [past and future] worlds differ from the present world, they receive the name "distant. The Master [Vasubandhu], having finished his critique regarding the present world, now proceeds to challenge this [notion of temporal distance].

He then provides his own explanation: "According to correct reasoning, one should say that the past and future are called 'distant' because they are devoid of the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon;
for the future has not yet acquired the intrinsic characteristic of the phenomenon, while the past has already relinquished the intrinsic characteristic of the phenomenon."
The statement that "if one does not regress further, there will be no subsequent re-severing of afflictions" is based on the principle that if there is regression, one must sever them again;
thus it says "non-regression. This accords with the traditional interpretation.

If this were so, even for one who regresses from the fruit, since the afflictions previously abandoned have already ceased to exist, how could they constitute a "re-severing"? According to the traditional view, this is stated in terms of the general category [of afflictions].

Regarding the statement "re-cutting" (*punar-viccheda*), my detailed examination now suggests that whether one has regressed or not, there is no such thing as "re-cutting" after which [the defilement] arises again, for it would then not be the same as the prior affliction.
Thus, when speaking of the "superior advancement" (*viśeṣa-gati*) of the Path, the claim that a "superior acquisition" (*viśiṣṭa-prāpti*) arises repeatedly is addressed by the *Śāstra*, which says:

"Although there is no principle of gradual superior advancement for the disjunction (*visamyoga*) already obtained, at the time the Path advances, it is possible for that superior acquisition to arise repeatedly. (The commentary explains: "That which is obtained...")

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be discussed in terms of superiority or inferiority; however, the Path (*mārga*) possesses the principle of progressive advancement because its nature is determined according to the attainment of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*). Thus, the superiority or inferiority of the attainment arises in accordance with the Path that realizes it.
Regarding the expression "arising through counteraction" (*pratipakṣa-ja*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states that this term refers to two meanings:

if it refers to abiding in that which can realize disjunction, it denotes the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); if it refers to abiding in that which actually realizes disjunction, it denotes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

The abandonment of those five categories constitutes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). Furthermore, although there is a subsequent fruit that arises from its antidote, because one category is missing, it is said to be attained at the same time as the five [moments];
this refers to the attainment of the fruit within the four [stages], excluding the first two. Regarding the statement that among the four attainments of the fruit, the first three are excluded:

this refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), who attains the second fruit only after having abandoned seven or eight categories of afflictions, thus excluding the first two times of fruit-attainment. As for the exclusion of the first three among the four attainments of the fruit, this refers to the non-returner.

Because a person is currently abandoning the afflictions of the upper realms to be abandoned by cultivation, the three [attainments] resulting from the acquisition of the fruit are excluded. Furthermore, the treatise states:

"Thus, this is explained according to the principle of possibility; for those of sharp faculties, in each of the preceding stages, the attainment resulting from the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is excluded.
Moreover, for those who enter the noble path by means of leaping over [stages], there is accordingly the exclusion of the attainment of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and so forth."

Regarding the statement that untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*), there is one opinion in the *Mahāvibhāṣā* that it also applies to tainted [knowledge], meaning that what is extremely clear through hearing, reflection, and cultivation is also called "thorough knowledge," with the exception of conventional knowledge associated with attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa-manasikāra*).

Regarding the expression of applying the name of the cause to the effect: it is as when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are called "karma," because they are the fruit of karma. This is asked in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

If it is said that what is abandoned by cultivation is the fruit of knowledge (*jñāna*) and can thus be called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*), then how can what is abandoned by seeing be called "thorough knowledge" when it is the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*)?

The commentator (*vibhāṣā-vādin*) says: One should state it thus—because patience is an attendant of knowledge, the name "knowledge" is applied to what is accomplished by patience, just as the deeds performed by a minister are also called the deeds of the king.
Furthermore, regarding the establishment of a single thorough knowledge for the abandonment of both suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*): it is because...
Regarding these two truths, because the pervasive afflictions mutually bind one another, it is only by extinguishing both causes that universal knowledge (*parijñā*) is attained;

therefore, they are collectively established as a single truth of cessation and a single truth of the path. Since the causes belonging to other realms have already been extinguished, one attains universal knowledge of each respective truth through mere cognition.

The same applies to the higher realms. As for the statement that the collective [attainment] is called the "universal knowledge of the exhaustion of the lower-tier fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*): [it refers to this].

This refers to the statement at this time that the six distinct names for the previously mentioned "vision of the truths" constitute the single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Question: Why is it not called the "thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of sensual desire" (*kāmarāga-parijñā*), but rather the "thorough knowledge of the five lower fetters"?

Answer: Because at that time, one transcends the realm (*dhātu-vyatikrama*) and attains the fruit (*phala-prāpti*); thus, the thorough knowledges of the origin (*samudaya-parijñā*) and the thorough knowledges of the phenomena of the origin (*samudaya-dharma-parijñā*) are established together with the preceding [knowledge].

Therefore, one asks: since the three [fetters] among the five lower-tier fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*), such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), have already been abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), how can it now be said that there is a "full knowledge" (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of all five lower-tier fetters? The answer is:

although the first three are indeed abandoned through the path of seeing, it is only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that greed and hatred are abandoned; because at this time all five fetters are exhausted, the general name is taken to establish the designation of "full knowledge."

Because this [knowledge] is universally known and was established previously, and because it takes the three preceding realms and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its objects during the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there is no fault.

Furthermore, although delusion (*moha*) and conceit (*māna*) are also abandoned at this time, they are not included among the five fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore, while their names are mentioned, they are not explicitly designated.

It is for this reason that many people become confused regarding the statement that the abandonment of afflictions in the form realm reaches the exhaustion of craving for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-tṛṣṇā*).

At that time, the "knowledge of non-aggregation" (*asaṃgraha-parijñā*) takes as its essence the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state resulting from the abandonment through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);

therefore, it is called the "knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters" (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya-parijñā*). This is because at that moment, one transcends the realms and attains the fruit, thereby aggregating the knowledges. As for the sequence:

because it takes as its essence the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all [defilements] of the three realms, it is called the "knowledge of the exhaustion of all fetters. Regarding the phrase "form and formless": [it refers to the abandonment of the form and formless realms].

The statement that "the cultivation of afflictions differs between the two realms" means that while the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are abandoned separately in each stage (*bhūmi*), they are nonetheless collectively referred to as being in "two realms" when contrasted with the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), which are abandoned simultaneously across all three realms.
Thus, although the afflictions of cultivation are abandoned stage by stage, they are spoken of generally as belonging to the two realms in relation to the afflictions of view.

Next, the results are explained in total as six pairs. Regarding the statement that "the six kinds of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) are obtained through patience (*kṣānti*)," this means that within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), patience serves as the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) for abandoning the afflictions;

because one attains thorough knowledge upon their abandonment, they are called the fruits of patience. Regarding the three kinds of thorough knowledge obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), these are:

the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*), and the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-kṣaya*). These are the three types.
Since thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is realized through the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the treatise further asks:
"Why is the fruit of patience (*kṣānti*) called thorough knowledge? The answer is: because patience is an attendant of wisdom (*jñāna*), and because patience and wisdom share the same fruit.

Regarding the statement that the fundamental stages cannot eliminate the afflictions of the desire realm, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā* school, this is because the higher paths do not sever the defilements of the lower realms, whereas the lower [paths] can sever those of the higher.

The principle that the fundamental dhyānas cannot serve as remedies for the desire realm is likewise the same here. Therefore, it is said that the four thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are not [attained] through the fundamental [dhyānas];
these consist of three from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the desire realm and one from the five fetters bound to the lower realms (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

This is because they are fruits obtained solely through the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration. As for the phrase "induced by a distinct path," this refers to the cultivation of the four dharmas of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) within the fundamental [dhyānas].

Because it reaches the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) which is the antidote that severs [the afflictions], it is called the "distinct path" (viśeṣa-mārga). Some say it is called "distinct" in contrast to the contaminated (sāsrava).

Regarding those who do not cultivate the five lower-tier fetters (pañca-avara-bhāgīya), it is taught that the path for severing delusions arises based on the fundamental dhyānas; such a person necessarily attains the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin). Among those abiding in the stage of the candidate for Non-returner, they are in the position of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga);

when they reach the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), they abide in the fruit rather than the candidate stage. Regarding the cultivation of the faculties (indriya) for severing [delusions] in the desire realm: *Note: The original text contains technical terminology related to the Abhidharma system of the paths of seeing and cultivation, the distinction between the candidate (pratipannaka) and the fruit-dweller (phalastha), and the role of the fundamental dhyānas in the process of severing afflictions.*

Fundamentally, there is no one capable of abandoning the nine grades [of afflictions] through the path of desire, because these are subsumed under the paths of approach for the second and third fruits.
Furthermore, for those non-returners who practice "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*), it is impossible for them to cultivate the antidote that abandons those [afflictions].

As for the statement that the contaminated path arises from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space, it is only this preparatory stage that can abandon the defilements of the fourth dhyāna and attain the full knowledge (*parijñā*) of the exhaustion of craving for the form realm; there is no such attainment based on the preparatory stages of the higher [formless] realms.

One is able to become detached from the defilements of this stage. Regarding the statement that [the paths] excluding those of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) belong to the Formless Realm and that only the three lower stages possess the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) capable of detaching one from the Peak of Existence:
this is because the stage of the Peak of Existence lacks the untainted path and thus lacks the fruit of universal knowledge (*parijñā-phala*); therefore, it must be excluded.

Regarding the statement that there are two types of conventional fruits (*sāṃvṛta-phala*): this refers to the fact that conventional wisdom (*sāṃvṛta-jñāna*) cannot specifically sever the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) pertaining to the Desire and Form Realms.

One cannot attain the six fruits of the path of seeing because the outflows (*āsrava*) are not abandoned; nor can one attain them in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as all fetters (*saṃyojana*) have not been exhausted there.

Furthermore, the six modes of cultivation (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*) are unable to sever the afflictions of the desire and form realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation. Therefore, one attains two types of universal knowledge (*parijñā*): the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya*) and the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*).

As for the statement that the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) can sever the afflictions of the three realms to be abandoned through cultivation, this is because the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) and the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) perform this function through cultivation.

Within the stages of the Path (*mārga-avasthā*), because [the subsequent knowledge] is simultaneously able to counteract the higher [defilements of the] form and formless realms, it does not counteract the afflictions of the Path of Seeing;

therefore, it lacks the fruit of the Patiences (*kṣānti*) and possesses the fruit of the six Subsequent Knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*). Furthermore, because Subsequent Knowledge does not counteract the desire realm, it also excludes one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely the thorough knowledge of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Regarding the phrase "of the same category" (*samāna-jātīya*): although Patience and Knowledge differ, they are both "Dharma" [knowledges]; thus, Subsequent Knowledge is likewise [of the same category].

In the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are two further pairs [of fruits] not mentioned in this treatise: first, the fruits of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); second, the fruits of the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
These are not stated here because they are redundant.

As for the question, "Why is a separate 'thorough knowledge' (*parijñā*) not established for each individual abandonment?"—the intent of the question is: what is the purpose of the eight truths of the path of seeing?

Question: Regarding the eighty-one categories of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), why is "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) not established for each individual category that is abandoned, but rather established only with respect to the nine stages?

Answer: It is not said that complete knowledge is established according to the quantity of the objects of bondage (*bandhana-vastu*). One who establishes complete knowledge must do so by way of the fullness of conditions (*pratyaya-sampad*).

Since one intends to clarify those conditions, the question is first raised. To say that one "attains" the untainted cessation through deliberation (*anāsrava-pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) refers to the time of the patience and knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna-kṣānti-jñāna*).
This [category] distinguishes it from the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the five classes of afflictions (*kleśa*), they do not collectively constitute a single [unit].

For instance, at the time of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*), one abandons the first class of afflictions pertaining to the realm of suffering. The reason this condition is required is to manifest the characteristic of permanent abandonment.

Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Alternatively, although the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the remaining [afflictions] may arise upon their abandonment, it has not yet become firm and solid—the very head of saṃsāra."

Regarding the statement that although the defilements of the eighth stage have been repeatedly abandoned, they have not yet been eliminated, and thus one falls back into the hells of the evil destinies:

as for the "two causes," one interpretation follows the chapter [of the *Abhidharmakośa*], while the new commentary states: those belonging to the same category and the same grade are called "self-causes" (*svahetu*);

those belonging to other grades within the same category, as well as all those belonging to other categories, are called "other-causes" (*parahetu*). This is because when the noble ones abandon the afflictions of the view-division (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), the nine grades are abandoned simultaneously as a single grade. If...
When one abandons [the afflictions] of one's own category (*nikāya*) and sub-category (*prakāra*), one abandons those of other categories within the same category;
it is not by means of other categories that full knowledge (*parijñā*) is achieved, but rather it is not achieved by means of other categories alone.

Regarding what is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), full knowledge is not achieved by means of other categories, but rather it is not achieved by means of other categories alone, because one must first abandon the causes belonging to other categories.

The *Vibhāṣā* states that for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), another category [of afflictions] serves as a single cause, while for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), another grade [of afflictions] serves as a single cause.

Regarding the statement that the other three categories take suffering (*duḥkha*) and origination (*samudaya*) as their universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*): this means that for the three categories of the path of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path [of cultivation], there are no universal afflictions;

they take only the universal afflictions of the two categories of suffering and origination as their causes. Regarding the statement "ordinary beings... until the deficiency": [this refers to the fact that ordinary beings lack the path of seeing].

Regarding the other two conditions: this refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who, though they can indeed aspire to the higher realms and loathe the lower ones to sever all afflictions, are unable to attain the untainted acquisition of abandonment (*anāsrava-prahāṇa-prāpti*).
Furthermore, they lack the untainted acquisition of abandonment and are deficient in [the abandonment of] the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

As for the statement that "the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*) is either present," it is because this patience remains conjoined with the acquisition of doubt (*vicikitsā-prāpti*) and has not yet attained liberation; therefore, it is not termed "deficient. Thus it is said.
"Non-accomplishment" refers to this power of patience (*kṣānti*): it merely causes the acquisition of delusions (*kleśa-prāpti*) to decline so that they do not project future results;

thus it is termed "abandonment. However, as long as it remains in the present, coexisting with the patience itself, it is still termed "accomplished. It is only upon reaching the stage of knowledge (*jñāna*) that one is finally able to separate from the body [of the afflictions], and is therefore termed "non-accomplished.
Regarding those who attain through leaping (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), during the fourth and fifth moments of mind, both causes [are present].

At the stage of the knowledge of the dharma of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nirodha-dharmajñāna*), one attains the untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*); at the stage of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*), the three conditions for the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) are deficient.

Since these are now complete, why is "complete knowledge" (*parijñā*) not established? The answer is: the establishment of complete knowledge is explained according to the method of gradual progression (*ānupūrvika*).

For those who practice by leaping over stages (*vyutkrāntaka*), the status of complete knowledge is established only when they reach the position of complete knowledge according to that gradual sequence; it is not established in the preceding positions.
Although the three conditions are present, [the path] is still not established. Regarding the further mention of "transcending the realm" (*dhātu-saṃkrānti*):

one asks why the three conditions for the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are not established as transcending the realm, while they are independently established for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The traditional explanation states:

although the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) have been abandoned, one is still bound by the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) and has not yet transcended the realm; therefore, if the condition of transcending the realm were established at the stage of seeing, it would be untenable.

Therefore, while only three conditions [are established] for the *miśra-citta* (mixed mind), that master establishes four conditions for the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and five conditions for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Now, speaking generally of "five causes," this refers to those factors such as the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) of mind and mental states which, though not of the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*), can serve as causes;
however, they cannot be said to be "bound" (*saṃyukta*). This is because of the difference between broad and narrow [definitions]; thus, he excludes them.
This treatise does not establish [this category] separately because, at the time when both causes are extinguished, the function of being freed from both fetters is not distinct;
therefore, it is not established separately. Thus the treatise says: "Even though there are differences in meaning, they are not explained separately. Furthermore, the treatise says:

"Although all transcendences of realms involve the extinction of both causes, the extinction of both causes does not necessarily mean one has transcended the realm; therefore, [the extinction of both causes] is [treated as a distinct category]."

Externally, a separate condition for transcending realms (*dhātusamatikramaṇa-pratyaya*) has been established; however, the universal knowledge (*parijñā*) that extinguishes the dual causes of the three stages has not yet been established. (The commentary explains:

because the extinction of the dual causes bound by both [desire and form] must necessarily be identical, they are combined into one "transcending-realm dual cause"; yet, since their meanings differ, although the defilements of the three lower stages—desire, form, and formlessness—are extinguished by the dual cause, the realm has not yet been transcended.)
Regarding the statement that "only one [complete knowledge] is established at the stage of the subsequent-knowledge-tolerance (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) regarding the origin," the question asks:

In the previous section on the conditions for attainment, it was stated that upon reaching the stage of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding the origin, three conditions are fulfilled and one complete knowledge is attained. Why, then, in this present section, is it said that even upon reaching the subsequent-knowledge-tolerance regarding the origin, only one is established?

The answer is: The previous explanation was based on the principle of the "attainment of complete knowledge" (*parijñā-prāpti*), according to which the dharma-knowledge itself actually attains it. This present explanation, however, is based on the "person's accomplishment" (*pudgala-sampadana*), and although...

Since those [knowledges] of the preceding stage have already been attained, and because one attains only one more at the time of the subsequent *anvaya-kṣānti*, they are subsumed within the stage of *dharma-jñāna*.
The statement that "six are accomplished through cultivation" means that at this time, the *parijñās* (full knowledges) are not yet accumulated, and thus six are established.
As for the question regarding the previous statement that six *parijñās* are attained in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it refers to the sixth *parijñā*.

Although this is a path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because it is obtained as the fruit of "patience" (*kṣānti*) through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is categorized under the path of seeing.

Now, in this context, the discussion is restricted to the person's attainment at a specific time; since this refers to the stage of "subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayajñāna*), it is subsumed under the path of cultivation.

Regarding the statement "having completely abandoned the defilements of desire up to becoming one," there are two types of persons here: first, those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); second, those who have regressed from the abandonment of the defilements of the form realm.

In total, only one [complete knowledge] is established because it is the collective complete knowledge (*saṃgraha-parijñā*); thus, the preceding six are not established. Two types of complete knowledge are established. In total, there are three categories:

first, those who gradually abandon the defilements of the form realm; second, those who, having previously abandoned craving for the form realm, leap directly into the path of insight (*darśana-mārga*);

and third, those who, arising from the state of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*), fall back into the defilements of the formless realm. Referring to the chapters, it can be seen that the Arhat establishes only one, which refers to the collective [complete knowledge].

Because one also knows the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) within the three realms, it is said that "by possessing two conditions, there is a collective universal knowledge" (*parijñā*);

this explains the reason why, among the nine [universal knowledges], only five correspond to the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarva-saṃyojana-parikṣaya*). The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, only when two conditions are present is there a collective [knowledge]."

Regarding the single "thorough knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-parijñā*): 1. When one transcends any one of the three realms (*dhātu*) among the three realms; 2. When one exhausts any one type [of birth] among the five destinies (*gati*) and four modes of birth (*yoni*), thereby attaining either the first or second fruit of the path (*phala*).

When both of these two conditions are absent, there is the attainment of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin-phala*) at the time of becoming free from attachment to the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*); here, one condition is absent and the other is attained.

When neither of the two conditions is absent—namely, when one transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and exhausts the human destiny (*manuṣya-gati*) while bypassing birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*)—[one attains the fruit of stream-entry].

When one attains the fruit of Arhatship, it also possesses two meanings: first, transcending the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); second, exhausting the celestial destinies (*devagati*) by transcending birth by transformation (*upapāduka*).

Regarding the gate of the thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*), for the sake of clarity in explaining the meaning from the few to the many, there are three categories within the single [category] of abandoning one [defilement]. First, no...

There are two types of abandonment regarding the learner (*śaikṣa*): [abandonment] of the two [lower realms] and [abandonment] of the craving for the form realm. There are three types of abandonment regarding the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*): [abandonment] of the desire realm, [abandonment] of the form realm, and [abandonment] of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Regarding the abandonment of the intermediate state, there are two kinds:

first, the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who is free from the defilements of the form realm but falls away due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm; second, the non-learner who abandons the two previous [knowledges] through the attainment of the universal knowledge (*sarvājñātājñāna*).

In reality, the solitary realizer (*pratyekabuddha*) also abandons the two previous [knowledges], yet they are referred to as "arhats" based on the terminology used for the śrāvakas. Furthermore, regarding this abandonment, there are some cases where...

The essence of "abandonment" (prahāṇa) is like the retrogression from a fruit (*phala-parihāṇi*) and so forth; there are cases where the name "abandonment" is applied while the essence is not abandoned, such as when the [knowledge of] "not-yet-thoroughly-known" (*aparijñāta*) has not yet been fully realized.

Regarding the abandonment of five: when a person who has leaped over (*vyutkrāntaka*) reaches the *mārgānvaya-jñāna*, they do not obtain the sixth thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), but directly obtain the five abandonments of the lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-prahāṇa*).

These are the fruits of the patience (*kṣānti*) that abandons the five lower fetters. Regarding the abandonment of six: this refers to the sequential realization of the path according to the dharma, whereby one attains the exhaustion of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) within the desire realm.

Because of the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the aggregates, one abandons the six fruits of patience (*kṣānti*); it should be known that among these abandonments, there is no abandonment of the third, fourth, seventh, eighth, or ninth.

This means that for one who attains or has not yet attained the nine thorough knowledges, because they attain at the time of first realizing the path a thorough knowledge previously never before attained, they are called "attained" as each is gradually acquired.

First, it is called "attained" when arising from the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) and regressing; second, [it is so called] when [the fruit] is first realized.
This means that when one first attains the complete knowledge (*parijñā*) of the origin (*samudaya*) of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one abandons the previous two types [of acquisitions];

the phrase "now arising from the regression of afflictions and regaining" refers to this. Sixth, it means that when one previously realized the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and abandoned six [acquisitions] to obtain one, now arising from the regression of afflictions, one loses that one acquisition and regains the six.
Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa (Abhidharmakośakārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā) Treatise Volume Twenty-Two Narrated by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.

The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "One who possesses manifold talents and conduct is called a 'worthy' (*xian*). The *Guiyuan Zhucong* states: "One who is unimpeded in all matters is called a 'sage' (*sheng*).
The *Renwang Jing* states that those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) are 'worthies,' while those on the stages and above are 'sages. This treatise states:

"A sage" refers to one who has already attained the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), thereby distancing themselves from all unwholesome dharmas; thus they are named 'sage,' having obtained ultimate liberation (*visamyoga*).

Having attained [the path], one may infer from the aforementioned sūtras and śāstras that those in the seven stages of the *upāya* (preparatory means) are called "Worthy Ones" (*bhadra*), while those above the stage of "Endurance of Suffering" (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) are called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*).
Herein, the term "Worthy" (*xian*) is explained as "harmonious and virtuous," and "Noble" (*sheng*) as "sacred correctness"; these are thus etymological definitions.

As for why this is clarified after the "Chapter on Latent Tendencies" (*anuśaya-varga*): the preceding chapter elucidated abandonment, which pertains to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); this chapter elucidates the Noble Ones, which pertains to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

It is explained next because it serves as the cause for cessation. If one follows the structural outline (*xu-ke*), since the three grades of noble ones (*xiánshèng*) clarify the untainted (*anāsrava*), first comes revulsion (*yàn*) and then contemplation (*guān*);
subsequently come the tainted (*sāsrava*) and finally the untainted. Within this, the noble ones are the fruit and are therefore explained first, as extensively distinguished above.
As for the statement that they "can swiftly counteract the three realms," there are two reasons for this: first, they can swiftly sever the three [fetters].

Because the nine grades [of afflictions] of the two realms are abandoned instantaneously, [the path] is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); since the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) lacks this [quality], it pertains to both types.

The *Nyāyānusāra* (Correct Principle) objects, saying: "The claim that a single moment can instantaneously abandon the nine grades does not prove that the tainted [path] can also abandon the five categories (*pañcavarga*) combined within a single moment.
How could the mere fact of instantaneous abandonment mean it is subsumed under the untainted? The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (New Translation) says: "The *Nyāyānusāra*..."

If the nine grades [of afflictions] were abandoned simultaneously, it would necessarily require the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*); since abandoning the five categories together is easy, it employs the tainted path (*sāsrava-mārga*).
Why is it that taking the simultaneous abandonment of the nine grades as the cause makes the combined abandonment of the five categories difficult?

Regarding the statement that the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) is mentioned earlier [than the path of cultivation], this is because it follows the sequence of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and does not rely on the sequence of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This is because the observation of the truths (*satya*) in the path of cultivation is not fixed; furthermore, in the path of cultivation, one generally observes the truth of origination (*samudaya*) first.

As the *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "Why is suffering (*duḥkha*) presented first and origination (*samudaya*) later in the path of seeing, whereas origination is presented first and suffering later in the path of cultivation? The answer is: the path of seeing... [is fixed].

Based on the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) relies on the sequence of cause and effect (and so forth). Regarding the meaning of "clearly and perfectly awakening" (*abhisambodha*):
it refers to the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) which, facing toward the objects of the four truths, awaken to them with equanimity; this is called "clearly and perfectly awakening.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: Since there are four aspects that contemplate the fruit of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), why is it called only the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and not [the other truths]?

Regarding the truths such as impermanence (*anitya*), furthermore, the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*) is unique; only those phenomena that are *sāsrava* (tainted) are suffering, and not others, and for this reason it is called the Truth of Suffering.
The three [characteristics] such as impermanence are common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) shared with others;

because these three truths—impermanence and so forth—all possess the common characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and non-self (*anātmatā*) which pervade all phenomena, they are not termed "Truths of Impermanence" and so on. Question: There are four aspects (*ākāra*) through which one contemplates arising.

For what reason is the cause of death designated solely as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)? Furthermore, origination only brings about the gathering of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) regarding contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), and not regarding uncontaminated ones (*anāsrava*).

Since uncontaminated phenomena also possess the characteristics of being causes, births, and conditions—such as the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) being called a cause, a birth, and a condition—the Truth of Origination is established as a "Truth" because it is unique [to the defiled].
Question: There are four aspects (*ākāra*) for contemplating nirvāṇa; why is nirvāṇa... [the rest of the sentence is missing from the source text].

The Truth of Cessation alone is designated as such, while it is not called "peace" (*śānta*) or the other three aspects of the truths. Furthermore, because the Truth of Cessation is unique, it is established by the name "Cessation" (*nirodha*) alone to manifest ultimate cessation.

The term "peace" is ambiguous as it overlaps with meditative concentration (*samādhi*); "sublime" (*praṇīta*) avoids ambiguity as it refers to the Path (*mārga*), and thus it is not called the "Truth of Peace" or the "Truth of Sublimity.
Question: There are four aspects through which one contemplates the Noble Path; why then is the Noble Path designated only as the "Truth of the Path" (*mārgasatya*)?

They are not called the "Truths of Suchness" (*yathābhūta*) and so forth. Furthermore, the name "Path" (*mārga*) is established solely to reveal the road leading toward *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it does not receive the designation "Truth.

This is because the term "Suchness" would be confused with the correct principle (*nyāya*), while the practice (*caryā*) extends to include both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the transcendent (*anāsrava*), and the emergence (*niḥsaraṇa*) extends to include both cyclic existence and *nirvāṇa*. Thus, they are not called the "Truths of Practice" or the "Truths of Emergence.

Regarding the term "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*), the treatise explains that they are called "Noble" because they are the truths of the Noble Ones (*ārya*); that is, they are perceived as suffering only by the Noble Ones.

Because one truly perceives suffering up to the path, and because one perceives the path as the path, they are called the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*). Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) reckon suffering to be pleasure and reckon what is not the path to be the path;

because these are inverted and false views, they are not called the "truths of ordinary persons. Question: Why are space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) not truths?
Answer: The *Vibhāṣā* states: "If a dharma is suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, or the remedy for suffering, then it is [a truth] in the world..."

The Venerable One does not establish space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) as truths, because they are neither suffering nor the cause of suffering and so forth;

therefore, the Blessed One does not establish them as truths. Furthermore, because space and cessation not through deliberation do not fall within the world (*adhvan*), they are not the [first] three truths; and because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature, they are not the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

First, regarding suffering as suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*): it constitutes the nature of suffering by its very essence, as the Sūtra says: "All painful sensations are suffering when they arise and suffering while they persist.

Since both their arising and their persistence are suffering, we know that they constitute the nature of suffering by their very essence. Second, regarding the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*):

as the Sūtra says, "All pleasant sensations are pleasant when they arise and pleasant while they persist, but they are suffering when they change. Therefore, prior to their changing, during their arising and persistence, [they are pleasant].

Since all that is pleasant is only designated as suffering at the time of its destruction, we know that pleasure becomes suffering through destruction. Third, regarding the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*):

as the Sūtra says, "That which is impermanent is itself suffering," we know that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is not either of the former two [types of suffering], but rather constitutes suffering by virtue of being conditioned formations.

The Correct Principle (*Nyāya*) states: "There is no impure, impermanent phenomenon that is not suffering" (based on this, the *Śāstra* clarifies that the suffering of destruction is included within the suffering of conditioned formations).

First, suffering as suffering (duḥkha-duḥkhatā) is situated in the second [category]. Regarding "agreeable contaminated phenomena" (*iṣṭa sāsrava dharma*): this means that because they function in accordance with pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) due to the power of pleasant sensation, they are called "agreeable";
because they are conjoined with the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), they are called "the suffering of change. Second, regarding "disagreeable" (*aniṣṭa*):

this means that because they function in accordance with painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*) due to the power of painful sensation, they are called "disagreeable," and so on, up to those that function in accordance with neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*) due to the power of neutral sensation.

The term "feeling of equanimity" refers to the remaining [feelings] that are neither agreeable nor disagreeable. As for the statement that the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) because of their impermanent nature:
one might ask whether the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) should also be characterized as the suffering of conditioned existence. The answer is that the Truth of the Path is not suffering;

rather, it is the suffering of conditioned existence that is contrary to the noble mind (*āryacitta*). This is because the arising of the Noble Path does not involve being contrary to the noble mind; by means of this [Path], [one attains liberation].
Because it leads to the exhaustion of all suffering, the Path is not suffering. Who among the wise would wash an abscess with water?
No wise person would entertain such a notion. The verse says that which acts as the cause of suffering:

because pleasure gives rise to the fruit of future suffering and accumulates the fruits of various sufferings in the future, one is oppressed by suffering due to the craving for pleasure; it is for this reason [that the Path is not suffering].

Regarding the argument that the three causes are designated as suffering, the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes it, saying: "To be a cause of suffering is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*);
how could this pertain to the Truth of Suffering? The Sautrāntikas and Mahāsāṃghikas state that there is no real pleasure for two reasons:

first, scripture (*āgama*), and second, reasoning (*yukti*). As for scripture, it is as the Blessed One said: "Whatever sensation exists, none of it is anything other than suffering," and he also said: "You should..."
Regarding the contemplation of pleasure as suffering, it is further stated that to call suffering "pleasure" is called a perversion (*viparyāsa*).

How so? By reason of the fact that all causes of pleasure are indeterminate. That is to say, things such as clothing, food and drink, cold and heat, which sentient beings accept as causes of pleasure—if these are used at the wrong time or in excessive measure—they can instead produce suffering. Furthermore...

Because they constitute the cause of suffering, one knows that clothing and other such things are fundamentally causes of suffering; when suffering increases and intensifies, their true nature becomes manifest.

The principle that bodily postures can easily be discarded should likewise apply here. The Master [Vasubandhu] evaluates that the existence of pleasure is logical, because there is a sense of gratification and the like.

The appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) as effects are termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), while the appropriated aggregates as causes are termed the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*). This is capable of...

Because they are gathered together, suffering and its origin are distinguished by way of their nature as cause and effect. According to the Sarvāstivāda, suffering and its origin are one entity, while the distinction between cause and effect is merely nominal.
The Master [Vasubandhu] should understand that although these two—the nature of cause and effect—are distinct in name, the entity itself is not different.

However, regarding the two truths of cessation and the path, the entities themselves are indeed distinct. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "Is the establishment of the knowledge of the four truths based on substantial entities?"

If based on the truth of cause and effect, or based on the truth of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), or based on the truth of substantial entities (*dravya-satya*), there would have to be three truths of suffering and origin, because they are a single substance.
If based on the truth of cause and effect, there would have to be five paths, because there are both causes and effects.

If based on the truth of clear realization, there would have to be eight, because there are the eight truths of the higher and lower realms. Therefore, one should say that the Four Noble Truths consist of the combination of the nature of cause and effect within the path of cause and effect.

Because they are one: that is to say, the untainted (anāsrava) factors, which combine cause and effect, and the mundane (laukika) factors associated with suffering and outflows (sāsrava), are all established as a single category because they pertain to the practice for the ultimate cessation of birth and death.
Furthermore, while the truths of suffering and its origin each have four aspects (ākāra), the truth of the path has only four aspects in the lower realm;
thus, although there are eight aspects across the upper and lower realms, they are combined into one because their aspects are identical.
This refers to the Four Noble Truths.

For example, when a jar is broken, the cognition of it as a "jar" ceases; that is to say, once the jar has been broken into shards and the like, the conceptual understanding of it as a jar no longer arises.
The same applies to clothing and other objects. As for the phrase "wisdom analyzes the remainder," it is like using wisdom to analyze water.

When comparing odors, tastes, and so forth to water, they are considered "residues" (the remainder); the same applies to fire and the other elements. Regarding the statement that feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates can be analyzed down to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*):
since non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*) cannot be analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), they can only be analyzed through wisdom down to a single moment.

Question: Does this statement regarding the two truths (*satya*) apply to the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*) as well as to what is not a truth? Answer: According to the *Vibhāṣā* commentators (*vibhāṣā-vādin*).

The intended meaning is that all four truths pertain to both the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Regarding the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), the existence of things such as jars and robes is conventional;

the Buddha’s teaching on the truth of cessation (*nirodha*) as being like a garden or grove is also conventional; and the Buddha’s teaching on the truth of the path (*mārga*) as being like a boat or raft is likewise conventional.

However, when the Buddha teaches that each of the four truths possesses its own fourfold reasoning, these are all ultimate truths. Furthermore, it is said that both truths encompass the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).

Space and analytical cessation are also subsumed within the two truths. Regarding the statement "and the subsequently attained mundane right knowledge," this refers to the mundane right knowledge that follows the untainted fundamental knowledge (*anāsrava-mūla-jñāna*).
According to this master’s intention, because right knowledge apprehends its object without inversion, it is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
because right knowledge does not apprehend its object as real [in the conventional sense], it is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The phrase "one who is about to proceed toward the path of seeing the truths" describes the sequence of entering the path. First, one must generate the resolve (*cittotpāda*) to proceed toward the seeing of the truths;
second, one must abide in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*); third, one seeks the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-prajñā*) that accords with the seeing of the truths;

fourth, one engages in reflection (*cintā*); and fifth, one practices meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This means first abiding in morality and subsequently cultivating the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), as stated in the *Nyāya-ānusāra-śāstra*.
The conduct and practices cultivated during the stage of initial application for those seeking to perceive the Noble Truths are extremely extensive and detailed;
those who wish to understand them thoroughly should seek them within the various treatises on contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) compiled by the noble ones. To state the essentials:
a beginner should cultivate a profound intention toward liberation, contemplate the state of *nirvāṇa* with joy, and first employ skillful means to turn away from the faults of *saṃsāra*.

Associating with virtuous friends is so called because such friends serve as the foundation for all [spiritual] practices; by possessing the power of hearing and so forth, they receive the name "virtuous friend.
As it is explained at length, for example, regarding the wisdom produced through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) which takes both names and meanings as its objects:

the treatise states that sometimes meaning is drawn out by means of the phrasing, and sometimes the phrasing is drawn out by means of the meaning, for one does not yet entirely abandon the phrasing while contemplating the meaning.
The analogy states: For example, suppose there is a person swimming in deep, swift water. One who has never learned to swim does not let go of their support;
one who has learned but not yet mastered it may either let go or cling to it; whereas one who is well-trained in swimming crosses by their own power without depending on a support.

The three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) are likewise so. Furthermore, it says that the expression "that which is accomplished" indicates that these three superior wisdoms are accomplished through the three causes of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

It is just as when people in the world say that the life-force of a cow and so forth is composed of the grass it has eaten (the commentary explains this as meaning that the cause of a person's life is food,
while the cause of a cow's life is grass, and so on).
Regarding the statement that "the first two are easily accomplished," these refer to dwelling free from defilement and the absence of unwholesome vitarka. The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:

"By what means are these two easily accomplished? It answers: because those who possess few desires and contentment regarding robes and other requisites, yet seek many means of livelihood, associate with evil companions by day and give rise to evil vitarka and vicāra by night; consequently, there is no possibility for them to cause the mind to attain [these states].
Regarding the statement that "having attained" and "not yet having attained" are called "non-existent," this means that these two types of intense seeking do not exist;
rather, they are contentment with what one has and fewness of desires. Thus, these two are termed "non-existent. However, these two characteristics represent the fundamental meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*.
Since the Master [Vasubandhu] differs from this, the Master does not seek further, and he also takes what has not yet been attained as his object.

Otherwise, the distinction between the two would not be established; therefore, it should be stated here as follows: To be dissatisfied and unhappy with what one has already obtained—whether it be excellent or abundant—is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).
To seek excellence and abundance regarding things not yet obtained, such as clothing and so forth, is called "great desire" (*mahēcchā*).
Since contentment and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) serve as the antidotes to these, they should be understood as being the opposites of these [two].
Regarding the statement that "knowing the distinctions" (formerly called *saṃtuṣṭi* and *alpecchatā*, which were considered identical) "pervades the three realms," the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
By what is it proven that the form and formless realms also possess the antidotes of contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) and fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*)?

It is because we observe those born in the desire realm who, when arising from the form or formless realms, have the two types of afflicted states (*vipakṣa*) currently active; since these are distant, the two types of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are manifest.
Because their practice increases, they are said to be able to give birth to the various noble ones (*ārya*); thus, they are called "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*). The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Since all noble ones are born from these four, they are transmitted in succession without interruption; the former serves as the lineage for the latter, which is universally established in the world.
The dharmakāya of the noble ones is entirely produced by the power of contentment with robes and so forth; therefore, it is 'noble'."
Regarding the statement that "the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are also thus," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
Just as within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), although there is no object of resentment, the wholesome root of non-hatred (*avyāpāda-kuśalamūla*) can still exist;

and just as within the formless realm, although there are no garments and so forth, the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha-kuśalamūla*) can still exist—so too, one who is not greedy for the body is likewise not greedy for material requisites.

Because they are fully possessed [of these], it is said that those in the formless realm possess the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Regarding the statement "delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation," one explanation is as given in the chapter.

Furthermore, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) is called "delighting in abandonment," while the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is called "delighting in cultivation. Alternatively, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called "delighting in abandonment," and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is called "delighting in cultivation.
As for the phrase "abandoning desire-greed (*kāmarāga*) and existence-greed (*bhavarāga*"), "desire-greed" refers to the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Regarding the craving of the two upper realms, the *Nyāya* asks: "Is it not the case that the fourth [root] is also able to counteract hatred and so forth?

Then it should also have non-hatred (*adveṣa*) and so on as its nature. This is not incorrect; however, because the first three serve as its provisions, those first three are exclusively of the nature of non-greed (*alobha*).
Since this [fourth root] likewise functions as an antidote to greed, it is described primarily in terms of its predominant quality. Question: Why is this so?
Is it that contentment alone is the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*) and not fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*)? The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* answers:
"Fewness of desires operates with respect to things not yet obtained in the future, whereas contentment operates with respect to things already obtained in the present.

It is not difficult to refrain from taking even a single coin in the present, but it is difficult to be content with the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) in the future; therefore, it is established as a noble lineage. Thus it is said.
Regarding the establishment of the two matters, these are the requisites (*pariṣkāra*) and activities (*karma*), which constitute the two.

As for the statement that they serve to counteract the arising of the four types of craving, the treatise says: "Therefore, the Sūtra states: 'O Bhikṣus, listen attentively! Craving has clothing as its cause;

it arises when it should arise, it persists when it should persist, and it is grasped when it should be grasped. Thus, craving has food, drink, bedding, and seating as its causes, and likewise non-existence and existence."

Thus, it is said that in order to counteract these four [types of craving], the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are established. Question: Why are medicinal substances not established as a noble lineage? Answer:

According to the correct principle, they are not so established because craving does not arise toward them. The Sūtra states only that craving arises in four ways; therefore, medicinal substances are not established as a noble lineage.
Alternatively, they are already included within the first three [noble lineages]. This is because medicinal substances may be contained within clothing, food, or shelter.

There are those included among garments (such as wrapping the abdomen with a cloth when suffering from cold), those included among food and drink (such as consuming much kudzu powder when suffering from heat), and those included among bedding (such as those who suffer from cold using many cloths for their bedding).

Therefore, they are not established separately. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, regarding the "destruction of wealth" and "medicines," it says there is no pleasure in abandoning [sensual] pleasure, but rather pleasure in cultivation; this differs from the *Śāstra*.

It is said that there are two essential requirements for entering the gateway of formal cultivation. Generally, there are many types of gateways for entering cultivation because the modes of conduct among sentient beings are manifold;
thus, the gateways for entering cultivation are also manifold. In detail, they are numerous, but in brief, there are five:

namely, the meditation on impurity for those with excessive desire, the meditation on loving-kindness and compassion for those with excessive hatred, and the meditation on dependent origination for those with excessive ignorance.

For those who are attached to a self, there is the contemplation of the differentiation of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*); for those who engage in discursive thought (*vitarka*), there is the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
However, as for the most concise and essential gateway, these two alone are mentioned. Regarding the statement that these can eliminate distracted discursive thoughts, other masters say:

"This mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is able to stop distracted discursive thoughts because it does not have many objects; whereas the [contemplation of] impurity has many objects, as it involves the distinct features of visible forms and thus induces many discursive thoughts."

Therefore, [the meditation on] impurity has no power to remedy that [restlessness], as it is said that this mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) operates within the internal door and can thus suppress discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), whereas impurity mostly operates through the external door and is thus like visual consciousness, having no power to remedy that [restlessness].

According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, however, impurity can also remedy discursive thoughts, and mindfulness of breathing can also remedy greed; the present statement is made based on what is most frequent.

Regarding the mention of "greed for color" (*varṇa-rāga*), this refers to greed for exquisite colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth. "Greed for shape" (*saṃsthāna-rāga*) refers to greed for excellent forms and so forth.

"Greed for touch" (*spraṣṭavya-rāga*) refers to greed for exquisite qualities such as softness of bone and so forth. "Greed for service" (*paricaryā-rāga*) refers to [greed for] excellence in postures such as bowing and looking up.

These take as their objects such things as the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) and so forth, which are the opposites of exquisite blue and so forth; they take as their objects those who have been devoured by jackals, wolves, and so forth, which are the opposites of handsome features. They take as their objects... [the rest of the sentence].

Because worms, maggots, and the like are the opposite of exquisite tactile sensations, and because the unmoving corpse is the opposite of acts such as honoring and serving, these four types of impurity each counteract one type of greed.
If one contemplates the skeleton, it universally counteracts all four types. According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, this refers to those of dull faculties;
for those of sharp faculties, they first observe their own internal bodies to counteract the four types of objects of greed. The text is extensive and will not be detailed here.
