Regarding the statement that "perverse views have only a partial object" and so forth: To sever the afflictions, one must employ attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) and universal attention directed toward a single location;

only then can the afflictions be severed. Because this attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣamanasikāra*) regarding the contemplation of the skeleton has only a partial object, it cannot sever the afflictions;
it can only suppress them. Among the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), there should be a fault in the fourth, as both [the object and the subject] are deficient.
The third [alternative] and the third "neither-nor" are in the fourth [alternative]; according to the *dharmatā*, the same applies to the treatise (*śāstra*). Question:

According to the verse, it says that from the feet up to the midpoint of the head is called "the cultivation of the object is matured. This refers to the maturation of the attention (*manasikāra*) regarding the object;

how then can it be said that the maturation of the attention regarding the object extends to the ocean? Answer: What is stated in the verse is based on the initial stage of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Once it has been accomplished, when one contemplates it again, it is also permissible to contemplate it extensively; therefore, there is no fault.

Regarding the statement that the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its essence, one master in the *Vibhāṣā* says it is wisdom (*prajñā*), while another master says it is revulsion (*nirveda*).
The critique states: "This meditation on impurity has non-attachment as its essence, not wisdom, nor revulsion. Why is this so? Because..."

Because it remedies greed, its nature consists of five or four aggregates along with their attendants. Regarding the statement that it "generally relies upon the ten stages," this means that all ten stages can take the desire realm and the form realm as their objects.
It does not rely upon the formless realm; as the *Vibhāṣā* states, this is because in the formless realm there is no impurity contemplation (*aśubha-saṃjñā*) that takes form-dharmas as its object.
The statement that it "takes only the desire realm as its object" refers specifically to visible form and shape.
The principle is as follows: The power of this contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is able to take as its object all forms (*rūpa-āyatana*) subsumed within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If it is argued that the Venerable Aniruddha was unable to perceive the heavens as impure, and that Śāriputra and others were likewise unable to perceive the physical body of the Buddha as impure, how then can this contemplation universally take all forms of the desire realm as its object? This is the objection.

Otherwise, since those who have attained victory over extinction (*vibhava-nirodha*) are able to contemplate the color of celestial beings as impure, and the Buddha is able to contemplate his own subtle and wondrous physical body as impure, this contemplation must necessarily take the entirety of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as its object.

As for the statement that it occurs "only in the human realm," this means that it can first be manifested only in the three continents of the human world; as the treatise says: "It does not even exist in other realms."
Moreover, regarding its arising in other realms, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that it first arises only among humans, and subsequently it can also manifest when one is born in other places.
As for the term "impure," the treatise says: "Since the name 'impure' is established, only the aspect of impurity serves as its cognitive object (*ākāra*).

Regarding the phrase "taking its own world as an object," this is because this contemplation through mental resolve (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) takes only the present environment as its object—just like the five sensory consciousnesses—and does not extend beyond it. If it were to transcend...
"Past" refers to conditions such as those of the past. As for the statement that non-arising phenomena (*anutpattidharma*) can take all three time periods as their objects:
this is because the categories of non-arising phenomena are manifold, and because their objects flow through the three times, as explained in the section on "past fetters" (*pūrvāntasaṃyojana*).

Since these are merely conceptual constructs (*parikalpita*), they are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are entirely real and are not produced through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Since this [attainment] is acquired through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), it is comprised solely within the category of the contaminated (*sāsrava*). Regarding the statement that it is "acquired through the abandonment of defilements by prior cultivation" (*vairāgyalābhika*):

this means that although one had previously attained this meditative absorption before abandoning defilement, one lost it in the interim; subsequently, upon abandoning defilement, one regains it and thus it is called "acquired through the abandonment of defilements.

Alternatively, because any dharma of a particular stage that is obtained simply by abandoning defilement is termed "acquired through the abandonment of defilements," the *Nyāyānusāra* states: [text follows].

Because when one becomes detached from the defilements of various stages and attains the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of those respective stages, one simultaneously acquires the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) of those stages;
thus it is said there are "eight gates. The "new" [commentary] speaks of nine gates by adding the first explanation regarding the definition of inhalation and exhalation;

however, this present chapter combines the first two as one, hence there are only eight gates. Regarding the term "wind of the breath," according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, it is explained as follows: [it refers to the wind] belonging to... (the text continues).

The bodily winds are briefly of six kinds: (1) the wind of inhalation, (2) the wind of exhalation, (3) the wind that initiates speech, (4) the wind of expulsion, (5) the wind that follows movement, and (6) the wind that moves the body (and so forth).
Although this [wind] is actually wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called "mindfulness" (*smṛti*);

this is because mindfulness is predominant, and thus it receives the name "mindfulness. It is by the power of mindfulness that objects are perceived with clarity and the task to be accomplished is achieved.
Therefore, just as the four foundations of mindfulness have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence yet are called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), so too regarding the five stages:

because the fourth dhyāna lacks vitarka, they are restricted to the three lower dhyānas, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*). As for "suffering and pleasure being conducive to vitarka," this means that suffering in the desire realm is conducive to inducing vitarka;
since this contemplation remedies vitarka, [suffering] does not arise simultaneously with it. Furthermore, the joy and pleasure of the form realm are able to oppose it.
This meditation focuses exclusively on the object of the inhalation and exhalation; because it focuses solely on this object, the three feelings do not arise together.
To clarify this meaning: since "suffering" already includes "grief," and "pleasure" already includes "joy," they are not explained separately.
Regarding the statement that it "depends solely on a body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)," one theory in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* holds this to be so;

another theory holds that it depends on both the desire and form realms (*rūpadhātu*) but not the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), though at the time of its initial arising, it must necessarily depend on the desire realm.

Regarding the statement that it is "attained in two ways," according to the *Nyāyānusāra*, it is attained solely through application (*prayoga*) and not through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*); for one who has not yet abandoned defilements, it necessarily manifests through application.

Therefore, it is not obtained through detachment from defilements (*vairāgya-lābhika*), because it is comprised within the stages [of meditative attainment] (and so forth). Regarding the statement that it is "only the attention consisting of reality" (*tattvamanasikāra*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states that it also extends to the attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanasikāra*).
Regarding the statement that it is "cultivated only through the Buddha’s teaching," this is because Pratyekabuddhas and Buddhas can arise [to this state] by themselves;

Śrāvakas can arise through the power of the causal teachings; and outsiders cannot arise [to it] as they lack such teachings and do not realize subtle phenomena. Thus, [this state] does not exist among them.

Furthermore, the *Nyāyabindu* states that because this [recollection] is utterly incompatible with the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), such recollection is absent where there is the grasping for a self.
Regarding the fault of confusion, the *Nyāyabindu* says: "Counting five inhalations as five exhalations, and counting five exhalations as five inhalations.
According to this text, counting inhalations and exhalations separately and then combining them makes ten. Furthermore, regarding the three faults, the first is...
There are three faults: being too lax is the first fault; being too hurried is the second fault; and confusion is the third fault. Regarding the fault of being too lax:

it means that because the force of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is excessively slow and slack, the mind becomes entangled by indolence (*kausīdya*) and torpor (*styāna-middha*), or else the mind is allowed to run wild and scatter toward external objects.
Regarding the fault of being too hurried: it means that because the preparatory application is too restless and impetuous, it causes an imbalance to arise within the body and mind.
If at that time one forcibly and repeatedly inhales and exhales until the breath becomes constricted, it causes an internal disharmony that gives rise to wind.
Because of this wind, first the various channels of the body’s limbs become distended and dispersed;

as this wind increases in intensity, it can induce the onset of disease, and so forth, as explained at length regarding the signs of impairment and benefit, and the confusion resulting from their loss. That is to say, through mental distraction, one becomes subject to all manner of afflictions.
Regarding "affliction and subjugation," the treatise further states that when counting the breaths, one should first count the inhalations;

since the inhalation occurs at the moment of birth and the exhalation is the last at the time of death, by thus observing the stages of birth and death, one is gradually able to cultivate the perception of impermanence.
Regarding "following the breath," the treatise further states that one should be mindful of each inhalation and exhalation respectively.
Regarding "extending far": what is meant by this? Mindfulness of the inhalation of the breath is practiced as pervading the entire body;

mindfulness of the inhalation is practiced as following it part by part, proceeding from the throat, the heart, the navel, the hips, the thighs, the calves, and down to the toes, with mindfulness constantly following along.

As for the exhalation of the breath, mindfulness follows it as it leaves the body, whether it extends for a span (*vitasti*) or a fathom (*vyāma*), with mindfulness constantly following it wherever it goes. This is called "stopping" (*sthāpanā*). Regarding the treatise:
It further says: "Observe that the breath abides in the body like a thread within a pearl; is it cold or warm? Is it harmful or beneficial?

To say that one also observes the breath together with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), etc., means observing the four great elements that act as the creators, the derived matter of color, odor, taste, and tangibility, and even the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), whether internal or external, such that there is no self (*ātman*) to be found, because one has abandoned the inversions (*viparyāsa*), and so on until [liberation] is attained.

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): The *Śāstra* states that "shifting" means transferring the awareness of the breath-wind (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) from its object and placing it within progressively superior wholesome roots, up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

The phrase "entering the path of vision" (*darśanamārga*) and so forth includes the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). The *Śāstra* further states:

"Other masters say that the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is the beginning and the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is the end; this is called the 'transformation' (*parivarta*), culminating in the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)."

The term "pure" (*śuddha*) refers to these [stages]. (According to the former master, that which precedes the untainted (*anāsrava*) is called "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*), while that which follows it is called "pure. According to this [latter] master, that which possesses afflictions (*kleśa*) is called "defiled," while that which lacks them is called "pure. Bao says:

"According to the former master, everything prior to the attainment of the untainted is called 'transformation' (*parāvṛtti*), and from the attainment of the untainted onward is called 'purity. According to the latter master, up until the attainment of the state where afflictions still exist, it is called 'transformation,' and when the afflictions are exhausted through their eradication, it is called 'purity.'"
To say that breath is subsumed under one part of this body is because the wind—which constitutes one part of the person (puruṣa) formed by the six elements—is a single component.
To say that it lacks the other two conditions refers to the wind-path and the pores (though only "two" should have been mentioned).

According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, if one considers birth from a womb, then at the stage of the *kalala* (embryonic mass), the inhalation and exhalation would cause the body to move and vibrate, as it is still extremely subtle.

Therefore, the bodies in the three stages beginning with the *arbuda* must disintegrate; although these bodies gradually become thicker, they lack pores and fissures, and thus the breath does not circulate.
As for the statement "if a body is born in the fourth dhyāna," the former refers to a body in this realm entering the fourth dhyāna, while the latter refers to a body existing in that stage itself.
In the former case, there is an absence of two conditions—the coarse mind and the pores—while in the latter case, there is an absence of the breath.

The earth and the pores differ because of two distinct conditions. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "If one is born in that realm where the body has no pores, how could one produce speech upon being born there?
It is not the case that the production of speech necessarily depends on the pores;

rather, it can also be produced through mere movement, just as the sound of a mechanical device does not depend on the pores. Regarding the phrase "counting breaths," this refers to the enumeration of sentient beings.
This [wind] exists only within the body; apart from the body, it is neither inhalation nor exhalation, because it does not belong to the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*).
Regarding its being "non-appropriated" (*anupātta*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states that this is because breath lacks the characteristics of appropriation;

thus, although there is wind within the body that is appropriated, this wind of breath is exclusively non-appropriated. Regarding its being "of the nature of outflow" (*niṣyandaja*), according to the treatise:

It is not produced by nourishment (*aupacayika*), because when the body grows, it diminishes; it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*), because after being severed, it continues again later as a result of its nature as a natural outflow (*naiṣyandika*);
it is not of a single moment, nor is it unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); thus, it does not pertain to the ultimate reality (*dravya*).

Regarding the statement that the breath of the first dhyāna has only three stages as its object: among the four dhyānas, this excludes the fourth absorption because there is no breath there, nor does it take the lower stages as its object.
By this principle, one should determine that the breath of the desire realm has all four stages as its objects.

While it is true that giving rise to a mind of a lower stage is not a mind that takes the breath as its object, what is stated here is that this [contemplation] is mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and it is not said that the three [sensory] consciousnesses are able to observe it.

Because [the breath] has ceased, one borrows the consciousness of a lower stage to give rise to the deportment-mindfulness (*airyāpathika*) and so forth of a higher stage; however, this only takes as its object the karma-initiating [breath] and does not take the breath-wind of the higher stage as its object.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "What are the characteristics of the completion of mindfulness of breathing?

It means that if a practitioner focuses their attention on the observation of the breath flowing subtly and slowly—pervading the entire body like a single hole in a tube—the breath-winds flow in continuous succession."

Just as when one holds a mani-jewel in the hand, it cannot move the body nor give rise to body-consciousness; up to this point, one should say that the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) is perfected.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa), Fascicle 23.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.
Regarding the reliance on the two preceding gates, these refer to the impurity meditation (*aśubhā*) and breath-counting (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) as the two gates.

As for the statement "to cultivate the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) through contemplation," "contemplation" here refers to this stage of the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vastuka-citta-sthiti*); it is a state where, in order to arrest distraction, one exclusively cultivates tranquility (*śamatha*). At that time, [it is] provisional...
To dwell with the mind focused on a single image, such as a chain of bones, is called *śamatha* (calm abiding).

At the stage of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one grasps the distinct characteristics of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena; furthermore, within the body itself, one grasps various distinct characteristics.

Because this eliminates the four inversions and gives rise to seeing things as they truly are, it is called *vipaśyanā* (insight). Regarding what are termed "distinct images" and "general images," herein [the latter] refers only to...

Observing the body, feelings, and so forth individually is called "distinctive perception" (*pṛthak-saṃjñā*); observing them collectively by way of the four [foundations] is called "collective perception" (*sāmānya-saṃjñā*).

This does not refer to "collective" or "distinctive" in terms of the aspects (*ākāra*) such as impermanence. Within the initial distinctive perception, there are three parts: first, distinctive observation by way of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

second, distinctive observation by way of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); and third, collective observation of the four. Regarding the first, distinctive observation by way of specific characteristics, the *Nyāyapraveśaka* states: "That is to say, one observes..."

Examining the ten bases within and without the body, one sees that their intrinsic natures are each distinct; from the eye to the tactile faculty, each possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, when correct knowledge arises regarding these respective phenomena, it is called "contemplation of specific characteristics.

When this contemplation of specific characteristics reaches fulfillment, a path-form (*mārga-rūpa*) arises; at that time, the "mindfulness of the body as a lineage of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-gotra-kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*) is established.

Abiding in conventional terminology, one first contemplates that the body, like other conditioned phenomena, is impermanent; this is done by observing it through its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
Having thus briefly explained the contemplation of the body, the same principle applies to the other three [aggregates]. Regarding the statement "contemplating the body down to a single atom":

this means contemplating the physical body as being established by the accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*)—both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*)—as well as the five sense faculties (*indriya*) and the five objects (*viṣaya*). In this manner, one gradually reduces [the object of observation] to its subtlest limit.

Subsequently, observing a single ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is called the fulfillment of the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the observation of feeling, mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-citta-dharma*) down to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*):
this means that one first observes the nature, duration, and temporal extent of feeling and so forth, gradually abbreviating them until they reach the duration of a single moment;

this is called the fulfillment of feeling and the others. The statement that "the power of mindfulness causes wisdom (*prajñā*) to abide upon its object" follows the tenet of the Vaibhāṣika school; thus, the treatise says: "Vai... [and so on].
The Vaibhāṣikas say that because mindfulness (*smṛti*) increases in this stage, it is by the power of mindfulness that wisdom (*prajñā*) is sustained and able to proceed;
it is like an axe cutting wood, which proceeds by being supported by the force of a wedge (this is a case of naming the effect after its cause).

Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* further provides a simile, stating that the wholesome roots increase in successive stages, like water overflowing and spreading through a field. Or, it may be said that it is by the power of wisdom that mindfulness is [sustained].

As for those that "dwell upon objects," this is the Master’s own explanation; thus the treatise states: "In truth, one should say that it is wisdom (*prajñā*) which causes mindfulness to dwell [upon its object];
therefore, the name 'foundation of mindfulness' (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is established for wisdom. This is because mindfulness can clearly remember whatever is contemplated by wisdom.

Regarding the "foundation of mindfulness as the object of focus" (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*), this refers to the objects of wisdom, which also include wisdom itself, because all phenomena are subsumed within the totality of objects of focus. Regarding "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*)...

Regarding the statement that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), this treatise contains no explicit textual passage for it; rather, this meaning is established by implication alone.

As for those that are not co-existent (*sahabhū*): among the objects of perception (*ālambana*), there are some that do not exist simultaneously with their corresponding perceiving subjects (*ālambaka*), because they can perceive phenomena across the three periods of time.
The body is the coarsest because it is material form (*rūpa*). Next, sensation (*vedanā*) is coarse, as expressed in such statements as "my hand hurts."

This [sequence] is established by way of grossness and subtlety; mindfulness is established by way of its arising. Regarding the statement that there are only four [foundations] as antidotes to the perversions, the *Nyāyānusāra* further states:

"Because they serve as antidotes to the four types of craving, there are only four. Regarding the statement that among these four, three are called "non-mixed objects," this means that the body, feelings, and mind can only be taken as distinct objects;
if one were to combine the body with the mind to take them as a single object, one would not be able to take the mind as the object.
Because one contemplates the impurity of the body in meditative concentration, the third is called "unmixed.

Next, regarding the difference between this general characteristic mindfulness (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*) and the preceding specific ones, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The foundation of mindfulness that takes phenomena as its object in a general way (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) has three types, namely those consisting of two, three, and four [foundations].
Only that which takes all four as its general object is what is being cultivated here; the preceding 'mixed' [foundation] is not merely the two, three, and so forth."

Having distinguished it from what preceded above— from the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vasthā*) up to this end of the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*)— the following clarifies the stage of internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*).

Regarding the statement "from this general mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) until the subsequent arising of the stage of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*)," this accords with the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra* concerning entry into the Path.

Following the sequential cultivation of the dwelling in mindfulness amidst mixed objects, one practices the contemplation of the three meanings and the seven points of mastery (*saptasthānakauśalya*);

only then does one enter from the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) into the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*). This treatise omits these details. The "contemplation of the three meanings" refers to contemplating the meanings of the three categories: the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

The "seven points of mastery" refers to knowing, as they truly are, the suffering of form, the origin of form, the cessation of form, the path leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the peril of form, and the escape from form; this applies equally to feeling and the other four aggregates, though here they are referred to collectively as the "seven points. However, this treatise...

It is said that through the gradual accomplishment of the mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) by taking the common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as its collective object, one eventually reaches the highest of the high grades.
Following this mindfulness, there arises the first root of merit (kuśalamūla) conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), which is called "Heat" (uṣmagata).

Regarding the statement that one "fully contemplates the four noble truths through the sixteen aspects," this refers to a contaminated mind (sāsravacitta) in training that observes the four truths but has not yet attained clarity.

It is understood as being like viewing various forms and images through a thin gauze. The new commentary states that, according to the subsequent section on the "reduction of conditions in practice," one contemplates the four aspects within each of the Four Truths before moving on to the next truth.
Regarding the statement that the arising of roots of goodness is called the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
"The practitioner cultivates these roots of goodness of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*), progressing gradually through their lower, middle, and upper grades."

Increasing one’s compliant faith in the Buddha’s teachings on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, and observing that all states of existence are constantly being incinerated by fierce flames, one develops within faith in the Three Jewels a supreme faculty. Following this, the roots of virtue produced through cultivation that accord with the stages leading to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) arise;
these are termed the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage. Regarding why the Summit is called "supreme," the *Nyāyānusāra* further states:

The term "summit" (*mūrdhan*) indicates that this is the most excellent meaning; just as it is said in the world that when a matter of auspiciousness reaches its fulfillment, "this person has reached the summit.

Regarding the statement that the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) consists solely of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*): this means that because the path of seeing is so rapid, there is no opportunity for separate contemplation;

thus, it consists only of the mindfulness of phenomena. The new commentary states: "Separate-object contemplation is inferior and cannot shift one's stage; it is through the power of general contemplation [that one does so]."

Because it possesses the superior capacity to shift one’s state, all [roots] in this initial stage are therefore called "Dharma Mindfulness-Abiding" (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the statement that "endurance" (*kṣānti*) refers to the most excellent acceptance of the Four Truths:
the roots of goodness in the preceding stages do not lack such acceptance; however, because this stage is uniquely distinguished as the most supreme, it alone receives this name.
If that were so, the "Worldly Supreme Stage" (*laukikāgradharma*) should also be called "endurance. The *Nyāyānusāra* explains: although the Worldly Supreme Stage, with respect to the Noble Truths...
Furthermore, because one who endures [the truths] is certain to enter the Path of Seeing without interval, there is no possibility of falling back;
yet, it is not that they do not fully contemplate the principles of the Four Noble Truths. Because this stage does fully contemplate them, it specifically receives the name "Patience" (kṣānti).

Regarding these roots of goodness of Patience, which are categorized as inferior, medium, and superior, according to the text of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are collectively divided into three grades: "Heat" (uṣmagata) is the inferior grade, and "Summit" (mūrdhan) is...

Regarding the statement that "one contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm for a single moment" in reference to medium patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which are here classified as superior (*adhimātra*), the treatise states:
"Because they are contiguous with the supreme mundane dharma.

Based on this principle, it is already established that the roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth are all capable of fully taking the suffering and other truths of the three realms as their objects, as there is no distinction made [in the texts]. Thus it is said.

"Subtracting one category" refers to the category of formations (*saṃskāra*). When it is said that at the time of subtracting the conditions (*pratyaya*), the formations are also subtracted, this is because these conditions and formations differ in name but are identical in essence;

thus, these eight conditions are also subsumed under formations. That is to say, they are termed "conditions" (*pratyaya*) based on what they rely upon, and they are termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*) based on their mode of activity and characteristics.
For example, the "path of practice" (*mārga-caryā*) is both the path (*mārga*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); the same applies to the other Truths.

It is likewise; thus, the convergence of conditions and formations is fully elucidated in the chapter on the "Diminution of Conditions and Formations. If one were to provide further explanations, it would instead increase confusion.

Regarding those who cultivate sixteen, twelve, eight, or four [factors], one should infer from this that there are no instances of cultivating fifteen, fourteen, thirteen, eleven, nine, seven, six, five, three, two, or one [factor]. As for the statement that "only one factor arises":

This means that because the mind engaged in the essential practice of cultivation observes the principles of the Truths (*satya*) with focused presence such that multiple minds do not arise simultaneously, only one [momentary] attainment occurs;
it does not hinder the fact that many mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) may also be present. Regarding the statement that the sequence of names proceeds from the end toward the beginning:

this refers to the sequence of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), which are reduced from the end toward the beginning because "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) is at the very end, and thus it is the first to be subtracted. Question: [Why is this so?]
Regarding the question of what mental aspects (*ākāra*) are employed during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) for each of the other three Truths:

the answer is that one employs whichever aspect was previously habituated. According to this principle, when contemplating the remaining Truths, one does not employ the aspects associated with suffering (*duḥkha*).

As for the phrase "the intended suitability is appropriate" (*niyi yīxiāng chāngzhě*): "intended" (*niyi*) means directed toward, and "suitability" (*yī*) means correspondence; these refer simply to the sequential correspondence [of the contemplation].

They are considered to be continuous. Regarding the statement that it is "foremost in the world," according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*’s question-and-answer section, it is called "foremost" because it is superior to all others from the very beginning.

Regarding the statement that it "is free from homogeneous causes" (*sabhāga-hetu*): prior to the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), [all dharmas] are collectively contaminated (*sāsrava*);
from this point onward, they are entirely uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Therefore, this stage of the supreme mundane dharma is able to be free from homogeneous causes.

Furthermore, it is said that the attainment (*prāpti*) is excluded from being the essence of the four roots of goodness (*śuklavidarśanā*) because one fears the error of having the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the noble path manifest again;
thus the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "For one who has already seen the truths, the manifestation of the preparatory stage would be useless.
Moreover, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "Why is attainment the essence of the fruits of śrāmaṇya, whereas the 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are not? It answers: "The fruit of śrāmaṇya..."

Because it is manifested through the accomplishment of its essence, one attains the fruits of *śrāmaṇya*; because the noble ones do not again give rise to the roots of goodness such as *ūṣmagata* and so forth, one does not attain those [roots] such as *ūṣmagata*.
Furthermore, it is asked: why are the characteristics of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth considered the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), yet not considered "attainment" (*prāpti*)?

Answer: Because the characteristics of arising and so forth share the same fruit as that [Supreme Mundane Dharma], follow it in its course, are inseparable from it, and are eternally conjoined with it, they do not precede it.
Furthermore, the acquisition (*prāpti*) and that which is acquired (*prāpya*) have never been separated from one another;

for this reason, the acquisition of the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) is not of the same fruit as those dharmas, nor does it follow along with them, because their natures are distinct and they do not coalesce—whether the acquisition precedes or follows the acquired dharma, they may at times be separated, just as tree bark may sometimes be separated from the tree. Therefore, the acquisition is not itself the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
The same applies to the attainment of the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*.

As for the statement that there is no path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): one who enters the path of seeing must necessarily take the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as an object, whereas the mind of the formless realm does not take the desire realm as its object.

Regarding the claim that "the desire realm is added [to the objects of the formless realm]," this is not the correct meaning; the *Abhidharma* refutes it by stating that such a position violates correct principle (*nyāya*).
The various masters do not accept that [the roots of goodness] are not produced through hearing or reflection, because they are factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Therefore, it is said that the first three roots of goodness arise for the first time in the three continents. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "For what reason can they not arise for the first time among the gods? It answers:

"Because in those places there is no superior attention (*manasikāra*) such as disenchantment (*saṃvega*) and so forth. It further asks: "Is there not superior attention such as disenchantment and so forth in the evil destinies (*durgati*)?"
Why do these roots of goodness not arise [there]? Answer: In the miserable realms (durgati), there is no superior physical basis (āśraya).

Even if there were superior renunciation (nirveda), if there were also a superior physical basis, then one would be able to first give rise to them. Among humans, both conditions are present; therefore, they can first give rise to the fourth root of goodness.
As for the gods, they too can first give rise to them. Since it is only a single moment (ekakṣaṇa) that does not arise, once it has arisen, it must be called "first" among the gods.
Since it is admitted that one enters the Noble Path from within [the stage of Heat], the gods first give rise to this wholesome state.

Regarding the statement that "one who possesses the preceding roots of goodness attains both," this means that if one attains one [root], the others are merely accomplished (*samanvāgata*) but do not necessarily arise simultaneously;
therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "The Heat produced in a female body is both attained, present in the body, accomplished, and manifested; as for the male body..."

Having attained "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), it is not present within one's own continuum; rather, its accomplishment is non-manifest. As it is said regarding the dharma of Heat, so it is for the Summits (*mūrdhan*) and Patience (*kṣānti*).

For men, this is stated accordingly: because these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are identical, they are mutually attained. Regarding the statement that one attains the "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female body:

this means that if one was originally a male body who has subsequently realized the state of an Arya, there is no further transformation into a female; thus, with respect to the female body, one attains non-analytical cessation.
If cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) were originally female, it would not be the same as this [case], because an Arhatī remains female even after attaining sainthood.
If one was originally a woman, after realizing the state of an Ārya, she may be transformed into a man; thus, while the fourth category of women can attain two [results], men can attain only one.

Regarding "transmigrating to a higher stage," it is like being in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and, relying on the first dhyāna, giving rise to the stages of *uṣmagata* and so forth, thereby producing the first [fruit].

While in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is not called "losing the stage" because one remains identical with the fundamental basis; only when one is born into the second dhyāna is it called "transferring to a higher stage.
If one dies in this stage and is reborn in this same stage, it is said that one does not relinquish [the attainment], because the noble ones possess the support of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*);

thus, although they die, they do not relinquish it until they must transfer to a higher stage. It is only at the moment the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the higher stage arises that it is relinquished.

Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) also relinquish [the roots] through falling away (*parihāṇi*) in the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*; this is because these two are "shakable" roots of goodness (*cala-kuśalamūla*), and thus there is also relinquishment through falling away.
By analogy, the loss of the stage (*bhūmi-hāni*) applies only to the noble ones (*ārya*) who fall away, whereas death (*cyuti*) as the cause of relinquishment applies only to ordinary persons.

Regarding the statement that one must necessarily see the truths (*satyadarśana*) based on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*): this means that if one gives rise to the four roots of goodness based on the fundamental stage, one will necessarily fulfill them within three lifetimes and then, in the subsequent birth...

Regarding those who enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) while arising in the *anāgamya* stage or the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) through the development of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, it is not necessarily the case that they will realize the Truths (*satyadarśana*) within this very life;
this is because their balance of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) is uneven, and their mind of revulsion toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is not intense.

Furthermore, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, there is likewise no falling back from "Heat" or "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) when they arise in the fundamental dhyānas. As for the statement that these must be attained through great preparatory effort (*prayoga*), this refers to...
Because they have not previously practiced, the time for their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to reach fruition is brief;

this is unlike other contaminated concentrations (*sāsrava-samādhi*), which require great effort to arise because they have been cultivated since beginningless time. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Even regarding what was previously abandoned, there is no reverence.
As for the phrase "encountering a teacher who has attained the stage of realization and who skillfully expounds the Dharma," it means knowing that the person before one possesses roots of goodness.
Having understood their stage, once they have attained the stage of *ūṣmagata* (Heat), one explains to them the stages of *mūrdhan* (Summits) and so forth.

As for the statement that there is no prolonged transmigration: while those in the preceding stage of *mokṣabhāgīya* (Aids to Liberation) attain the state of an *ārya* at most after three births, those in the present stage of *nirvedhabhāgīya* (Aids to Penetration) attain it as quickly as in this very life.
This is because these [stages] give rise to superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "although there may be regression, etc.," the term "etc. includes the possibility of performing unwholesome karma and so forth;

however, this differs from the previous case in that the roots of goodness are not severed, while the rest remains the same. One must carefully examine the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Principles of Reasoning).

Taking the sublime qualities of the Triple Gem as the gateway, one generates pure faith. As for the statement, "From those born from eggs or moisture... until attaining non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)," it is precisely [as follows]:

Regarding the theoretical explanation: those born from eggs or moisture are generally characterized by great ignorance; the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Great Brahmā realm are abodes of distorted views;

the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*) lacks direct realization (*abhisamaya*); the *kaṇṭha* (or *kaṇḍu*) and similar beings possess manifold afflictions (*kleśa*); a noble one (*ārya*) will certainly not undergo an eighth existence;

and afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) would necessarily not arise [in such states]. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* states that the physical forms of the *kaṇṭha* and others are as follows:

Because they are base and lowly, these are the evil destinies among humans; once the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) is attained through superior roots of goodness, one will certainly not undergo further rebirths.

(The commentary explains that the mention of the "eighth existence" merely excludes the desire realm and does not exclude the higher realms, because those who ascend in succession (*ūrdhvasrotas*) undergo many births. As for the statement that the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) leads to the departure from birth, it is still contaminated (*sāsrava*);

therefore, while remaining an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) at the present moment.

Leading [the mind] toward the state of arising is called "entry" (*praveśa*). The Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is like the path of non-interruption (*anantaryamārga*), while the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is like the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*);

these two together abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). However, because the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering has not yet been fully accomplished at the moment it is currently arising, one is not yet called a noble one (*ārya*).
Because it arises immediately following [the preceding state], it is called "immediately antecedent" (*samanantara*).
It is said that those at the two stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit) may turn toward Buddhahood because those at the stage of *mūrdhan* can still fall into the evil destinies.

If one who has not yet planted the seeds for the Buddha-vehicle’s factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) within the Śrāvaka lineage should turn toward the Buddha-vehicle, they will do so after three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and a hundred eons have passed since the arising of those *uṣmagata* and other stages.
If one turns toward the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, it is after a hundred eons have passed since the arising of those *uṣmagata* and other stages.

Since all [Bodhisattvas] attain enlightenment while seated upon a single throne, this discussion regarding "turning back" (*parāvṛtti*) or "not turning back" (*aparāvṛtti*) concerns only the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).

Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* discusses turning back or not turning back in relation to the preceding stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-dharma*). As for the statement that a Bodhisattva who seeks to benefit others must necessarily fall into the evil destinies (*apāya*), the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
because a Bodhisattva exclusively pursues the task of benefiting others, they make a great vow (*mahā-praṇidhāna*) out of a desire to rescue and deliver infinite sentient beings.
Because one adorns the *Sūtra* over immeasurable eons, one goes to the evil destinies as if to a garden; were it otherwise, there would be no possibility of attaining Buddhahood.
Regarding the statement that those at the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* may still turn away from the path to become *pratyekabuddhas*:

this means that since *pratyekabuddhas* do not go to the evil destinies, their stage of *kṣānti* can still be diverted [toward that goal]. By analogy with this, it is also possible for those in the "Worldly Supreme Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) stage to divert themselves toward becoming *pratyekabuddhas*. However—
Because time is short, it cannot be diverted. Regarding the "rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddha," this distinguishes them from the "group-dwelling" type;

as explained in the case of the śrāvakas, the group-dwelling type can be diverted, whereas the rhinoceros-like type has no possibility of diversion, its meaning being identical to that of a Buddha. Therefore, the treatise states:
"There are other pratyekabuddhas who, unlike the rhinoceros metaphor, may give rise to the first two roots of goodness of their lineage and turn toward another vehicle."
In principle, there is no obstruction to the statement that [the practitioner] proceeds from the stage of *uṣmagata* until reaching *bodhi*. As the treatise states:
"Other masters say that from the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one does not rise from one's seat until the attainment of *bodhi*."
Regarding the statement that "the maximum is three lifetimes," it is, for example, like a field: first the seed is sown, second the sprout forms, and third the fruit ripens;

these three stages are distinct. The cultivation of the path is likewise: in the first lifetime one enters the *dharmatā*, in the second lifetime one achieves [realization], and in the third lifetime one attains liberation.
The Correct Principle (*Nyāya*) states: "In the first lifetime, one produces the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); in the second lifetime, one achieves..."
Regarding the third life, one arises in the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and immediately enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

If it is claimed that one arises in the aids to penetration in the second life and enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*) in the third life, such a statement would contradict what was previously stated— namely,

that those who give rise to "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and the other stages based on the fundamental dhyānas must necessarily enter the vision of the truths in that very same life, or else they must admit [the possibility of doing so] at the very fastest.

The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* offer this defense: those who rely on the fundamental dhyāna stages (*maulabhūmi*) to give rise to the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages must have already given rise to them in a previous life;
alternatively, it may be that one is only able to rely on the fundamental stages to give rise to them in the fourth life.

However, by speaking of the "maximum speed" and "maximum slowness," it is shown that there is no fixed standard for the number of intervening lives. Regarding the statement that the three types of karma constitute its essence, the treatise says: "Although..."

Since the most excellent [roots of merit] consist solely of mental action (*manas-karman*), yet this volition (*cetanā*) also encompasses the arising of bodily and vocal actions, they are thus designated as "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*) and are understood to comprise all three types of action.
Furthermore, the treatise states that one plants these roots of goodness upon encountering a Buddha appearing in the world;

other masters say one may also encounter a Pratyekabuddha (the commentary explains that both the Buddha and his teaching are termed "the world of the Buddha"). Regarding the mention of "giving a single meal" or "observing a single precept," it refers to... [the Bodhisattva] Po.
Śāriputra said: "There are those who, by giving even a single morsel of food or a single tooth-stick, are able to plant the seeds of liberation, such as Cāṇūra and others.
They make this vow: 'May I, by means of this, certainly attain liberation.
On the other hand, there are those who, despite hosting a great *vaiśvadeva* assembly, are unable to plant the seeds of liberation, such as Aghamaṣa."
"Equal to them" means that some who practice giving seek only worldly wealth, nobility, and fame, rather than seeking liberation;

or some may observe the eight precepts for a single day and night and thereby plant the seeds of liberation, while others may observe the precepts for the duration of their lives yet fail to plant the factors conducive to liberation.
(The above concludes the seven stages of skillful means.)

From here below, [the text] distinguishes [the stages] according to the noble levels (*ārya-bhūmi*). Next, regarding the knowledge of the dharma (*dharma-jñāna*): this contemplation involves the sixteen moments of mind (*citta*) that cycle through the eight truths of the upper and lower realms.

The *Nyāyapravēśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states: "Since one repeatedly cycles through and agitates the objects of the four noble truths within the three realms, how could this not constitute an obstacle to clear realization (*abhisamaya*)?
In the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*), one frequently reverses [one's understanding] regarding the objects of the various truths."

Because it has already become thoroughly matured through revolving, the phrase "taking the subsequent outflow as the distinguishing mark" means that while the fourth root of goodness, *kṣānti* (patience), is of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) nature, the *kṣānti* in this context is of an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) nature.
Fearing confusion with the former *kṣānti*, one cites the fruit of *dharmajñāna* to reveal its uncontaminated nature and distinguish it from the former *kṣānti*.
That is to say, this [state] is able to produce *dharmajñāna*, and thus it is the cause of *dharmajñāna*.

The "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) is named after it, like a tree bearing flowers and fruit. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: This untainted receptivity takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object and is thus called "receptivity to the knowledge of the phenomenon of suffering" (*duḥkhadharmakṣānti*).

It means that regarding the phenomena of suffering, which have been deludedly grasped as "self" and "mine" by the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) since beginningless time, one now for the first time perceives them as being solely the nature of suffering;
this present state of patient acceptance is called "receptivity to the knowledge of the phenomenon of suffering. Question:

Regarding the eight truths of the upper and lower realms, why is suffering in the desire realm observed first? The *Vibhāṣā* explains: "The desire realm is not a stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*);
therefore, it is observed first. Since the [suffering] of the two upper realms is both subsumed under stages of meditative concentration, they are observed together later.

It is said that the subsequent object and cognition are established with the name "subsequent" (*anvaya*) because they are of the same category as the preceding ones; for example, the knowledge of suffering in the upper realms is of one category with the knowledge of suffering in the desire realm.

Because they are identical, they are termed "categories" (*jāti*). Furthermore, the commentary concludes by stating that subsequent [moments] follow and verify the preceding object; thus, the meaning of this "patience" (*kṣānti*) is also the same as previously explained.
Regarding the statement that "there are three types," this describes the distinctions among the three types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

Only wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to see; other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), not being of the nature of wisdom, cannot see the truths and are therefore merely called "conditions" (*ālambana*). As for the fourth...
Because the factors of equality (*samāna*) are not mental states (*caitta*), they cannot take objects as their cognitive domain;

yet, because they perform the same function as wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others, they are termed "realization of the task" (*kṛtyābhisamaya*). Thus, wisdom possesses three names, while associated factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*) possess two, and the factors of equality possess only one.
The statement, "Alternatively, from the view-afflictions up to 'unable to reach full maturity,'" constitutes the second explanation regarding their arising.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Furthermore, because the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other [afflictions] are stubborn and difficult to subdue, like the wildness of a beast, they are called 'birth' (*jāti*).

Regarding the statement that these two explanations are the same as the former, it means that the basis (*āśraya*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the object (*karman*) are identical to the previous case of "entry into the state of rightness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

To examine the term "rightness" (*samyaktva*) in detail, it generally encompasses both *nirvāṇa* and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); however, entry into the state of certainty (*niyāma*) refers exclusively to the latter.

Since both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation] involve direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), both of these names apply to both interpretations. Regarding the designation "entering" (*praveśa*) for the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, the treatise states:
"Once this receptivity has arisen, one obtains the name of a noble one (*ārya*); because it exists in the future, it abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

The commentary explains: "Just as when a lamp arises, it is precisely at that moment capable of extinguishing darkness; once it is established, the darkness is already extinguished. Likewise, when the characteristic of arising appears, it is precisely at that moment capable of producing the dharma."
At the time it has already arisen, this patience (*kṣānti*) also correctly abandons the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) at the very moment of its arising;

since it has already been abandoned by the time one abides [in it], it is said that "it is not obstructed by the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions. This means that at the time of severing the afflictions, the substance of the affliction does not manifest, but rather their acquisition is severed;

thus, it is said to be unobstructed by acquisition. The *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) raises an objection, stating: "The Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrakāra*) explains that this refers to the acquisition of the severance of the afflictions."

If it is argued that it is called the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*) because nothing can obstruct it, then the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) should also be called "uninterrupted," since it too cannot be obstructed when it arises simultaneously with the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*). Therefore, it should be explained as follows:

it is called "uninterrupted" because there is no interval; being uninterrupted, it is the path, hence it is the "uninterrupted path. This is because no other path of the same class (*sajāti-mārga*) can act as an interval between them.

This means that while the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*)—which do not serve as conditions for the continuity [of defilements] regarding the path of liberation—are each limited to a single moment, the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) may either be single moments or continuous.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is likened to a pursuer of thieves, signifying that the afflictions are driven out from the body;
knowledge (*jñāna*) is likened to one who closes the door, signifying that the afflictions are prevented from re-entering the body.

To say that the first fifteen moments of mind are called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) refers to the fifteen moments from the "patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvaya-kṣānti*) onwards.

"Patience" (*kṣānti*) is termed "seeing" (*darśana*), while "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is termed "wisdom" (*jñāna*). By the time one reaches the fifteenth moment, one has already seen the principle of each and every truth;

thus, there is nothing previously unseen. Although one knows the eight truths, one has not yet attained complete mastery of them. Here, we clarify the Path of Seeing and do not clarify [the Path of Meditation].

Because one knows [the truths], there is no fault. If it is said that "knowing" refers to the sixteen aspects being fully encompassed, this is an illustration provided by way of analogy to explain the meaning:

just as other paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are called "cultivation" because they have been previously seen, so too this sixteenth moment is called "cultivation" because it has also already been previously seen.
To say that "this refers to the truths (*satya*) and not to the moments (*kṣaṇa*)" means:

Regarding the analysis of whether [the path] is pervasive or non-pervasive based on the eight truths, rather than the sixteen moments of mind, it has already been seen that the path of the higher stages is boundless;
since only one moment remains unseen, how could it be called "not yet having seen the truth" based on such a small portion?
Therefore, the treatise states: "Furthermore, because the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) is subsumed under the category of the fruit-path, one again cultivates the eight truths."

Because it possesses the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*), because it abandons the previous path, because it arises in a continuous succession, and because it is like other paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),

it is not included within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Regarding the statement that "it arises in the interim before the truths have been fully known," this refers to the arising of the seven knowledges (*jñāna*) during the interval while one has not yet reached the ultimate realization of the eight truths.
Regarding the meaning of "practicing in accordance with the words of others": this refers to first believing that others are correct, and then initiating practice by following that faith;

thus it is called "following-faith practice" (*śraddhānusārin*). Because one's prior actions consist solely of following the words of others rather than personally investigating the teachings, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"By means of faith as a precursor, one first enters the Noble Path. Such a type of person (*pudgala*) has been so from the very beginning.

Because his nature is largely characterized by faith, if he hears others exhorting him, "You should engage in agriculture to sustain yourself," he does not reflect upon whether it is appropriate for him to do so or not;
rather, if it is appropriate, he acts upon it, and if it is inappropriate, he desists.
Upon hearing such things—even regarding traveling with merchants, serving kings, or training in writing, arithmetic, and various arts—he likewise acts in accordance with the Dharma.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that up until the point where one enters the Noble Path by means of wisdom first, such a type of *pudgala* has, from the very beginning, possessed a nature characterized by abundant wisdom.

Thus, if they hear another exhorting them, "You should engage in agriculture to sustain yourself," they immediately reflect and examine whether this is something they ought to do or ought not to do, and so forth. This refers to the period prior to [the attainment of the Path].

Regarding those who sever the afflictions of the cultivated path (*bhāvanā-heya*) through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*): this refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who, while at that stage, have not yet used the six types of contaminated contemplations (*sāsrava-ṣaḍākāra*) to sever the afflictions.
Upon reaching the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they are termed "candidates for the first fruit" (*prathamaphala-pratipannaka*);

this means that from the stage of "patience with suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the fifteenth moment of mind, they are collectively called "candidates" (*pratipannaka*) and not yet "fruits" (*phala*). As for the mention of "sixty-four persons," this refers only to those starting from the third candidate.
The treatise states: If one includes both the first and second stages of the path of approach (*pratipannaka*), there are seventy-three persons who are all on the path of approach;
this is because this chapter establishes [the practitioners] based on fifteen moments of mind, and thus they have not yet attained the fruit (*phala*).
Regarding the statement that one abides in the fruit by following the three inclinations (*trīṇi mukhāni*), the treatise says:

"The fruit of Arhatship can never be attained for the first time [by one following these inclinations], because there is no possibility of abandoning the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and because the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) cannot effect liberation from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Therefore, the fourth fruit [Arhatship] can never be attained for the first time [in this manner].

Regarding the term "faith-understanding" (*śraddhādhimukta*), the *Vibhāṣā* states: "It refers to obtaining faith subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) based upon faith subsumed under the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)."

Regarding "resolute confidence" (*adhimokṣa*): it is also called "attaining the fruit through reliance on and orientation toward faith," and it is also called "liberation of the mind preceded by faith, thereby being freed from the three fetters," hence it is named "one liberated by faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*).

Regarding "one who has attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*): it is also called "attaining the vision subsumed under the path of cultivation by relying on the vision subsumed under the path of seeing," and it is also called "liberation of the mind preceded by vision, thereby being freed from the three fetters," hence it is named "one who has attained through vision"; furthermore, it is [defined] by means of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because right view is manifested through the power of predominance (*adhipati-bala*). Regarding "that which is reached," it is as explained in the commentary.

As for the statement that "the two noble ones—those of faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)—increase in faith and wisdom respectively," in reality, faith increases for the former and wisdom increases for the latter. The term "mutually" (*itaretara*) is used here to indicate that they do not possess both qualities;
thus, "mutual increase" does not mean they see each other like people facing one another from east and west.

Regarding the statement "the path of superior fruit has not yet arisen," the *Nyāyānusāra* says: "Furthermore, it is not the case that at the very moment of attaining the fruit, there arises the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) from the afflictions abandoned by the path of superior fruit;
for the patience regarding the category of the path (*mārga-jñāna-kṣānti*) cannot induce that acquisition of disjunction.

Based on this, the previously abandoned afflictions, according to their respective antidotes, give rise to a further superior path which induces the acquisition of disjunction; this is what constitutes the 'path of superior fruit'."
The statement that "not all stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) undergo seven returns" means that there are also those among them who attain *nirvāṇa* before completing the seven [returns].
Regarding the explanation of the term "stream-enterer": the various untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) are collectively termed "streams" because these untainted paths flow toward *nirvāṇa*.
To "enter" (*prati*) for the first time and thus obtain [the name] is what was previously called "entering" (*praveśa*).
The meaning of "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*) is likewise the same. To say that it should refer to the eighth [stage] means that the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* occupies the eighth position;

thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun) states that the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is called the "ground of the eight persons. Furthermore, an ancient interpretation states that among the four candidates and four fruits, counting from the last toward the first, the first candidate is the eighth;
thus the *Vibhāṣā* says that the "eighth noble one" refers to those practicing through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those practicing through dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

Since it is the eighth when counted from the most excellent [fruit], neither this chapter nor the new commentary provides this interpretation. Regarding the fact that the Once-returner and Non-returner fruits are not necessarily attained for the first time:

if one attains them through "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*), they are attained for the first time; if one proceeds through the "gradual sequence" (*anupūrvin*), they are not attained for the first time.
As for this fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), it cannot be said that it has already been attained [previously]; because it must necessarily occur at the beginning, it is called "the first."

To establish this: first, for one who has attained both the path of approach (*pratipannaka*) and the fruit (*phala*), among the sixteen moments of mind, the first fifteen are the path of approach and the sixteenth is the fruit;

therefore, they possess both paths. Second, for one who has attained both the untainted (*anāsrava*) paths of seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*), since the sixteenth moment is the path of cultivation, they likewise possess both paths. Third, [this applies] throughout the sixteen moments of mind.

"Attainment" (*prāpti*) refers to the attainment that reaches the body through traversing all sixteen moments of mind; it does not mean that the name "attainment" is applied simply because one has attained the fruit.
Regarding the statement that the eighth [moment] lacks all three meanings: first, it is merely the path of approach (*pratipannaka-mārga*) and thus lacks the path of fruition (*phala-mārga*);

second, it consists solely of seeing (*darśana*) and thus lacks cultivation (*bhāvanā*); third, it is merely the first moment and has not yet traversed the sixteen moments of mind. Although it is indeed the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*), it is not termed "entry."

Regarding the "fruit of the stream-winner" (*srotāpanna-phala*), because it is said that "all [attain] seven [lifetimes] at most," those who speak of "at most seven births" (*sapta-kṛtvah-parama*) are discussing them collectively.
Although there are four types of "seven births" and so forth, because they all consist of seven, the term "seven births" alone encompasses them all. This is like a "seven-leaf tree" (*saptaparṇa*):

although every individual branch has seven leaves, one does not say there are only seven [leaves in total]; rather, because the number on each is equal, one simply says "seven. According to the treatise, this refers to the "seven births" (*sapta-janman*).

This is stated in reference to one realm (*gati*), not two realms; furthermore, it refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not the higher realms, because for an *ūrdhvasrotas* *anāgāmin* who reaches the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there can be an eighth birth.

Because of the great power of its four limbs, the snake does not diminish [its stride] beyond seven steps; because of the force of its venom, it does not exceed seven steps.
Regarding quartan fever—formerly called "various fevers"—the times of their onset differ: some manifest for half a day and do not manifest for the other half;
some manifest for one day and do not manifest for the next; and some are extremely slow, manifesting on the first, second, or third day.

If it does not manifest until the fourth day, it will inevitably manifest by the nature of things (*dharmatā*); this is called "malaria of the fourth day. The Noble Path (*āryamārga*) is also like this:
by the seventh birth, one will necessarily sever the remaining afflictions and attain *parinirvāṇa*.

This takes the extremely slow limit of the natural order as a metaphor for the seventh [birth], rather than taking the literal number as a metaphor for the correct principle. It is refuted by saying: "It is like being bitten by a 'seven-step' snake"—this is the metaphor.

Not so. For those whose lifespan is fixed, they may continue to abide even beyond this limit; thus it is said that this is a natural law (*dharmatā*), such that the power of poison does not extend beyond seven paces.

for example, while fire can burn and water can drown—both of which can kill a person—Jyotiṣka was not burned by fire and Sāriputra did not drown when mindful of the Buddha. How could this be the nature of fire and water?
Is this not an analogy? Regarding the statement that one naturally acquires the physical form and appearance of a bhikṣu by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* says:

"For example, five hundred sages were practicing the path on Mount Iṣigiri. Originally śrāvakas, they appeared in a Buddha-less age; a monkey manifested the appearance of a Buddha’s disciple to them, and they all followed his example.

Because it possesses the characteristics of the Path: first, by not producing or growing karma that leads to decline and downfall—meaning one does not create new karma for the miserable realms;

second, by opposing the production and fruition of such karma—meaning that previously acquired indeterminate karma for the miserable realms cannot yield its fruit, as one who possesses determinate karma for them cannot attain the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*);
third, by possessing powerful roots of goodness—meaning those which are untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is a root of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). Fourth, one who possesses both pure preparatory application (*prayoga*) and pure intention (*āśaya*) attains the restraint of non-action (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*).

Fifth, regarding the statement that "even the states of miserable rebirth (*durgati*) do not arise for one who possesses patience": this is an illustration of the inferior by means of the superior (*hīnena viśiṣṭopamā*), and it is interpreted in two ways.
First, because one does not fall into the miserable rebirths due to patience, the karma of the miserable rebirths cannot produce [the arising of] patience-virtue.

How much more so for one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry? Second, it is said that "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the non-arising of karma leading to the miserable realms; thus it is called "the patience of non-arising.

Furthermore, according to the previous interpretation, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Although those who are stream-enterers have not yet permanently abandoned the fetters to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they have already permanently abandoned the fetters to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Lacking but a single factor of the provisions [for rebirth], they do not fall into the miserable realms, just as a cart [cannot proceed] if it lacks one wheel."
A two-wheeled vehicle can carry a load, and a bird with two wings can fly through the void; if either is missing, success cannot be achieved.
This is likewise the case here: therefore, one who has attained the stream-entry (srotāpanna) does not fall into the evil destinies.
