Furthermore, whether the births one undergoes are many or few, all the karma that draws forth such birth was created while one was an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not during the stage of an *ārya*.

Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that one does not create new projecting karma, because one has turned one's back on saṃsāra and is directed toward nirvāṇa. It is said that there is certainly no case where even one great category (*mahāpakṣa*) of defilements remains unsevered.

Regarding those bound by existence and subject to birth and death, because the mind directed toward the fruit of rebirth is powerful, if one [link] is severed, necessarily three are severed; if five are severed, necessarily six are severed.

According to the traditional interpretation, even for those who have severed one grade or two grades, or five grades, and are permitted to fall back or emerge from meditative absorption, there is still no birth and death.
As for the term "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula), it is called "house-to-house" because they are not born into a single family. It is said that they may be reborn in two heavens.

Regarding "places," this refers to the differences between celestial realms such as Cāturmahārājakāyika and Yāma. As for the phrase "or two continents," this refers to places such as the eastern and western continents;
according to the *Śāstra*, it is permitted that within a single celestial realm or a single continent one may undergo three or two births.
The *Pāṣa* (Vibhāṣā) is the same in this regard, for that treatise states: "In one celestial realm, or two celestial realms, or three celestial realms, one undergoes one [birth]."
Regarding the "two or three births," it is further stated that one may be born as a *deva-kula-kuśala* (family-to-family deva) in one, two, or three families, or for one, two, or three births.

As for the "two or three [births] among the devas" and so forth, these refer to the variations of the family-to-family (*kulaṃkula*) type. According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, there are also cases of the "two or three [births] among the devas" type of family-to-family.
Now, upon careful examination, if the number of births among the devas is not equal [to the number of families], it is not classified as family-to-family.

Those who attain the Path among humans and enter *nirvāṇa* in the heavens are named after that place of *nirvāṇa*. As for those of "equal birth," they attain the Path in the heavens and also enter *nirvāṇa* in the heavens;

they are named according to these two meanings of attaining the Path and entering *nirvāṇa*. Regarding all "house-to-house" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioners, there is no discussion of their initial attainment of the Path or their birth;
rather, all [categories] are explained in terms of the births they undergo after having already attained the state of an *ārya*. New [practitioners] are not included here.
The statement that one who has abandoned three or four grades [of afflictions] will undergo three or two births is also made from the perspective of the maximum limit;

it is not that there are no cases where fewer than three or two births are involved. If one who has abandoned three grades, after passing through one birth, completely severs the remaining fetters and enters *nirvāṇa*, this is also included within the category of "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) over three births.
The principle for the "family-to-family" over two births is the same. Regarding the phrase "in the third birth":
Regarding the exhaustion of afflictions (*kleśa*), in principle, one must indeed sever the afflictions of the upper realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*) before realizing *parinirvāṇa*.

As for the statement that one returns once more to the human realm and then attains *parinirvāṇa*, this refers to a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone rebirth and will not go to be born in other realms;
because they attain *parinirvāṇa* upon their subsequent birth in this very realm, the treatise states: "Beyond this, there is no further birth. However, this...

In this chapter, the stages of the candidate for the fruit of Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka) and the fruit itself (sakṛdāgāmi-phala) are explained as consisting of three categories: first, the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula); second, the candidate for the fruit of Once-returner; and third, the fruit of Once-returner.

Regarding the statement that "the meaning is as previously explained," it refers to the explanation given earlier concerning the "family-to-family" practitioner. As for the phrase "transcending those ninth-grade afflictions" and so forth:
"Flowing fruit" (*nisyanda-phala*) refers to the fact that the subsequent moments of those afflictions do not continue; thus it is called "transcending the stage of outflow" (*nisyanda-bhūmi*).

"And transcending the stage of maturation" (*vipāka-bhūmi*) means transcending the stage of maturation produced by those delusions, just as one who has abandoned desire does not undergo the fruits of the desire realm.
Because the severance of these delusions possesses this superior capacity, even a single grade of delusion can act as an obstacle to the attainment of the fruit, though the specific obstacles differ.
Because the Once-returner lacks this superior function, a single grade of affliction cannot obstruct the fruit. Regarding the term "ekavīcika" (one-intervener), the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Vīci is a synonym for 'interval' (*kṣaṇa*). This means that in that stage, there still remains one separation capable of containing one more birth;

because one has not yet attained nirvāṇa and possesses this one interval, one is called an 'ekavīcika'. (The above explains the meaning of "ekavīcika"; the following explains how the person receives that name. As for the word...

Regarding the third candidate (*tṛtīya-pratipannaka*), if this "one-interval" (*eka-vīcika*) lacks the necessary conditions, they are merely termed a "non-returner candidate" (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*).
As for those who pass away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"It refers to a certain class of persons (*pudgala*) who have already attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the fetters of birth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*), but not so regarding the fetters of arising (*abhinivṛtti-saṃyojana*); such persons, within the desire realm..."
When oppressed by the conditions of afflictions, he is able to exert himself to cultivate the superior application for abandoning the remaining fetters.

While his application is not yet complete, he encounters the conditions for death and thus passes away. Due to the power of the fetters that have arisen, he undergoes a material intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
because he is weary of its many sufferings, he relies on the path previously generated to advance and abandon the remaining fetters, becoming an Arhat and attaining parinirvāṇa.
Question: For what reason is there no one among those in training (śaikṣa) who has not yet abandoned desire and greed that attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarābhava)?

Answer: Because the body upon which the intermediate state of the desire realm depends is weak and lacks the capacity for manifold activities. Therefore, while even remaining in the state of the prior existence (pūrvakālabhava), it is already difficult to transcend the phenomena of the desire realm;
how much more so could one transcend the desire realm from within the intermediate state? This is the correct principle regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa after two births (upapadyaparinirvāyin).

The treatise states: There is a certain class of *pudgala* who, because they previously performed and accumulated karma conducive to birth in the form realm, pass away from the desire realm and take birth in the form realm;

because they possess the path of swift progress through diligent cultivation, they do not long after being born before becoming *arhats*, and only upon reaching the end of their lifespan do they enter *parinirvāṇa*.
This is described as "having a remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) with reference to the basis of existence.
One who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth does not attain it immediately after being born, because they lack mastery over their lifespan during that interval.
This treatise also states: "The parinirvāṇa spoken of here refers to that with a remainder of substrate.

The new edition of the treatise provides this explanation immediately following the discussion on *upapadya-parinirvāyin* (attaining nirvāṇa upon birth), rather than providing it after the discussion on *antarā-parinirvāyin* (attaining nirvāṇa in the intermediate state). Therefore, we know that parinirvāṇa occurs within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Parinirvāṇa" means that having attained *sopadhiśeṣa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), one immediately attains *nirupadhiśeṣa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).

It is said that those who possess both "diligent cultivation" (*prayoga*) and "swift progress" (*kṣiprābhisamaya*) attain parinirvāṇa immediately upon being born; therefore, we know that diligent cultivation is accompanied by the ability for swift progress.

Regarding those who have diligent cultivation but lack swift progress: because they possess diligent cultivation, they are called "with effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra*); because they lack the path of swift progress, they abide in "attaining nirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).

Only after a long time did he finally attain it. It is said that those who lack both diligent cultivation and swift progress are equivalent to those who possess application but lack diligence, because they do not cultivate with effort;
thus, they follow after those with application. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"There is a certain class of persons who, previously within the desire realm, by relying on the power of the 'uninterrupted' (*anantarya*) samādhi, sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) and realize the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*)."

Those born later in the form realm who, after a long period, are still able to advance and cultivate the aforementioned type of path to become arhats, are called "those with effort" (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) and "those without effort" (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin);

those who are the opposite of this are [the others]. Regarding the statement that the Sautrāntika interpretation is what the Master accepts, it means that the Master, in his critical evaluation, took the Sautrāntika position as correct.
For those of sharp faculties who are without effort, there exists a swift-advancing path (*kṣiprābhisamaya-mārga*) prior to [their attainment].
Those of dull faculties who practice the path of no rapid progress should be placed later; this is not the same as the position of the [Vaibhāṣika] school.

Furthermore, since those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) obtain the most rapid and supreme grade of the path prior to the path of non-application (anabhisaṃskāra), this serves as proof that those who practice with application (sābhisaṃskāra) abide later.
Regarding those who go upstream (ūrdhva-srotas), although the first four types are born in the higher realms, they attain parinirvāṇa in the very place where they were born and do not ascend further.

Because they possess the meaning of "superior practice" (*ūrdhva-gamana*), those such as the "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) are not termed "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhva-srotas*).
Furthermore, because they only ascend and do not descend, they are called "Upstreamers. Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) may also have an upward flow, they also have a downward flow;
therefore, they are not termed "Upstreamers. Moreover, because the first four types definitely attain *parinirvāṇa* within this very body, they are specifically associated with *parinirvāṇa*.

The term "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) refers to one who is capable of undergoing many births before attaining *parinirvāṇa*; because this is not fixed, the term "attaining *parinirvāṇa*" is not explicitly stated.
As for the statement that they may "retreat and lose the three higher dhyānas due to conditions," this means that if they do not retreat, they would proceed directly to the fourth dhyāna;
therefore, it must be that they first retreat from the higher concentrations, becoming exclusively attached to the flavor of the first dhyāna, and are thereby reborn in the first dhyāna.
Having already [attained the first three], one is now born for the fourth time; this is called "Full Leap" (*skanda*). Regarding the "Half-Leap" (*ardha-skanda*):

a question is raised as to how it can be called a "half-leap" when, in this context, some undergo three births while others undergo fifteen. The answer is: this is called "half" because it is not complete, not because it is the opposite (or complementary) half.
Regarding the statement that one is not born in the realm of the Great Brahma King (*Mahābrahmā*), one interpretation is as stated in the chapter. Furthermore, the *Śāstra* says: "One Teacher."

Therefore, when asked why "excluding the non-percipient beings" (*asaṃjñin*) is not mentioned, the answer is that according to the Sarvāstivāda school, the heaven of non-percipient beings is not established;
thus, it is said that there is no need to exclude them. Regarding the term "universal exhaustion" (*sarva-vyaya*), the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:

because those [beings] universally possess inferior degrees of attachment (*āsvādana*) toward each of the sixteen locations within the four dhyāna stages, this serves as the condition for the arising [of rebirth], starting from the Brahmakāyika heaven.
Because one passes away from each individual celestial realm and only attains parinirvāṇa upon reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven, they are called "those who pass away everywhere" (*sarvasthānacyuta*).

Furthermore, the treatise states: "There is no non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who undergoes a second birth in the very place where they were born, because such a person may seek further progress within that birth rather than remaining equal or inferior.
It is precisely for this reason that the meaning of "non-returner" is fulfilled; they will certainly not return to be reborn there again.
Since they have already been born in their original place, they do not even return there; how much less would they be born in a lower realm?

As for the statement that "those who delight in meditative concentration" (sukha-vihārin) Anāgāmins are included within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*): although these individuals are subsequently born in the Formless Realm, because the sūtra states they were born in the Form Realm, they are categorized as "Upstreamers" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) of the Form Realm and are not called Anāgāmins of the Formless Realm.
Next, it says that there are four types of those who proceed to the Formless Realm (*ārūpya*).
This refers to those who are born directly from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) without passing through the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

To say that these are collectively termed "formless *anāgāmins*" means that the four names—such as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) and so forth—are no different from those previously mentioned; they are not established separately, but are collectively designated as "formless *anāgāmins*.
The only exception is the "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*), which differs from the case of the form realm.

Regarding what is illustrated by the analogies of the three types of fire: it should be understood that the analogies of the small, medium, and large sparks of wood-fire and iron-fire, as well as the distinctions of near, intermediate, and distant, and of swiftness and non-swiftness, are likewise as previously explained.

Question: From the "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyin*) at the beginning, up to the "one who goes upward to the pinnacle" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) at the end, all are established in relation to the three paths of swiftness and so forth;
how do they differ from one another? Answer: Within each of these three, there are their own [subdivisions].

Regarding the discussion of "fast" and "not fast" within these stages, it is because they are like the nine grades of rebirth (*upapatti*); thus, when viewed in relation to one another, there is no error of confusion.

As for the statement regarding "arising in accordance with activity," this means that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a "rebirth" (*upapatti*), but is merely termed an "arising. However, among these, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is the most swift and sharp;

the one who goes upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is slow due to lower afflictions and superior faculties; and the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon being born (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) is of middling faculties due to superior afflictions.
The delusions are equal. Regarding the three types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who go upstream), they are distinguished by means of delusion, faculties, and karma.

As for the *ūrdhvasrotas*, they are "destined for future lives" (*parāyaṇa*) starting from the third birth onwards and continuing through many births; because this duration is broad and long, they are designated as such. Thus, they are distinguished by karma.

Among these, there are two types born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), both of which constitute a single birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*); within these, one cannot further differentiate specific karmic distinctions.

Regarding the statement, "Therefore, these nine [types of] non-returners differ by way of their afflictions and faculties," this refers to those born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and not to those [born there] by way of karma;
thus, the concluding phrase cannot specify "karma. However, when discussing the three types of non-returners, they all possess distinctions in terms of afflictions, karma, and faculties.
Nevertheless, the mention of "distinctions in karma, afflictions, and faculties" within the present verse is stated in terms of their general characteristics.
The treatise says: "If this is so, why does the Sūtra speak of seven 'destinies of the virtuous person' (*satpuruṣagati*)?

Since we have already established that there are nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), why does the Sūtra mention only seven virtuous destinies? Furthermore, regarding the statement that all seven go upward to the higher realms and do not return again:
previously, they were called 'virtuous destinies' in reference to their wholesome conduct; here, they are so named in reference to their upward movement."

The "wholesome destination" (*sugati*) refers to those who do not return, because they proceed only upward and no longer return to lower realms, whereas others do return to lower realms. The new commentary states that the latter interpretation is superior.

If one were to define a "noble person's destination" (*satpuruṣagati*) as merely practicing wholesome deeds, then even those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would qualify, as they too practice only wholesome deeds;
why, then, is this not stated? It is because the Arhat possesses the meaning of "no further birth."

Regarding the statement "one who is weary of birth in the desire realm": because one has previously understood that birth in the desire realm is characterized by painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*), and since even such a brief birth is difficult to endure, one develops a profound weariness toward the long lifespans of the higher realms and thus does not go there;
hence, one attains the state of *anāgāmin* (non-returner). Because one is weary of being born in the upper realms, it is said:

"having undergone birth, the faculties (*indriya*) cultivated through practice have become extremely mature. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Because one has already experienced birth within its own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)."
Because it continues to accumulate the noble path, making it extremely firm and stable, the fourth dhyāna is said to be the most capable;
that is to say, it is the most excellent among all pleasant practices and is free from the eight calamities.

Therefore, one first cultivates the fourth dhyāna and only thereafter cultivates the lower ones. It is said that the intermediate state is with outflows (*sāsrava*), while those preceding and following it are without outflows (*anāsrava*).

The treatise states: "The first two moments resemble the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the third moment resembles the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). The commentary explains:

"The first two [moments] directly sever the hindrances, and thus resemble the path of uninterrupted transition; the third [moment], having already severed the hindrances, resembles the path of liberation.

Because it is easy to enter the contaminated (*sāsrava*) from the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), whereas it is difficult to enter the uncontaminated from the contaminated, one [path of uninterrupted transition] and one [path of liberation] are established."

Regarding the path of liberation, it is said that the cultivation [of the fruit] by a non-returner (anāgāmin) extends from the first three [vimokṣas] up to the exclusion of one who is to be reborn [in the Pure Abodes].
This is stated in terms of general characteristics; however, according to the treatise, it must be analyzed accordingly. Thus the treatise says:

"Among non-returners, those with sharp faculties [cultivate these] for the sake of happiness in the present life and for birth in the Pure Abodes; those with dull faculties also cultivate them for the sake of preventing regression, as they fear falling back."
By thus practicing mixed cultivation, one distances oneself from the meditative attainments associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samādhi*);

therefore, for Arhats who possess sharp faculties, it serves as a basis for happiness in the present life, while for those with dull faculties, it also serves to prevent the arising of afflictions and subsequent regression.

Regarding the second category, from six up to fifteen: these all involve the repeated arousal of the three minds, which, when combined with the preceding, are counted as a renewed cultivation that progressively increases in excellence to constitute the "superior grade" (*uttama*).

As for the statement that they "elicit the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) in successive order," this means that the inferior grade elicits the Avṛha heaven, continuing up to the superior extreme grade which elicits the Akaniṣṭha heaven. The *Śāstra* states that there are others.

The Master says that through the successive predominance of the five faculties beginning with faith, one brings about rebirth in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). (The intention of this Master is that the predominance of faith brings about the first Pure Abode, while the predominance of wisdom brings about the last Pure Abode.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Is the attainment of the five Pure Abodes due to the power of karma or the power of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*)?

If it were by the power of karma, then the mixed cultivation of dhyāna would be rendered futile. If it is by the power of mixed cultivation, [it must accord with] what is taught in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*..."

The contradiction is as stated in that treatise: regarding the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and birth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens by means of karma, it is determined herein that both powers are required, because one is not born there if either one is lacking.

Regarding the statement that one who has "transformed their name" is called a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin): this refers to one who has attained the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmin) and possesses the eight liberations.

Because they have the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) within their body and thus obtain a state resembling nirvāṇa, they are called a "body-witness. Question: Why is he not called a "mind-witness"? Answer:

Because there is no mind [during cessation], and because [the attainment] arises in dependence upon the body, he is not called a "mind-witness. If one follows the Master’s own explanation, it means that [the designation "body-witness"] applies from the time one arises from the meditative attainment of cessation.

Having attained bodily tranquility that closely resembles *nirvāṇa*, and because one has thus realized this bodily tranquility and wisdom is manifest before one, it is called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*).
Regarding the Blessed One’s statement that there are two kinds of fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), the correct principle explains that the Blessed One told Anāthapiṇḍada:
"Householder, you should know that there are two kinds of fields of merit. As for the five types of *anāgāmin*, these are as follows:
In reality, apart from the four paths and fruits mentioned above, there is no separate entity; they are listed together merely because their names and meanings differ.

As for the statement that the extinction attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is not a supporting cause (*āśraya-hetu*), this means it is not the support for those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This explanation of it not being a cause actually implies it is also not a fruit. The Treatise states: "That [attainment] is said to be a coarse distinction of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*)."
If these characteristics are analyzed in this manner into minute divisions, they number in the thousands;
when totaled across five categories, they amount to twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty, as explained in detail in the treatise.

Regarding the statement that it culminates in the severance of the eight grades of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the final stage: this is because one proceeds from the severance of the first dhyāna, then the second dhyāna, and so on, until finally severing the Peak of Existence;
since the ninth grade is termed the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*), it is said to culminate at the eighth grade.
Regarding the phrase "like a diamond, it crushes all": this concentration is firm and sharp, and thus its metaphor is likened to a diamond.
Because the ninth grade of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is most subtle, it is difficult to eradicate;
since this meditative absorption can eliminate them, it is known that it must certainly be able to counteract the remaining afflictions as its most excellent function.

This is just as a great light can dispel subtle darkness, while coarse darkness is necessarily dispelled by even a small light—though because the small light first breaks the coarse darkness, it is said to dispel only the subtle, yet it is not that it lacks the power to dispel the coarse.

One might ask: "If the delusions of view regarding non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) are also the most subtle among those of the nine stages, and the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is able to sever them—thus they should be compared to a diamond (*vajra*)—then how can it be said that the nine grades of these delusions are severed by a single grade?
In response: One should know that the power of those delusions is weak and inferior.

Since the Path of Seeing serves as the antidote for such inferior delusions, it follows that it cannot destroy all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). If there were something capable of destroying them [completely], [it would indeed be like a diamond].
When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) arises, what obstacle prevents it from destroying the remaining afflictions such that it cannot receive the name "diamond-like" (*vajropama*)?

It is said that it can induce the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), which occurs simultaneously with the attainment of the exhaustion of these afflictions. Here, "attainment of exhaustion" refers to the attainment (*prāpti*) regarding the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of the ninth grade [of afflictions];
because the knowledge of exhaustion arises at the same time as this attainment of exhaustion, it is called "simultaneous" (*sahagata*). This is the diamond-like [concentration].

The first interpretation holds that concentration is called "arising" (*utthāna*) because it can induce these two [the attainment of exhaustion and the knowledge of exhaustion] to reach the state of manifestation.

Furthermore, the second interpretation clarifies the meaning of the phrase "concomitant with the attainment of exhaustion" (*kṣayaprāpti-sahagata*) in the context of the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*): it indicates that the knowledge of exhaustion is concomitant with the attainment of exhaustion;

by citing the "attainment of exhaustion," one thereby takes the "knowledge of exhaustion" which is concomitant with that attainment. This latter interpretation is superior. Thus, it is said: "the knowledge of exhaustion arises."
"One who has already attained the fruit of no-more-learning" means that one becomes a no-more-learner (*aśaikṣa*) only when the fruit of knowledge is present;

it is not at the moment of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) that one becomes a no-more-learner. As for the term "no-more-learner," a treatise states: "Because there is nothing further to be cultivated for the sake of attaining another fruit, one receives the name 'no-more-learner'.
This implies that such a person should perform only deeds for the benefit of others. The commentary explains: "It is simply for the sake of attaining benefit."

The faculties and various merits are that which one should train in; however, because there is nothing further to be trained in regarding the attainment of a distinct fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
It is said that one "abandons dull fruits and attains sharp faculties," yet this is not a distinct fruit.

As for the statement that one "should receive offerings from gods and humans," it means that with all fetters and burdens completely extinguished, one is capable of receiving such offerings. Furthermore, the treatise states that the meaning follows from what was previously discussed.

The four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) and the three fruits (*phala*) are all designated as "those in training" (*śaikṣa*), because they constantly train for the sake of attaining the bliss of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). There are three essential requirements for such training, namely:

higher virtue (*adhiśīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*). Furthermore, it is said that they are called "in training" because their intention is not yet fulfilled, just as a traveler briefly rests;

and it is also said that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not called "in training" because they have not yet seen the principle of the Truths (*satyadharma*). Moreover, the treatise states: "The four..."

Regarding the designations for the four fruits, although there are eight names, there are only five actual entities: namely, those abiding in the four fruits and those in the first fruit-directed stage (*pratipannaka*);
this is because the latter three fruit-directed stages are not separate from their respective preceding fruits.

Regarding the statement that "the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) has nothing superior to be sought," if that were so, why would one not rely on the path of that very level to abandon [defilements]? The answer is:
because the afflictions of one's own level increase in accordance with [the path]. Thus, the treatise says:
"If those afflictions increase in accordance with this path, this path can certainly not remedy those afflictions; if the power of this path is able to counteract those delusions, then those..."
Because delusion regarding this path certainly does not increase concomitantly with it, the path of its own stage cannot treat that same stage—just as a person who is bound cannot free themselves.
Regarding the statement that detachment from the defilements of the eight stages occurs through both paths: since there is a higher stage to be sought after, it involves the contaminated path;
the uncontaminated path is likewise understood.
Regarding the statement that each induces two acquisitions of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*):

first, when the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) eliminates afflictions, it is primarily able to induce a contaminated acquisition while concurrently inducing an uncontaminated acquisition, because their functions are identical; the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is likewise.

Regarding the statement that one cannot be free from a lower level because one has already become free from it: this means that since there is no Path in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), one relies on the Unsurpassed (*anāgamya*) stage of the higher realms to abandon its own remaining outflows.

These untainted [paths] exist only in the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*) and not in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*). One attains the higher stages only at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the lower levels;
for this reason, the other stages do not counteract the lower levels.

Regarding the statement that "it is difficult for there to be entry or non-entry when transitioning into a different feeling," this means: if the aspiration for the higher [realms] is strong, one enters;

if the aspiring mind is weak, one does not enter. Furthermore, it is for those practicing dhyāna that there is entry, while for those seeking liberation there is no entry, as explained in detail above.

Regarding the statement that one may give rise to any one of the three modes of activity (*ākāra*) within the three types of practice, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "This is said in terms of what is possible;

it does not mean that every sentient being, at the stage of becoming free from defilements, necessarily possesses all three [modes] in both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "In the path of uninterrupted transition, what is the mode of activity, and in the subsequently arising path of liberation, what is the mode of activity? The critique (*pūrvapakṣa*) says:

This matter is not fixed; following the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) characterized by the aspect of coarseness (*audārikākāra*), one may subsequently give rise to any of the three types of aspects—calmness (*śānta*) and so forth—as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

The same applies to suffering (*duḥkha*) and the other [aspects]. This is because these six kinds of impure (*sāsrava*) aspects arise according to the inclinations of those who are free from defilement (*vairāgya*).
(Based on this, it is not necessary that the upper and lower [aspects] must arise as direct opposites. It is said that they are called "coarse" because they are not tranquil (*aśānta*).
It is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*) because it can only be transcended through great exertion and because it is not pleasant;
it is called an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) because it is not an escape, as it is capable of hindering transcendence of its own level—just as thick prison walls obstruct one's departure.
This is because it is contravened by the heavy burden (*dauṣṭhulya*) of manifold afflictions (*kleśa*).

The statement that "one must necessarily give rise to the knowledge of non-arising" means that this must be determined: after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one must necessarily give rise to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*);
only thereafter does right view arise, and one never again gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Since this clarifies the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it speaks only of the arising of untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) and does not speak of the arising of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); yet in reality, the arising of conventional knowledge is also possible."

Regarding the statement that "all untainted paths constitute the nature of a śramaṇa": this clarifies that one who possesses such a path is called a śramaṇa, thereby indicating that it is the person who is named a śramaṇa.
As for the phrase "because of exerting effort to pacify the afflictions," this explains the etymology of the term *śramaṇa*. The treatise states:
as the Sūtra says, "Because one is able to exert effort to pacify and eliminate various evil and unwholesome dharmas," and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, they are called śramaṇas; however, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cannot be [true] śramaṇas because they are unable to reach the ultimate nirvāṇa without further distinction.

Furthermore, the Correct Principle states: "Although ordinary beings may be able to sever the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), because various faults still remain, they merely find temporary tranquility and do not reach the ultimate; thus, they are not true śramaṇas. It is said that there are eighty-nine such [paths].

Regarding "types" (*prakāra*), this refers to the extensive enumeration; thus the treatise states: "The Sūtra speaks of these distinctions as being fourfold, but in reality, according to their positions, there are eighty-nine and so forth.

As for the phrase "arising of a single type of superior acquisition" (*ekajātīyaviśeṣalābha*), it is because acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not unitary that the term "single type" is used. A new commentary states: "This explains what precedes."

Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) obtained within the preceding fruits, up until the present fruit-stage, there is only a single "possession of the fruit" (*phala-prāpti*) that possesses this unconditioned;
therefore, it is not the case that many unconditioned phenomena are possessed by a single "possession.

As for the statement that "it is not so in other stages," this means that among the eighty-nine [stages], the remaining stages—excluding these four—are not established as fruits because they do not possess the five causes.
Regarding the explanation of the two fruits realized through the mundane path, the first section concerns what is attained and sustained by the untainted [wisdom] of the path of seeing;
the second concerns what is induced and sustained by the untainted [wisdom] of the mundane path. These chapters can be understood by following the text.
The Sūtras also speak of those called *brāhmaṇa*. According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), all śramaṇas are distinct from *brāhmaṇas*;
however, according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the nature of a true śramaṇa previously described is also called *brāhmaṇa*.

"Śramaṇa" means "one who strives and rests," while "brāhmaṇa" means "one of pure resolve"; since both are far removed from afflictions (*kleśa*), their meaning is the same. [In modern terminology, it is rendered as] "one of pure conduct."

This is identical to Jingzhi’s [view]. Regarding the statement that the World-Honored One is called a *brahman*, the *Śāstra* says: "The Buddha is also called 'Tranquil' (*śānta*) and also called 'Cool' (*śītala*.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Silence, meditative concentration, and sublime detachment are termed *brahman*; because the Buddha possesses these qualities, he is given the name *brahman*. Having attained self-awakening, he causes others to awaken;
by turning this over and bestowing it upon others, it is called the *brahma-cakra* (Wheel of Brahmā). As for the phrase "resembling the world":

Regarding the "wheel of intervals" (*antara-cakra*), the *Nyāya* states: "The wheel of the noble king (*cakravartin*) revolves without ceasing; the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is likewise, for there is no interval or rest between them.
Just as the movement and function of the noble king’s wheel are swift, so too is the path of seeing.

To say that one "abandons the preceding truth and takes up the subsequent truth" means that one abandons objects such as suffering (*duḥkha*) and takes up [objects] such as origination (*samudaya*); this demonstrates that the four noble truths are necessarily not simultaneous.

At that time, the descent [of the wheel] subdues those not yet subdued and stabilizes those already subdued; likewise, the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) also descends to subdue what is not yet subdued and stabilizes what is already subdued.

Regarding the statement, "having observed the suffering of the upper realms, one observes the suffering of the lower realms," this follows the sequence of meditative practice (*yogācāra*), wherein one first observes the suffering of the lower realms and subsequently observes the suffering of the upper realms.
Now, here it is merely stated for the sake of linguistic convenience as a summary, saying: "By virtue of this, the Path of Seeing alone..."
It is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). As for "Kauṇḍinya," what was formerly called "Kauṇḍina" is a corruption;
this means "Fire-Vessel," which is his clan name (*gotra*), while "Arjuna" is his personal name. It is also called "First-Knower" because he was the first to realize the Path.

According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, "A" means "non-" and "rjuna" means "like"; thus, Arjuna originally refers to one who first heard the Dharma and was the very first to attain realization among the assembly.
Because it is peerless among those in the middle, it is said that there is none like Ci'en for explaining the surname Kauṇḍinya.

The statement that "the Wheel of Dharma was already turned at the time the Path of Seeing arose" means that since Kauṇḍinya first gave rise to the Path of Seeing, he had not yet initiated the Path of Cultivation;
thus, the claim that the Wheel of Dharma was already turned makes it clear that the Wheel of Dharma exists only within the Path of Seeing. If this were not the case, it would be illogical.

Having said this, "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering," which reveals the Path of Seeing up to the Path of No-More-Learning—this threefold revolution is collectively termed the "revolution of indicating characteristics" (*lakṣaṇānvayaparivarta*), because it reveals the three paths through its words.
Furthermore, some explain that "This is the Noble Truth of Suffering" refers to the "revolution of indicating characteristics," because it displays the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering.
"This should be fully known" refers to the "revolution of exhortation," as it exhorts one to know [it].
Because it is suffering. This has already been fully known; this is the citation that establishes the turning [of the wheel of Dharma]:

"This Truth of Suffering has already been fully known by me; therefore, you too should know the Truth of Suffering. Since this is so, regarding the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering], one should say:

"This Noble Truth of the Origin should be abandoned; this has already been abandoned. Regarding the Noble Truth of Cessation: "This should be realized; this has already been realized. Regarding the Noble Truth of the Path...

One should contemplate this, one should cultivate this, and having cultivated this—within these twelve chapters formed by three turns for each [truth], it is only regarding the Truth of Suffering that they are explained in detail, while the other truths are indicated briefly.
Furthermore, each chapter takes vision (*cakṣus*), knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*) as its four aspects.
Thus, there are twelve aspects across the three turns of each truth. If one follows the *Caturvargika-vinaya*, at each turn, the supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*) is generated.

The six kinds of qualities, such as clarity (*vidyā*), cannot be assigned to twelve aspects (*ākāra*). For this reason, the *Śāstravyākhyā* (Shizong) adopts two interpretations from the section on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of impermanence (*anityatā*) and so forth:
that sight (*cakṣus*), knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*) are all two-fold explanations found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The former explanation assigns these four qualities to the wisdoms (*jñāna*) and patiences (*kṣānti*) of the upper and lower levels of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the latter explains them more generally according to their meaning, clarifying that the former [explanation] applies only to...

After the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one penetrates all three paths. The statement that "the Vaibhāṣika masters teach thus" concludes that their own school [the Sarvāstivāda] maintains it is exclusively the path of seeing.
Regarding the statement that "according to the Sautrāntikas, it is not only the path of seeing," this refers to how the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes the Sarvāstivāda:
"If that were so, since the three turnings and twelve aspects (*triparivarta-dvādaśākāra*) are not exclusive to the path of seeing, how can it be said that they exist only [there]?"
The designation "Turning the Wheel of Dharma" (dharmacakra-pravartana) is established with reference to the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga);

therefore, it is only this [Path], through its three turnings, that can rightly be called the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma (the Master accepts this teacher’s view as correct). Regarding the statement that it causes others to understand the meaning within their own continuums:

this means that the twelve aspects of the dharma, having turned from within one's own continuum, proceed into the bodies of others, causing them to understand the meaning; thus it is called "turning. (The above is from the Sūtra.)

[Commentary on the Section] Furthermore, the Master himself explains: "Alternatively, all noble paths (āryamārga) are the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), because they turn within the bodies of those to be converted.
Since they have already reached the beginning of turning when the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) arises in the continuum of another, it is said that [the wheel] has 'already turned'.

(Note: According to the treatise, from the Sautrāntika school onwards there are two explanations—namely, those of other masters and the Master himself. The former masters discuss this in terms of the teaching (*deśanā*), while the Master applies it to all paths. In this chapter, these are combined into one; however, the underlying meaning is that in reality, all three paths are so named.)

The term "Dharmacakra" (Wheel of Dharma) refers exclusively to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the Path of Seeing is the beginning of the Wheel of Dharma; thus, it is designated by its initial stage and does not depend on the other two paths. Furthermore, the word "already" (*ya*) indicates that [the turning] has already reached the commencement of the revolution.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: When Kātyāyanaputra’s Path of Seeing arose, it was called the "Blessed One’s Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

This is intended to reveal that those [disciples] obtained the turning of the Wheel of Dharma fundamentally through the Blessed One; therefore, this is attributed to the Buddha so that those to be converted may give rise to reverence.
Therefore, if it were not so, the celestial deities would have said that the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma beneath the Bodhi tree;
they would not have proclaimed, "The World-Honored One is now in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Thus, the act of transmitting it to others is here termed "turning."
Regarding the statement that those who attain the first three fruits rely on the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):

this means these fruits are attained solely by relying on the nine bodies of the desire realm—namely, the six heavens of the desire realm and the three continents. As for the fourth fruit, it is attained by relying on bodies throughout all three realms:
nine in the desire realm, sixteen in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), totaling twenty-nine bodies upon which it is realized.

Regarding the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattva-phala*): the statement that there is no path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) above [the realm of form] explains why one cannot attain the third fruit from a higher stage.

There are two aspects to this proof: first, the principle (*nyāya*), and second, the teaching (*śāsana*). This refers to the principle: if one attains the third fruit by becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and if it is through the gradual path (*anupūrva-mārga*), one must necessarily rely on a body within the desire realm;

having already attained the preceding fruit while free from the defilements of the desire realm, one can only then be born in a higher realm. If, however, it is through the leap-over path (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), [it is otherwise].

One who transcends [the lower realms] must necessarily rely on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) to attain the third fruit; since the path of seeing must arise based on a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the third fruit relies exclusively on the desire realm.
As for the statement that there is no disenchantment (*nirvid*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth: first, because there is no disenchantment with suffering;

second, because they are attached to superior bliss. Therefore, there is no path of seeing there. Regarding the scriptural evidence from the teachings below this point, it is stated that the higher realms include both the form and formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).

*Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun Based on the Original Treatise, Fascicle Twenty-five *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun Based on the Original Treatise, Fascicle Twenty-five
Regarding the statement that one may regress from what has been attained upon encountering minor conditions, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle) states:
"This refers to one who has acquired such faculties and abides in them; when these faculties encounter conditions for regression, they regress from what was attained.

One who lacks conditions for regression enters parinirvāṇa, or perhaps through diligent effort attains a superior nature. Regarding the statement that one constantly contemplates self-harm, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Constantly..."
One should reflect in this way: "May I not encounter illness or other such obstacles that cause me to lose my right mindfulness and lead to slackness in my application;

for through such slackness, I would fall away from my progress. By reflecting thus, one may give rise to the thought of self-harm, or consider that it will be only through great hardship that one reaches the superior state.
Regarding "self-protection," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains: "He reflects in this way..."

Reflecting that I am as yet unable to cultivate the faculties for the sake of attaining the state of one who dwells in the Dharma, I shall instead be diligent and heedful in protecting the liberation through wisdom born of self-love; such a category is called "guarding the Dharma.

Regarding "dwelling," this nature neither advances nor retreats when two superior conditions are absent—it simply dwells; however, upon encountering those two superior conditions, it may either advance or [retreat].
Or [there is] regression. Regarding those called "unshakable" (*akopya*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"There is a certain class whose faculties are preeminent, who have mastery over their practice, and who have attained the wisdom of skillful means regarding the abandonment of afflictions and secondary afflictions; they cannot be shaken by any dharma of regression caused by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)," and so forth at length.
These five are collectively termed "those liberated by time" (*samayavimukta*). They should be fully understood as follows:

The term "liberation through waiting for time" (*samaya-vimukti*) is an abbreviation; it is like the expression "butter jar" (which, according to the commentary, abbreviates the initial word "containing" to simply say "butter jar").
Liberation is likewise abbreviated: by omitting the initial word "waiting," it is called "time-liberation. Regarding the six kinds of time, this refers to the *Vibhāṣā* text;

this treatise merely states that one enters meditative absorption only when favorable conditions—such as necessary requisites, freedom from illness, and a suitable location—converge. First, "obtaining excellent robes" means...
Regarding the phrase "this is the time for good robes," this must also be stated as "time" up to the sixth [category], though it is omitted in the section on "time.

If it were not so, could one call things such as "good places" "time"? As for those who speak of "subsequently liberated through non-time" (*akopyadharma*), this refers to the fact that among the six types, the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) occupies the very last position;
thus, by mentioning only its "subsequent" nature, it indicates that it is immovable and will certainly never fall away.

Therefore, it is called "immovable"; because greed and the other afflictions are exhausted, it is called "liberation of mind. Because it does not depend on favorable conditions such as fine robes and the like, it is called "untimely" (*akālika*).
Thus, the Treatise says: "That is to say, samādhi manifests according to one's wish, without depending on the time when superior conditions come together."
To say that the lineage of the "one subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*) must necessarily exist from the outset means that this nature of falling away is the most inferior;
there is no case where one was not previously of this nature and later becomes so.

To say that the one subject to falling away does not necessarily fall away, and so on up to their existence throughout the three realms, is because the names such as "one subject to falling away" are established based on what is possible. Thus, the six types of Arhats are obtained.

The phrase "pervading the three realms" means that if one were to regress from meditative absorption, it would extend even to the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder); this is an explanation by way of contrapositive.

If the regression of the dharmas and so forth were not possible for those who establish [the Arhatship], then only the desire realm would possess the six types of Arhats, while the higher realms would lack the four [types].

Since it is stated that they "possess the six," we know that regression is not restricted to the regression of meditative absorption and so forth. That the higher realms lack the four types of regression and so forth is as stated in the verse:
Regarding this and those who are reborn in the higher realms, since they neither transform their faculties (*indriya*) nor undergo retrogression, one might ask:

"If these four do not exist there, how can it be said that those [beings] possess six types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*)? The answer is: although they do not undergo retrogression, they are nonetheless persons belonging to these lineages; therefore, they are designated as "those subject to retrogression" and so forth.
The statement that "only those of the four lineages, such as the *cetanādharmā*, may fall" distinguishes [them] from the first and last two types:

the first because it is extremely inferior and thus does not fall, and the last because it is immovable (*akopya*). Since only these four possess an inferior nature that can be lost, it is said that the five, beginning with the *parihāṇadharman*, are all susceptible to falling;
whereas the former [statement] concerned the lineage of falling—limited to the four starting with the *cetanādharmā*—this treatise concerns the falling from the fruit itself.

Therefore, although those subject to falling back (*parihāṇadharman*) do not fall back from their lineage (*gotra*), they do fall back from the fruit; thus it is said that "both possess the possibility of falling back.

Alternatively, "both" may refer to the four types [of noble ones] taken together, or to the lineage and the fruit taken together. Regarding the statement that "what is accomplished by the Learners (*śaikṣa*) and Non-learners (*aśaikṣa*) is firm," this means that the support provided by these two paths is extremely stable and solid.
As for those in the stage of Learners who previously resided in a particular lineage during their status as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*):
There is no principle by which one could fall away from this nature, because it is firmly established by both mundane and supramundane paths.

The verse states that those who were not previously included among the "those liable to fall" (*parihāṇadharman*)—namely, the four types beginning with the "thoughtful" (*cetanādharman*)—do not fall away if they existed previously, whereas those who attain it later are admitted to fall away;
thus, the phrase "not previously" is used for qualification. Now, although the nature of being "liable to fall" (*parihāṇadharman*) is necessarily...

Because one who has previously attained [a fruit] may also fall back from it, the phrase "previously" refers only to the *cetanā* (volitional) and other [faculties], and does not concern those subject to falling back (*parihāṇadharman*). The old commentary states that this text’s wording is not definitive;
rather, it speaks from the perspective of the majority. In reality, even for those subject to falling back, there is first the attainment of the fruit, followed by the statement that they fall back.

Regarding the statement that "afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) delude with respect to phenomena (*vastu*), leading to loss of mindfulness and thus falling back," this means that while afflictions of cultivation are delusions regarding phenomena, the afflictions of seeing (*darśana-heya*) which delude with respect to principles (*tattva*) do not [fall back].

The afflictions of the realm of objects (*vastu-kleśa*) and the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) arise from delusion regarding coarse objects; thus they are called "afflictions with objects. The *Śāstra* states:

Furthermore, the afflictions abandoned through cultivation do not arise from deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*), because their nature is dull and obtuse. The afflictions abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) arise from deliberation, because their nature involves investigation and inference.

When a Noble One (*ārya*) does not deliberate upon a coarse object, an affliction of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) arises; it is not so when there is deliberation, as in the case of suddenly [mistaking] a rope for something else.

This means that because the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are like snakes, an Ārya may fall back and give rise to them; however, views (*dṛṣṭi*) cannot arise through such sudden impulse.

If an Ārya reflects carefully, they perceive the principles of the Truths (*satya-dharma*). Therefore, there is certainly no possibility of falling back from what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).

As for the statement that the Mahāsāṃghikas hold that *srotāpannas* can fall back while Arhats cannot, it is because the afflictions of a *srotāpanna* are not yet exhausted and their noble realization (*ārya-adhigama*) is not yet complete.
Therefore, as for why the Arhat is excluded [from falling back]: their afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been exhausted and their noble realization (*ārya-adhigama*) is already complete;

thus, there is no falling back. According to the Sautrāntika school, a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) certainly does not fall back from the fruit. This point regarding the non-retrogression of the Stream-enterer is the same as the Sarvāstivāda school.

However, the point regarding the non-retrogression of the Arhat differs from the Sarvāstivāda school. The Master [Vasubandhu] offers this evaluation: "The explanation of the Sautrāntikas is logical. How is this known to be so?
How is this known through both reasoning and scripture? Regarding scripture, the Sūtra states: "O Bhikṣus, when one abandons the afflictions through noble wisdom, it is called 'true abandonment'...
and so on, up to: "Even those in training (*śaikṣa*) should remain heedful; they are not yet Arhats. How is this known through reasoning?

If an Arhat has not yet produced this path, he would be unable to permanently uproot the seeds of the afflictions, and thus he would not be one whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*). If his outflows were not exhausted, [he could not be an Arhat].

It is more reasonable to say that they are subject to regression; for according to the intention of this school, even Arhats may still regress from the "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

This means that due to the fault of being disturbed by gain and honor (*lābhasatkāra*), there is the possibility of falling away from the abiding in happiness in the present life that has been attained.

Regarding the statement that there is regression from any one of the four types of higher mental states (*adhicitta*) that have been realized: the "four types" refers to the four dhyānas, and "mental states" indicates meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This explains regression from the attainment of the "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

As for the regression of the "unshakable liberation of mind" (*akopyā cetovimukti*) attained through the absence of causes and conditions—meaning the fruit of the unshakable dharma (*akopyadharman*) which is itself non-regressive—how could the unshakable regress from the abiding in happiness in the present life?

Regarding the one who dwells [in the fruit]: since the intent of this question states that one has not regressed from the fruit of the "unshakable and immovable dharma," how could there be a regression from dwelling in the happiness of the present life?
It is answered by means of three types of regression. As for the "immovable" [fruit], it refers to regression in terms of enjoyment (*paribhoga-vihāni*). To this, the questioner asks:
"Since it was stated that Arhats of sharp faculties possess the middle and last two types of regression, why now is it explained solely in terms of the single regression of enjoyment?"

Does this resolve the objection? The answer is: This explains in general that for an Arhat of Immovable Dharma (*akopya-arhat*), there is no "retrogression from what has not yet been attained" with respect to all [attainments] already acquired.

Since it is stated here that he has already attained the four types of mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*), there is no retrogression from what has not yet been attained; however, because the four types cannot manifest simultaneously, there is "retrogression from enjoyment" (*upabhoga-parihāṇi*).

Regarding the statement, "That which one does not do while abiding in the stage of fruition (phalasthāna) will certainly not be done [even later]": this means that after falling away from the fruition, one does not perform the activities for the sake of attaining that fruition;
furthermore, while at the time of the fruition, one neither falls away nor performs such activities. Thus, it is said that "one does not do" what was previously exemplified.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks: "Who is subject to falling away, and who is not? Those who enter the Noble Path by practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*)..."
There may be those who regress from the cultivation of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), but there is certainly no regression for one who has entered the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

Furthermore, in which realm (*dhātu*) or destiny (*gati*) could there be regression? Only in the three continents of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is there regression. Those who attain the fruits of the noble state in the six heavens of the desire realm are called those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*);
therefore, they do not regress, because their superior wisdom and understanding are able to subdue the mind and turn it away from sublime desires.
Because the sphere has entered the Noble Path, some say there is falling away; this occurs due to the lack of necessary conditions or because the physical basis (the body) is unbalanced.

In the abodes of the six desire-realm heavens, neither of these two factors exists. Furthermore, although those of dull faculties who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) may be born there, there is no logical possibility of their falling away from the state of a noble one (*ārya*).

Regarding the nature of each of the five types of regression and so forth, it is said that because those who are immovable do not undergo the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they are simply called "five.
This is explained by means of an analogy, just as one who has first attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"When one in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) cultivates the refinement of faculties, the number of paths cultivated is like the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in the higher realms; for that [refinement] only involves its immediate neighbor..."

Question: Since the path at the time of attaining the fruit is similar [to the path of preparation], do the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) each have nine uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga), as in the case of the refinement of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) for one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?

And do the eight patiences (kṣānti) of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) each have eight uninterrupted paths, as in the case of the refinement of faculties for one in training (śaikṣa)? Answer: Regarding the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (darśana-heya), there are eight truths (satya) across the upper and lower realms; within each single truth, there are naturally nine grades of affliction. However, in this case, they are combined into a single grade and abandoned all at once. Therefore, there are only eight uninterrupted paths.

This is because the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing are abandoned simultaneously according to their respective truths, whereas those to be abandoned by cultivation are abandoned gradually, grade by grade. Thus, while the latter require nine uninterrupted paths per grade, the former require only one. Furthermore, in the case of the refinement of faculties for one beyond training, since the nine grades of afflictions are abandoned simultaneously, there are likewise nine uninterrupted paths. In contrast, for the refinement of faculties for one in training, because the afflictions are abandoned gradually, there are eight uninterrupted paths corresponding to the eight patiences of the path of seeing. Consequently, the analogy does not hold.
When considering a single truth, one uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are established;

however, when not considering different truths, because the nine grades of abandonment are distinguished within a single stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), nine uninterrupted paths and so forth are thereby established.

Regarding the number of uninterrupted and liberation paths explained above, there are differences in quantity between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); yet, if one discusses the preparatory application (*prayoga*), they are uniform—one uninterrupted path and one path of liberation.
Regarding the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the *Śāstra* states that there is one [moment] for each stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
"For what reason is it called 'refining the faculties' (*indriya-saṃcāra*)? It answers: "Because one disciplines the faculties so that they may increase.

That is to say, by the power of the path, one causes the continuity of the faculties to abandon the lower and attain the middle, and to abandon the middle and attain the higher; this gradual enhancement is called "refining the faculties. Therefore, it is called *saṃcāra*.

The term "roots" (*indriya*) signifies the meaning of the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*). The statement that they are "exclusively untainted" (*anāsrava*) clarifies that this refers to noble beings (*ārya*); therefore, they are exclusively untainted.

If ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) were to transform their faculties, it would logically follow that they would possess tainted [faculties]. The statement that they occur "only among humans in the three continents" is because those three continents possess the fear of falling back [from the path];

thus, one cultivates the transformation of faculties there. This is because the evil destinies (*apāya*) and the northern continent (*uttarakuru*) lack the Noble Path, and within the heavenly destinies, it does not exist.

Regarding the statement that because they have regressed, those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) rely on nine stages: when one who is in the stage of no-more-learning refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), it is like attaining the fruit of arhatship;

since attaining the fruit itself is common to all nine stages, the refinement of faculties is likewise common to all nine stages. Regarding the statement that what is attained is only the fruit and it relies solely on six stages:

this means that when one in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) refines their faculties, it is also like attaining the fruit; however, because one cannot attain the fruit of a trainee in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the refinement of faculties [for a trainee] does not occur there.

They do not rely on the formless realms (*ārūpya*) because the first two fruits of one in training (*śaikṣa*) rely solely on the *anāgamya* stage, while the third fruit, that of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), can rely on all six stages.
This is because, according to this intent, the formless realms lack the fruits of one in training; it is not that there are no "candidates" (*pratipannaka*) for those fruits.
Since one who has refined their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) attains only the fruit and not the candidate stage, we know they do not rely on the formless realms. Question: For what reason?

The answer is that when one abandons the path leading toward the fruit (*pratipannaka-mārga*), one attains only the fruit itself; this is because the mind that refines the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) seeks only the fruit.
Thus, what is attained is exclusively the fruit, as the intention is to entirely discard the inferior; for this reason, one abandons the path leading toward the fruit.

Regarding the statement that there are differences based on the nine grades of faculties, such as the "inferior-inferior" and so forth: the *parihāṇadharman* (one subject to falling away) is the most inferior by virtue of the "inferior-inferior" faculty, up to the Greatly Awakened One (*mahābuddha*), who possesses the "superior-superior" faculty.

Regarding the two types of the "immovable" (*akopya*) category: the first refers to those who were originally of sharp faculties and are designated as "non-retrogressive" (*aparihāṇadharman*) without having undergone the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*);
the second refers to those who were initially of dull faculties but later attained [the state] through the refinement of faculties, who are called merely "immovable" and not [by the other name].
Non-retrogression.

Based on differences in their faculties, the next two types of noble beings are established: those in the stage of cultivation who possess dull faculties and an increase in faith are called "those resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*);

those with sharp faculties and an increase in wisdom are called "those who have attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). The meaning is as explained previously. Regarding liberation, it is undefiled by the obstacles to liberation.
Regarding the nature of that which is known [as the obstacle], the *Nyāya* (Principles) states: "What is the essence of the obstacle to liberation?

It is a state of inferior ignorance (*ajñāna*) that is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), which by its very nature can obstruct liberation. By the power of that [ignorance], it acts as an impediment, causing one to lack mastery over those meditative absorptions.
The statement that "each of the three paths has two" means that each consists exclusively of the two types of noble ones: the sharp-witted and the dull-witted.

The first, "bodily witness" (kāyasākṣin), refers to those who have attained through faith (śraddhādhimukta) or through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta); the second, "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta) and "both ways liberated" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), refers to those who are liberated at specific times (samayavimukta) and those who are not dependent on time (asamayavimukta).

Regarding the statement that the designation "learner" (śaikṣa) is considered complete due to three causes: among learners, one is not yet called [perfected] while possessing only the first two fruits.

Because it is complete, the third [fruit] is called "fulfillment of the fruit" (*phala-paripūri*). Since its faculties, meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth may be either attained or unattained, the designation "fulfillment" is established in relation to these factors.
Because the fruit of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa-phala*) is invariably complete, it is not designated as "fulfillment" by way of the fruit itself.

Now, one who attains the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is necessarily a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*); this clarifies that among those in training (*śaikṣa*), fulfillment of this attainment necessarily entails fulfillment of the fruit.
Therefore, the treatise states: "There are no learners [who attain fullness] merely by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or by means of both faculties (*indriya*) and concentration.
Based on this, the two remaining phrases can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the statement that "the path" (*mārga*) refers to the basis for seeking, the previous explanation took "path" as a specific name for a road; here, it is used in the sense of a basis (*āśraya*).

The commentary states that "seeking" (mārga) necessarily relies upon a path, for one seeks nirvāṇa by relying on these four paths; thus they are also called "vehicles" (*yāna*), in the sense of being that which is relied upon for movement. Question: The stages of application (*prayoga*) and immediate succession (*ānantarya*) may be called "paths" as they tend toward nirvāṇa. However, how can liberation (*vimukti*)—which has already reached the stage of excellence (*viśeṣa*) and transcended [the path]—be called a "path"? There are three explanations in the treatise: First, it is said: [The first explanation: ... [text continues] ... It is said: "Because it is the basis for the attainment of nirvāṇa, it is called a 'path'. This means that because one attains nirvāṇa by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Furthermore, because it is the basis for the attainment of the fruit, it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the fruit by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Alternatively, because it is the basis for the attainment of the cessation of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the cessation of outflows by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the state of an Arhat, it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the state of an Arhat by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows, it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the exhaustion of outflows by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the knowledge of non-arising by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the knowledge of destruction by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the state of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the state of a Stream-enterer by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the state of a Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the state of a Once-returner by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the state of a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the state of a Non-returner by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the state of an Arhat, it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the state of an Arhat by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the fruit of Stream-entry, it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the fruit of Stream-entry by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. Or, because it is the basis for the attainment of the fruit of Once-returning, it is called a "path. That is to say, because one attains the fruit of Once-returning by relying upon this, it is designated as a "path. First, because it evolves as a superior grade, similar in nature to the Path; second, because the power of each preceding stage reaches the subsequent ones;
and third, because it enables one to enter the Nirvāṇa without remainder. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on the Correct Principles) states:
"The noble beings of the two vehicles traverse this as their path, swiftly reaching the two types of Nirvāṇa realms."

To say that it is called "ease" (*sukha*) because it proceeds spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) means that what is not difficult is termed "ease," and this does not refer to the feeling of pleasure (*sukhavedanā*).

For example, although the fourth dhyāna lacks the feeling of pleasure, it is still called an "easy path" (*sukhapratipad*); likewise, although the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) lack the feeling of suffering, they are also called "difficult paths" (*duḥkhapratipad*).
The *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) states: "Because it proceeds spontaneously, like riding a boat or raft, it is a 'difficult path'."

Regarding the statement that "walking is like riding a horse on land," when it says that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are unequal, this refers merely to an imbalance in their increase or decrease, not to the presence or absence of untainted (*anāsrava*) states.
