Although the objects of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) regarding phenomena (*dharma*) are vast, they do not take that which is not a truth as their object; therefore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), such as space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), are excluded.

The phrase "excluding its own category" clarifies that there is not a single moment of knowledge that knows all phenomena; although conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) can observe them, it does not know them in their entirety.
Even when one contemplates all things as non-self, one cannot yet observe that the simultaneous dharmas are distinct in their nature as object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*).

Here, "object" refers to the apprehended (*ālambana*), and "subject" refers to the apprehender (*ālambaka*). If conventional cognition were admitted to take itself as its own object, then there would be no distinction between object and subject;
therefore, it cannot be said that they share the same object. For example: [as in the following analogy].

When a multitude of people gaze at the new moon together, they do not see one another; yet, if their conditions correspond, the very act of perceiving that object is lost. The explanation is as follows:

just as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) share a single object of perception (*ālambana*), if the mind-king depends on feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, and those [factors] such as feeling must in turn depend on feeling and so forth, then it constitutes self-perception (*svālambana*).

(End of preceding section) Regarding "not perceiving what is co-existent" (*na sahaja-ālambana*): this means not perceiving the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), such as arising and so forth. As for...

The eye does not see the color-form that supports it (*āśraya-rūpa*) and so forth because they are extremely close together; therefore, these three factors do not constitute the object of this cognition at a single moment.
This [cognition] consists only of that which is produced by hearing and reflection (*śruta-maya* and *cintā-maya*), excluding that which is produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).

The *Śāstra* states: "Because the wisdom produced by cultivation has distinct objects. If it were otherwise, one would have to abandon defilements instantaneously. (The commentary explains: "Because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) takes [all things] collectively as its object, whereas the wisdom of cultivation takes [them] individually; therefore, it is not the wisdom of cultivation. *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
The *Nyāya* school maintains that [this knowledge] also extends to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), which differs from this treatise.

Regarding the attainment of wisdom by way of persons, there are three stages in total: first, the stage of gradual increase; second, the stage of detachment from desire; and third, the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and a noble one (*ārya*) at the first moment [of the path of seeing] definitely possess one type of knowledge; this refers to the first stage. All nine types of noble ones [possess all].

Because one has not yet abandoned desire, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not established. Although a noble person at the initial moment of the receptivity to the suffering of others (*paracittakṣānti*) possesses untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*), it is not yet termed "knowledge" (*jñāna*);
they possess only conventional knowledge, which is identical to that of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

Upon reaching the second moment, the stage of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) are added to the preceding conventional knowledge, thereby establishing three knowledges.
Although the essence of this dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and suffering-knowledge (*duḥkhajñāna*) is one, they receive two names because the perspectives from which they are viewed differ.

Thus, within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are generally seven knowledges; these are all explained with reference to those who have not yet abandoned desire (*avītarāga*). Within the path of seeing, six stages are established in total:

in the first momentary stage, there is only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); in the second moment, three knowledges are established; and subsequently, four stages are distinguished, thus making six [knowledges] in total.

Furthermore, it is only in these six stages that there can be an increase in knowledge (*jñāna-vṛddhi*); in other stages, there is none. For instance, although there is knowledge in each of the stages of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), their names do not differ from those previously mentioned, and thus there is no increase. Likewise, in all the stages of the receptivities (*kṣānti*), there is no increase in knowledge.

At the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), it is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). This concludes the second section of the chapter concerning the increase of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) for one who is free from desire.

Speaking in terms of the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is said that there are eight [knowledges] attained; however, according to the principles of the treatise (*śāstra*), in each of the preceding stages, they increase sequentially:

for example, in the first stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becoming an noble one (*ārya*), there was previously one and now there are two; in the second momentary stage, there were previously three and now there are four, continuing up to seven previously and eight now—only then can the full reasoning be exhausted (and so forth).
Since all these stages involve the transcendence of desire (*vairāgya*), it is said that there is no time when [the knowledges] are absent.
Liberation refers to "liberation at any time" (asamayavimukti).
Regarding the analysis of cultivation according to the stages, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "One should first investigate what is meant by 'cultivation' (*bhāvanā*).

It is the practice that brings about the fulfillment and mastery of conditioned wholesome phenomena; this is the meaning of cultivation. When patience (*kṣānti*) is actually arising, one cultivates future patience. This means:
Previously, this lineage had not been attained; now, having been attained for the first time, its power is not yet extensive.

Therefore, one cultivates only the similar [types] and cannot cultivate them laterally. Thus, the treatise states: "Because one fully cultivates the aspects of the various practices of one's own truths, the applications of mindfulness, and even the objects of counteraction, all are determined.
(Note: The commentary explains: On the Path of Seeing, the eight patiences are determined to take the eight truths as their objects and abandon the afflictions of the eight truths.

The path of cultivation does not involve mutual intermingling; this is not the case here. According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it is discussed in detail that this applies only to the forbearances (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*), which constitute their own respective homogeneous classes.
(End of citation). Regarding the phrase "the final stage of clear observation" (*abhisamaya-paścima-bhāga*): this refers to the three types of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

They are called the "final stage" because, at the conclusion of each truth, the knowledge that observes that respective truth attains fulfillment. This is not yet fulfilled during the stage of cultivating the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) in the subsequent final stages.
Therefore, one cannot practice [the supramundane path] at this stage. As for the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), it is said to be by way of two meanings:

first, that which was previously known since beginningless time—such as suffering and so forth—is now known again; and second, that this conventional knowledge, which has not been abandoned since beginningless time regarding the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), is now abandoned.
Through the arising of joy and the attainment of sympathetic rejoicing (*anumodanā*) toward this single task of present realization (*abhisamaya*), it is cultivated.

This means that because they share the same knowledge of suffering and the same activity of abandoning the origin, it refers to the "contemplation of phenomena" (*vastu-abhisamaya*) among the three types of contemplation.

As for the statement that there has never been a contemplation of phenomena within the Path, this means that since beginningless time one has never attained the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), and thus lacks the shared activity;
therefore, the Path is not cultivated—this is one interpretation. Furthermore, "necessarily not yet," and so forth, constitutes the second [interpretation].

The *Yishu* (Exegesis on Meaning) explains that regarding the statement "the truths of the path have not been cultivated" (*dangdi*), this means that although the three truths of suffering, origin, and cessation have already been fully encompassed (*zhou*), one is still unable to cultivate conventional wisdom (*suzhi*) within the truth of the path;
how much less could one cultivate conventional wisdom when even the truth of the path itself has not yet been fully encompassed?

Furthermore, the *Lun* (Treatise) states: "Although the extremes of origin and cessation have not yet been universally severed or realized, within their respective stages, severance and realization have already been achieved."
The Path of the Cycle (*cakravartimārga*) is not like this, for its lineages (*gotra*) are manifold. (Note: This explains the objection.

"When one's position is already complete" means that although one has not yet severed all origins (*samudaya*) nor realized all cessations (*nirodha*) during the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), one will necessarily complete it during the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Thus, the Path is not like this; it is not only the Path of Vision that does not cultivate all [factors] of No-More-Learning.

The character "zhāng" (章) in the phrase "not universally cultivated in the section on stages" (*bù biàn xiū zhāng*) is pronounced as a departing tone (*qùshēng*); the ancient interpretation is likewise the same. (End of citation). Regarding the statement that there are instances where [the word] has a departing tone:

this refers to the question, "For what reason is there a mention of 'limit' (*biān*) regarding the Truths of Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Origin (*samudaya*), whereas in the case of the Path (*mārga*), one speaks of 'cultivation' (*xiū')?

This implies that while the Path does indeed possess a departing tone—where "tone" (*shēng*) refers to the sound of speech—the Buddha also attains cultivation of the Path such that both [types of] cultivation are not exhaustive; this is an instance of citing the superior to illustrate the inferior.

If even the Buddha does not exhaustively cultivate them, how much less so other persons? Because the Buddha does not practice the paths of the śrāvakas and others, he does not exhaustively cultivate the "cultivation by acquisition" (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), as he does not give rise to the "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāpti-prāpti*).
He does not exhaustively cultivate the "cultivation by presence" (*sammukhībhāva-bhāvanā*), because [the defiled states] do not manifest before him.

He does not exhaustively cultivate the "cultivation by practice" (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), because there is no possibility for them to arise during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), since it is impossible for outflowing (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) minds to coexist. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks: "If that is so, why is it not..."
Regarding the statement that this wisdom does not manifest for even a moment during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is because this wisdom arises immediately [upon its completion];

since the Path of Seeing has no sense of interruption between moments, there is no possibility for this wisdom to manifest therein. This is because it would contradict the preceding arguments regarding its actualization.

Furthermore, once the stage of the Path of Seeing has passed, there is no possibility for it to arise. Even if one were to assume it did arise within the stage of the Path of Seeing, what then would it be called?
Because it is cultivated as something previously unattained that is now being attained for the first time, it is said:

"That which does not manifest even for a moment during the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga)—this wisdom (jñāna) arises [at that time]. Since there is no sense of "momentary interruption" (*kṣaṇa-viccheda*) regarding the Path of Seeing, this wisdom has no occasion to manifest [during that stage].
An objection is raised: "Question: It is said that at that time, although one has attained mastery over its arising, its essence does not manifest due to the obstruction of other conditions."

The preface states that there are six levels in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), namely: the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:

Why is it that when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) operates within these six levels, one is able to cultivate the lower-lower [levels] but does not cultivate the higher? Answer: The superior surpasses the inferior, just as the inferior cannot approach the superior;

the superior does not approach the inferior. This case is likewise. It is said that at the limit of suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*), the cultivation is subsumed under the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

This means that because suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) take as their objects the four spheres of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena (*dharma*), they pertain to all four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Cessation (*nirodha*), however, takes only phenomena as its object, and thus pertains only to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
The path (*mārga*) is not discussed here because it is not cultivated [in this context]. Regarding which truth serves as the object:

this means that whichever truth—suffering, origin, or cessation—becomes the object, its aspects (*ākāra*) differ according to whether they belong to the lower or higher realms; in each case, that truth serves as the object.

Regarding the statement that one cultivates six or seven knowledges (*jñāna*), there are two types of cultivation: cultivation by practice (*pratipatti-bhāvanā*) and cultivation by acquisition (*prāpti-bhāvanā*).

"Practice" refers to actual manifestation; "acquisition" refers to the arising of attainment. At the first moment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one practices two knowledges—namely, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

Although their substance is one and not two, they are distinguished sequentially or through transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*) in this same manner. Regarding the three types of acquisition, the sixth and seventh knowledges differ.
In this current chapter, only *pratilambha-bhāvanā* (cultivation by acquisition) is discussed and not *niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā* (cultivation by practice), as this is an exegesis based on the verses;

however, according to the *Śāstra*, both types are fully explained, and this applies to all paths. Regarding the statement below that "one who has already abandoned desire adds the knowledge of others' minds," the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:

"For what reason does one who has already abandoned desire and entered the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*)? This is because [the knowledge of others' minds]...

The stage of mental investigation (*citta-vicāra*) is comprised within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), and it is only at this point that there is the sense of "cultivation. Within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because the preparatory application for observing the principles of the truths (*satya-naya*) is rapid and urgent, one cannot cultivate [this wisdom].
Now, at the time of the sixteenth moment, the knowledge of the path-type (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), it is a stage of leisurely investigation;

therefore, one cultivates this wisdom. Because it is not the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one does not cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). One does not cultivate conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), as in the previous case.

It has already been stated above that this [path] does not counteract the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) cannot counteract the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, there is no sense of a common object of counteraction, and thus it is not cultivated.

Furthermore, although conventional wisdom is cultivated as a counteraction to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) on the side of the three Truths, it is cultivated there because its objects are distinct;
since this [wisdom] lacks such distinct objects, it is not cultivated. Regarding the "uninterrupted paths" (*ānantaryamārga*) for abandoning the eight stages, there are three types in total herein.
Example One: (1) The uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the eight stages; (2) the remaining paths with desire; and (3) the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Although these three categories differ in the wisdom they cultivate, they are identical in the number of their seven factors; therefore, the verse treats them in the same section.

The reason it specifically mentions only the "uninterrupted paths of the eight stages" is that while those at the Peak of Existence do not cultivate conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), these eight uninterrupted paths do cultivate it.

Because it is conventional, it is designated separately; since conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) does not counteract the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) but does counteract the lower stages, it is said to be different.

Regarding the statement "excluding the ninth liberation": this is because the ninth liberation belongs to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), and thus is not what is being elucidated here.

As for the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and other paths involving desire that cultivate the seven knowledges, these include both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Therefore, one cultivates the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of the four truths, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Because these pertain to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and other paths for those still subject to desire, one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Furthermore, because one is not yet an adept (*aśaikṣa*), one does not cultivate the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

However, the mutual cultivation of the knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge occurs because they support one another through the power of their causes; that is to say, they are mutually similar as being of the same category. The following explanations should be understood according to this principle.

Excluding the mundane [paths], when the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) is added because it is the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and because it excludes the mundane paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), seven [knowledges] are established.
Regarding the statement "in the higher uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) up to the cultivation of six": because they are uninterrupted paths, the knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated;

because they are the antidotes to the Peak of Existence, the mundane [knowledge] is not cultivated; thus, only six are cultivated. This refers to the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for abandoning the desire realm.
Because the Path has already abandoned desire, it attains knowledge of others' minds. Regarding the "abandonment in the upper seven stages," this excludes the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

As for the "eight grades of afflictions" mentioned in the context of the various paths of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), these exclude the ninth grade; otherwise, they are the same as the preceding eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).

However, because the first liberation is characterized by the severance of fetters (*visaṃyoga*), it does not include conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); since this [knowledge of others' minds] does encompass conventional knowledge, it is explained separately as being "conjoined with conventional knowledge."

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): because it is not an antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is conventional (*saṃvṛti*) rather than an uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*);

therefore, the knowledge of others' minds is added here. Within this, there are four general cases where eight knowledges are cultivated simultaneously: (1) the ninth liberation and the subsequent advancement (*viśeṣamārga*) in abandoning the desire realm;

(2) the liberation and subsequent advancement in abandoning the seven higher stages; (3) the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the eight higher stages; and (4) the abandonment of the Peak of Existence.

The eight grades of the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) are all comprised within the stage of one-in-training (*śaikṣa*); therefore, they exclude [the knowledges of] exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), reaching at most eight.

As for the statement that there are either ten or nine knowledges in the stage of one-beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*), this is said in terms of the cultivation of attainment (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*). If one discusses the two types of cultivation—namely, cultivation by practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*) and cultivation of attainment—[both are included].

One cultivates only four [knowledges], namely: the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and either the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

This is because that initial moment of mind takes only the four aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object. Question: How can the initial moment of mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)? Answer:

Although conventional knowledge lacks the capacity for that [supramundane state], at the stage of no-more-learning all qualities are fully perfected; it is like a king ascending the throne, where everything [is established] simultaneously.
Because the myriad nations all come to pay court and offer congratulations, conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) arises and attains this coming to court.

Regarding the six [knowledges] cultivated in the future during the various paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) when those in training (*śaikṣa*) refine their faculties: the term "various" (*nānā*) is used because the five spiritual lineages (*gotra*) are not one;

however, in reality, their nature is but one, and since one cannot speak of "various" in a single uninterrupted path, and because they are in training, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is excluded.

Because one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds. Regarding the cultivation during the single path of uninterrupted transition for the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) of those in training (*śaikṣa*):

when the ignorance induced by the abandonment of the afflictions of the view-division is severed, and at the time of the "patience corresponding to the subsequent knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) within the path of seeing, the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are severed;

because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is not cultivated at that time, only six knowledges are cultivated. As for the statement that those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who refine their faculties cultivate seven knowledges in the future during all paths of uninterrupted transition, it is as follows: [the same applies].

Because they treat the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they do not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). This refers to the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*anantaryamārga*) in the refinement of faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);

these eliminate the obstacles induced by the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), just as one eliminates the defilements of the Peak of Existence. Since all refinements of faculties are like the attainment of a fruit, and because these practitioners have dull faculties, they exclude the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*);
otherwise, they are the same as those in training (*śaikṣa*). Regarding the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) for the refinement of faculties by those in training, up to the sixth [moment]...

Because it resembles the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the path, one does not cultivate conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*); furthermore, having excluded the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), one cultivates only six.

Other masters state that at the stage of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one also cultivates conventional knowledge—this implies that, as in the case of the three subsequent knowledges, one is able to cultivate conventional knowledge at their conclusion.

If the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) extends up to and includes conventional knowledge, this is similar to how the preparatory path of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) possesses conventional knowledge.
Therefore, both [types of knowledge] are added because they do not sever the obstacles; for those who have already abandoned desire, the term "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*) is added.

Regarding the five beginning with "regression," this refers to the six lineages (*gotra*), excluding the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), as the latter possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*) and thus is not mentioned at all in the context of the training of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
As for the "first eight liberations," the ninth liberation is added as "knowledge" (*jñāna*); this is why it is mentioned first.

Regarding the explanation of the cultivation of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*): since it is stated that these belong to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and are necessarily associated with liberation, they must include the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

However, because these individuals possess dull faculties, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is excluded. As for the non-cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), this is because it serves as the antidote to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Thus, it is said that by adding conventional knowledge to the aforementioned eight, [the total becomes nine]; however, this refers to the initial attainment of the fruit of arhatship, and because these individuals still possess dull faculties, the knowledge of non-arising remains excluded.
Regarding the fifth lineage (*gotra*) up to the tenth [moment] of cultivation, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is added.

Because the first eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) do not possess the knowledge of non-arising for all five lineages, they are explained together in one place. However, regarding the ninth liberation, the first four lineages have not yet attained the knowledge of non-arising, whereas the fifth lineage has attained it;
therefore, it is mentioned separately as the "path of superior progress" (*viśeṣa-mārga*), being "dull" for the nine [lineages] and "sharp" for the [fifth] lineage.

Tenth: because it does not abandon the obstacles, there is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); because it does not counteract the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

For those in training (*śaikṣa*) who practice mixed meditation—that is, mixed dhyāna—as well as for those possessing the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), these are included among the six supernormal powers, excluding the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).

Regarding the supernormal power of the mind (*ceto’bhijñā*), as previously explained in the context of first attaining the fruit of arhatship, it is not further clarified here. As for the seven knowledges, they are common to all.

Because it includes both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), because it incorporates the mundane path of immediate succession (*laukikānantarya-mārga*), because it pertains to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who do not possess the knowledge of others' minds, and because it excludes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), only seven knowledges are cultivated;
other paths cultivate eight. Since these are not paths of immediate succession, the knowledge of others' minds is added.

Furthermore, since it is stated that this involves "mixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) and the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it clarifies that one has already abandoned desire (*vītarāga*); thus, there is no need for further qualification, except to exclude the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising.
Because they have not yet been attained and because they are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), they are not called "cultivated" (*bhāvita*).

Regarding the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and liberation, only three are wholesome (*kuśala*) and two are indeterminate, as will be explained below. It has already been established above that what is indeterminate is not cultivated.

As for the phrase "the remaining four dhyānas," this refers to the purely tranquil states, excluding those involving mixed cultivation. The statement "those who have not abandoned desire are called seven" refers to those in the world.

Ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) do not possess the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). If they have already abandoned desire (*vītarāga*), and if they further cultivate the knowledge of others' minds:

upon attaining the ninth liberation of the abandonment of desire, they acquire the knowledge of others' minds pertaining to the first dhyāna; continuing thus until, having abandoned the defilements of the third dhyāna, they acquire the knowledge of others' minds pertaining to the fourth dhyāna.

However, because one cannot acquire the knowledge of others' minds if one has not abandoned the defilements of the fourth dhyāna, ordinary worldlings who rely on the four dhyānas possess both types of knowledge.

Regarding the remaining stages, one cultivates only the conventional [truth]. Furthermore, the treatise states that in the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one certainly does not cultivate the knowledge of others' minds, because these are the immediate attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

As for the statement that "the various paths" refers to the two contaminated paths, the new commentary explains them as the four: the preparatory (*prayoga*), the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), the liberation (*vimukti*), and the advancement (*viśeṣa*) paths.
The various paths are mutually accessible; this chapter explains that "relying on" (*niśraya*) refers to the aforementioned paths arising according to whichever stage (*bhūmi*) they manifest in.

"Attaining this" (*prāpti*) refers to when one relies on a contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) of a higher stage to separate from the defilements of a lower stage, or when one relies on a pure path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of whichever stage to separate from defilements—specifically at the moment of attaining the ninth liberation (*vimokṣa*) of a higher stage, where one cultivates only [the pure path].
The wholesome dharmas of that stage are not cultivated because the stages of other levels are firmly bound by contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas;

thus, there is a distinction between these two meanings. Regarding the basis according to which [a dharma] arises in the present: when one becomes detached from the defilements of a lower level, one first attains the fundamental [attainment] of the higher level.

As for "attaining one" to become detached from this: it means that when a noble one (*ārya*) becomes detached from the defilements of whichever level they are based upon, they cultivate... [the path of cultivation].

When one is free from the defilements of the first dhyāna and so forth, one attains the second dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) states of that level and below; this is just like when one relies on the first dhyāna to become free from the defilements of the second dhyāna.
The traditional explanation says that when speaking of "cultivating" these lower levels in relation to the stage of freedom from defilement, it does not refer to the stage upon which one relies.

Even if it were in relation to the stage of reliance, it is still called "cultivating the higher," because both [the higher and the lower] are attained. In all such cases, regardless of which stage a noble being relies upon...
When one attains the second, third, or higher dhyānas on a particular stage, one cultivates those second, third, or higher dhyānas as well as the lower untainted (anāsrava) states.

Regarding "the arising of these," this refers to when a noble one (*ārya*) manifests the second, third, or higher dhyānas during the time of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*); at that time, they cultivate those second, third, or higher dhyānas as well as the lower untainted states of the stages below.

Question: Previously, it was stated that one cultivates tainted (*sāsrava*) states; why was it not said that this is for the sake of detachment (*vairāgya*) from them? Answer: Because of their function... [text fragment].

When one abandons defilements through the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*) or the uncontaminated path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one cultivates the contaminated [dharmas] of that stage; this is no different from when one relies upon that stage or attains that stage.

Furthermore, when one gradually abandons the defilements of a higher stage by relying on the path of a lower stage, one again cannot cultivate the contaminated [dharmas] of the higher stage—unlike the cultivation of the uncontaminated [dharmas]—and therefore this is not mentioned separately;
its arising is the same as what was previously stated regarding reliance upon that stage.

In the preceding [stages], both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) paths are employed; therefore, one cultivates [the antidotes] for those [stages]. In the intermediate [stages], it is only the abandonment of these that differs.

Regarding the statement "one cultivates the untainted of the lower [stages]," the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Because they are equally capable of acting as the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) against the defilements of the higher [stages], one attains the cultivation of the lower.

Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The untainted [path] based on a higher stage necessarily cultivates the lower, because it is autonomous and not bound [to a specific level]. Question: Why?

Therefore, regarding the untainted [factors], one does not cultivate those of higher stages. This answers the previous two categories: because they have not yet attained a higher stage, they cannot cultivate what belongs to it.
Within the third category, although it is possible that one has already abandoned the defilements of a higher stage, this is not certain; therefore, it is not said that one cultivates them.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of afflictions, since one attains the stages through gradual progression, it is not said that one cultivates the afflictions of a higher stage; for one lacks mastery over the higher stages, and thus does not cultivate what belongs to them.

Regarding the statement that "this term [‘abandonment’] applies to both sets of four paths," this means that in terms of the counteracting agents (*pratipakṣa*), it applies to both sets of four paths, but not to the paths that are the objects of abandonment (*vipakṣa*).

This is because the phrase "by abandoning these" restricts it to the cultivation of the untainted (*anāsrava*). As for the statement that "it extends only from the initial knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) up to the tainted virtues (*sāsrava-guṇa*)," the *Nyāyānusāra* asks:
How is it that at the time of this initial knowledge of exhaustion alone, its power is able to cultivate all tainted states universally?

Virtue is able to eliminate all roots of goodness and afflictions that have existed since beginningless time, just as when a common enemy of a kingdom is defeated and subdued, everyone comes together to rejoice, rely [on the victor], and praise his excellence.

Furthermore, because the bonds of affliction are severed without remainder, it is like the breath of the bound being released once the binder has been cut. Therefore, only the wisdom of the initial exhaustion can universally cultivate this; thus it is called "self-."
The mind is first like a king; from the time it attains the fruit until its arising, it comes to court.

When ascending to the throne in the western direction, water is sprinkled upon its crown, and various rare treasures arrive as tribute from every quarter. The King of Mind is likewise: when first realizing the ultimate fruit, it well comes to court.
One born in a higher realm does not cultivate the lower, for if one is born in a higher meditative absorption, the lower tainted states cannot be accomplished.

Because it is wholesome, one is born in the higher realms; however, one cannot cultivate the lower stages there. It is said that although one may now regain them, this is not called "cultivation," for the treatise states:
"It is not attained through arduous effort."
Regarding the statement that the two cultivations of "remediation" (*pratipakṣa*) and "expulsion" (*vinirdhāvana*) depend upon contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*):

only contaminated phenomena can be subject to these two cultivations, because uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava*) are faultless and thus cannot be remediated or expelled. Therefore, contaminated phenomena universally possess all four cultivations, whereas uncontaminated phenomena possess only the two cultivations of "attainment" (*pratilambha*) and "practice" (*niṣevaṇā*).
As for the inclusion of the cultivation of "protection" (*ārakṣā*) and the cultivation of "observation" (*vīkṣaṇā*), the treatise states: "As it is said in the Sūtra..."
What is the cultivation of the faculties? It refers to the thorough restraint and protection of the six faculties, and so forth, as explained at length. Furthermore, a sutra asks:
"What is the cultivation of the body? It refers to contemplating one's own body from the hair of the head and body, the nails, and so forth, as explained at length.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa), Fascicle 27.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun.

Regarding the statement that "the grounds of possibility and impossibility (*sthānāsthāna*) have the ten knowledges as their essence," there are two parts here: first, their essence; second, the explanation of their names.
The initial statement that "the ten knowledges constitute its essence" means that the Buddha’s ten knowledges, as appropriate, know all phenomena;

because he knows what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), it is said: "As it has been taught, wholesome causes can bring about desirable results. This means that things such as the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action can produce results such as those of humans and devas—this is indeed possible.
It is like what people in the world say when they declare, "Such a thing exists," and so forth. As for the unwholesome... [the text continues].

By reversing this, one can understand that what is called "creating unwholesome causes" refers to those who, like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), cling to chickens, pigs, and so forth as the cause of their precepts, while denying the existence of the fruits of the path that lead to purity;
all such acts are termed evil causes. Because these necessarily cannot yield desirable fruits, they are called "impossible cases" (*asthāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "This knowledge universally takes both sentient and insentient objects as its conditions."
This is not in contradiction with all-encompassing omniscience; it is merely stated here in brief because it is difficult to realize through little effort.

Furthermore, within this context, the remaining nine [factors] are extracted. In the *Bhagavat-bahudhātuka-sūtra*, they are analyzed in detail by the Blessed One himself. Regarding the eight types of karma:
according to the older tradition, if one considers them from a distant perspective, karma is said to be the cause and its maturation (*vipāka*) the fruit. However, if one analyzes them minutely:

It is said that moments [of consciousness] are mutually related as cause and effect when compared with their own kind across preceding and succeeding instants; because they pertain to both the Truths of Suffering and its Origin, the nature of this [knowledge] consists of the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Alternatively, it is called the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*svakarmasvakatājñānabala*).

This refers to the correct discernment that such-and-such a type of fruit is summoned by the power of the karma created by oneself, and cannot be taken away or bestowed by others, such as a wife or children; and that such-and-such a type of karma [is likewise determined]."
It necessarily draws forth its own fruit; it cannot be bartered or exchanged; and unimpeded wisdom is called the power of knowledge regarding one’s own karma.
Regarding the mention of the "third dhyāna," this refers to the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) being the third among the ten powers, not to the third of the four dhyānas.
As for "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), since liberation is the fruit of concentration, it is also subsumed under the power of concentration according to correct principle.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself spoke regarding the characteristics of the powers, saying: "Bhikṣus, listen attentively!

The Buddha knows, as they truly are, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), as well as their defilement, purification, and establishment," and so forth at length. Regarding the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*):
it means knowing, as they truly are, the distinctions among the classes of faculties possessed by sentient beings that enable them to establish the sublime Dharma, without obstruction.

The power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*) is defined as the wisdom that discerns the superior and inferior [faculties]. Although there are those with middling faculties, they are not separately specified because they are subsumed under the categories of superior or inferior.
Furthermore, even in the mental continuum of one who has severed the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), there still exist past and future wholesome factors such as faith.
Regarding the phrase "various dispositions" (*nānā-dhātu*): it refers to the volitional tendencies (*śīla*) formed through repeated practice throughout the beginningless past of sentient beings.
To know, as they truly are, the various distinctions among sleep and the natures of all phenomena without obstruction is called the power of nature (*dharmatā-bala*).

Regarding the statement that its essence consists of four powers and nine knowledges (*jñāna*): because it encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), it comprises all nine knowledges;

however, because it takes conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as its object, it does not include the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). Regarding the statement that "all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are capable of tending toward their results," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:

This meaning reveals that the Buddha is able to know, as they truly are, the courses leading to saṃsāra, the courses leading to nirvāṇa, and the various sub-categories within each course—ranging from those leading to the hells up to those leading to the heavens—and likewise the various sub-categories within each course leading to nirvāṇa, which includes the distinctions of the three vehicles.
Based on these general categories, the name "universal course" (*sarvatraga*) is established for each (the above is the explanation of the name). If...
This refers to the explanation of their essential nature [as follows]. Regarding the statement "one who can know past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*)," the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:
"This refers to the unimpeded knowledge that knows, as they truly are, the distinctions between one's own and others' past lives; this is called the eighth power.
Regarding "one who can know the death and rebirth of sentient beings," the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "If one knows, as they truly are, those various classes of sentient beings..."
The unimpeded knowledge regarding the continuity of birth and death of sentient beings in future ages is called the ninth power.

An extensive analysis of these two [powers] appears in the section on the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Regarding the essence of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) mentioned previously, it refers to the six knowledges—namely, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)—because all six of these knowledges can take cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) as their object.

Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "These latter three powers are identical to the three supernormal knowledges (*vidyā*). Among the six supernormal powers, these three are particularly distinguished;
when established in the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are termed the 'three supernormal knowledges,' and when present in the body of a Tathāgata, they are also called 'powers.

As for the power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi*) and the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), even if they exist in the body of a Buddha, they lack great utility and are therefore not termed 'powers. (The above [sections] all fully explain the names and identify the essential nature; these may be seen in the relevant chapters. From here below:

Regarding the analytical exposition of the categories of meaning, the statement that "the two powers rely upon the four dhyānas" has two aspects. First, regarding the aspect of the supporting levels (*bhūmi*):

since these two powers are of the nature of the five supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), they necessarily rely upon the fundamental dhyāna levels (*mauladhyāna*). As for the other knowledges, they extend across eleven levels;

this means they do not necessarily arise from the meditative states (*samāpattibhūmi*) and thus are known to extend through the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the other levels. Regarding the phrase "the male body of a Buddha," this is the second [aspect], relying upon...
Although the physical gate is indeed the Buddha’s body and he is also a male, it is called "the remainder of speech" because it is that which is to be remedied.
As for the noble ones not being so, this distinguishes them from those of the Two Vehicles, who cannot be called "possessing power" in the same way as the Buddha.

For example, during the time of the Buddha's presence in the world, there was a man at the entrance of Jeta’s Gate who sought ordination. Śāriputra and others observed that this person had not [attained the fruit] for eighty thousand kalpas.

Having planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation, because they lacked the causal conditions for renunciation, he set them aside and did not ordain them. He praised their seeking ordination and did not abandon them;
later, when another Buddha came and saw them, he ordained them, taught them the Dharma, and they attained the fruit [of Arhatship].
Śāriputra and others were astonished and questioned the Buddha, who told them: "In the past, in the kingdom of Nāgara, I lived together with these people."

While sweeping and sprinkling water to cleanse the streets and preparing various offerings with the intent to invite and make offerings to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, he sought to save others by entering the city to sell firewood.
Upon learning of this matter, he immediately made a vow: "I shall gather more firewood, obtain money, and offer it as sustenance.
When he reached that mountain, he was bitten by insects; as his life was about to end, he called upon the name of that Buddha, yet forgot and could not remember it.
Even down to the phrase "Namo to those who were welcomed within the city," this is what is called planting the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
Although these roots of merit were planted in the past, because the time elapsed was so remote, Śāriputra and the others were unable to know them;

nor could they know such things as the number of births during the two periods—the past and future—of the pigeon pursued by the hawk, as detailed extensively in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. [The full account] is not related here due to its length. Question:
Question: If the slowest śrāvaka requires only sixty kalpas, why is it that one does not enter the state of an ārya beyond eighty thousand kalpas? Answer:
The figure of sixty kalpas is based on continuous cultivation; if there are interruptions, there is no impediment to requiring many more kalpas.
Regarding the explanation of physical strength, there are three general accounts: first, that it is equal to that of Nārāyaṇa; second, that every joint possesses such strength;
and third, that physical strength is boundless. Were it not so, one would be unable to sustain the boundless power of the mind.

As for the term "human seed-spirit" (rénzhòngshén), based on a seven-hundred-year calculation, *nara* is translated as "human" and *nāyana* is translated as "birth"; thus, it refers to the origin of human birth.
This is none other than the Great Brahmā King himself; because the non-Buddhists claim that all people are born from Brahmā, it is so called.

Regarding the "hooked joints" of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, this refers to the joints of the limbs being hooked together, which describes a copper-wheel-turning king. As for the phrase "bones and joints linked like chains," this pertains to a gold-wheel-turning king.
As for the term "ordinary elephant," in the Western lands, this refers to the common elephants used for daily purposes, [as well as] the incense-elephant.
As for the "elephant," in the Western lands there is a distinct class of large elephants called *gandhahastin* (fragrant elephants), which are employed for use in battle;
thus, the "sevenfold increase up to seventy-seven" refers to the calculation of their strength. These seven comparisons all involve an increase of tenfold. The *Śāstra* states:
"Some say that the first sixty [elephants] increase tenfold [in strength], reaching the power of half the body of Nārāyaṇa. This is one measure of that strength.
The *Dviguṇa-nārāyaṇa-śāstra* states: "In the commentary [on this], it is said that among those things described, only that which is most consistent with reason [is correct].

Regarding 'the specific great elements (mahābhūta) within the tangible': the term 'tangible' excludes the 'tactile organ' (*spraṣṭavyendriya*), for the tactile organ is the body. Thus, because the great elements are predominant, they are called 'bodily power' (*kāyabala*).
They are termed 'specific' (*viśeṣa*) because they differ from other great elements. In the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, it is stated that when earth is predominant, it is called 'body'."
Regarding the statement that power is augmented, the commentators say that both the four great elements and the derived tangible objects constitute bodily power;
that is to say, when they are in harmony, both are termed bodily power, whereas if they are not considered harmonious, both are termed bodily weakness.

Regarding the statement "like the second power," this refers to the factors that constitute obstacles, namely suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), as previously explained in the context of the second power.
Regarding the "fearlessness in proclaiming the path leading out of suffering" as being like the seventh power, this refers to the power of the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*).

While in the former case both cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and the transition to nirvāṇa were included, in this context only the practice leading to nirvāṇa is taken, encompassing both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths.

Because all paths can lead to nirvāṇa, or if one considers only that which leads [to it], the nine knowledges constitute its essence; if the goal itself is included, then it encompasses all ten knowledges.
Regarding the term "Perfectly Awakened One" (*samyaksaṃbuddha*): the Buddha has awakened to all phenomena equally, such that there is nothing he does not know;

thus he is called the Perfectly Awakened One. As for the objection raised based on the reliance upon the Dharma: an external opponent poses the challenge, saying, "The Buddha asked Ānanda about what he had heard..."
When the heavens rain, why do the birds not cry out? The bhikṣus dwell in peace and happiness;

they do not perceive any of these dharmas before them, yet how can you say that he is the Samyaksaṃbuddha? This name is established based on the Dharma. The Buddha’s intended meaning in answering was this:
he questioned Ānanda in order to ensure thorough examination. If he knew even when asked, how much more so would he know what he does not currently perceive for the sake of the bhikṣus?

Because it establishes the standard [of practice], it is said that right view has no cause; this means that even when subjected to external challenges, the arising of right view is not something that occurs through being coerced or through the production of fear.
"Cause" (you) refers to a causal basis. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states, "right view has no cause.

Regarding those who have exhausted their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), an external challenge asks: "How could one revile Devadatta? [This refers to] anger. [The Buddha] then spoke words of consolation to Rāhula.

(Regarding greed: Since both greed and anger exist, how can it be said that the outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted? To provide a comprehensive explanation, the Buddha stated: "Because Devadatta was stubborn and fierce, I rebuked and scolded him;

because Rāhula was disciplined and compliant, I used gentle words. These were all demonstrations of specific circumstances. An objection is raised: "If defilement (*saṃkleśa*) does not constitute an obstacle [to the exhaustion of outflows], [it contradicts the teaching].

(Defilement refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like, which necessarily obstruct the Noble Path. An external objection states: "As is known from the fact that those in the first and second fruits [of the path] are permitted to have their own wives."
Regarding the fact that the defiled dharma does not obstruct the Noble Path, the Buddha provides a comprehensive explanation, stating: "The Noble Path is of two kinds: first, the Noble Path itself;

second, the path of detachment from desire (*vairāgya-mārga*). For one who engages in non-celibate conduct with one's own wife, this only obstructs the path of detachment (which obstructs both the tainted and the untainted), but it does not obstruct the Noble Path.

However, for one who engages in sexual misconduct, it obstructs both paths. If an external opponent were to object, saying: "The path is not the means for escaping suffering," [the response would be as follows].
An opponent raises an objection, saying: "Kālodāyin was defiled by excrement, and Aṅgulimāla was burned by fire; since they have both attained the Way, why did they suffer such hardships?
To explain this away, the Buddha says: "Kālodāyin manifested these conditions to transform sentient beings, and it was the same for Aṅgulimāla.
Another interpretation states: "Before attaining Arhatship, they were still in the stage of 'those still training' (śaikṣa), yet they were destined to attain it."
Because they are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are called Arhats; this is the activity of those in training (*śaikṣa*) that brings about the state of being beyond training—it is not otherwise.

Regarding the statement that there were disciples who were single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha, such as when [the Buddha] fell into mud like sandalwood, or those who were disrespectful, such as [Devadatta], who [threw him] with a sword against his right flank:
due to these two conditions, he did not give rise to sorrow or joy. The *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on the Correct Principle) states: "By abiding in the correct..."
Mindfulness and clear comprehension do not give rise to joy or sorrow regarding the three types of objects.
That which has great compassion and conventional wisdom as its essence takes phenomena as its object;

for if it were otherwise, it would be unable to take all sentient beings as its object, nor could it manifest the aspect of the three types of suffering. This is because [great compassion], like ordinary compassion, has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature.

Because it takes as its object sentient beings of the desire realm by way of the aspect of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), it is said that its "provisions" (*sambhāra*) are great, meaning that for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) one cultivates merit and wisdom as provisions.

Regarding the "three sufferings," these are the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Regarding the statement that "compassionate pity is not impartial," this refers exclusively to the suffering of suffering.
Because they extract suffering and bestow happiness from within.

Regarding the phrase "provisions" (*sambhāra*) and so forth: it means that all Buddhas of the three periods of time have cultivated the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*).
Regarding the phrase "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) and so forth: it means that they all possess the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅgadharmakāya*). Regarding the length of their lifespan: as [stated]...
Regarding the statements that Śākyamuni lived for one hundred years while Maitreya will live for eighty thousand years, and that there are Kṣatriyas born into the Brāhmaṇa caste:
the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that as for those of distinguished lineage, there are four classes.

First is the Brāhmaṇa (*jingxing*, meaning "pure conduct"), who preserves the Way, dwells in integrity, and maintains pure操守 (conduct). Second is the Kṣatriya (*wangzhong*, meaning "royal lineage"; formerly called *Chali*). (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
[This is a brief summary. First are the Kṣatriyas, whose will is set upon benevolent governance. Second are the Vaiśyas [some say "Vipra" is a corruption of this], who are merchants;
they transport goods according to the presence or absence of wealth, pursuing profit from near and far. Fourth are the Śūdras [some say "Śaudra" is a corruption of this], who are farmers;

they exert their strength in the fields, laboring diligently at sowing and reaping. These four castes differ in their purity and turbidity; their marriages and gatherings do not intermingle, and they follow distinct paths as separate clans.
The name of the root branch is "clan" (*gotra*), while the name of the derivative branch is "surname" (*nāma-gotra*). This "clan-surname" is actually a general clan;
it is because within one specific type of clan there are many surnames. For example, the Buddha belongs to the *Kṣatriya* clan, and *Gautama* is simply one surname among those *Kṣatriyas*.
As for the term *Gautama*, it is called *Gautama* because it is produced from within the *Go* [clan].
In the past, it was said that the name Gautama was a corruption. I have heard that in ancient times, a member of the Kṣatriya caste had his throne usurped by bandits;
when his father died, the son fled. A benevolent seer took the boy in and raised him, intending to ensure that the lineage would not be extinguished.
Later, as he grew up, he became a sovereign ruler. From that enemy king of the Kṣatriya caste, there subsequently arose royal kings who were enemies of the [original] king.
He issued a reward and sought out those who would cast [the child] away; after he had departed, the child was eventually captured and brought before the King of Vengeance.
The King then ordered his body to be struck with a mallet. The "Virtuous Immortal" returned to his dwelling and, not seeing the child, perceived through supernatural knowledge where it was.
He went to that place and, knowing the child could not be saved, spoke from afar to encourage the child, hoping to leave behind at least its physical remains. The child—
Afflicted by distress, he could not follow the path of the immortals; thick clouds obscured him while a fine rain drenched him, momentarily relieving his hunger.
A woman appeared, stirring his desire, and the child consequently discharged semen onto the ground.
The immortal took it up, wrapped it in cow dung, and returned to a sugarcane field. There, touched by the rays of the sun, the ball of dung opened.

A man was born from a split [cow-dung], his appearance exceptionally wondrous; he later grew up to become a king, and thus it has been traditionally transmitted that he was of the "Cow-Dung Lineage" (*Gomīya*), also called the "Earth Lineage" (*Bhūmija*) or the "Sun Lineage" (*Sūryavaṃśa*).
As for the term *Kāśyapa*, this means "Drinker of Light" (*Ābhāsvara*);
it is one of the clans among the Brahmins. Some were sixteen feet tall, while others were a thousand cubits tall; this refers to the height of Śākya.

Regarding the duration for which the Dharma remains in the world—whether it stays for seven days, a thousand years, or for many kalpas—and the sixteen-foot Maitreya versus the thousand-fathom [Buddha]:
there are those who say the Buddha possesses three virtues, namely the marks (lakṣaṇa), which do not exceed these three. Within these three, one further distinguishes many types of causes.
For the sake of convenience, the former meaning has been briefly explained. Now, to exhort people to practice and study the Buddha-Dharma, I shall speak of the "Venerable One" (Bhagavat).

The "renewer" (the practitioner) reveres what is studied without any sense of stinginess, because they practice without pride. That which illuminates true reality through omniscience refers to the wisdom that takes the ultimate truth as its object;
it is also called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). That which illuminates conventional phenomena through omniscience refers to the wisdom that illuminates the conventional;
the various distinct phenomena are called "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*), and this is the latter [wisdom].

Regarding the attainment of wisdom: some say that fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is called "all-aspect" (*sarvākāra*) because it serves as the seed for subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*);
subsequently attained wisdom is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*) because it illuminates all conventional phenomena.

Non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) refers to the aforementioned two types of wisdom arising spontaneously without depending on further application (*prayoga*). As for the phrase "the severance of all afflictions": this...

They are the same as those of the two vehicles and the same as the Arhats of the three vehicles in that they have abandoned all afflictions (*kleśa*); however, they differ from Bodhisattvas in that they have not abandoned all cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This distinction from the two vehicles is made because Bodhisattvas possess immeasurable *samādhis* which the two vehicles do not attain. The term "ultimately abandoned" indicates non-retrogression, while the phrase "abandoning along with residual impressions" refers to the abandonment of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because all types of ignorance have been eternally exhausted, this is also distinct from the Two Vehicles, as the Two Vehicles have not yet severed their residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Regarding the perfection of majestic power (*prabhāva*), there are two sets of four kinds. The first four clarify the inconceivable supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); the latter four clarify that the subduing of sentient beings necessarily achieves its intended results.
While the former four were briefly mentioned previously, they are now described in full. Thus, the treatise states: "First, regarding external objects, [the Bodhisattva] manifests transformations."
The sovereign power of sustaining; second, the sovereign power over the duration of life, whether shortening or extending it;
third, the sovereign power of moving swiftly through space, overcoming obstacles, and traveling vast distances, as well as the sovereign power of small and large things entering one another;

fourth, the sovereign power that causes the various inherent natures of worldly objects, such as flowers and fruits, to naturally transform into something more excellent and marvelous. Regarding the characteristics of the latter four as stated in the text:
That is to say, the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics;
being endowed with great power as explained above, such as the strength of Nārāyaṇa and so forth—this clarifies that the perfection of the fruit consists of four sets of four, totaling sixteen kinds.
If one further expands upon the majestic power (*vibhūti*), there are another four, making twenty kinds of resultant dharmas. Thus, the inconceivability of the fruit is established.
The general designation "unshared dharmas" (āveṇika-dharma) refers exclusively to those possessed by the Buddha alone and not shared with the two vehicles; thus they are called "unshared.
As for the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa), although ordinary beings also possess them—though they do not fully possess all eight—they are nonetheless said to have them.

Regarding the term "non-contention" (*araṇa*), its Sanskrit name is *araṇa* (translated here as "without contention"). To explain it generally, there are three types of contention: first, that of the aggregates (*skandha*);

second, that of speech; and third, that of afflictions (*kleśa*). These have already been analyzed previously. Here, this "non-contention" specifically refers to the cessation of the third type of contention, namely afflictions.
The phrase "contemplating the suffering of sentient beings" clarifies its mode of activity (*ākāra*). As stated in the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā*: "There is an Arhat..."

The Bodhisattva recalls how, throughout many past lives, he assumed the bodies of various species and gave rise to afflictions in himself and others; through this continuity, he experienced undesirable fruits.

He then reflects: "If a body possessed of afflictions, when serving as a condition for the arising of delusions, still invites such bitter fruits, how much more so must this be the case for a body free from afflictions and endowed with supreme virtues?
Having contemplated thus, he gives rise to a cognition characterized by these marks. By means of this skillful method, he causes others to [realize the same].

Afflictions such as greed and anger do not arise toward one's own person; furthermore, according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, an Arhat is able to prevent the arising of those afflictions by cultivating five causes and conditions:
first, observing deportment—namely, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—in such a way as not to cause others to give rise to lust;
second, observing whether speech should be delivered or should not be delivered; and third, observing whether gifts should be accepted or should not be accepted.

4. Observing the dwelling place: Even if a location is peaceful and abundant with the requisites for life, if one’s previously arisen roots of goodness are exhausted, it may still be called a place where one ought not to dwell. 5. Observing the streets and alleys for the purpose of alms-seeking:
When about to enter a city or town, one first observes the streets and alleys to ensure that the men and women therein will not give rise to afflictions on account of oneself;

this refers specifically to the inhabitants of the three continents, as their faculties are extremely sharp and intense. Regarding the phrase "conditions have not yet arisen," it means... [text ends].

Because the afflictions that have already arisen cannot be turned back, they pertain only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This means that because afflictions of the desire realm can summon the various sufferings of the three miserable destinies (*durgati*), they cause sentient beings to abandon wholesome states and give rise to suffering;

therefore, it is specifically the afflictions of the desire realm that must be prevented from arising. Regarding those "afflictions without objective basis" (*avastuka-kleśa*) which cannot be warded off or prevented:

this excludes the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and refers only to the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). As for the phrase "arising internally in accordance with": [it refers to the fact that these arise] following [the internal mental states].
Regarding the statement that "one who takes the object as a collective whole cannot obstruct the afflictions of view":

this means that since the afflictions abandoned through seeing take internal objects as their collective characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and do not arise by taking one's own person as a specific object, how could one's own wisdom possibly prevent them?

Regarding the statement that "the vow comes first," the *Śāstra* says: When sentient beings wish to give rise to this knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), they first make a sincere vow seeking to know that object, and then enter the fourth dhyāna of the limit (*prāntakoṭika*) as the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Immediately thereafter, according to the strength or weakness of the power of the concentration entered, and in accordance with the force of the prior vow, the correct knowledge is induced to arise regarding the object sought.

Because it knows all objects exactly as they are, it is called "vow-knowledge" (*praṇidhijñāna*). Regarding the fact that the essential nature of this knowledge is the same as that of "non-contention" (*araṇā*): it means they are both of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

As for their basis, they both rely on the fourth dhyāna of the immovable nature (*āniñjya-svabhāva*). As for their scope, such as the three continents and so forth, they differ only in their objects of focus (*ālambana*):

namely, this [vow-knowledge] takes all phenomena of the three realms and the three times as its object, whereas non-contention takes only the desire realm and those [phenomena] not yet arisen as its object.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "name, phrase, and phoneme—these three are collectively termed 'name'":

although there are distinct names and phrases in their individual characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they are here collectively termed "name" because, in terms of their common characteristic of being able to express and indicate meaning, they function identically. Regarding the phrase "taking the signified object as its object": this refers only to taking...
Based on words, names arise; that which is manifested by names is the meaning, not the mere object of the mind’s general activity, which is designated as the "condition of meaning.

Regarding the "condition of regional dialects," the *Nyāyabindu* states: "If one possesses non-retrogressive knowledge (*avivartyajñāna*), one establishes the third [condition] by taking the conventional and noble linguistic expressions of various regions;
thus, one is able to understand secular scriptures and the diverse differences among the various regional dialects."

Furthermore, one who possesses the wisdom of non-retrogression and has attained the two paths of concentration and wisdom is able to correctly proclaim the Dharma, skillfully responding to the capacities of sentient beings.
Their speech does not contradict the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and is called "right principle" (*nyāya*). Their verbal expression is unimpeded;

they can analyze and resolve matters with mastery, independent of place or time, which is called "unimpeded speech. Moreover, all the merits already attained do not require further application of effort (*prayoga*).
The spontaneous, manifest, and sovereign capacity is called the arising of the two paths of concentration and wisdom.

Because these paths exist, one is skillfully able to respond to sentient beings, and speech functions without obstruction. Regarding the statement that the two unimpeded knowledges have "names" (*nāman*) and so forth as their objects:
names and the like are the expressive designations of phenomena, while various regional dialects are the objects of words; both are mundane matters and spheres of experience.

Regarding the fact that among the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), only the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) constitutes the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), which universally relies upon five stages (*bhūmi*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā* presents three general explanations.
However, there is no formal adjudication (*vinīścaya*) by the Master. The first states that the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena relies upon two stages; the second states it pervades five stages;

and the third states it pervades seven stages—namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas. Here, we follow the second explanation, as in the older tradition.

The first explanation states that because names are bound to speech (*vāk*), they are identical to words (*pada*). The second explanation states that because names are bound to the body (*kāya*), they extend to the higher stages, with the exception of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
A new interpretation states that it is correct to hold that names alone belong to sound (*śabda*);

thus, although the "body of names" (*nāma-kāya*) and so forth do not exist from the Second Dhyāna upward, there still exists the "unimpeded knowledge of phenomena" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) because one can specifically perceive the names and so forth of the lower stages.

Because one cannot cognize names and so forth belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), nor can one specifically take names and so forth of lower realms as objects, there is no unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).

From the second dhyāna upward, there is neither *vitarka* nor *vicāra*; since these two are the causes of speech, and since *vitarka* and *vicāra* are absent from the second dhyāna upward, there is no speech.
The ancient masters said: "Because it is difficult to take the phonemes (*vyañjana*) of other levels as objects, [the unimpeded analytical knowledge of expression] exists only within its own level."

Question: Since both the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) take names and terminology as their objects, why do they differ regarding the levels (*bhūmi*) upon which they depend—specifically, why does the former depend on two levels while the latter depends on five?

Answer: Because the analytical knowledge of language takes as its object that which is coarse and mobile, whereas the higher levels are tranquil; thus, it does not depend on them. The analytical knowledge of phenomena takes as its object that which is subtle, and since it is admitted to take the phenomena of the higher levels as its object, there is this distinction between the two.
Question: Since both the analytical knowledges of phenomena and language equally depend upon sound (*śabda*), for what reason... [the distinction remains]?
Regarding the distinction between coarse and subtle: although the answer is the same in that both rely on sound, conventional speech-terms are coarse while names and phrases are subtle.
Regarding the six knowledges as its essence: this excludes the knowledges of suffering, origin, the path, and others' minds, because these take conditioned phenomena as their objects;

it also excludes the knowledge of cessation, because cessation is not a verbal expression. Regarding the statement that it "generally relies on all stages": the *Nyāyānusāra* states that this refers to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the explanation that within the path of cultivation, it is admitted that any one [of these] may arise according to conditions, there is no fault in its being common to all stages (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, the statement that "one necessarily attains all four" means that at the time of the fourth *prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are necessarily all attained.
The treatise states: "It is traditionally taught that these four analytical knowledges arise through successive cultivation of calculation, reflection, the Buddha, and..."

Since one must first apply oneself to grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), linguistics (*vyākaraṇa*), and logic (*hetu-vidyā*) as preliminary practices, and because the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) cannot arise if one has not attained skill in these four fields,
