the Master of the Treatise explains: "The arising of the unimpeded analytical knowledges occurs only through training in the Buddha’s words as the preliminary practice" (the Master's intention being that all four are contained within the Buddha’s words).
"These six are all obtained by relying on the 'limit' (*prāntakoṭika*) concentration" means that all six types are induced by relying upon the fourth dhyāna.

"These six exclude [the sphere of] words" means that because words exist in the stages of vitarka and vicāra, although they are produced by relying on those stages, their essential nature is not subsumed under the bonds of those stages.
Regarding the explanation of the term "limit" (*koṭi*), first the meaning of "limit" is explained, and then the meaning of "edge" (*anta*) is explained; "limit" (*koṭi*) manifests its excellence.

Regarding the meaning of "manifesting the category" as being "without transgression" (*avyatikrama*): it means that within this meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is a sense of similarity in type (*jāti-sādharmya*).
For example, when a single verse consists of four lines and is called "four limits" (*catur-anta*), it is because there are four distinct divisions;

or, when a single realm has the boundaries of four oceans, these are all instances of the meaning of similarity in type. Regarding the meaning of "manifesting the ultimate": it is also like the description of the *vajra*.
The "actual reality" (bhūtakoṭi) is also called the "ultimate meaning" (paramārtha). This is because, by virtue of this meaning, it is definitively the most excellent among all categories;
it possesses the most preeminent qualities and is the most supreme among those practices that lead to the path of ease.

Next, regarding the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*) and the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and three demonstrations (*prātihārya*) shared with ordinary beings: although these are not shared with ordinary beings, they are included among the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

Thus, there is no fault in explaining them according to their general characteristics. As for the statement that "the miraculous (*ṛddhi*) refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*)," concentration is meditative absorption;

through concentration, one can perform miraculous feats. That which realizes the sphere of supernormal power (*ṛddhiviṣaya*) through wisdom without obstruction is called a "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*), meaning it arises from concentration.

Because it is named after its object and its capacity for realization, it is called the supernormal power of the knowledge and realization of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).

Although other powers also rely on meditative concentration, this power’s characteristics are so prominent that it is specifically designated by the term "psychic power" (*ṛddhi*). The supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are named after their sense faculties and their capacity for realization.

The supernormal power of knowing others' minds is named after its preparatory application (*prayoga*) and its capacity for realizing wisdom. Furthermore, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives refers to that which has already occurred in the past.
Regarding the past, these [supernormal powers] are named after their objects, their associated mental factors, and the realizing wisdom that accomplishes them.

As for the supernormal power of recollecting former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*) and the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*): "destruction of the outflows" refers to *nirvāṇa*, which is named after what is realized;

it is also named after the realizing wisdom. Furthermore, when referring to the body in which the outflows are destroyed as "the destruction of the outflows," it is named after both its basis and the realizing wisdom.

Regarding that which is subsumed under the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the treatise and its commentary state: "The term 'path of liberation' as used in reference to the fruits of śrāmaṇya signifies the meaning of emerging from obstructions.

(Commentary: This does not mean that it refers exclusively to the path of liberation; rather, because it signifies the act of emerging from obstructions, we know that by the logic of this statement, the path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) is also included. Fourth, regarding the fact that they pertain only to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*): because they take only phenomena as their objects, they are conventional knowledge.

Because the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*) pertains to both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), it comprises five types of knowledge, as has already been explained previously.

The first three supernormal powers (abhijñā) take material phenomena as their objects; therefore, they are all conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Since the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*) is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it encompasses five types of knowledge, as has already been explained.

As for why the first three supernormal powers take only material phenomena as their objects: the supernormal power of miraculous movement (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*) involves the transformation of matter, such as visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility;

the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) observes visible form, and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) observes sound. Thus, these three supernormal powers each specifically take material phenomena as their objects.
Regarding the statement that when first cultivating the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñānābhijñā*), one takes form (*rūpa*) as the gateway:

this clarifies that while the initial stage of the knowledge of others' minds provisionally uses form as its gateway, subsequently it takes only the mental object (*cittālambana*) as its focus, which differs from the [other] three [supernormal powers]. As for the phrase "manifesting in form" (*rūpeṇa saṃdarśayati*):

"manifesting" (*saṃdarśana*) means that the signs of joy or anger appear in accordance with their states within the form. Regarding the subsequent attainment of the knowledge of others' minds, the treatise says: "By means of... [and so forth].
Through this preparatory practice (*prayoga*), one gradually attains accomplishment;
having accomplished it, one does not observe the various forms of one's own mind regarding the minds of others and so forth—the term "and so forth" includes what is spoken of as the mind.

"Recalling the preceding moment" means first observing the mind that has just ceased, and then gradually observing in reverse order—this is called "observing in reverse. Regarding the distinctions of the ten stages, they begin from old age.

One contemplates the distinct characteristics [of the stages] from the embryo (*kalala*) within the womb up to the infant; furthermore, the treatise states that the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for recollecting others is likewise so.
This [recollection] is initially sequential, but when it has become habitual through practice, one can also skip over [the stages] to recollect.
Regarding the object to be recollected, it must have been previously experienced. The above merely clarifies the preparatory application for these two types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
Since the treatise clearly explains the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the remaining three [higher knowledges], it states:

"When cultivating the first three superknowledges—miraculous power (*ṛddhi*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)—one contemplates lightness (meaning one contemplates the body as light and buoyant), light (meaning one contemplates luminosity), and sound (meaning one contemplates sounds, taking what is near as far).
These serve as the preparatory stages. Once they are accomplished, one gains mastery and acts according to necessity; therefore, these five..."

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) do not rely on the formless realms (because the preparatory practices for the five supernormal powers are absent there). Regarding "the *anāgamya* concentration, etc.," the term "etc.
includes the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), as these also lack the equilibrium of calm (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). The same applies to the other four supernormal powers:

namely, the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, and the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), because they cannot perceive or hear objects belonging to higher planes. Furthermore, the treatise states: "Therefore, there is no capacity to grasp [them]."

Regarding the statement that the two supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) of others' minds and recollection of past lives have as their objects the two thousand, three thousand, or immeasurable world-systems, the *Śāstra* says:
"The scope and extent of the activity of these five supernormal knowledges toward the realm of worlds varies among the various noble ones (*ārya*).

Specifically, the Great Śrāvakas and the Rishyadeśīya (the Rhinoceros-like [Pratyekabuddha]—it should be noted that those who do not practice the stages of a lineage [gotrabhū] should be described as being like the Śrāvakas], and the Greatly Awakened One (Mahābuddha), when not exerting extreme mental attention (*manasikāra*), are able to [perceive] one, [two thousand, three thousand, or immeasurable worlds] respectively."
Regarding the sovereign functions of arising, acting, and transforming within the spheres of two or three thousandfold world-systems:

if one applies the mind to the utmost, one can accordingly [perceive] two thousand or three thousand, or even incalculable worlds (here, "two thousand" or "three thousand" is stated in reference to the application of the utmost mental effort; according to the *Māyājāla-sūtra*, Nanda perceives three thousand worlds).

This refers to the power of the Buddha’s majestic presence for those who have not yet cultivated such practice, as explained in relation to the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*). As the treatise states: "As if... [and so forth].

Regarding these five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*): if they possess superior efficacy and sharp intensity that one has never previously attained since beginningless time, they are acquired through preparatory application (*prayoga*).
If they have been practiced habitually in the past but lack superior efficacy—though they belong to that same category—they are acquired through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).

When they manifest before one, this occurs entirely through preparatory application. As for the Buddha, he acquires all of them through the abandonment of defilements; they manifest according to his will without requiring further effort.

Regarding the statement "because they arise by taking form as their object through preparatory application": this means that the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) takes the four external bases—form, odor, taste, and tangibility—as its objects;

the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) takes form as its object; and the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) takes sound as its object; therefore, these are all subsumed under the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). As for the two supernormal powers of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), they are subsumed under all four foundations of mindfulness;

this is to be understood according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, which states that they involve a general observation of the various distinctions in the stages of previous births as being merely... [the nature of suffering].

[The *smṛtyupasthāna*] that takes various phenomena as its object is subsumed under [the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*]. (The new commentary states: "This treatise applies to all four; it should be explained in terms of cultivation through acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), for they are not mutually exclusive. Furthermore, it says: "One should know that the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) pertain to the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Alternatively, it is not definitive that they are subsumed under the four *smṛtyupasthānas*"). Regarding the statement that the two supernormal powers are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*):

although the five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*) can be associated with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), these two supernormal powers are associated only with the indeterminate feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because their primary intention is merely to apprehend visible forms, sounds, and so forth. Thus, it refers to the eye and ear.

Regarding the statement that "the supernormal powers (abhijñā) acquired at birth are wholesome," this is the reason why the ancient commentators explained that both types of supernormal power are exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).

Within this, there are two points of contention: first, it is held that the five sensory consciousnesses are only those acquired at birth, and it is not admitted that those acquired at birth can arise in a different stage (bhūmi);

second, since these supernormal powers are associated with the two [mental] consciousnesses, even if they were admitted to be wholesome, they would—consistent with that previous explanation—be unable to arise in a different stage.

Since they arise in a different stage (*bhūmi*), it is known that they are not subsumed under the wholesome (*kuśala*). Next, regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and below, based on their arising from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), it is proven through reasoning that they are not wholesome;

for the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are induced by absorption, and one emerges back from that absorption. Thus, it is said that the "resultant of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Question: Since wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself the supernormal power, why is it called a "result"? Answer: It is precisely the supernormal power that is the result. The sense of being unobstructed is "supernormal power," while [the state] arising from absorption is the "result."
Because they are produced [by them], they are called "fruits"; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. Question:

Since both types of supernormal power (*abhijñā*) are associated with two consciousnesses, and the divine eye and ear consciousnesses exist only in the first dhyāna, why is it said that the two supernormal powers rely upon all four dhyānas? Treatise: There are two explanations. The first states:
Because they are described according to their bases (*indriya*), there is no fault. That is to say, they are induced by the power of the bases belonging to the four dhyānas.

They are subsumed under that same stage, or rather, they are said to pertain to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) because the supernormal power of the path of immediate succession relies upon four stages.

Only these three are called "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*) because these three are able to illuminate the events of the three time periods; since they dispel the delusions regarding the three time periods, they are specifically termed "clear knowledges.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Furthermore, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) recalls the suffering experiences of oneself and others in the past."

Through the supernormal power of knowledge regarding death and birth (*cyutyupapādajñānābhijñā*), one observes the suffering of oneself and others in future lives; because of this, one develops revulsion toward the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra and gives rise to the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā*) by contemplating the bliss of nirvāṇa. Thus, only these three [supernormal powers] are specifically established as "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*). Regarding the treatment of delusion concerning the middle period: it is said that by means of clear knowledge, one abandons the afflictions of the present; therefore, they are called the treatment for delusion concerning the middle period. Thus, [the sūtra] says: "Bhikṣus, I shall teach you the three clear knowledges. What are the three? Here, Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu dwells having realized through direct knowledge the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, which has been liberated and purified in this very life. This is called the third clear knowledge. Furthermore, Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu dwells having realized through direct knowledge the knowledge of the non-arising of the outflows, which has been liberated and purified in this very life. This is called the fourth clear knowledge. Furthermore, Bhikṣus, a bhikṣu dwells having realized through direct knowledge the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows, which has been liberated and purified in this very life. This is called the fifth clear knowledge. These five are collectively referred to as the three clear knowledges. Why? Because the first two are included within the third, and the last three are included within the fourth. Therefore, they are collectively designated as the three clear knowledges. Furthermore, there are four types of clear knowledge: first, the clear knowledge of the past; second, the clear knowledge of the future; third, the clear knowledge of the present; and fourth, the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows. Vasubandhu asked: "Why are only three of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) established as 'clear knowledges' (*vidyā*)? The answer is: Because they possess superior function. Regarding the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), there is aversion toward the prior limit;

regarding the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*), there is aversion toward the subsequent limit; and regarding the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), there is aspiration for *nirvāṇa*. It is said that these may be "true" (*bhūtā*).

This means that among those belonging to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), if they are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called "true" because they are dharmas of one beyond training. If they are tainted (*sāsrava*), they are not [considered true].
Regarding the statement that "there may be darkness and delusion": this refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have not yet exhausted their afflictions.

Although they may temporarily suppress the ignorance and obscurity of these afflictions, they are once again shrouded by them; therefore, this is not called "clarity. Only when darkness is permanently extinguished can it be termed "clarity. As for the Dharma (which consists of one portion of the exhaustion of outflows and one portion that is with-outflows), it is said that it "may exist" because it encompasses both [the tainted and the untainted].
Regarding the phrase "capable of showing and guiding": "showing" (*darśana*) is a synonym for revealing and instructing; "guiding" (*naya*) is a synonym for leading and teaching.
The treatise states that among these three types, only these lead those to be converted to first generate the resolve for awakening most excellently;
furthermore, only these three enable them to successively take refuge in, have faith in, accept, and practice the Buddha-dharma, thereby attaining showing and guidance.
The names of the other three are not so. Regarding *Khandarī*, the old [translation] states it is the name of a country; because she was born in that country, she is so called.
Furthermore, Paramārtha says there is a female deity named *Khandarī*, translated as "Earth-Sustainer" (*Dharaṇīdhara*); the spell is named after her, and from this, the person is given the name.

(The former interpretation states that the woman is addressed by this sound, while the men of the country pronounce it as *Khaṇḍala*). Regarding *Iṣṭāni*, Paramārtha says it is the name of a treatise (*śāstra*).
This means that when the treatise composed by the teacher of the naked ascetics (Ājīvika) was translated and examined, this mantra emerged from it and was thus named after that treatise.
Since these two [the Ājīvika teacher and his treatise] did not attain their powers through cultivation, yet were nonetheless able to manifest transformations and know the minds of others,
one knows that these two guides are not particularly superior.
Regarding the statement that the essence of *ṛddhi* (supernormal power) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"The Sūtras refer to the fruit of *ṛddhi* as 'ṛddhi' because they employ the coarse to manifest the subtle; furthermore, it is shown that superior meditative concentration is its proximate cause. However, the actual essence of the phenomena of supernormal transformation is not itself *ṛddhi*, as has been extensively explained previously.

The various phenomena of supernormal transformation are what are termed the "objects" (*viṣaya*). [As for the phrase "spiritual and wondrous qualities" mentioned previously, this is to be reconciled according to the *Nyāyānusāra*.]

Regarding the two types—manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) and transformation (*vikurvaṇā*): "manifestation" refers to not changing one's original form, while "transformation" refers to altering one's appearance.

As for the phrase "the power of intent belongs only to the Buddha," the treatise states: "Our World-Honored One’s supernormal powers are so swift that whether a place is far or near, he reaches it as soon as he directs his mind.
For this reason, the World-Honored One has declared: "The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable. Therefore...

As for the movement of power (*gati*), only the World-Honored One possesses it through superior resolve (*adhimukti*), as do other noble ones (*ārya*) when shifting their bodies (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇā*), as well as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

According to the correct principle, just as the sun extends its rays, so too does the stream of aggregates (*skandha-srotas*); because it can reach a distant place instantaneously, it is called "movement.

If one were to say otherwise, then since [the stream] would be severed between this world and that world, the meaning of "movement" would be non-existent. Alternatively, it is mentioned because the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*) is inconceivable.
The mind itself is ultimately immeasurable. Regarding the statement that it "appears as one's own body or the bodies of others," this term "appears" (sadr̥śa) should be understood accordingly:

just as the four external objects appear [as such], so too do they appear as one's own body or the bodies of others. According to the treatise, those designated as belonging to one's own body or the bodies of others are explained as follows:

the new interpretation states that when a transformation (*nirmāṇa*) occurs within one's own body, that transformation belongs to one's own body; if a person is transformed externally, that transformation belongs to the body of another. Furthermore, within one's own body... [there is] presence.

Manifest transformation with substance (*sapratigha-nirmāṇa*) is like the Brahmā King descending to listen to the Dharma; manifest transformation without substance (*apratigha-nirmāṇa*) is like the dispute over a cloth tied into the shape of a sheep.

These are called "transformation bodies" (*nirmāṇakāya*). There are likewise four types in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*): namely, transforming oneself and others within the Form Realm, and transforming oneself and others in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, the treatise states: "If one born in the Form Realm creates a transformation in the Desire Realm, how is it that [the transformed being] does not possess fragrance?"
The loss of flavor is like a garment or an ornament that is made but not completed.

As for the statement that "the mind of transformation arises from the supernormal power of the divine realm" (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*): this means that the transformative mind arises subsequent to the supernormal power of the divine realm;

by the power of the resulting transformative mind, one is able to produce all manner of transformations. This is explained according to the simultaneous production of the transformative acts. It does not [refer to the initial arising].

Regarding the statement "transformations are pervasive": if one considers them in terms of pervasion, they are also called "transformations. This is because a mind of a lower stage does not produce a fruit of a higher stage;

thus, a transformation produced in the first dhyāna cannot travel to the second dhyāna. However, if there is no reliance on the second dhyāna, one can perform transformations of the desire realm or the first dhyāna that reach as far as the second dhyāna.
Regarding "arising from the pure [state] by itself," there are two types therein: first, arising from...

The two [types of] arising can give rise to two [types of minds]: that is, the first moment of the transformation-mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) arises from the pure meditative absorption (*śuddha-samādhi*), while from the second moment onward, they arise from their own kind.
The final moment can give rise to the pure meditative absorption, and the moments immediately preceding it—the initial moments—both give rise to the transformation-mind.

This mind necessarily lacks the sense of "directly exiting the contemplation," which explains the arising of the pure mind; that is to say, when one ceases the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is necessarily...
It returns to belong to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*), just as one enters through a gate and exits through that same gate; thus it is here as well.

Regarding the claim that speech and [the mind] must necessarily coexist, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Even for the Buddhas, the Lords of Transformation, and those who are transformed, the minds that produce speech are distinct in their preceding and succeeding moments.

What is called 'simultaneity of speech' refers to their extreme rapidity. In reality, the mind that produces speech arises first, and once the transformative mind has arisen, the former no longer exists."

The intent of this question is as follows: Since the mind that initiates speech (*vāg-utthāpaka-citta*) is distinct from the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), once the mind that initiates speech has arisen, the mind of transformation would no longer exist;

thus, one's body should cease to exist. However, because the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) arises from a mind directed toward transforming others, it is said that the transformation-body which is "retained" can also persist after death.

The old [translation] states: "Since it is said that he 'retains' a transformation-body, it is clear this is not his own original body. Regarding the bones, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states that they do exist.
Regarding the matter of retaining emanations, some say there is no such thing, while others say that there is indeed the retention of emanations.

For this reason, it is said that Mahākāśyapa has already entered *parinirvāṇa* (according to this treatise and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, he is said to have entered *parinirvāṇa*; however, other sources state that he entered the *nirodha-samāpatti* and awaits the appearance of Maitreya, which differs from this account).
As for the term "many emanation-minds," it means that initially, one must employ many moments of emanation-mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) before being able to complete a single emanated object.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "A beginner, by means of many transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*), must rely upon a support (such as a stone or other object) to produce a single transformative act.
Once the practice is perfected, one can, by means of a single transformative mind, produce numerous transformative acts without relying on a support.
Regarding the phrase "like ghosts and spirits," according to the treatise, it refers to those such as devas and nāgas who possess the power of transformative minds.
One can also transform ten bases of form for oneself and others, or nine bases excluding sound; however, in principle, there is no capacity to transform the sense organs (*indriya*).
Nevertheless, because the transformed objects do not exist apart from the organs, it is not erroneous to say that nine bases are transformed.

(According to this, those acquired through cultivation can only transform four types of objects, as they abide attached to the organs and thus do not separate from them; those acquired at birth can transform nine bases, as they are mixed with the characteristics of the organs and thus do not separate from them. The following passage is the main text of the Master of the Treatise.
Regarding what is called the "clairvoyance of the eye and ear": it refers to the cultivation of preparatory application (*prayoga*) by taking light and sound as objects;

thus, based on the four dhyānas, one brings forth within the vicinity of the original eyes and ears the two faculties of the pure form (*rūpa-prasāda*)—the eye and ear organs—which are derived from the subtle primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of that stage.

Seeing forms and hearing sounds through these is termed the "divine eye" and "divine ear. Furthermore, the treatise asks: "Why are these eyes and ears called 'divine'? The answer is: "Their essence is..."

Because this [category] is subsumed under the realm of the gods (*deva*) and the realm of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), although there are gods who are not subsumed under the realm of meditative concentration, those subsumed under the realm of meditative concentration must necessarily be gods.
Therefore, taking "being subsumed under the realm of meditative concentration" as the reason serves to prove that they are gods.

As for the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*), the ministers among the wheel-turning kings, the Bodhisattvas, and the various nāgas—these are all "resembling gods" (*devopama*). Among these three categories, the first two are included in the aforementioned [definition].

Regarding the categories, there are two explanations: the "divine eye" and "divine ear" are *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds; if "the deity itself is the eye or ear," they are *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds;
the third is a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compound. In reality, these are not entirely the divine eye or ear, yet they are designated by the names "divine eye" and "divine ear.

(The [category of] Bodhisattvas is omitted in the treatise, but it exists according to the *Śāstra*. As for the statement that they are "always of the same class" (*sabhāga*), it means they are always conjoined with consciousness.)

Furthermore, because it is neither impaired nor deficient, the Treatise states: "It is unobscured and unimpaired; like sentient beings born in the Form Realm, it can perceive objects according to their capacity, including those that are obstructed.

According to the Treatise, there are some who say this eye can instantaneously see all visible objects in the ten directions, while others say it cannot. Rather, when facing a single direction, one can see whatever one desires without having to turn around; therefore, regarding the object— [The text continues: ...it is said that the eye does not travel to the location of the object. As for the manner of seeing, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The eye sees by means of its own nature (*svabhāva*). This means that the eye perceives the object through its own essential character, rather than by traveling to the place where the object resides. Regarding the distance of what can be seen, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that the eye can see objects at a great distance, such as the moon and stars, yet it cannot see objects that are extremely close, such as the eyelashes.

This is because the eye’s power of vision has a specific range of efficacy; it is not that the eye lacks the capacity to see nearby objects, but rather that the proximity prevents the visual faculty from functioning effectively. Thus, the eye perceives objects within its own sphere of operation, neither reaching out to them nor remaining fixed in one place. This concludes the discussion on the nature and function of the visual faculty.
They are able to see the ten directions.
Those who obtain it through birth include devas, nāgas, birds, and the like. Those who obtain it through spells or medicine do so by means of incantations or medicinal substances.
Those who obtain it through karma include King Mandhātṛ and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), who are able to fly without relying on the observation of signs.

Because they are equal [in nature], there is no other-mind [knowledge] that relies on divination or signs. The old translations state: "divination" (*zhan*) refers to fortune-telling, and "signs" (*xiang*) refers to observing appearances.
This is because one who wishes to know another's mind must rely on a specific mark (*viśeṣa-nimitta*), yet the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of that mind is subtle and difficult to perceive;

therefore, it cannot be accomplished through medicinal substances or ritual actions. Regarding the three [supernormal powers] consisting only of the divine eye and so forth, these do not depend on medicinal substances, mantras, or divination/signs.

Because it is attained through equality and because it is difficult to accomplish, it is not achieved by means of mantras, medicines, or divination. Because the eyes and ears are dull, it is not accomplished by mantras, medicines, or the observation of signs;

it is known solely by the mind. Furthermore, although the body is material form, it is manifested through its characteristics such that divine mantras and medicinal ointments can enable one to fly—this is unlike the eyes and ears.
Since knowing the past is difficult, the recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsa*) is not achieved by means of mantras, medicines, or divination.
However, the three faculties of the eye, ear, and so forth each have distinct functions because their causes differ; the causal relationships between phenomena cannot be fixedly generalized.
Just as amber picks up mustard seeds and a magnet attracts needles, their operations are each distinct. Therefore, among humans, there are none who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) by birth.

It is said that this is because [such powers] are obscured and impaired by the knowledge of marks (*nimitta-jñāna*), as well as by the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).

Regarding the statement that "others may possess it because they are obscured [by other factors]," this means that the cultivation of spells, medicines, rituals, and divination may all potentially exist [in those realms], but they are not necessarily present;
hence the use of the term "may" (*yōng*). As for the claim that "birth-attained [clairvoyance] exists in all four destinies," the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"Among animals, there are those with the intelligence to remember many lifetimes—for instance, a wolf may recall the events of five hundred births—and the same can be known for the other destinies."

Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa Recorded by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun Based on the Original Treatise, Fascicle Twenty-Eight The Abhidharmakośa-kārikā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā Recorded by the Śramaṇa Dunlin of Fuchun Based on the Original Treatise,
Fascicle Twenty-Eight. Narrated by Dunlin.

The reason the "Chapter on Concentration" (*Samādhi-paṭala*) is explained next is as follows: the "Chapter on the Noble Ones" (*Ārya-paṭala*) clarifies the fruit, and the "Chapter on Wisdom" (*Jñāna-paṭala*) clarifies the cause.
Since concentration is the condition for wisdom, and conditions are more remote than the fruit, concentration is clarified next.

Furthermore, the preceding "Chapter on Wisdom" clarifies that which depends upon concentration (the fruit), whereas this "Chapter on Concentration" clarifies the cause upon which wisdom depends; thus, this chapter follows after the "Chapter on Wisdom. This is why the four dhyānas are explained first.
Regarding *dhyāna*, the *Śāstra* states: "Since all virtues for the most part depend upon *dhyāna*, one should first distinguish the varieties of *dhyāna*.
There are four *dhyānas*. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks: "Are there not unique names and designations for the various *dhyānas*, such as 'loving-kindness' (*maitrī*) and so forth?
Why then are distinct names established here only according to the four numbers, beginning with the first? The answer is: "It is not that there are no unique names herein."

In brief, these [attitudes] are entirely subsumed under the category of the wholesome (*kuśala*). If one includes their associated factors (*sānucara*), they have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their nature.

Since these two [categories] are identical in this regard, it is difficult to discern their distinct characteristics. Although there is no difference [in their essential nature], the stages (*bhūmi*) differ;
thus, to manifest these differences between the stages, their names are designated according to their numerical order. Therefore, they are called the first through the fourth. Thus ends the question.

"What is meant by 'one-pointedness of mind'?"—this is the question of the Sautrāntikas. "It is that which causes the mind to focus intently upon a single object"—this is the answer of the Vaibhāṣikas.
The treatise states: "If that is so, then one-pointedness should be established as a state of the mind itself when it is concentrated on a single object;
there should not be a separate mental factor (caitta) [named samādhi]. The answer is: "A distinct factor causes the mind to operate upon a single object."

Regarding the term *samādhi*, the Sautrāntika masters who differ [from the Sarvāstivādins] state that it is not the essence itself, but rather the continuous flow of the mind upon a single object (*cittaikāgratā-saṃtati*) that is called *samādhi*;
thus, it differs from the Sarvāstivāda school (and so forth). As for the word "deliberation" (*vicāra*), it means the sense of actual discernment;
in Sanskrit it is *vitarka*. This term is derived from the verbal root *vi-tark* (to deliberate), which is applied to the element of the earth (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, *vitarka*...
*Samādhi* (Sanskrit) is translated here as *dhyāna*, which may also be called *chán* (meditation), *chíhēnà* (dhyāna), or *chíhēnà*;
these latter terms are all corruptions. It refers to the state where the concentrated mind is stilled and serene, contemplating and deliberating upon objects; thus it receives the name *dhyāna*.

Because the wisdom born of concentration (*samādhi*) is free from turbidity and distraction, it is said to be capable of "deliberately and precisely contemplating. Regarding this, the treatise establishes a metaphor, stating: "Although a rotten seed lacks..."
Birth can receive the name "seed" (*bīja*), whereas other factors such as the earth or defiled meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) cannot; this is likewise the case here.

Although it is not identical to wholesome deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), it receives the name "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) because it is a state of tranquility. The Blessed One also spoke of "evil meditative absorption," which serves as scriptural evidence.

When it is said that the first dhyāna possesses investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*), it means it possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*); however, the verse does not mention applied thought (*vitarka*).
Because the second [dhyāna] is free from *vicāra*, it differs from the preceding; thus, only *vicāra* is mentioned.

The treatise states that by this, the presence of *vitarka* is also clarified, because they necessarily function together, like smoke and fire. It is not the case that *vicāra* possesses *prīti* and *sukha* while lacking *vitarka*. (The commentary explains:

because the intermediate dhyāna lacks *prīti* and *sukha*, there is *vicāra* without *vitarka*; in all other cases where *prīti*, *sukha*, and *vicāra* exist, *vitarka* must also be present. This means that the factors of *prīti* and *sukha* are established as being distinct from *vicāra*.
Regarding the second point: although here [in the third dhyāna] there is also actually an absence of vitarka, the preceding text spoke only of the triad of vicāra, prīti, and sukha;
now, because among those three there is both prīti and sukha, it is said that it is "only" free from vicāra.

If one were to claim that when prīti is absent there is only the factor of sukha, then since the third dhyāna is free from prīti yet possesses sukha, even though the sukha of the second dhyāna is pliancy (praśrabdhi) and the sukha of the third dhyāna is [sensory] pleasure, [the two would be indistinguishable].
Because the names for experiencing pleasure and pleasure itself are identical, they are spoken of collectively. As for the statement that one subsequently gradually abandons the preceding factors:
it is like the second dhyāna abandoning *vitarka*, which was listed before; and the third dhyāna abandoning *prīti*, which was before *sukha*.
Regarding that which was already explained in the *Lokadhātu-nirdeśa* concerning birth in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), as stated in the *Loka-paṭala*: "Birth is of four kinds," etc.

For one who is born having departed from the fourth dhyāna, there are two meanings for "birth" (*jāti*): first, defiled phenomena are called "birth" because they act as a source of affliction, just like raw food remaining in the stomach;
second, it refers to the process of taking birth, for at the time of departing from the defilements of the lower stages, one is able to leave behind both types of faults associated with birth.

To call it "separated from the signs of form of the lower stages" means that because the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) takes the fourth dhyāna as its object and forms its cognitive aspect (*ākāra*), the signs of form have not yet departed;
it is now called "formless" (*ārūpya*) with respect to the absence [of form] in that stage.

As for the statement "because form is subtle," this is the answer to the objection raised by the Sarvāstivādins. For example, even a slightly yellow object may be called "yellowless. The Sarvāstivādins challenge this, saying: "If you grant..."

What are the characteristics of form (*rūpa*) within that realm? If it is argued that it is because the dimensions of the body are small, then even microscopic aquatic insects and atoms (*paramāṇu*) should also be called "formless" (*ārūpya*).
If it is argued that it is because those bodies are extremely pure and subtle, then the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) should also be called "formless.
To say that this is the Master’s explanation based on the Sautrāntika school is because, in the Sarvāstivāda tenet system, there is no doctrine of seeds being formed through perfuming (*vāsanā*).

(Now, examining the intent of the detailed discussion: since the Sautrāntika explanation cited here addresses the objection of the Mahāsāṃghikas, its meaning should be the same as the Sarvāstivāda’s admission of the formless realms. Regarding the statement that "the name is established based on the preparatory application (*prayoga*"):

this means that during the preparatory stage of the first three dhyānas, one contemplates space, consciousness, and so forth; however, in reality, the fundamental [dhyāna] also takes other dharmas as its object and does not exclusively take space as its object.
Therefore, the name is established based on that preparatory application, not based on the fundamental state. As for "dwelling in tranquility," it refers to the devas.

The *Taishe* (Commentary on the *Śāstra*) states: "To take only a single consciousness as its object and produce infinite modes of activity is called 'Nothingness' (*ākiṃcanya*), which is equivalent to having existent phenomena.

However, this [state] is not like that; it is called "Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception" (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) because it possesses a dull and inferior aspect of perception—it does not mean that perception is entirely absent.

Regarding the statement that "the name is established based on its essential nature," this means that the name is established through both negation (*paryudāsa*) and affirmation (*vidhi*) with respect to the dull and inferior perception of the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*).
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Even at the time of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one forms this thought: 'All perceptions are like a disease, like an arrow, like an abscess.

If perception were entirely absent, it would be identical to a state of blind darkness; therefore, it is only within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—which is the opposite of the aforementioned—that [the name is established].
It is peaceful and sublime, yet the name is not established based on this preparatory stage. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "These four formless [attainments]..."
All are called "bases" (*āyatana*) because they are the places where various states of existence arise and grow.
Regarding the clarification of the eight attainments (*samāpatti*): in general discussion, there are three types of meditative names. First, *samādhi* (in Sanskrit;

translated here as "equipoise" or "even-holding") applies to both concentrated and non-concentrated states, to all three moral natures, and refers exclusively to the mind, as explained previously. Second, *samāpatti* (in Sanskrit; translated here as...)
*Samāpatti* (equipoise) pertains to both states with mind (*sacittaka*) and without mind (*acittaka*), and is exclusively meditative concentration (*samādhi*) rather than distraction.

If it involves a state with mind, it is called *samāpatti* because one has reached this concentration through the abandonment of agitation and the attainment of equilibrium. If it is a state without mind, it is called *samāpatti* because within the concentration, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are in a state of equilibrium;

this is as explained in the *Indriya-varga*. In Sanskrit, it is *samāhita* (translated here as "equilibrated induction"), which refers exclusively to a state with mind and exclusively to concentration, not to distraction; that is to say, it is capable of...

Regarding the name given to this meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—namely, that it is associated with craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—a question is raised: why is it not said to be associated with other afflictions?
The correct response is as follows: concentration is defined as being focused and unwavering;

since absorption associated with craving is likewise one-pointed toward its object, it receives the designation "absorption. Other afflictions do not function in this way; therefore, if *samādhi* were associated with craving...

"Both are single-pointedly focused on a single object and resemble the wholesome; 'pure' refers to worldly wholesomeness because it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), thus distinguishing it from the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is what is excluded by the term 'worldly. Because it is pure, it is not 'tasting' (*āsvādana*);

this is what is excluded by the term 'wholesome,' as it is associated with white dharmas such as non-attachment (*alobha*). Therefore, it is called 'pure. Having taken as its object that which has already ceased, it is pure and profound."
Regarding the arising of attachment: it is said that craving takes only past pure meditative absorption (*śuddha-samādhi*) as its object, and not the present or the future.

This is because there is no impure meditative absorption currently arising in the present that could serve as a basis for purity, and because future pure meditative absorption has never yet been experienced.

Regarding the four joys, they refer to the joy of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding the five types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the treatise states: "In this context, the verse refers to 'concentration' (*samādhi*);

since the term 'concentration' differs in name but is identical in essence to 'meditative absorption' (*dhyāna'), the Sūtra speaks of 'mental concentration' (*citta-samādhi*) and 'equilibrium concentration' (*samatā-samādhi') as 'right concentration' (*samyak-samādhi').
This is also termed 'one-pointedness of mind' (*citta-ekāgratā'), the meaning of which has been explained previously. Furthermore, the treatise says: 'It is traditionally taught...'"
Only concentration (*samādhi*) is both dhyāna and a limb of dhyāna; the remaining four limbs are limbs of dhyāna but not dhyāna itself. The Master explains:
"According to the true meaning, just as in the case of a four-limbed army, it should be understood that the remaining limbs of dhyāna are likewise.

(The commentary explains: "Just as a four-limbed army cannot be designated as an 'army' based on one single limb alone, yet it is also a limb of the army, so too it is with the remaining limbs of dhyāna. Regarding the first [limb], equanimity (*upekṣā*), this refers to wholesome equanimity.

Because it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it is designated by the name "equanimity of formations" (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), which differs from the equanimity that is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*). The *Nyāya* asks:

"In this context, what is the meaning of the term 'limb' (*aṅga*)? The answer is: it signifies the sense of "manifesting completion" (*pariniṣpatti*), meaning it manifests the completion of this being the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;
or it signifies the sense of "conformity" (*anukūla*), meaning each of the eighteen limbs conforms to its own respective [dhyāna].
The term "limb" (*aṅga*) is explained in the sense of being a basis or a requisite. Regarding the distinction between the general and the specific established from the lower [stages] upward:
since the first two [dhyānas] do not establish equanimity of formation (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*), they establish pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on Correct Principles) states:

"Equanimity of formation and pliancy mutually exclude one another; where one exists, the second is absent. Pliancy counteracts lethargy, its characteristic being buoyant activity, while equanimity of formation counteracts restlessness."

Because their characteristics are quiescent, tranquility (*śamatha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) mutually cover and obscure one another. Regarding the question of the single-faith practitioner, the explanation is as in the chapter.
Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "Moreover, in the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are like fire and the consciousness of the body is like mud;

they cause the mental continuum to become heated, turbid, and agitated, so that faith is not clear and pure—just as a reflection does not appear in hot mud. In the second dhyāna, such things do not exist."
The aspect of faith is clear and pure, like an image appearing on the surface of calm, cool water. In the third dhyāna, there is the feeling of extreme joy;
in the fourth dhyāna, there is the superior feeling of equanimity. Because these feelings cover the continuum of the mind, the aspect of faith does not manifest.

To say that one is "addicted to this pleasure and does not delight in the higher stages" is because the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "That which is tasted in the third dhyāna is the most extreme within the midst of saṃsāra, the most excellent among all conditioned existences."
Because it is characterized by bliss, it is logically appropriate to establish the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā*) for the purpose of observing and relinquishing [attachment].

If one lacks wisdom, one cannot even accomplish the wholesome roots of one’s own stage, let alone progress toward the superior; thus, wisdom is established as a factor (*aṅga*) to remedy such faults of one’s own stage.

This is not the case for the other stages, and therefore wisdom is not established as a factor there. As for the second dhyāna, because one is overwhelmed by the excellence of joy (*prīti*), [wisdom is not established].
Regarding "obstruction" (*pratigha*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states: In the second dhyāna, there is a supreme joy (*prīti*) that is restless and agitating, like a rākṣasa;
in the third dhyāna, there is a supreme pleasure (*sukha*) that is extremely difficult to relinquish, like the exquisite sensual desires of the gods.

In the third and fourth dhyānas, one departs by means of equanimity (*upekṣā*); although [the lower levels] have already been abandoned as appropriate, one establishes mindfulness out of fear that they might arise again through regression.

Because wisdom (*prajñā*) prevents and guards against the [defilements] of other stages, it is not established as a factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*). Regarding the number of factors, this is also the correct principle;

there is no textual passage in this treatise [to the contrary]. For one who follows the "leap-over" meditative attainments (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*), the term "leap-over" requires that one side [of the stages] be equivalent in number;
thus, it is easy to leap from the first dhyāna to the third dhyāna because their factors are equal in number. The same applies to the second and fourth [dhyānas]. Question: As for using...

Regarding the third dhyāna that transcends the sphere of infinite space, or the fourth dhyāna that transcends and enters the sphere of infinite consciousness: since those [higher stages] lack [the formal] factors (*aṅga*), how can they be said to "accord" with them?

The answer is: because it is difficult when first transcending, one provisionally posits the factors to accord with them; however, for subsequent times when it is easy, such provisional accord is not required.
The three factors being the same as before means that the factors of joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*) are the same as those in the first dhyāna.

The addition of the remaining four factors refers to equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and bliss (*sukha*). Regarding the fourth dhyāna, the three factors being the same as before means that equanimity and mindfulness are the same as the factors of the third dhyāna, while the other factors are the same as those in the preceding [dhyānas].
As for the statement "constituting eleven," if explained according to the seventy-five dharmas, it constitutes four [categories].

The feelings of the [lower] stages are all identical, consisting of only nine stages as their substance; however, when explained in terms of the five feelings, joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) each increase by one, and thus they consist of eleven substances.

As for the statement that the five consciousnesses do not exist within meditative absorption (*samādhi*), this is based on a general statement that applies to the association of the five consciousnesses with what is termed "bliss.
If one were to argue according to the specific reality, it should be said that within the third dhyāna, three consciousnesses are absent.

Furthermore, regarding those who have already abandoned the five dharmas—formerly called the five factors conducive to the lower realms (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni*) or the five hindrances (*pañca nivaraṇāni*)—it is also possible for deep faith to arise within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
This means that while one has previously departed from the distracted stage within the first dhyāna, now, in the second dhyāna, one departs from the stage of tranquility.
Having personally attained the second dhyāna and departed from the first, it is likewise possible [to attain faith] within that very stage of concentration.
When deep faith arises from being free [of external disturbances], that faith which is thus produced is called "internal serenity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*).
Because it is a characteristic of purity, it is designated by the name "purity. To explain the meaning of "purity": faith is called pure because it is free from the defilement of lack of faith.

It is called "internal serenity" because it flows evenly within, being free from external agitation; since concentration flows evenly within, it is termed "internal serenity. And as for "internal serenity"...
Therefore, the establishment of the name "internal purity" (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) is a collective explanation.

As for the claim that there is a distinct entity of joy (*prīti*) which is not the feeling of joy (*prītivedanā*), it is because they assert that all factors of bliss within the three dhyānas are the feeling of joy; thus, the entities of joy and the feeling of joy are each distinct, as extensively proven in the treatise.

Regarding the statement that [the first dhyāna] is not "separated from joy and bliss born of seclusion," the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The defiled meditative absorption (*kliṣṭa-samādhi*) is also associated with joy;

however, because it is not 'born of seclusion' (*vivekaja*), it is not included among the factors (*aṅga*). Regarding the absence of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) within the third [defiled dhyāna], the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

'Although mindfulness and wisdom exist within defiled meditative absorption, because the mindfulness there is a mindfulness of loss (*pramoṣaka-smṛti*), it is not established as the factor named "mindfulness"; therefore, these three [factors] are absent.'"

Regarding the statement that "among the defiled [mental factors], there are no equanimity or application [of mindfulness] except for those subsumed under the universal wholesome ground-factors (*mahā-bhūmika-kuśala-dharma*)," this is analogous to the fourth [case].

Therefore, this does not preclude them, because these two types are universal wholesome ground-factors. As for the claim that "those two are exclusively wholesome," thus they are definitely absent in the defiled, and since they further proceed toward the wholesome or the defiled, both are permitted;
the correct principle is that their statement holds: among the defiled, joy, faith, mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth all exist.

Since both are included among the factors (*aṅga*) and are equally pervasive of defilement (*kliṣṭa*), faith (*śraddhā*) is precisely the factor of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). However, faith is also a universal wholesome mental factor (*mahābhūmika-dharma*);
that it is said to be pervasive of defilement refers to its specific function (*pṛthag-artha*).
Regarding those who are unmoved by the eight calamities: when these are correlated with the antidotes for the desire realm and with inhalation and exhalation, they are said to be eight;

however, if they refer only to what exists within the form-realm meditative absorptions, then they consist of the abandonment of vitarka, vicāra, prīti, and sukha. In the treatises, a second meaning is cited from a sutra.

Regarding the statement that pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is associated with three consciousnesses: this refers to the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body, excluding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Neutral feeling (*upekṣā*) includes mental consciousness as well, and thus it pertains to all four consciousnesses. Second, joy (*prīti*) and neutral feeling are associated with mental consciousness;

this is because the [other] three consciousnesses are absent, and because bodily pleasant feeling is absent—since mental joy is coarse—and because there is no pleasant feeling on the level of the mind itself, there is only joy. Third, pleasant feeling and neutral feeling...

"Joy" refers to the subtle remnant of mental delight; thus, there is pleasure within the mental stage (*manobhūmi*). "Equanimity alone" in the fourth [dhyāna] means that because the mind has become utterly tranquil, there is only equanimity.

Regarding the statement that the two meditative attainments give rise to two kinds of distinctions: it means that among those born therein, it is not said that there is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth.

Regarding the statement that the three lower consciousnesses arise and that the mind which initiates expression occurs: because the higher stages lack vitarka and vicāra, they possess neither the three bodies of consciousness nor the mind that initiates expression.
However, when one desires to see, hear, or touch, one borrows the consciousness and the mind that initiate expression belonging to the first dhyāna to perform these superior functions;
since these consciousnesses are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, they are all bound to the first dhyāna. As for the word "if": [it refers to the case where...]
That which arises [as an indeterminate state] is the traditional meaning of "indeterminate regarding deportment" (*airyāpathika-avyākṛta*); it is merely a new way of saying this.

It cannot be that the ear-consciousness is an "indeterminate mind of deportment," nor can it be that the verbal informative action (*vijñapti-karma*) produced by such a mind is an "indeterminate mind of deportment," for this would contradict the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

Since matter subsumed under the "indeterminate" does not exhaust all matter, what harm is there in the four types of indeterminate minds not exhausting all minds? However, this "borrowed consciousness" is itself... [text ends].
"Nature is indeterminate" (note says: the commentary explains that the ear-consciousness is not [of the nature of] deportment; in the higher stages there is no craftsmanship or transformation;
it exists only as mental [consciousness]; it is maturation and does not arise from a different stage). For this reason, it is known that it is exclusively indeterminate by nature (end of passage).

Second, the explanation of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). This section of the text stands independently; according to the old commentaries, it divides the preceding eight attainments into two parts:
first, the acquisition of *dhyāna*, and second, the explanation of the three types of attainment. Here, it corresponds to the second part, the explanation of the three attainments.
The phrase "when arising from a higher stage into one's own stage" likely resulted from an error in the transmission of the structural outline (*ko-wen*).

This is because, when viewed in relation to the meditative stage (dhyāna-bhūmi) actually attained, it is said to be "of its own stage" (*svabhūmika*); however, if viewed in relation to coming from a higher stage, one should say it is "born in a lower stage.

Question: Why is birth necessarily taken from either a higher or a lower stage? Answer: When one attains the two higher meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) from a lower stage, as soon as one is freed from attachment (*vairāgya*), that attainment is already subsumed under the aforementioned principle;
it does not depend on the moment of being born. Since it was already obtained prior to the time of birth, [the attainment] is required [to be categorized by the stage of birth].

Regarding the statement that "birth occurs through the upper and lower [realms]": this refers to the initial attainment of birth. When it speaks of the "seven upper attainments," it does so in relation to the desire realm;
since these are distinguished from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), one might expect it to say "seven lower.

Therefore, the treatise states: "the seven lower knowledges. However, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* explains: "In this context, only the fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*) are mentioned, because the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) have not yet abandoned defilement."

There are cases where [the attainment] is not fully accomplished through application (*prayoga*), yet it is obtained as untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the untainted, there is that which is obtained through a single condition: namely, because the untainted does not fall within the confines of the realms (*dhātu*) or stages (*bhūmi*), it is not obtained through rebirth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*). Question: Is it not the case that upon entering the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one also attains for the first time the untainted meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)? Why, then, do you say they are obtained only through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*)? Answer: One attains this [attainment] upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). However, that which is attained through the abandonment of defilements is the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*). Therefore, it is said that the attainment of the fruit is obtained through the abandonment of defilements, while the attainment of the path is obtained through application. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, regarding the statement "obtained through a single condition": since the untainted is not bound by the realms or stages, it is not obtained through rebirth; therefore, it is said to be obtained through a single condition. As for the statement "not fully accomplished through application," this refers to the fact that the untainted is not obtained through the application of the mundane path.
