It is not certain; for although those who transcend the human realm by entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) from the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) do attain it, those who enter sequentially have not yet attained the fundamental stage.
Therefore, this is not certain. Since this context discusses only those who definitely attain it, the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"At the time of abandoning the defilements of a lower level, one necessarily obtains the fundamental untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) of the higher level. Thus it is said.

Regarding defilement through falling away: as previously explained, one who has already become detached from the first dhyāna may at some time relinquish that detachment from the first dhyāna and subsequently give rise to the defiled state of the first dhyāna, or regain the defiled concentration.
This condition is the direct opposite of the condition for becoming detached from defilement within the pure [dhyānas] mentioned above; it applies analogously to both the higher and lower stages.
Regarding the statement "up to the third," one's own level is counted as the first, the level immediately above it as the second, and the level separated by one intermediate stage as the third.

For this reason, the first dhyāna can only produce six [types of attainments], because the first dhyāna has no lower levels from which it could arise, and only untainted (*anāsrava*) and pure (*śuddha*) attainments can reach the third level; defiled (*kliṣṭa*) concentrations cannot do so, as explained in the text.

Regarding the statement that "in this context, the first dhyāna is explained first, followed by nothingness, and finally the four dhyānas," this means that the sequence is established by moving from the fewer toward the more, rather than being based on the hierarchy of upper and lower stages.

Furthermore, it clarifies that the untainted (anāsrava) serves as the producer, whereas the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is merely that which is produced. Thus, it is said that [the Peak of Existence] exists.

Regarding the statement that "immediately after the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), six [minds] arise": because the preceding meditative absorption was untainted (*anāsrava*), the Peak of Existence was excluded;

now, since we are clarifying the tainted (*sāsrava*) state, it is included. Furthermore, because its number is the minimum, it is explained first. As for why only six arise: because there is nothing superior to be produced from it;
because within its own stage, there is only the defiled and the pure (one); and because in the lower stages, there are only two: the pure and the untainted.

Therefore, because one does not give rise to the defilements of the lower [stages], there are only six; in the first *dhyāna*, there are seven, because while previously there were six pure states, now the defilement of its own stage is added.
Thus, as before there were eight, now there are nine, and so on up to where previously there were ten, now there are eleven.

Regarding the fact that one also respects the pure concentration (*śuddhaka-samādhi*) of the lower stages, this is the mind that guards concentration; that is to say, the practitioner makes such a vow: "I..."

It is better to give rise to lower wholesome states through cultivation than to give rise to higher defilements; for when one is later pressured by the afflictions of one's own level, one is able to give rise to the lower wholesome states by virtue of the power of a prior vow.
Thus the treatise says: "Just as one first makes a vow before falling asleep and is then able to awaken at the appointed time," and it further says:
"The untainted and the defiled do not necessarily arise together; since these [wholesome states] arise together [with the defiled]."

Regarding the three distinctions arising from birth-acquired virtue (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*): that which gives rise to the defilements of the three realms refers to the virtue acquired through application (*prayoga-ja-kuśala*), because it lacks the sense of "ending with death.
As for what is "birth-acquired," the mind at the moment of taking birth is necessarily defiled; therefore, it gives rise to all [defilements].

However, in both the Desire and Form Realms, it gives rise to the two types of existence (*bhava*) that are defiled; in the Formless Realm, it gives rise only to the defilement of existence (*bhava-kleśa*), and does not give rise to the defilements of higher [realms].

This means that if one is free from defilement when giving birth to a higher plane, it cannot be through a defiled mind that one passes away; if one has not yet become free from defilement, one simply does not give birth to a higher plane.
Therefore, there is no principle by which a defiled mind could produce rebirth in a higher plane.

Regarding the statement that there are only three [stages] at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*): although there is no untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma within its own stage, it can nevertheless favor the arising of the untainted;

therefore, it possesses these three parts. Although there is no Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the formless realm, because it can generally give rise to the untainted, it may also be termed a "factor conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
As for their mutual relationship, here we refer exclusively to the pure meditative absorptions (*śuddhadhyāna*) as they relate to one another.
This does not refer to the untainted (*anāsrava*) or the "tasting" (*sāsvāda*) concentrations. Regarding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), they can only produce one [subsequent state].

However, while the higher preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) all arise in succession without interval, the initial aid to decline (*parihāṇabhāgīya*) can only produce two and cannot produce the latter two because they are separated by a great distance.
Only this fourth [aid to penetration] produces its own kind and does not produce the superior or progressive states.

Regarding the previous point of difference, the *Xinyi* (New Translation) explains its underlying intent as follows: because one who abides in the stage of "decisive distinction" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) delights in severing all forms of existence (*bhava*) and cultivates the untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not produce the "further progress" stage (*viśeṣabhāgīya*).
According to one interpretation in the *Nyāyānusāra*, this is the same as the present treatise;
another interpretation also holds that the further progress stage is not produced, as these stages arise in immediate succession without any interval.

"Similar types" (*sabhāga*) refers to the uniform cultivation (*sama-bhāvanā*) of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) within their own respective categories; "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*) is the opposite of this.

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the leap-attainments (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), there are six stages in total: the first five constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*), and the last one constitutes the fulfillment (*niṣṭhā*).

Within the former [five], if it is uniform cultivation, the contaminated and uncontaminated are explained separately; if it is alternating cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), both are [explained together].
Regarding the dual analysis of practicing with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is said that there are eight stages; if one speaks of those without outflows (*anāsrava*), there are only seven stages.

As for the initial mention of the eight stages being practiced in both forward and reverse order: this means entering from the first dhyāna into the second dhyāna, and so on up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which is called "forward";

then returning from the Peak of Existence to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and so on down to the first dhyāna, which is called "reverse. One practices only [the stages] with outflows.

Because the outflows (āsrava) are uniform and do not transcend their respective stages, they are termed "sequence" (anukrama); this concludes the first section. The state of being without outflows (anāsrava) is understood by analogy, with the exception of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), which constitutes a difference.

Regarding the sequence of alternating cultivation (vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā) in both forward and reverse order as described above: for instance, when one enters from the contaminated (sāsrava) first dhyāna into the uncontaminated (anāsrava) second dhyāna, because these are of different classes, it is an "alternation";
yet because it does not transcend the stage, it is still termed "sequence. Within the fundamental states, there is alternation in both forward and reverse order.

Regarding "leaping" (*sādhara*): for example, when one enters from the contaminated first dhyāna into the uncontaminated third dhyāna, or from the contaminated peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) into the uncontaminated sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), or from the uncontaminated sphere of infinite space into the contaminated attainment of the fourth dhyāna, and so forth—the treatise states that such leapers can only leap over one interval;
therefore, there is no capacity to leap and enter the fourth [dhyāna] directly. Nevertheless, within this context, one may indeed leap.

Because it is difficult, it is called "fundamental" (*maula*); because it is either uninterrupted or non-interrupted, or interrupted yet not bypassed, it is relatively easy, and thus is merely termed "preparatory" (*prayoga*).

Regarding the term "Arhat person": the word "person" (*pudgala*) serves to distinguish [the practitioner] from gods; therefore, no distinction is made for those who lack faculties or are of both genders, as these are not saints and thus require no such qualification.
Furthermore, because they possess mastery over meditative absorption (*samādhi*), they are distinguished as being "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*).

Because they are free from afflictions (*kleśa*), [these attainments] distinguish them from those in training (*śaikṣa*) and others. The *Nyāyānusāra* states that they occur only in the three continents; however, they apply to both men and women.

Regarding the claim that there is no purpose for arising lower meditative absorptions once a higher one has been attained: this means that one cannot abandon the afflictions of the higher realms, nor can one manifest supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.

As for a noble being (*ārya*) born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) arising in the untainted attainment (*anāsrava-samāpatti*) of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which is lower: the term "noble" distinguishes them from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), as ordinary beings do not arise in such states.

Because the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) lacks the untainted (*anāsrava*), it does not give rise to [an untainted path] belonging to the lower seven stages; since those lower stages possess their own untainted paths, there is no utility for [the Peak of Existence] to produce them.

Regarding the fact that the neutral (*avyākṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) do not take the untainted as an object: this refers to the two unconditioned phenomena—space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which are exclusively neutral.

The outflows (*āsrava*) do not take [the pure concentrations] as their object; however, if they are pure concentrations, they can take the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) as their object, such as the fundamental wholesome formless attainments (*ārūpya*) like the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).

Here, "fundamental" excludes the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and "wholesome" excludes the defiled. Regarding the fact that they do not take the lower impure stages as objects, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Because the dharmas of the lower stages are not tranquil, whereas the fundamental wholesome formless attainments are extremely tranquil. Thus, [the outflows] take only [the higher] as their object.

Regarding those that can take as their object the category of the Path of Subsequent Knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of a lower level: because uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas do not fall within the bounds of the realms (*dhātu*), when they take one stage as their object, they take all nine stages as their object.
Therefore, the Knowledge of Dharmas (*dharma-jñāna*) does not take them as its object, because it is not a complete antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to them;

this is explained in the same way as the afflictions taking [higher] objects. Furthermore, it does not take the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of a lower level as its object. As for the access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realm (*ārūpya*), they also take lower levels as their objects. This means:

Because the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space takes the fourth dhyāna as its object through coarse, painful, and other such aspects as the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and so on,

up until the preliminary stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception takes the Sphere of Nothingness as its object through three aspects, all four preliminary stages are able to take the lower levels as their objects.

As for the statement "it is said that one has already abandoned [the lower defilements]," this means that if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of a lower level, one cannot attain the fundamental dhyāna of a higher level.

Since it is clear that one has already abandoned the defilements of the lower level upon attaining the fundamental dhyāna of the higher level, at what point, then, would those [lower] defilements be severed?

Regarding the statement that there are eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) as gateways to the eight fundamental dhyānas: this means that because each fundamental dhyāna has its own preparatory stage, there are likewise eight.

As for the term "preparatory stage" (*sāmantaka*), it refers to the sphere of influence proximate to the fundamental dhyāna; all [preparatory stages] are associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is one meaning according to the treatise. Furthermore, the treatise states:

"Because they have not yet abandoned fear of the lower realm, the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna also includes the untainted (*anāsrava*). This is intended to distinguish [the preparatory stage from the fundamental].
The remaining seven are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*). The reason for this is stated in the *Nyāyānusāra*:

"The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher realms lack the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state because they do not feel revulsion toward the phenomena of their own respective levels. Only the first preparatory stage is permeated by the outflow-free state because it is able to feel revulsion toward the phenomena of its own level;
this stage is extremely close to the realm of many calamities and afflictions, for all desire-attachment arises from..."

Investigation (*vitarka*) and analysis (*vicāra*) arise here because they are accompanied by investigation and analysis. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that only the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) of the first dhyāna is called "unattained" (*anāgamya*), in order to distinguish it from the other preliminary stages.

It is not that the activity of this preliminary stage arises prior [to the main dhyāna], nor is it that one who dwells in this [preliminary stage] has already given rise to the relish (*āsvādana*) [of meditative absorption].
Based on such meanings, the name "unattained" is established. Moreover, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* says: "Unattained..."
The fundamental [attainments] are established under the name "unapproached" (*anāgamya*), which signifies that the fundamental state has not yet manifested.

As for the statement that these eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) are all free from defilement (*kliṣṭa*), the treatise says: although the minds of the preparatory stages involve the defilement of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), this statement is made because they exclude the defilement of meditative absorption (*samāpatti-kleśa*).

Regarding the phrase "the path of freedom from defilement," this means that those "tasting" absorptions (*āsvādanasamāpatti*) are not paths of freedom from defilement; rather, it refers to the arising of freedom from defilement through deliberate effort.
Because it is stained and arduous, craving does not arise.

Regarding the statement "from the intermediate [dhyāna] up to the fully endowed," this refers to the *āsvādana* (tasting), *śuddha* (pure), and *anāsrava* (untainted) attainments. The treatise states:

"Because there is a superior dharma that can be relished, although one is born in those stages, one does not enter the untainted state. Here, however, we are considering the basis (*āśraya*), and thus [the attainment] may be either present or absent.

Regarding the statement that the "outflows" (*āsrava*) correspond only to equanimity (*upekṣā*), this is because they proceed through effortful application. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that because the three consciousnesses do not exist there, there is no pleasure (*sukha*) or joy (*saumanasya*);

because it proceeds through self-exertion, there is no sorrow (*daurmanasya*) or suffering (*duḥkha*); and because one has already emerged from the desire realm, it corresponds exclusively to the sensation of equanimity.
By this same principle, the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) likewise lacks the three consciousnesses, for those three consciousnesses are associated with vitarka.

As for the establishment of the name "intermediate" (*dhyānāntara*) because it is associated with vicāra and lacks vitarka: the Master [Vasubandhu] states that above this level there is no such intermediate dhyāna stage through which one could ascend or descend;

thus, those who practice it extensively become Great Brahmās (*Mahābrahmāṇaḥ*), while those who practice it only slightly become Retinue of Brahmā gods (*Brahmapurohitāḥ*), as they belong to the same single location.

"Lower" refers to those who have not yet reached [the first dhyāna]; since "samādhi" (equipoise) encompasses both meditative concentration (*samāhita*) and non-concentrated states (*asamāhita*), the term "lower" would otherwise include the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, as this passage clarifies the state of meditative concentration, it specifically uses the term "not yet reached."
"Emptiness is the emptiness of 'mine' and 'non-self'; that which is its self, though distinguished into the categories of 'self' and 'mine,' is none other than the gate of liberation of emptiness.
Regarding this, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The meditative concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) is the direct antidote to the view of a personal identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

This view of a personal identity also possesses two modes of activity (*ākāra*): namely, the mode of activity of emptiness directly counteracts the view of 'mine' (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*), while the mode of activity of non-self [directly counteracts] the view of 'I' (*ahaṃkāra-dṛṣṭi*)."
The antidote for the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is the contemplation of phenomena as non-self; this is called the aspect of non-self (*anātmanākāra*).
The contemplation that there is no self within these [phenomena] is called the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatākāra*). As for the distinct term "signless" (*animitta*), the *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Alternatively, 'sign' (*nimitta*) is a synonym for 'cause. Since nirvāṇa is causeless, it is called signless. Alternatively, 'sign' refers to the worldly aggregates (*skandha*) categorized as inferior, middling, or superior; since nirvāṇa is free from these, it is called signless."
It is called "signless" (*animitta*) because it is distinct from those [signs]. The five signs refer to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

Since *nirvāṇa* is a phenomenon (*dharma*), it is not said that its characteristic of being a phenomenon (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is excluded; rather, its characteristic of abiding (*sthitalakṣaṇa*) is excluded, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of *nirvāṇa* is eternally abiding and cannot be non-existent.
Regarding these two truths, although there are six modes of practice, they are subsumed under two names: the truths and the paths.

Just as one who has used a boat or raft should discard it once they have reached the other shore, it can be said that "having caught the fish, one forgets the trap. Thus, suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) are tainted (*sāsrava*) and are therefore to be loathed;
the Path (*mārga*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), yet it is simply said to be "to be abandoned. These two forms of abandonment are not the same:

while the former refers to total detachment, the latter is called "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*) because one no longer seeks or delights in them. To say that one "transcends" the suffering and its origin currently confronted is the explanation of "wishlessness."
The meaning of "wishlessness" (*apraṇihita*) is that one desires to transcend suffering, its origin, and the path in order to reach *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called wishless. Question:
If one does not wish for the Noble Path, for what purpose is it cultivated? Answer: It is for the sake of seeking *nirvāṇa* that the Noble Path is cultivated;

since the Path is like a raft that must necessarily be abandoned, it is just as one has no desire for the Noble Path in one's underlying inclination (*āśaya*), because that was the original intention of the mind.

Regarding the statement that they resemble *nirvāṇa* because of weariness with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*): this means that these two modes of practice are devoid of male and female characteristics, just as *nirvāṇa* is devoid of the marks of male and female.

Regarding the statement "repeated twice": this refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*); because emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are each repeated, they are called "repeated."
Regarding the two types of emptiness being concordant with revulsion, where the superior [emptiness] is non-self:
the *Nyāya* states that even for one who perceives non-self, the arising of a mind of revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is not as effective as perceiving emptiness.

This is because those who have already seen that all phenomena are non-self may still give rise to attachment and delight toward existence (*bhava*), since they do not clearly perceive emptiness within their mental formations (*saṃskāra*). For this reason, [the perception of] emptiness...

Although the two aspects [of emptiness and non-self] coexist within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is designated only as "emptiness" and not described as the "understanding of non-self. The explanation is as follows:

the aspect of emptiness is established in opposition to the removal of "what belongs to a self" (*ātmīya*). When one perceives in the world that things are not owned by a self and thus does not greedily seek to grasp them, this is precisely the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā*).

The *Nyāyānusāra* explains: based on this, it is possible to take the path of revulsion as its object; therefore, the statement that these five are not the characteristics of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is correct.
This refers to the fact that when one is weary of the Noble Path and establishes the "heavy" aspect of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), these five objects of focus are not the untainted Noble Path;

Now, since the "vow of non-existence" (*apraṇihita*) specifically increases weariness toward the path, one contemplates the path through its impermanence and views its defects; thus, the four aspects such as the path cannot serve as objects for the cultivation of weariness.

As for analytical cessation, it is attained through the abandonment of afflictions; since there are no afflictions to be abandoned in the case of the untainted, there is no analytical cessation.

This is also not the case. It is said that one takes non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which is itself devoid of characteristics—as its object; yet this non-analytical cessation is also free from all characteristics.

Taking the "characterless" as its object is what is meant by "taking the characterless as its object. Therefore, this meditative absorption is named after its object, which risks being confused with "non-eternal cessation" (destruction).

As for those who do not take the characteristic of cessation as their object: if this [absorption] were to take the path to cessation as its object, it would risk being confused with "non-eternal arising" (the characteristic of impermanence).

Because it extinguishes arising and ceasing, it is not "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). That which is "only with outflows" (*sāsrava*) means that while the path of observation that is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is entirely an act of joyful engagement, this [state] is one of aversion;
therefore, it is not without outflows. Regarding "not occasional" (*akālika*) and "one beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*): these refer to those of sharp faculties. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Because those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) cherish the noble path. As for "excluding the seven higher preparatory stages" (*saptordhva-sāmantaka-varja*), "higher" excludes the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*).

The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) exclude the fundamental [dhyānas] and so forth because the aforementioned seven levels lack superior dharmas; thus, it is possible for them to arise in all other eleven levels.
If one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they arise after the noble path (*āryamārga*) subsumed under the *anāgamya* stage;
if one is at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they arise after the noble path of the *ākiṃcanyāyatana*; in all other cases, they arise after the noble path of their own respective level.
"Cultivating all virtuous meditative absorptions" refers to the four fundamental dhyānas. "Abiding in happiness in the present life" means abiding in the happiness of the phenomena of the present;
that is, by being detached from [the lower levels], one experiences joy and bliss with certainty, and thus abides only in the happiness of the present life.

It does not say "abiding in happiness in future lives" because the fruit is not necessarily experienced in subsequent states. "Obtaining the divine eye and superior knowledge and vision" is because...
Because the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can see at a distance, one cultivates this [wisdom].

"All preparatory virtues" (*prayoga-kuśala*) refers to all dharmas—whether produced through hearing, reflection, or cultivation, or being untainted (*anāsrava*)—from the desire realm up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). These virtues are able to induce the arising of wisdom, which functions by discerning among various objects.
The term "preparatory" (*prayoga*) is used to distinguish these from those acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).

Regarding those for whom immeasurable sentient beings are the object (*ālambana*): they are named after the object; they lead to immeasurable merit because of the [immeasurable] cause; they result in immeasurable fruit because of the immeasurable [cause];

and they are immeasurable in their fruit because they arise from taking immeasurable sentient beings as objects. Because one takes immeasurable sentient beings as objects, one obtains immeasurable merit;
because of immeasurable merit, one obtains immeasurable fruit. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states there are three explanations: first, it is the immeasurability of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
First, because of the affliction of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); second, as an antidote to the immeasurable affliction of negligence (*pramāda*);
third, these four kinds are the vast playgrounds of the noble ones (*ārya*), and are thus called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). Regarding the fourth obstacle, the *Nyāyānusāra* explains:

"Hatred (*vyāpāda*) refers to the desire to kill sentient beings or the desire to harm sentient beings; it is a mental factor (*caitasika*) called 'malevolence' (*vihiṃsā'), characterized by an attachment to sense objects."
The cause for not delighting in dwelling upon the various categories of wholesome qualities is called *anabhiraddhi* (lack of contentment).
To give rise to defiled attachment and longing for the objects of exquisite desire, with a mind never satisfied, is called *kāmarāga* (sensual lust).

It is said that the antidote to these four frequently occurring obstacles—which "frequently occurring" means being predominant by nature—is as follows: loving-kindness (*maitrī*) counteracts ill-will (*vyāpāda*), compassion (*karuṇā*) counteracts harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) counteracts lack of contentment.

Regarding the statement that "equanimity has non-hatred as its essence" and that "the two—compassion and loving-kindness—have non-hatred as their essence," the ancient masters of the *Mahāvibhāṣā* explain that the Master [Vasubandhu] considers compassion to be non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). The *Nyāyānusāra* explains:

Some say that compassion is non-harming because it is the direct antidote to harming; this is indeed the case in principle. However, harming resembles non-hatred, and thus compassion is designated by the name "hatred."
The aspect [of this state] resembles non-hatred (*adveṣa*), and thus it is given the name "non-hatred," though in reality it is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*).

This is the ancient interpretation, which explains that when one harbors a mind of attachment toward a friend or relative, and subsequently perceives an enemy who might harm that friend, hatred arises.
The Master corrects this, stating that both factors are employed; this differs from the ancient view. The distinction between their characteristics is as follows: [text continues].

The *Vyākhyāyukti* further states that the Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus: "Bestowing benefit is the characteristic of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); removing misfortune is the characteristic of compassion (*karuṇā*);
rejoicing in [others'] attainment of equanimity is the characteristic of sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and forgetting [self-interest] with impartiality is the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the phrase "taking sentient beings of the desire realm as objects," "desire realm" excludes those above it, and "sentient beings" excludes non-sentient things. As the *Śāstra* says: "Thus it accords with the truth."

When the Sūtra speaks of cultivating the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth toward one direction or one world-system, it cites the vessel to reveal what is contained within that vessel.
Those who have not yet reached the threshold [of the form realm] are excluded because they cannot participate and because they for the most part lack freedom from desire (*vairāgya*).

If one intends to include those in both the meditative (*samāhita*) and non-meditative (*asamāhita*) stages within the category of the "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*), it is because they all take immeasurable sentient beings as their object and bestow [their benevolence] upon them.

Because it brings benefit, removes decline, provides consolation, and attains equanimity regarding loss and ruin, it is said to be "associated with attention through resolute conviction" (*adhimukti-manasikāra*).
This means that although one has not actually caused others to obtain happiness or be freed from suffering, one merely gives rise to this mental conception;

for even though they have not yet actually attained it, one causes them to obtain happiness and so forth by means of aspiration. Thus, it is not a distortion (*viparyāsa*). It is said to be "suppressed during the stage of application" (*prayoga-avasthā*).

Regarding "hatred and so forth," the treatise states: This means that even when one has not yet reached the fundamental [dhyāna], there are states such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) that resemble those cultivated to completion as the fundamental immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).
By means of these, one subdues the obstacles of hatred and so forth, thereby inducing the arising of the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), which is capable of severing all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Once the afflictions have been severed, it is only in the stage of being free from defilement (*vairāgya*) that one attains the four fundamental immeasurables. Even if one encounters powerful [obstacles] in this subsequent stage...
Conditioned by this, and not being overwhelmed or suppressed by hatred and the like, one first contemplates the happiness experienced by oneself;

then, upon hearing descriptions of the happiness experienced by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, one forms this thought: "May all sentient beings likewise attain such [happiness].
One begins with those who are superior kinsmen because it is easier to direct [the mind] toward what is difficult; thus one cultivates compassion and sympathetic joy.

The same applies to the seven categories of the higher realms (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya*). If one cultivates equanimity (*upekṣā*), it arises from the state of neutrality (*madhyastha*), which differs from the aforementioned cases;

this is because it is easier for one who has first abandoned neutrality to enter into equanimity, whereas it is difficult for one who has first abandoned attachment toward superiors to enter into equanimity. Regarding the final statement that obtaining one necessarily results in three:
if one obtains one in the first or second dhyāna, one necessarily obtains four; if one obtains one in the third dhyāna or above, one necessarily obtains three.
Because there is no joy (*prīti*), it is now established by convention that there are three [meditative stages] and not four.

Regarding the statement "having the perception of form within the internal body" (*adhyātmaṃ rūpasaṃjñī*), this is the traditional interpretation: because one possesses the craving for the perception of form, it is called "having the perception of form. The new interpretation states:
it refers to the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) wherein one contemplates one's own body being devoured by worms and so forth, thus seeing the internal body.
Because one perceives the signs and sees external insects, it is said: "Having the perception of internal form, one perceives external forms; this is liberation.

This differs from the [standard] chapter because it uses the perception of the body (*kāyasaṃjñā*) as "perception of form" (*rūpasaṃjñā*). Regarding the second stage, "having no perception of internal form," there is also the old interpretation, but the new [interpretation] says:

through the mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanaskāra*), one perceives one's own body being devoured by insects and so forth; one does not see the characteristics of the body, but sees only the insects and so forth.

Regarding the statement "internally perceiving no form, one contemplates external [forms] as liberation," the characteristics of these first three liberations are explained in detail in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*;

as they would be too cumbersome to cite in full, I shall merely introduce their essential meaning. The term "abandonment" (*pratikṣepa*) signifies the act of casting aside; thus, these eight are collectively termed the "eight abandonments" (*aṣṭa-pratikṣepa*).

The older tradition states that the first two liberations involve abandoning attachment to form (*rūpa-rāga*), while the third liberation involves abandoning the mind that contemplates impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā-citta*). This concludes the initial section.
Regarding the statement that "the nature of its cultivation is exclusively non-greed; its nature as a retinue consists of the five aggregates; and it is the direct antidote to greed":

this means that while it is primarily capable of counteracting greed, it may also incidentally counteract other defilements. Regarding its nature as having the five aggregates as its companions: because it exists within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are the five aggregates that function in accordance with it.
As for the third liberation being based solely on the fourth dhyāna: this is because by contemplating pure form (*śubha-rūpa*), greed does not arise; this is the ultimate [limit].
Because these difficult [liberations] can only be accomplished by relying on superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they depend on the fourth dhyāna.

The older tradition states that the other three dhyānas and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) also possess the first two similar liberations (*pratirūpaka-vimokṣa*); furthermore, the other three dhyānas and the desire realm also possess the third similar liberation.
However, because these are not predominant (*an-adhipati*), they are not established as such. This should be understood by analogy with the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) according to the treatise.

It is called "liberation" (vimokṣa), yet it is not so designated [in this context] because the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) and uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) paths take lower stages as their objects; therefore, they are not termed "liberation.

There is an interpretation that those who experience aversion toward sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) refer to what is elsewhere called the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*).

Another explanation holds that aversion toward all minds that have an object of cognition refers to being universally averse to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); for this reason, it is so named.

The meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—according to the new [translation], there are only two interpretations and no third—regarding the terms "perception" (*saṃjñā*) and "mind" (*citta*): these refer to coarse perception and mind. The first two objects are loathsome because one contemplates impurity;
the third is lovely because one contemplates pure form. Regarding the fact that they take as their objects suffering, origin, and cessation of their own or higher stages:
this is because the lower stages are inferior and because one turns away from them; thus, they do not take the lower as objects. Furthermore, they take nine [stages] as objects.

Regarding the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the stages: because the formless realms do not take the lower desire realm as an object, they do not take dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) as an object.

Since these four formless states are able to take everything as their object, they are able to take non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and space (*ākāśa*), etc., as objects. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:

"Whether one considers it a single entity or multiple entities, all are taken as objects. It further states: "The liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-vimokṣa*)..."

Regarding the object of focus, since there is no greed induced by visual consciousness within the third dhyāna, this mental state is like that of the desire realm where greed is induced by visual consciousness;

therefore, liberation is established for the first dhyāna. Since there is likewise no greed induced by visual consciousness in the second dhyāna, it is not established [as a separate liberation] for the third dhyāna.
As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya* (Chapter Text) that "in the third dhyāna there is no greed induced by visual consciousness," this is not based on the [Abhidharma] Śāstra.
Because these are the second dhyāna, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* further states:

"The first two liberations (vimokṣa) each rely upon the first and second dhyānas, as they can counteract the craving for visible forms within the desire realm and the first dhyāna. Since it does not say they counteract [craving] in the second dhyāna, we know that in the second dhyāna there is no eye-consciousness to induce craving.
If this is so, since the third dhyāna likewise lacks eye-consciousness to induce craving, why [is it said to be free from such craving]?

Regarding the establishment of liberation within the fourth dhyāna: it is said that one establishes liberation in the fourth dhyāna because, having first abandoned craving, one contemplates the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) within that stage;
it is not established by means of counteracting the craving induced by the visual consciousness. Furthermore, the treatise states:
"For two reasons, practitioners of yoga cultivate the liberations and so forth: first, so that those defilements already abandoned may become further removed."

Because one attains supreme mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to give rise to qualities such as the "pure" and "non-pure" as well as the noble supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

through this, one can transform various phenomena and perform diverse functions such as prolonging or relinquishing them (based on this principle, the cultivation of liberation for the sake of manifesting supernatural powers is likewise the same as in the Mahāyāna).
Regarding the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), they are distinguished as a specific differentiation branching out from the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*).
The liberations are the cause and the spheres of mastery are the fruit, because one enters the spheres of mastery by practicing the liberations.

While the first three liberations can only grasp the general perception of impurity or purity among all forms, the eight spheres of mastery differentiate between the quantity [of forms] among all forms.

Regarding the statement that the distinct characteristics of blue and so forth can "restrain" the object of perception (*ālambana*), this means analyzing and subduing them so that they follow the movement of the mind.

That "the mind is superior to the object" explains the name [of the *abhibhvāyatana*]. Because it is able to restrain and subdue, it is called "superior" (*abhibhu*) to the object; thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Because one overcomes the object and destroys craving, it is called a 'sphere of mastery' (*abhibhvāyatana*)."

Regarding the term "totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*): it is so called because one takes the ten aforementioned bases as objects in a pervasive manner; thus they are named "totalities. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"In this context, the Sūtra says that there is 'one perception'—above, below, and across—without duality, immeasurable, and that one contemplates pervasively throughout all places without interval or gap;
therefore they are called 'totalities. Alternatively, they are established as 'totalities' because they pervade the bases. Or...
These roots of goodness are called "universal" (*kṛtsna*) because their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is all-pervasive;

furthermore, the term "universal" as it is taught indicates that while the modes of activity are equal, the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are distinct. Therefore, the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are divided into ten types.

The first eight are like the pure liberations (*śubha-vimokṣa*), meaning that the eight—earth and so forth—are all objects of observation consisting of pure form (*rūpa*), and they have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their basis.
Because their natures and so forth are identical, this supporting consciousness has no distinct support; this explains why, when not cultivating the higher [realms], there are only ten.

Furthermore, it is said that in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one relinquishes the aspect of vastness (*vipula*); how then could one cultivate the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totality spheres) therein?

Regarding the previously explained categories of the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), and faculties (*indriya*): it was stated that these are attained solely through application (*prayoga*) and arise only in noble beings (*ārya*).
As for the phrase "other liberations, etc.," the "etc. includes the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

Regarding the statement that "others arise only in the human realm," "others" refers to the three liberations and the eight spheres of mastery; because they depend on the power of the teachings, they arise only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

First, regarding the cause, there are two characteristics: (1) although one has not previously practiced it repeatedly, because it arises through proximity, one is now able to produce meditative absorption;
(2) although it does not arise through proximity, because one has practiced it repeatedly, one is able to produce it.

Both of these are due to the power of the cause, meaning they are present homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) that induce birth in a higher realm as karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*). This should be understood by analogy with the following.

The treatise maintains that only karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is considered here, because karma to be experienced in the next life is subsumed under the power of causes. If Master Baofa were to include both karma to be experienced in the next life and subsequent lives, his intention would be as follows:
one first attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and by the power of this concentration, one brings about rebirth in the higher realms to be experienced in the next life or subsequent lives;

even through falling away from that state, by the power of the previously acquired karmic concentration, one is again able to give rise to meditative concentration. This above is a general summary of the three powers.
To distinguish them separately according to the three realms: the formless realm [attains its state] by two powers; the form realm by three powers; and the desire realm by four powers.
As for the gods such as Anabhraka (Cloudless) who are free from calamities, it is because the fourth dhyāna is not destroyed by the three calamities;
they do not arise in the formless realm through the natural law (*dharmatā*) of entering the formless attainments, nor does the "natural law" apply to the lower three dhyānas.
Because they are destroyed by calamities, there are those for whom the natural state is further augmented by the power of instruction; as the *Nyāyānusāra* states:
"This refers to the three continents of humans and the gods, who also hear the instruction, though it is subtle and thus not explicitly mentioned.

There are those who maintain and preach the teachings, and because of them the Dharma remains; 'maintaining' refers to those who recite the instructions, while 'preaching' refers to the Dharma itself."
The Master’s reason for citing these two cases is that if one merely upholds [the Dharma] but cannot explain it, the meaning of "transmitting the lamp" is lacking;

if one merely explains it but forgets to uphold it, then one abandons it through forgetfulness and fails to practice it. Therefore, when both are possessed together, the Dharma does not fall into decline.

When the holy teachings state in general that [the Dharma] will abide for only a thousand years, this implies that both the teaching (śāsana) and the realized Dharma (adhigama-dharma) will last for only a thousand years.

Some say that the period of the teaching of the Dharma exceeds this; others recount a divergent view, the meaning of which is that after a thousand years have passed, one cannot enter the state of an *ārya*.

Thus, it is proven that the Dharma lasts for only a thousand years. Although there are no more who attain sainthood after a thousand years have passed, there are still those who uphold and expound it;
therefore, these two views differ. The "New" school adopts the latter view because the teaching of the Dharma exists at the present time. Now...

To explain in detail: if one discusses the Buddha-dharma as a whole throughout its entire duration, it is reasonable to designate it collectively as the "True Dharma" (*saddharma*). However, if one discusses the "True" and "Semblance" periods specifically, this proof is not logical.
Nevertheless, the various sūtras provide different accounts according to the capacities of sentient beings and cannot be recorded in full here.
According to the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the Tathāgata’s True Dharma lasts for one thousand years; because of the ordination of Gopikā, five hundred years were subtracted from that period.

Because the Buddha commanded the practice of the Eightfold Respectful Precepts, and because the Śākya women he ordained all became Arhats—thus increasing the number by one thousand—the True Dharma was restored for another millennium;
according to other treatises, this is the standard calculation.
In the age of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), the various treatises are numerous but incomplete; their explanations mostly rely on that [Abhidharma].

"Those who explain the Abhidharma" refers to those who mostly rely on the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* for their exegesis. The frequent use of the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) indicates that there are few alternative paths—for instance, regarding the existence or non-existence of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) or the future (*anāgata*).
The infrequent use of "few" (*alpa*) is a modest depreciation by the author of the treatise; this is the meaning of the term "Vibhāṣā."
It constitutes a fault because I have rashly disparaged the Great Holy Disciples of the Blessed One; thus it becomes a transgression.

Regarding the new commentary (*Xinyun*), it states that based on this intent, one should infer that the *Mahāvibhāṣā* preserves the six *pādas* and the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*), for the six *pādas* and the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* were composed by the Great Disciples.
As for the "repeated lamentation," the new commentary states that the preceding verse laments the teaching (*śāsana*).

In this context, the lamentation concerns the fact that the Dharma is being lost because there are no "fishermen" of the True Dharma. Concentration and wisdom are like the fishing line, while the afflictions are like a mad elephant;
without the line of control, the elephant wanders east and west at will. Likewise, without the line of concentration and wisdom, the afflictions drift and drown as they please.
It is for this reason that it is proven the Dharma is about to perish.
Commentary on the Verses of the Abhidharmakośa (End)
